5 Conclusion
The dance movement quality robustness evaluation system based on causal inference 
and invariant learning proposed in this study has achieved significant breakthroughs in 
cross-domain generalization, noise-resilience, and cross-data-set robustness by com -
bining a causal inference module with an invariant learning module. The experimental 
data show that the motion recognition accuracy of the system on the multi-scene dance 
motion data set is 92.5% where the 95% confidence interval ranges from 91.2% to 93.8%. 
Compared with the baseline model, the average absolute error in the cross-domain gen -
eralization test is reduced by 38.7%, and the correlation coefficient remains stable above 
89.1% with a 95% confidence interval between 87.5% and 90.7%. All these performance 
gains are statistically significant because the p-value is less than 0.05, which verifies the 
system’s high robustness evaluation ability in complex dance scenes.
1. Behind the excellent performance of the system in the cross-domain generalization 
test, and the average absolute error is reduced by 38.7%, is the ability of the causal 
inference module to decouple the essential characteristics of the action. In cross-
domain verification across four major motion capture datasets, including Human3.6 
M and CMU MoCap, CIDES achieves the lowest cross-domain mean-squared error, 
resulting in an average reduction of 62.3% compared with traditional deep learning 
methods. Under the interference scenarios where rhythm stability fluctuates ± 15% 
and ambient illumination changes ± 30%, the system still maintains a classification 
accuracy of more than 92%, which proves that it can effectively strip off the interference 
of environmental noise on action quality evaluation.
2. Compared with the traditional Baseline model, CIDES is significantly better than 
Baseline’s 0.8-1.0 interval in the cross-domain MSE peak interval. The comparison 
of module effects shows that the invariant learning module improves cross-domain 
performance by 15%, and that the error of the causal inference module reduces 
by 30–40% under the single-module configuration. Under the complete model 
configuration, the MAE of the system in the Master-level difficulty scenario is as 
low as 0.59, the average deviation between the prediction score and the expert score 
is only 0.32 points, the prediction error in the high-score area is controlled within 
± 0.5 points, and the Spearman correlation coefficient is concentrated in The range of 
0.6–0.8 improves the positive correlation stability by 40% compared with the Baseline 
model.
3. Through noise interference stability test and cross-data set generalization ability 
verification, the system constructs a multi-dimensional index system including 
average absolute error, Spearman correlation coefficient, prediction score deviation, 
etc. In the noise interference scenario, the standard deviation of the system’s quality 
score within the action complexity interval is reduced by 40%, and the trend line 
slope is increased by 18%, indicating that the causal inference feature effectively 
enhances evaluation stability. The cross-dataset generalization verification shows 
that the system achieves the lowest cross-domain MSE across the four major motion 
capture datasets, demonstrating its generalization universality. To sum up, this study 
constructs a highly robust dance movement quality evaluation system by integrating

Genotype imputation is fundamental to association studies, and yet even gold standard panels like
TOPMed are limited in the populations for which they yield good imputation. Speci ﬁcally, Paciﬁc
Islanders are poorly represented in extant panels. To address this, we used whole-genome sequencing
from 1,285 Samoan individuals combined with 1000 Genomes Project (1KGP) individuals to construct
an imputation reference panel that better represents Paci ﬁc Islander, speciﬁcally Samoan, genetic
variation. Here we show that this panel yielded up to two times more well-imputed ( r2 ≥ 0.80) variants
than TOPMed-R3 and 1KGP and was enriched for moderate and high impact variants. There was
improved imputation accuracy across the minor allele frequency (MAF) spectrum; accuracy ( r2)w a s
greater for population-speciﬁcv a r i a n t s( h i g hﬁxation index, FST) and those from larger haplotypes (high
LD score). However, the gain in accuracy over TOPMed-R3 was largest for small haplotypes, reﬂecting
the Samoan panel’s ability to capture variation not well tagged by other panels.
Genotype imputation is fundamental to modern genome-wide association
studies (GWAS), yielding a much de nser association landscape in which
ﬁne-mapping of causal variants and genes can occur than can be obtained

tation depends upon the haplotypes that make up the reference panels. This
is especially critical in populations that are underrepresented in genetic
research, as imputation is much poorer when the reference panel does not
contain good haplotype matches to that of the target population. Existing
panels like 1000 Genomes (1KGP)1, the Haplotype Reference Consortium
(HRC)2, and the Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine version R3
(TOPMed-R3)3 catalog human genome variation of numerous majority
populations worldwide, especially those with Western European ancestry.
The TOPMed-R3 panel contains the most ancestrally diverse set of parti-
cipants and has addressed disparities in representation, especially for
Hispanic- and African-admixed populations, greatly improving imputation
accuracy in these populations3,4. However, there are still populations for
which these reference panels are inadequate. This is obvious in looking at the
representation of Paciﬁc Islanders, who are underrepresented in health
research. In common publicly available reference panels (1KGP, HRC, and
TOPMed-R3), there are no participants explicitly from Oceania, and so the
totality of genetic variation present in Paciﬁc Islanders cannot be adequately
represented in genetic association studies. This may further exacerbate the
health disparities faced by Paci ﬁc Islanders, who are not only under-
represented in research but have a disproportionate burden of non-
communicable diseases compared to majority populations.
For example, the Paciﬁc Island nation of Samoa, which has a unique
population history consisting of founder effects and bottlenecks5–8, also faces
some of the highest rates of non-communicable disease globally9–13.D e s p i t e

this, most existing knowledge about disease etiology comes from majority
ethnic groups, even though disease presentation, progression, and response
to treatment can differ by ancestry11,14–21. Speciﬁc to genetic studies, Paciﬁc
Islanders more broadly are often grouped into an“other/mixed” ancestral
category, which itself is still <1% of GWAS participants22. However, because
of their unique population history, there are regions of the genome for which
Samoans have different variant frequencies and haplotype structure (LD)
from other majority populations, making the aggregation of them with
other Oceanic- or Asian-ancestry individuals inappropriate. Moreover,
advances in knowledge on the genetic underpinnings of human phenotypic
variation from majority populations are often assumed to apply to all
populations globally, which is premat u r ea tb e s t( b u t ,m o r el i k e l y ,c o n -
tributing to racial health disparity)23,24.
To combat this, greater representation of Paciﬁc Islanders is needed in
gene-mapping studies. However, this cannot happen without additional
whole-genome sequencing and/or im proved genotype imputation. Evi-
dence of this comes from studies based on cohorts of Samoans and
American Samoans recruited in 1990–199525–27, 2002–200328,29, and 201012.
We have performed GWAS to dissect the genetic architecture of cardio-
metabolic disease traits in these cohorts. Through this, we have identiﬁed
variants of high frequency in Samoa and not appearing (at least at high
frequency) in other non-Paci ﬁc-Islander populations that are associated
with body mass index30 and lipid traits31. They may be at high frequency due
to founding events and bottlenecks. Interestingly, these variants were not
present in initial GWAS using genotyping array data only. They were dis-
covered using imputation based on Samoan haplotypes. In the two loci
harboring Samoan-speciﬁcv a r i a n t s30,31,t h eg e n e t i ca r c h i t e c t u r eo ft h e
GWAS signal looks markedly different after imputation, with the location of
the sentinel variants shifting post-imputation dramatically. The discovery of
these associations offers a case studyinto how genetic studies in Samoans
and other Paci ﬁc-Islander populations will bene ﬁt from improved
imputation.
In this study, we describe the strategy we employed to create a Samoan-
speciﬁc reference panel containing phased haplotypes from 1KGP partici-
pants and Samoan participants with whole-genome sequencing (WGS)
from the Samoan Study, part of the TOPMed Consortium. Importantly, the
Samoan Study, which consists of 1285 participants of Samoan ancestry that
are part of the TOPMed Consortium, was not included in the TOPMed-R3
reference panel. Prior admixture studies have demonstrated that some
Samoan genomes share some overlap with other global ancestry popula-
tions (mostly East Asian and European)8. To impute well in individuals with
such admixture, it is necessary to include diversity such as that of the 1KGP
in the panel.
We investigated this panel derived from Samoan participants with
WGS and compared it to several other reference panels to determine the
extent to which adding Samoan participants to the existing 1KGP reference
panel impacted imputation quality. Speciﬁcally, we sought to address these
questions:
1) How does the imputation for a re ference panel of 1285 Samoans plus
1KGP compare to other existing panels?
2) How many population-speci ﬁc sequences are necessary to add to
1KGP to achieve good imputation accuracy?
3) Does the phasing of the reference panel impact imputed accuracy and
genotype frequency?
4) How does meta imputation of a population-speci ﬁc panel with the
TOPMed-R3 panel perform compared to the panels separately?
Here we show that the combined Samoan and 1KGP panel yields many
more well-imputed variants than TOPMed-R3 and 1KGP, with improved
imputation accuracy across the allele frequency spectrum. We also show
that imputation accuracy is gr eater for population-speciﬁc variants and
those from larger haplotypes; but the gain in imputation accuracy over
TOPMed-R3 is largest for small haplotypes, reﬂecting the Samoan panel’s
ability to capture population-speciﬁc variation not well tagged by other
panels. Moreover, the variants that are uniquely well imputed with Samoan-
speciﬁc panels are enriched for moderate and high impact.
Methods
Participants for this study came from the Soifua Manuia (“good health”)
study, a population-based sample of 3504 Samoan adults recruited in 201012.
The study was approved by the institutional review board of Brown Uni-
versity (#0903992671) and the Health Research Committee of the Samoa
Ministry of Health. All participants gave written informed consent via
consent forms in the Samoan language. Genotyping was performed for a
subset of 3182 Samoan adults usingGenome-Wide Human SNP 6.0 arrays
(Affymetrix) and extensive quality control was conducted via a pipeline
developed by Laurie et al.32. Additional details about sample genotyping and
genotype quality control are described in Minster et al.30.As u b s e t(n = 1285)
from this cohort also had WGS data from TOPMed. These 1285 individuals
were optimally selected for WGS by using the rankings from INFOSTIP33 to
capture the cohort’s genetic diversity (http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~itsik/
software/INFOSTIP.html)(Figs. S1 and S2). In addition to the Samoan
participants, 2,504 individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project Phase III
(1KGP) with WGS through TOPMed were included where appropriate.
Construction and comparison of the reference panels
We constructed 14 in-house imputat ion reference panels, varying the
number of Samoan participants, the inclusion of 1KGP individuals, and
using different phasing strategies, to assess differences in imputation quality
across a variety of settings (Fig. 1,a n dT a b l e1). We included high-quality
(i.e., passing all QCﬁlters and with a minimum read depth of 10), bi-allelic
markers from the TOPMed freeze 9b call set.
We created the Soifua Manuia reference panel by combining 2504
1KGP individuals with all 1285 Samoan participants (protocol 2). For
comparison, we created panels with only 1KGP (protocol 3) and only
Samoan participants (protocol 4).
To assess the relative gain from having additional population-speciﬁc
participants in the reference panel, we created panels by combining 1KGP
with varying numbers of Samoan pa rticipants: 4, 24, 48, 96, and 384
(representing fractions/multiples of a 96-well plate; protocols 5–9). These
participants were the ﬁrst 4, 24, 48, 96, or 384 individuals based on the
INFOSTIP ranking so that the reference panels reﬂected the most Samoan
genetic diversity possible at that sample size (Fig. S2).
For calculating genotype concordance among the panels with the most
Samoan representation, we constructed panels with 1275 Samoan partici-
pants (protocols 10 and 11, with and without 1KGP respectively), holding
out 10 participants distributed uniformly across the INFOSTIP rankings of
individuals (ranks 120, 240, 360, 480, 600, 720, 840, 960, 1080, and 1200,
chosen for generalizability and to speciﬁcally compare the performance of
the panels with <100 Samoans).
All the haplotypes from panels described above were phased in a
population-unaware manner by the TOPMed Informatics Research
Center3, along with all other individuals present in freeze 9b. For protocols
12–15, we phased the sequence data comprising the reference panels
separately using Eagle v2.4.134, such that protocol pairs 1 and 15, 4 and 13, 10
and 14, and 11 and 12 only differ fromeach other in the way the reference
panel was phased.
Analyzes comparing reference panels andﬁgures were created with R
version 4.4.135, unless otherwise noted.
Imputation
We imputed genotypes using all reference panels into Samoans with
Affymetrix genotyping array genotypes as the target. We imputed genotypes
on chromosomes 21 (for computational ef ﬁciency) and 5 (to measure
imputation in a Samoan-speciﬁc variant of interest— rs200884524, a stop-
gain variant associated with lipid levels in a prior study 31) for all Samoan
participants in the 2010 cohort who were not part of any reference panel
(n = 1834). To ensure that conclusions drawn from these two chromosomes
Communications Biology | (2026) 9:1191 2
did not misrepresent genome-wide trends, we also imputed genotypes on all
autosomes for 100 randomlyselected participants.
Prior to imputation, Affymetrix genotyped variant coordinates were
converted from hg19 to the hg38 genome build using LiftOver ( https://
genome.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgLiftOver)to align with the build of the WGS
data comprising the reference panel (mimicking the steps taken by publicly
available imputation servers36). Then, data were aligned to the reference
panel using Genotype Harmonizer37, using the mafAlign option to align to
the minor allele when LD alignment failed, and the minor allele frequency
(MAF) was ≤ 30% in both the input and reference sets. The resulting
variants were then phased with Eagle v2.4.134, and genome-wide imputation
was performed using Minimac436.A ne x a m p l eo ft h ei m p u t a t i o nc o d ei s
available at https://github.com/jennaccarlson/imputation.
To benchmark the performance of the in-house panels, we imputed
variants in the same sets of Samoans using the TOPMed-R3 reference panel
via the TOPMed Imputation Server3,36,38 (protocol 1). We also performed
meta imputation between the TOPMed-R3 and 1285S imputed variants
(protocols 1 and 4) with MetaMinimac2 39 (https://github.com/yukt/
MetaMinimac2). Importantly, MetaMinimac2 requires that the genotyp-
ing array data be phased consistently prior to meta imputation. Thus, we
pre-phased the genotypes of the n = 1834 Samoan participants with the
TOPMed Imputation Server prior to imputing with our in-house 1285S
reference panel for the meta-imputation comparison only.
We extracted imputation metrics from the resulting info ﬁles and
tabulated the number of well-imputed (r2 ≥ 0.80), non-monomorphic var-
iants for each imputation. For each variant, we predicted functional con-
sequence and impact using VEP 40, and calculated enrichment for each
variant consequence and SnpEff impact group 41 f o rv a r i a n t st h a tw e r e
uniquely imputed in a Samoan panel ( r2 ≥ 0.80 in either 1285S or 1KGP
+1285S and r2 <0 . 8 0o ra b s e n tf r o mb o t hT O P M e d - R 3a n d1 K G P )c o m -
pared to shared variants ( r2 ≥ 0.80 in either 1285S or 1KGP +1285S and
either TOPMed-R3 or 1KGP). Consequence and impact groupings are
listed in Table S3. Enrichmentp-values were calculated with a two-sidedz
test for the proportion of variants with the given annotation within the MAF
stratum.
Additionally, we merged imputed variants by position and alleles,
accounting for possible reference and alternate allele ﬂips, and calculated
mean and median r2 for the intersection of variants across MAF bins. We
examined empirical r2 for the genotyped variants. We also assessed the
impact of the reference panel to impute rs200884524, a population-speciﬁc
variant of interest mentioned above, by examining imputed MAF andr2.
To assess if the imputation quality gains from using a reference
panel that includes Samoan haplotypes were due to allele frequency
differences or haplotype size, we calculated ﬁxation index (FST) using the
Weir and Cockerham formula and LD score. FST was calculated using the
Soifua Manuia panel (protocol 1) with vcftools 42; the population labels
used were derived from the super populations listed in 1KGP (AFR,
AMR, EAS, EUR, SAS)1, with the 1285 Samoans listed as a separate sixth
population. LD scores were calculated using the Soifua Manuia reference
panel (protocol 1) in GCTA 43 with the default block size (1 Mb with an
overlap of 500 kb between blocks). For visualization, F ST and LD scores
were each stratiﬁed into low and high at the median value within a given
MAF bin (Table S8).
Additionally, we compared genotype concordance for 10 hold-out
participants with WGS from imputations using the following reference
panels: TOPMed-R3, 1KGP, 1KGP + 4S, 1KGP + 24S, 1KGP + 48S,
1KGP + 96S, 1KGP+ 1275S, 1KGP+ 1275S in-house phasing, 1275S, and
1275S in-house phasing (protocols 2, 3, 5-11). We calculated non-reference
discordance (NRD) for each of these panels’imputed genotypes for the 10
hold-out participants with WGS on chromosome 21 using bcftools44 using
the formula NRD = 100 * (xRR + xRA + xAA) / (xRR + xRA + xAA +
mRA + mAA), where xRR, xRA, and xAA represent the counts of dis-
cordant homozygous reference, heterozygous, and homozygous alternate
genotypes, and mRA and mAA are the counts of the matching heterozygous
and homozygous alternative genotypes.
We also investigated if the phasing of the reference panel impacted the
imputation of population-speci ﬁc variation. We hypothesized that for
Samoan-speciﬁc variation, the phasing of genotypes when done alongside
supermajority populations with very different allele frequencies might be
biased toward the haplotypes not common in Samoans, thereby decreasing
the Samoan-speciﬁc allele frequency. To investigate this, we compared
imputation quality (r2), MAF, and non-reference discordance for two sets of
imputed, Samoan-speciﬁc variants, deﬁned as those in the 99th percentile of
FST and with MAF > 0.05.

Results
We compared the average imputation quality (r2), genotype concordance,
and the number of well-imputed variants (r2 ≥ 0.8) across 11 sets of imputed
genotypes to assess the performance of the various imputation reference
panels which included TOPMed-R3, 1KGP, 2 panels of 1285 Samoan
participants, and 8 panels constructed by combining 1KGP with varying
numbers of Samoans (Table1).
Panels with more than 24 Samoans yield more well-imputed
variants than TOPMed
Panels with 1285 Samoan participants (1KGP+ 1285S and 1285S) resulted
in the largest number of well-imputed variants, yielding ~300,000 more
variants on chromosome 5 and ~70,000 more on chromosome 21 than the
TOPMed-R3 panel, with over 25,000 and ~6500 of these having a MAF of at
least 0.05 on chromosomes 5 and 21, respectively (Fig.2,a n dT a b l eS 1 ) .T h e
yield in well-imputed variants increased as the number of Samoans included
in the reference panel increased across all MAF bins (up to a 55% increase in
the total number of well-imputed variants compared to the TOPMed-R3
imputation). The largest gains were se e nf o rv a r i a n t sw i t hM A F<0 . 0 5 ,w i t h
up to a 187% increase in well-imputedvariants compared to the TOPMed-
R3 imputation. Moreover, the panels with the most Samoans (1KGP +
1285S and 1285S panels) had over 200,000 and 60,000 well-imputed unique
variants (not seen in TOPMed-R3 or 1KGP imputations) on chromosomes
5 and 21, respectively, in addition to the variants shared across panels
(Fig. 3). We annotated these shared and unique variants for consequence
and impact and observed enrichment in several categories among our
uniquely imputed variants, including signiﬁcantly more modiﬁer, moder-
ate, and high impact variants (Fig.4,a n dT a b l e sS 4a n dS 5 ) .
We also examined “lost” variants, those with imputation quality
r2 < 0.80 in the 1KGP imputation, to see how many could be“rescued”(had
imputation quality r2 ≥ 0.80) across other panels (Fig. 5,T a b l eS 2 ,a n d
Fig. S16). The proportion of lost variants rescued was highest for variants
with greater MAF across all panels, with nearly 100% of lost variants
recovered in some cases (MAF ≥ 0.05 for the 1KGP + 1285S panel). The
panels with at least 48 Samoans included rescued more variants overall than
TOPMed-R3 (15.0% to 35.5% for Sam oan panels compared to 12.2% to
13.2% for TOPMed). Over 95% of lost variants with MAF ≥ 0.05 were
rescued for the reference panels with 384 or more Samoans. Even for the
1KGP + 4S panel, 29.4% to 37.1% of variants with MAF ≥ 0.05 were res-
cued. As a control, we also examined the reverse scenario — variants that
were of high-quality (r2 ≥ 0.80) in the 1KGP imputation that were dropped
(r2 < 0.80) when using other reference panels. We found very few variants
that were dropped (Fig. S15), demonstrating that variants the 1KGP panel
imputes well are generally also imputed well with other panels.
Similar imputation quality to TOPMed is achieved with as few as
24 Samoans
Imputation quality increased as the number of Samoans represented in the
panel increased. The panels with 48 or more Samoans included out-
performed the TOPMed-R3 panel for all variants with imputed MAF ≥
0.001 (based on the 1KGP + 1285S imputation), while the 1KGP + 24S
performed similarly to TOPMed-R3 (Fig.6,a n dT a b l e sS 6a n dS 7 ) .W h e n
looking at empiricalr2 for genotyped variants only, which is a more robust
metric for evaluating imputation for lower-frequency variants, the panels
including at least 24 Samoans outperform both the TOPMed-R3 and 1KGP
panels (Fig. S4). This trend was consistent across all autosomes (Fig. S10).
Average imputation quality tended to be lower when examining variants
based on TOPMed-imputed MAF instead of 1KGP+ 1285S-imputed MAF

(Fig. S17). However, even when using TOPMed-imputed MAF, the panels

expected due to higher conﬁdence in matching haplotypes with population-

Discussion
The Soifua Manuia reference panel consisting of 1KGP + 1285 Samoans
outperformed all other panels tested, especially for low-frequency var-
iants. There were substantial gains in imputation quality ( r2) and in the
number of well-imputed variants across the allele frequency spectrum,

with more pronounced gains for low-frequency variants. Compared to
the commonly recommended TOPMed-R3 panel, the number of well-
imputed variants available across chromosomes and MAF ranges
increased by 8% to 182% with the 1KGP + 1285S panel and average
imputation quality increased by 3% to 42%. When examining meta
imputation between a population-speci ﬁc panel (1285S) and the
TOPMed-R3 panel, we observed lower imputation quality on average
with meta imputation compared to the population-speci ﬁc panel, con-
trary to prior work demonstrating the superiority of meta imputation to
single reference panel imputation 39,46. This demonstrates that while the
TOPMed-R3 panel has improved imputation quality for many diverse
populations, there are still populations that are not well represented by
this or other publicly available panels.
Additionally, there was an enrichment in high-impact, coding variants
among those that were uniquely well-imputed by a Samoan panel (1285S or
1KGP + 1285S) compared to TOPMed-R3 and 1KGP. This phenomenon,

founder and bottleneck effects. This has important implications for genetic
association testing and ﬁne-mapping of GWAS loci, as measuring asso-
ciation with these variants that likelyimpact gene function would elucidate

for similar population-speciﬁc variants, as they may be poorly imputed or
imputed with fewer non-reference ge notypes (i.e., with lower MAF) by
panels not including population-speciﬁch a p l o t y p e s .
In looking at variants with low imputation quality in the 1KGP
imputation, a large proportion of them were “rescued”,i . e . ,h a dh i g h
imputation quality, in panels containing 48 or more Samoans. These panels
rescued more variants, especiallycommon variants, than the TOPMed-R3
panel did. Across the variant frequency spectrum, with only 24 Samoans, we
achieved the same imputation performance as TOPMed-R3 and had greater
performance with all panels with 48 or more Samoans. Importantly, this
sample size is not necessarily prescr iptive for future studies planning to
perform WGS to create their own population-speci ﬁc panel as these 48
individuals were not randomly selected— they were chosen to maximize the
genetic variation present in the orig inal set of ~3000 participants, which
were all of Samoan ethnicity (de ﬁned by participant self-reporting four
Samoan grandparents) and therefore comprised a quite homogeneous
population with little to no admixture8.T h e s eﬁndings may reﬂect the fact
that in this cohort, the 48 individuals yielded over 70% of the information
content from INFOSTIP (Fig. S2). In other populations, the number of
individuals needed to see improved imputation will depend on the genetic
variation of the target population. Forp o p u l a t i o n sw i t hl a r g e rg e n e t i ch e t -
erogeneity, including those with lots of admixture or different haplotype
sizes, more individuals will likely be needed to achieve improved imputation
accuracy over extant panels.
The trends in imputation quality byFST and LD score suggest that these
improvements inr2 for theSoifua Manuiapanel are driven by differences in
both the LD patterns and haplotypes of Samoans and allele frequency dif-
ferences across populations. While imputation quality was highest for high
LD score variants, the gains in imputation quality for the Soifua Manuia
panel over the TOPMed-R3 panel were the largest for low LD score variants
across the MAF spectrum. This suggests that the gains in imputation quality
for the Soifua Manuia panel over TOPMed-R3 are driven by population-
speciﬁc variants in small LD blocks that would not be predicted well by other
reference panels.
We hypothesized that the phasing of reference panel haplotypes would
affect imputation quality, speciﬁcally, that phasing taking place in large
multiethnic consortia might bias thephasing of the reference panel haplo-
types more common in majority-represented populations. In this study, we
observed an opposite effect to what we hypothesized — the imputation
quality was slightly lower for population-speci ﬁc variation within a
population-speciﬁc panel (1285S) phased separately. We did not observe
this trend with the cosmopolitan panel (1KGP+ 1285S). We also observed
differences in genotype concordance by phasing of the reference panel—
with those having been phased sepa rately (1285S in-house phasing and
1KGP + 1285S in-house phasing) having slightly higher discordance than
those phased with other studies as part of a consortium (1285S and
1KGP + 1285S). Based on ourﬁndings in this study, it does not appear that
separate phasing yields better imputation.
These ﬁndings of substantially improved imputation quality by
including population-speciﬁc sequences to existing cosmopolitan reference
panels conceptually extend to other populations with a similar evolutionary

history to the Samoan population included here. Samoans are an isolated

extended haplotype blocks with high LD scores and reduced
heterozygosity8,52.T h eﬁndings here mirror those from other isolated and/or

imputation strategies.
Taken together, this work highligh ts the utility of augmenting cos-
mopolitan extant panels with population-speciﬁc sequences, resulting in
more well-imputed variants for associ ation testing, higher imputation
quality overall, and better imputation of population-speciﬁcv a r i a t i o n .I n
this work, these gains were the greatest for low-frequency population-spe-
ciﬁc variants in smaller LD blocks. These results suggest that adding even a
small number of population-speciﬁc haplotypes can substantially increase
the number of well-imputed variants available for analysis compared to
gold-standard extant panels, which may allow for better inclusion of even
more diverse populations in genetic association studies. This improvement
in the representativeness of genetic studies, by extension, will lay the
foundation for more equitable access to personalized medicine innovation
in this and other Paciﬁc populations.

title: Progress and challenges of biological reference standards for vaccine quality control and evaluation
summary: Progress and challenges of biological reference standards for vaccine quality control and evaluation
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Introduction Advances in the development, manufacture, and testing of biological products, along with the application of the ‘Replacement, reduction and refinement,’ have driven a paradigm shift in the establishment and application of biological reference standards (BRS) for vaccine quality control and evaluation. Traditional WHO International Standard(s) (IS), historically used for potency harmonization, now face multiple challenges stemming from vaccine diversity, platform complexity, and other factors.Areas covered This review summarizes recent updates to WHO and other regulatory guidelines on BRS, analyzes 2019–2025 BRS practices of WHO and regional/national regulatory authorities, highlights the need to develop BRS to support the advancement of novel platforms/technologies, and emphasizes harmonized coordination among WHO, regional/national BRS, and manufacturers’ in-house quality control working standards.Expert opinion To ensure that the establishment of BRS could keep pace with vaccine evolution, the following are required: (1) establish rapid-response mechanisms to address emerging pathogens; (2) retain traditional BRS for vaccine quality control and evaluation to maintain traceability of measurement values; (3) develop platform and quality-control BRS for novel technologies; and (4) support manufacturers in developing a product-specific working BRS using Quality by Design (QbD) principles – traceable to phase III protective efficacy.

title: Integrated groundwater quality assessment using Water Quality Index, complex fuzzy MCDM and GIS Techniques
summary: Integrated groundwater quality assessment using Water Quality Index, complex fuzzy MCDM and GIS Techniques
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Groundwater contamination, mainly caused by human activities, is a major environmental issue affecting the availability of safe drinking water. In this study, groundwater quality in Dharmapuri district, Tamil Nadu, India, was assessed using a complex Multi-Criteria Decision-making Model (MCDM). Physicochemical parameters, including total dissolved solids, nitrate, calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chloride, sulphate, bicarbonate, fluoride, pH and electrical conductivity, were measured from 31 wells over the period 2015-2022. The Water Quality Index (WQI) was computed for each sampling location and spatially represented using GIS to classify groundwater into six categories: excellent, good, mediocre, poor, very poor and unsuitable for drinking. The WQI values ranged from 0.00 to 1.00 with a mean value of 0.5, indicating that the groundwater is generally suitable for drinking purposes in the study area. Statistical validation using descriptive measures and Z-score analysis confirmed the relative performance of sampling locations, highlighting significant deviations for high-ranking wells. The model showed strong predictive capability with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) value of 0.993, indicating excellent classification accuracy.

title: Water for Energy Generation and Production
summary: Water for Energy Generation and Production
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Energy is used for many applications in modern society including heating, cooling, and lighting. There are substantial links between SDG6 for clean water and sanitation and SDG7 for affordable and clean energy, ventilation, transportation, electronic devices, and communications. Renewable and nonrenewable sources of energy are employed. Renewable energy sources include the use of solar, hydro, wind, and biomass, while fossil fuels (crude oil, natural gas, and coal) are considered nonrenewable due to their extensive production periods. Although water requirements for energy production are substantial, they are often not well documented. In the transition to renewable energies to reduce carbon emissions to mitigate carbon, attention must be paid to available water resources. These resources will also be impacted by climate change as the result of droughts or water shortages. Water assessments in the development of renewable energies must be included. Water for energy has not been studied as intensively as energy for water. Implementation of water resource management is needed through policy development. Comparisons can be difficult, however, as data is limited, and the boundaries for the comparison are not always the same. Water quality and thermal pollution are not usually considered. A more unified approach is needed for determining water consumption in relation to electricity and energy generation.

title: From water deficit to growth suppression: meta-analytic evidence  for a functional hierarchy of drought adaptation in Hippophae rhamnoides
summary: From water deficit to growth suppression: meta-analytic evidence  for a functional hierarchy of drought adaptation in Hippophae rhamnoides
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Drought constrains shrub establishment and persistence in arid and semi-arid restoration systems. Although Hippophae rhamnoides is widely planted in northern China, its drought responses vary among studies, hindering the identification of stable indicators. We synthesized 3,855 treatment-control comparisons from 49 controlled experiments across 12 Chinese provinces using random-effects meta-analysis and structural equation modeling. Results showed that drought adaptation in H. rhamnoides follows a functional cascade. Water status and membrane stability were the most consistent early constraints, followed by strong suppression of photosynthetic and gas-exchange traits. Photosynthesis acted as a key mediating factor linking water deficit, hormonal adjustment, and growth reduction. Under severe drought, membrane permeability increased by 89.5%, while leaf water content, net photosynthetic rate, transpiration rate, and stomatal conductance decreased by 37.2, 83.3, 91.2, and 92.9%, respectively. Therefore, drought evaluation should prioritize water status, membrane stability, photosynthetic performance, and growth traits.

title: Reducing turnaround time to improve the performance of the quality control laboratory: A case study of the pharmaceutical industry
summary: Reducing turnaround time to improve the performance of the quality control laboratory: A case study of the pharmaceutical industry
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

The quality control laboratory of any industry must ensure the quality of products to meet the regulatory compliances. However, the quality control in healthcare industry and pharmaceutical firms are highly relevant as its products’ quality directly impacts the human health. Hence, quality control laboratories in pharmaceutical firms needs to conduct several tests to ensure drug substances’ efficacy, safety and regulatory compliance to maintain the highest quality standards of effectiveness and precision. Though value stream mapping (VSM), a lean tool, has been widely used to enhance operational efficiency in manufacturing and healthcare operations but their application with pharmaceutical quality control laboratories remains relatively unexplored. Thus, the primary objective of this paper is to propose an optimized methodology for reducing turnaround time in quality control processes of pharmaceutical firms. Existing research primarily highlights production environments or conventional healthcare processes, often examining the factors responsible for efficient performance and waste management in pharmaceutical firms, daily operations and the associated supply chains which do not properly address the unique operational constraints, validation requirements and procedural difficulties essential in quality control laboratories. This research addresses this gap by applying work study based digital VSM framework to identify inefficiencies, reduce turnaround time and enhance operational performance while maintaining regulatory compliance by finding the causes of problems faced by analysts during testing. The proposed integrated framework was validated in a pharmaceutical case company that reduced turnaround time by 38.31%, significantly minimizing errors and decreasing potential delays in the supply chain to the market.

[“Quality: Judge Literary and Artistic Merit” explains that judging literary merit is a necessary critical move. While ever-changing perspectives allow us to find value in nearly everything we read, watch, and experience, we certainly don&s;t have time to consume everything. We have to make a choice, and our choice is often based on our sense of quality. As theorists of value, we may argue with others about the qualities and functions of a “well-crafted” text, and as critics who judge value, we argue with others about whether or not a particular text has the proper qualities or valued functions, and those are two different kinds of debates.]

title: Energy for and from Water and Wastewater Treatment
summary: Energy for and from Water and Wastewater Treatment
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

In this chapter, energy requirements for the various aspects of water management are discussed. Energy consumption corresponded to approximately 4% of all electricity consumed worldwide in 2014. Another 50 million tons of oil and diesel are required for irrigation and desalination of plants. Energy requirements are expected to double by 2040. There is a requirement, therefore, to shift to less energy-intensive water. There are numerous opportunities to accomplish a reduction in energy consumption and increase efficiencies in the water sector, which will be discussed. An understanding of water–energy integration is needed to develop integrated practices. Energy requirements must be reduced, and sources of contamination must be eliminated to maintain water quality and supply. Water must be conserved and managed properly. Various remediation technologies have been developed to treat water once it has been contaminated. The selection of these techniques requires examination of energy requirements and emissions, wastes generated, and water quality requirements. Development of more energy-efficient technologies to clean contaminated water resources is necessary to meet water and energy resource requirements. The wastewater sector can benefit from energy savings by improving energy efficiency and benefiting from the embedded energy in water. Practicing energy recovery can lead to up to the generation of up to 55% of the electricity needed for the municipal wastewater treatment sector. Reducing water losses can save substantial amounts of energy.

source: Eating and Weight Disorders - Studies on Anorexia, Bulimia and Obesity
summary: Night eating symptoms and sleep quality: the mediating role of somatization and depressive symptoms
content:

This study aims to explore the mediating role of depressive and somatization symptoms in sleep disturbances observed in individuals with elevated night eating symptoms. Four hundred and sixty medical students who were receiving training in the preclinical period were included in the study. The participants were asked to complete the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Night Eating Questionnaire (NEQ), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15), Panic module (P-5), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) scales. Analyses were conducted using comparison, correlation, and statistical mediation analysis with 5.000 bootstrap resamples. The mean age of participants was 19.90 ± 1.35 years. The mean PSQI score was 6.98 ± 2.66, with 30% ( n = 138) having good sleep quality (PSQI ≤ 5) and 70% ( n = 322) having poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5). No significant differences in sociodemographic characteristics were found between good and poor sleep quality groups ( p > 0.05). Participants with poor sleep quality had significantly higher NEQ, PHQ-9, PHQ-15, and GAD-7 scores ( p < 0.001). PSQI scores were positively correlated with NEQ (r = 0.498), PHQ-9 (r = 0.493), and PHQ-15 (r = 0.422). Mediation analysis revealed that PHQ-9 (β = 0.093, 95% CI: 0.008, 0.086) and PHQ-15 (β = 0.079, 95% CI 0.019, 0.063) significantly mediated the association between night eating symptoms and sleep quality, while P-5 and GAD-7 did not ( p > 0.05). Depressive symptoms and somatization exhibited a significant statistical mediatory role in the association between night eating symptom severity and sleep quality. Addressing these psychological factors could be critical in managing sleep disturbances in individuals with elevated night eating symptoms. Further research is needed to explore these relationships in more diverse populations.

Abstract
Background The present study evaluated the biological parameters (parasitism rate, fertility, emergence rate, adult 
longevity, and offspring sex ratio) of seven generations (F₀, F₁, F₃, F₅, F₇, F₈, and F₁₀) of the parasitoid wasp Telenomus 
busseolae Gahan (Hymenoptera: Scelionidae) reared on eggs of the sugarcane stem borer Sesamia nonagrioides 
Lefèbvre (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae) under laboratory conditions.
Results A host colony was established from field-collected S. nonagrioides, and fresh eggs were provided to T. 
busseolae females from generations F₀ (field-collected), F₁, F₃, F₅, F₇, F₈, and F₁₀; 30 female wasps per generation were 
randomly selected for the parameter recording. Significant declines were observed across generations: parasitism rate 
decreased from 85.2% (F₀) to 61.3% (F10), fertility from 42.1 to 25.7 parasitized eggs/female, emergence rate from 92.3 
to 71.8%, female longevity from 9.2 to 5.8 days, representing an a approximately 37% reduction. The offspring sex ratio 
shifted from 75% female (significantly female-biased) to 45% female, which did not differ significantly from a 1:1 ratio.
Conclusions The results demonstrate a gradual decline in the biological quality of T. busseolae under laboratory 
rearing. Consequently, periodic introduction of field populations, optimization of rearing diets, and stringent 
environmental control are recommended to sustain the efficacy of T. busseolae in biological control programs.
Keywords Telenomus busseolae, Parasitism rate, Biological parameters, Generational decline, Rearing, Biocontrol

 Background
As a cornerstone of industrial agriculture in tropical 
and subtropical regions worldwide, sugarcane ( Saccha-
rum officinarum L. hybrids) fulfills a vital role, supply -
ing approximately 70% of global sugar (Hunsigi 2012). 
The crop’s economic significance extends far beyond 
sugar; it holds remarkable potential for generating a 
diverse portfolio of industrial outputs, including bagasse, 
straw, molasses, filter cake, and ethanol (Paturau 1989). 
Iran’s sugarcane industry is predominantly centered in 
Khuzestan province, a region whose very name (“the land 
of sugar”) reflects its agricultural identity as the country’s 
primary cultivation area (Hamdi 2016).
Sesamia spp. (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), known as the 
sugarcane stem borers, ranks as a primary threat to sug -
arcane cultivation in Khuzestan province, with additional 
impacts on maize and rice (Agah-Manesh et al. 2021). 
Larval damage manifests as “dead heart” in young plants 
and structural compromise or death in mature plants 
through stem boring. Consequently, larval infestations 
cause substantial reductions in sugarcane juice volume 
and quality. The pest exhibits four yearly generations in 
this region. Its nocturnal adult females deposit eggs spe -
cifically behind the leaf sheaths of living sugarcane plants 
(Khanjani 2009).
Chemical control proves ineffective against Sesamia 
nonagrioides Lefèbvre (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae) because 
its larvae are protected from chemical exposure by dint 
of feeding within the sugarcane stems (Halabian et al. 
2013). This limitation has led to the adoption of inocu -
lative releases of the egg parasitoid Telenomus busseolae 
Gahan (Hymenoptera: Scelionidae) as the principal con -
trol measure in Khuzestan’s sugarcane agroecosystems 
(Nikpay and Goebel 2016). However, this parasitoid wasp 
does not consistently suppress pest populations below 
damaging levels across a range of sugarcane cultivars 
(Halabian et al. 2013).
Given the vital role of this wasp in controlling the 
insect pest, rearing this parasitoid under laboratory con -
ditions is essential and essential component of the bio -
logical control program. However, the biological quality 
of wasps in successive generations may deteriorate due to 
rearing conditions. Declines in parasitism rate, longev -
ity, fecundity, and optimal sex ratio in later generations 
can reduce field efficacy. Therefore, rigorous assessment 
of T. busseolae quality indicators across generations and 
comparison with wild populations is critical for opti -
mizing biological control strategies. Studies on various 
egg parasitoid wasps, including Telenomus remus Nixon 
(Hymenoptera: Platygastridae) (Pomari-Fernandes et al. 
2015) and Trichogramma brassicae Bezdenko (Hyme -
noptera: Trichogrammatidae) (Ghaemmaghami et al. 
2021a; b.), have shown that rearing conditions signifi -
cantly impact the biological quality and biological control 
efficacy of individuals reared over successive generations. 
Specifically, without rigorous quality assessment and 
the selection of robust isolines, parasitoids frequently 
exhibit reduced parasitism rates, fertility, and optimal sex 
ratios, which directly compromise sustained field efficacy 
against target pests (Chen et al. 2023). Therefore, rigor -
ous assessment of T. busseolae quality indicators across 
generations and comparison with wild populations is 
critical for optimizing biological control strategies.
The present study aimed to assess the impact of suc -
cessive rearing on the biological characteristics and effi -
cacy of biological control by T. busseolae, with the goal of 
applying the findings to the development of the biological 
control of sugarcane stem borers.
Methods
To establish a laboratory colony, S. nonagrioides lar -
vae were collected from infested sugarcane fields in 
the Imam Khomeini (31.801993, 48.767391) and Haft 
Tappeh (32.086303, 48.402481) agro-industrial com -
plexes. Infested stems were identified by desiccated api -
cal buds or larval entry holes containing darkened frass. 
The stems were ten dissected to extract 4th and 5th larval 
instars, thereby reducing the duration of the pupal stage 
before colony establishment. Larvae were reared in cylin -
drical plastic containers (25  cm height × 16  cm diam -
eter) and provided with fresh sugarcane stems under 
controlled laboratory conditions. After pupation, indi -
viduals were sexed based on genital slit morphology and 
isolated in separate cylindrical containers (5 cm height × 
10  cm diameter). For each oviposition cage, 10 pairs of 
newly emerged adults (sexed as pupae) were introduced. 
Mating was confirmed by observation of copulation, and 
only egg masses laid after confirmed mating were used in 
experiments. All developmental stages were maintained 
in a germinator at 28 ± 1  °C, 60 ± 5% relative humid -
ity, and a 14:10 (Light: Dark) photoperiod. Throughout 
the experiments, the same host colony was used as the 
source of eggs. While strict environmental and dietary 
controls were applied to maintain host quality, wild-type 
moths were not periodically introduced. We acknowl -
edge this as a study limitation, as any untracked decrease 
in host colony quality or potential artificial genetic bot -
tleneck effects from the initial field collection could have 
compounded the observed decline in parasitoid biologi -
cal parameters.
The parasitoid, T. busseolae was reared on its natural 
host, S. nonagrioides eggs. The initial culture was estab -
lished from parasitized S. nonagrioides egg masses col -
lected from the sugarcane fields. In the laboratory, host 
eggs (< 24  h old) were exposed to newly emerged para -
sitoid species. For oviposition, S. nonagrioides eggs were 
glued onto 15 × 2 cm strips of radiographic polyester film 
using a 14% honey-water solution and presented to the 
Page 3 of 6
Safaran et al. Egyptian Journal of Biological Pest Control (2026) 36:27 
parasitoid. The egg-bearing strips and parasitoids were 
maintained in cylindrical glass tubes (17  cm length × 
3  cm diameter), which were sealed with cotton plugs. 
Adult wasps were provided with filter paper strips satu -
rated with a 20% honey-water solution. All tubes were 
maintained in a germinator at 28 ± 1 °C, 60 ± 5% relative 
humidity, and a 16:8 (Light: Dark) photoperiod.
Biological quality assessment of Telenomus busseolae
Quality control parameters of T. busseolae were evalu -
ated across seven laboratory-reared generations (F0, F1, 
F3, F5, F7, F8, and F10), where F0 represented the field-
collected generation. For each generation, 30 randomly 
selected female wasps (mated for 24  h post-emergence) 
were individually housed in glass tubes. Each female was 
provided daily with 30 fresh host eggs (< 24 h old) until 
her death. The number of parasitized eggs was recorded 
daily, and the total parasitism rate was calculated as the 
proportion of eggs parasitized during the first 24  h of 
exposure (to standardize across generations). Fecundity 
was calculated as the total number of eggs parasitized 
over the female’s lifetime.
Statistical analysis
Data normality and homogeneity of variances were 
checked using Shapiro–Wilk and Levene’s tests, respec -
tively. For normally distributed data, one-way ANOVA 
followed by Tukey’s HSD test was applied. For propor -
tional data (emergence rate), data were arcsine-square-
root transformed before ANOVA. Sex ratio data were 
analyzed using a generalized linear model (GLM) with a 
binomial error distribution and logit link function (logis -
tic ANOVA), with generation as the fixed factor, follow -
ing the recommendations of Wilson and Hardy ( 2002). 
While arrhenotoky provides mated females with the 
physiological mechanism to control sex allocation, it is 
the population structure and mating system that primar -
ily drive the evolutionary expectation of female-biased 
sex ratios in parasitoid wasps (Hardy and Boulton 2024); 
therefore, deviations from a 1:1 ratio were interpreted 
within this ecological context. All analyses were per -
formed using SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, 
USA). Each experiment was repeated 30 times.
Results
Results indicated that the F0 generation (field-collected) 
exhibited the highest parasitism rate (Table  1). A grad -
ual decline in parasitism rate was observed across labo -
ratory-reared generations (F1 to F10). Tukey’s HSD test 
revealed significant differences in parasitism rates among 
generations (df = 6, 203; F = 31.2; P < 0.05). The lowest 
parasitism rate was observed in F10 (61.3%), which was 
28.1% lower than F0 (85.2%).
Female wasp fertility was assessed by counting the 
number of eggs parasitized by each female. There was sig-
nificant difference between wasp fertility in different gen-
erations (df = 6, 203; F = 27.6; P < 0.05) (Table 1). The early 
generations (F0 and F1) exhibited higher mean fertility 
with 42.1 and 39.5 eggs per female, respectively, com -
pared to subsequent generations. Furthermore, a decline 
in fertility was observed across successive generations. 
The lowest fecundity was observed in F10 (25.7 eggs per 
parasitoid), which was 39.0% lower than F0 (42.1 eggs). 
These findings indicated a gradual decline in reproduc -
tive capacity in laboratory-reared generations.
Results indicated a significant gradual decrease in 
the lifespan of female T. busseolae (df = 6, 203; F = 19.4; 
P < 0.001), with mean lifespan decreasing from 9.2 days in 
the F₀ generation to 5.8 days in the F₁₀ generation, repre -
senting a 37.0% reduction. (Table 1).
The emergence rate was calculated by dividing the 
number of parasitized eggs with exit holes relative to the 
total number of parasitized eggs. The emergence rate was 
the highest in F0 generation and decreased across sub -
sequent generations. The difference in emergence rates 
between generations was statistically significant (df = 6, 
203; F = 24.8; P < 0.001). Emergence rate of the parasit -
oid decreased by 22.2% from F0 (92.3%) to F10 (71.8%) 
(Table 1).
Logistic ANOVA (GLM with binomial distribution) 
revealed a significant overall effect of generation on off -
spring sex ratio (Wald χ² = 18.45, df = 6, P = 0.005). Pair-
wise comparisons against the 1:1 expectation showed 
that the sex ratio was significantly female-biased in the 
F0 ( P = 0.006) and F1 ( P = 0.033) generations. From F3 
onward, the offspring sex ratio did not differ signifi -
cantly from 1:1 ( P > 0.05), indicating a progressive loss of 
female-biased allocation in later laboratory generations 
(Table 2).

efficiency (Wang et al. 2022). These findings are consis -
tent with broader evidence showing that mass-reared egg 
parasitoids frequently exhibit reduced survival and flight 
activity over successive generations, necessitating contin-
uous monitoring of these vital quality indicators (Chen et 
al. 2023).
Laboratory rearing of T. remus has been reported to 
reduce foraging and flight capacity, compromising field 
efficacy in biological control programs (Naranjo-Guevara 
2020). These impairments are consistent with broader 
evidence that mass-reared egg parasitoids frequently 
exhibit reduced parasitism rates, fertility, host searching 
efficiency, and flight activity (de Paula et al. 2023). The 
decline in fecundity and parasitism rate may result from 
multiple interacting factors, including reduced foraging 
ability, inbreeding depression, host quality variation, and 
potential adaptation to laboratory conditions that may 
compromise field-relevant traits.
Fecundity is a critical determinant mass production 
costs and serves as a key quality indicator for parasit -
oids, however, it often declines during prolonged labora -
tory rearing rearing. In this study, T. busseolae exhibited 
a reduction in fecundity over 10 generations, mirroring 
with declines reported in T. embryophagum (Sadat et 
al. 2021) and T. brassicae reared on lepidopteran eggs 
(Ghaemmaghami et al. 2021a). Notably, the biological 
quality of T. busseolae, as reflected by fecundity and para-
sitism rate, declined within only 10 generations, a dete -
rioration that occurred disproportionately faster than in 
other parasitoid wasps such as T. brassicae, which main-
tained quality for over 40 generations under similar rear -
ing conditions (Ghaemmaghami et al. 2021b), or specific 
robust isolines of T. remus that require careful selection 
to avoid quality loss (de Lacerda et al. 2023). This sug -
gests heightened sensitivity of T. busseolae to artificial 
rearing conditions and inbreeding, necessitating colony 
restoration through wild-type supplementation.
Our findings align with Naranjo-Guevara et al. ( 2020), 
who demonstrated that prolonged laboratory rearing can 
select for parasitoids with reduced fecundity, aggression, 
and flight activity compared to wild counterparts. Wild 
Discussion
Biological fitness parameters (reproductive output, 
lifespan, emergence rate, and sex ratio) and parasitism 
rates of T. busseolae declined significantly across suc -
cessive generations under laboratory rearing conditions. 
This progressive decline could significantly compromise 
the effectiveness of T. busseolae as a biological control 
against S. nonagrioides.
Preserving the quality of natural enemies across mul -
tiple generations is critical, as prolonged mass rearing 
under stable insectary conditions may reduce their field 
efficacy (Bertin et al. 2017). Large-scale parasitoid pro -
duction for augmentative biological control demands 
significant labor resources while risking deterioration in 
agent quality over successive generations (Parra 2010). 
This degradation manifests as reduced environmental 
tolerance and altered host specificity, ultimately compro -
mising pest management efficacy (Sørensen et al. 2012). 
Consequently, rigorous quality control throughout rear -
ing and deployment progress is essential for biologi -
cal control program success. The observed reduction in 
parasitism rate and fertility can be attributed to multiple 
interacting factors, including adaptation to artificial labo-
ratory conditions, reduced host-searching efficiency, and 
nutritional deficiencies associated with continuous rear -
ing on the same host species (Chen et al. 2023). Recent 
studies on T. remus and Trichogramma spp. have demon-
strated that without rigorous quality assessment and the 
selection of robust isolines, parasitoids frequently exhibit 
reduced parasitism rates and fertility, which directly 
compromise their long-term efficacy under field condi -
tions (de Paula et al. 2023).
Furthermore, the significant decrease in emergence 
rate and female longevity observed in later generations 
indicates a loss of physiological vigor and developmen -
tal stability. This deterioration is often a consequence of 
inbreeding depression and metabolic changes induced 
by the artificial rearing environment (Ghaemmaghami 
et al. 2021). Reduced emergence rates may result from 
increased embryonic mortality due to the expression of 
deleterious recessive alleles, while shortened longevity 
reflects a decline in stress tolerance and overall metabolic

individuals consistently exhibit higher parasitism perfor -

A major concern in the mass-rearing natural enemies 
is inbreeding, definedas the mating between genetically 
related individuals, which triggers inbreeding depression. 
This evolutionary process manifests as reduced offspring 
fitness. In diploid females, inbreeding increases homo -
zygosity, thereby increasing the likelihood of deleterious 
recessive deleterious recessive alleles. In haploid males, 
deleterious alleles are inherently and always expressed, 
collectively compromise survival, reproduction, and 
adaptive traits (Charlesworth and Willis 2009). Recent 
genomic and ecological studies confirm that prolonged 
mass rearing of parasitoid wasps can rapidly reduce 
genetic diversity and host- searching efficiency unless 
these traits are actively monitored and managed (Li et al. 
2024; de Melo et al. 2024). The significant generational 
effect on sex ratio confirmed by logistic ANOVA further 
supports the progressive loss of female-biased allocation 
as a consequence of inbreeding. Although the specific 
molecular mechanism of sex determination in T. bus -
seolae has not been explicitly characterized in the litera -
ture, this rapid deterioration and sex ratio distortion are 
highly consistent with the effects of complementary sex 
determination (CSD). Under CSD, inbreeding increases 
the production of homozygous diploid males, which are 
often sterile or exhibit reduced fitness, thereby imposing 
a severe genetic load on mass-reared colonies (Cook and 
Crozier 1995). In arrhenotokous parasitoids, sex ratio 
manipulation is primarily controlled by females through 
differential fertilization of eggs; however, this ability 
may be disrupted by inbreeding depression (Russell and 
Stouthamer 2010). The male-biased shift observed in T. 
busseolae is likely a consequence of increased homozy -
gosity, which exposes deleterious recessive alleles that 
disproportionately affect female offspring survival or 
impair female reproductive capacity, including sperm 
storage and utilization (Charlesworth and Willis 2009). 
Recent studies further emphasize that such sex ratio dis -
tortions in mass-reared colonies can substantially reduce 
population growth potential and biological control effi -
cacy, underscoring the need for periodic genetic supple -
mentation with wild populations (Li et al. 2023).
Concern about the decline in the female sex ratio is 
another major challenge in using T. busseolae against 
the sugarcane stem borer. As emphasized in biological 
control literature, a shift in the sex ratio towards male-
bias and a reduction in females (the individuals directly 
responsible for parasitizing the host pest) will lead to a 
severe decrease in field efficacy (Russell and Stouthamer 
2010). Offspring sex ratios in parasitoid species are influ -
enced by multiple factors (e.g., parental age, temperature, 
host traits, density), primarily through female-mediated 
control of egg fertilization and differential survival).
Overall, the rapid deterioration of T. busseolae biologi-
cal quality within only 10 generations—a rate dispropor -
tionately faster than in other parasitoid species such as T. 
brassicae, which maintained quality for over 40 genera -
tions under similar rearing conditions (Ghaemmaghami 
et al. 2021a)—suggests a heightened sensitivity of this 
species to artificial rearing and inbreeding. The combined 
declines in parasitism, fertility, emergence, longevity, and 
sex ratio directly threaten the operational viability of T. 
busseolae in augmentative biological control programs. 
To mitigate these effects, rigorous quality control proto -
cols, including the periodic introduction of wild genetic 
material, optimization of rearing diets, and the potential 
use of iso-female line selection, are essential for sustain -
ing the efficacy of this parasitoid against S. nonagrioides 
in sugarcane agroecosystems (Fortes et al. 2023).
Although the arcsine-square-root transformation fol -
lowed by ANOVA provided robust statistical compari -
sons in this study, future research could further enhance 
the analysis of proportional data (e.g., parasitism rate, 
emergence rate) by employing logistic regression (GLM 
with binomial distribution). The models directly account 
for the binomial nature of the response variable and may 
provide a more appropriate framework for analyzing pro-
portion-based outcomes. (Hardy and Smith 2023).
Conclusions
The findings indicate that the biological quality of T. 
busseolae may deteriorate over successive generations 
(F₀–F₁₀) under laboratory rearing conditions. Critical 
parameters, including parasitism rate, fecundity, emer -
gence rate, adult longevity, and female-biased sex ratio, 
appeared to decline progressively, with the F₁₀ genera -
tion exhibiting reductions of 28–39% compared to the 
wild-derived F₀. This relatively rapid degradation (within 
10 generations) suggests that T. busseolae may be par -
ticularly sensitive to prolonged laboratory rearing and 
the inbreeding effects, although direct comparisons to 
other parasitoid species require standardized experimen -
tal protocols. Notably, these findings contrast with pre -
vious studies in which key quality parameters remained 
relatively stable across multiple generations. Recom -
mended interventions include periodic introduction of 
wild genetic material, optimization of rearing diets, and 
and strict control of rearing conditions. These measures 
may be critical for sustaining the operational viability of 
T. busseolae as a biological control agent and for ensuring 
consistent pest suppression in sugarcane agro-systems.

summary: Measurement of cervical cancer quality indicators using a population-based linked dataset in New South Wales, Australia
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

The aims of this study were to assess feasibility of measuring cervical cancer quality indicators (QIs) using a population-based linked dataset, assess the quality of care in the treatment of cervical cancer at a population level and to evaluate whether any sociodemographic variables were associated with quality of care. The primary data source was the NSW Clinical Cancer Registry, linked to NSW Cancer Registry, NSW Admitted Patient Data Collection and NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. Published QIs in cervical cancer were identified through a literature search. Feasibility of measurement was assessed according to available variables. QIs were measured where possible. Logistic regression analyses were performed to assess the impact of sociodemographic variables on QIs. There were 527 patients, of whom 160 (30%) had surgery, 259 (49%) radiotherapy and 153 (29%) chemotherapy. Only 16 of 93 (17%) published QIs could be measured. Only two of eight QIs with published benchmarks were met – postoperative deaths and duration of radiotherapy. The proportion alive at 1,3 & 5 years were 87%, 71% and 64%. Socio-demographic factors had limited associations with process QIs but were associated with outcome QIs. Increasing age, Australian country-of-birth, higher stage and squamous histology were associated with poorer survival. Population-based linked datasets are of limited value in measuring quality of care. Granular data collection at the institutional or multidisciplinary team level would allow improved measurement of quality indicators. Despite some QIs not meeting target benchmarks, survival from cervical cancer in NSW was comparable to other jurisdictions. Only 17% of published cervical cancer quality indicators could be measured from population-level linked datasets. Socio-demographic factors had limited impact on process quality indicators but were associated with outcomes. Survival from cervical cancer was comparable to published literature. Population-based linked datasets are of limited value in measuring quality of care.

title: Effects of cyclic hydrostatic pressure on the water absorption of polymer matrix solid buoyancy material

summary: Effects of cyclic hydrostatic pressure on the water absorption of polymer matrix solid buoyancy material
content:
Multiscale and Multidisciplinary Modeling, Experiments and Design (2026) 9:183 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s41939-026-01263-1
ORIGINAL PAPER
Effects of cyclic hydrostatic pressure on the water absorption
of polymer matrix solid buoyancy material
Wenjie Zhou 1 · Lei Chen 2 · Guoting Liu 2 · Fushun Liang 2 · Xiaoying Yan 2 · Peng Dong 1,2
Received: 7 February 2025 / Revised: 16 August 2026 / Accepted: 17 August 2026
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
From the perspective of service, the effects of cyclic hydrostatic pressure on the water absorption of polymer-matrix solid
buoyancy material (PSBM) are critical for the submarine safety. However, the underlying mechanism has not been fully
clariﬁed to date. This work is focused on the performance aging and underlying mechanisms of PSBM under cyclic hydrostatic
pressure. To comprehensively exhibit the actual service, a drying process was incorporated after each cycle during the
hydrostatic pressure tests. The results show that the water absorption of PSBM increases with the number of uses, and
long-term stress relaxation induces continuous internal stress redistribution, which exacerbates local stress concentration and
ultimately triggers the initiation of microcracks. Stress relaxation is attributed to such performance degradation. Moreover, a
model correlating the number of cycles to water absorption behavior was established, which enables the prediction of PSBM
water absorption behavior during cyclic service. These ﬁndings are beneﬁcial for improving the safety of submersibles and
provide signiﬁcant insights for the design of buoyancy materials in engineering applications.
Keywords Solid buoyancy material · Water absorption · Cyclic hydrostatic pressure · Lifespan prediction · Cyclic aging
1 Introduction
Polymer-matrix solid buoyancy material (PSBM) is a solid
compound formed through physical and chemical reactions
by ﬁlling inorganic materials such as glass microspheres into
the resin matrix (Xu and Zhang2016), which is necessary for
the submarine by providing the buoyancy to achieve deep div-
ing and surfacing. It has become the ﬁrst choice buoyancy
material in the deep-sea (Chenggui et al. 2017) ﬁeld, because
of its relatively low density, high strength, low water absorp-
tion, and low cost.
Water absorption (Li et al. 2009; Chen 2018) is one of the
most critical properties for the PSBM. It not only affects
the density and compressive strength but also determines
the buoyancy it provides. Currently, the water absorption for
almost all underwater equipment is required to be below 3%
in initial tests, even some standards targeting rates less than

1 Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Taiyuan
University of Technology, Taiyuan 030024, China
2 Shanxi Fenxi Heavy Industry Co. Ltd., Taiyuan 030027,
China
1%. At present, most of the research on the water absorp-
tion behavior of materials is to improve the composition and
processing of materials. Jiyouping et al. ( 2023) proposed a
vacuum-assisted isostatic pressing process. By fully accu-
mulating the internal glass beads, the internal pore defects
are reduced, thereby reducing the water absorption of the
material. Long et al. (2016) used a variety of silane coupling
agents to modify the surface of hollow glass microspheres,
thereby reducing the gap between the matrix and the glass
microspheres and the water absorption of the material. Liu
et al. (2023a) used the vacuum composite casting process to
increase the curing degree of the matrix by means of step-
wise heating curing, thereby reducing the water absorption
performance of the material. Unfortunately, people pay lim-
ited attention to the change of water absorption of PSBM after
multiple cycles, whether in practice or scientiﬁc research.
It is important to clarify whether the water absorption of
PSBM will increase after the repeated use of underwater
equipment, and it is also important to know the number of
cycles at which it will exceed the critical threshold. In fact,
previous studies have shown that visible cracks (Cui et al.
2018) were found on the solid buoyancy material block of a
deep-sea manned submersible after multiple uses. Kochetkov
and Maksimov ( 1996) found that the water absorption of

solid buoyancy materials continuously increases with time
when placed in the marine environment, leading to a gradual
decrease in compressive strength. Zhang and Zhang ( 2023)
found that the tensile strength, elongation at break, compres-
sive strength, tensile modulus and compressive modulus of
solid buoyancy materials decreased signiﬁcantly under cyclic
hydrostatic pressure. In this case, it is reasonably deduced
that the performance of the PSBM deteriorates with repeated
use, resulting in a severe threat to the safety of the sub-
mersible and its occupants (Grosjean et al. 2009; Helal et al.
2019). It should be noted that current research and tests on
the water absorption performance of solid buoyancy materi-
als keep specimens immersed in water all the time, without
considering that they may be removed from the water after a
certain service and continue to serve after a period of time.
The water absorption behavior of the material during this pro-
cess could potentially differ from that when it is consistently
submerged in water.
Therefore, cyclic hydrostatic pressure tests were carried
out on PSBM specimens, with a drying procedure imple-
mented after each loading cycle to simulate the practical
condition where the material is retrieved from the water
surface after service. The failure mechanism and water
absorption behavior of PSBM during cyclic loading were
investigated from the perspectives of microstructure evo-
lution and mechanical property variation. On the basis of
experimental data, a model was established to describe the
correlation between cycle number and water absorption per-
formance of PSBM, aiming to identify the critical transition
point in property evolution. This critical point facilitates the
prediction of the service life of PSBM under cyclic loading,
thereby improving its reliability and stability.
2 Experimental details
2.1 Experimental materials and preparation
The main part of PSBM used is composed of hollow glass
microspheres (HGM) and epoxy resin, with the remaining
components being curing agent, toughening agent and ﬁber.
A batch of the same PSBM samples was prepared for exper-
imental analysis. The ﬁller content is the ratio of the mass
of the insulating glass microspheres to the mass of the entire
composite material. Raw materials were obtained from the
following suppliers: epoxy resin is bisphenol F epoxy resin
(industrial grade), supplied by Nantong Xingchen Synthetic
Materials Co., Ltd.; curing agent is methyl tetrahydroph-
thalic anhydride (Me THPA, industrial grade), supplied by
Puyang Huicheng Electronic Materials Co., Ltd.; toughen-
ing agent is DMP-30; glass beads are hollow glass beads B;
and ﬁber was supplied by Bengbu Glass Industry Design and
Research Institute. The compressive strength of the tested
sample is 2.36 MPa, the density is 0.35 g/cm 3, the diameter
is 14.00 mm, and the height is 25.00 mm. The preparation
process is shown in Fig. 1. The parameters of hollow glass
microspheres (HGM) are shown in Table 1. The parameters
of epoxy resin are shown in Table 2.
2.2 Cyclic loading test
First, utilize the lathe to remove the outer surface of the
PSBM. Then weigh the material, and the initial mass was
recorded as m0. After the inﬁltration treatment, and the mate-
rial was placed in deionized water for immersion treatment,
the treatment time was 30 s, and then the surface of the sam-
ple was immediately wiped dry with a towel, and the mass
data were recorded as m 1.
The loading equipment is a hydrostatic pressure simula-
tion test device, as shown in Fig. 2a. Isostatic pressure is
used for loading. In accordance with Miner’s linear fatigue
damage accumulation rule and continuum damage mechan-
ics, the ultimate compressive loading test adopted herein
is regarded as an accelerated aging approach, which can
accelerate damage evolution and reveal the underlying aging
failure mechanism under limited cycles. The PSBM speci-
men was loaded into the permeable ﬁxture and placed into the
external water pressure experimental autoclave. The applied
pressure was set to 2.36 MPa, and the holding time was 10
h. Figure 2b shows the cyclic loading curve for three cycles.
According to this procedure, 30 cyclic loading tests were
performed. Upon completion of pressurization, excess mois-
ture on the surface of the PSBM specimen was immediately
wiped off with a towel, followed by weighing, and the mea-
sured mass was recorded as m 2. Next, the water absorption
of the specimen was calculated using Eq. ( 1). Subsequently,
the specimen was placed in an incubator and held at 60 °C
for 5h to ensure complete evaporation of penetrated water
molecules. The above procedures were repeated to complete
each full cycle. A pure thermal cycling control test without
hydrostatic pressure was supplemented, in which specimens
only underwent cyclic drying at 60 °C over 5 h. As shown
in Fig. 2c, analysis of the control group data shows that the
compressive strength remains nearly unchanged under pure
thermal cycling. This result demonstrates that thermal aging
can be distinguished from resin post-curing effects. It further
veriﬁes that cyclic hydrostatic loading and the accompany-
ing structural damage dominate the mechanical degradation
of the material.
