Lan Tang1, Qianghui Wang1, Haihua Xing1, Derui Zhao1, Yukai Ma1,Q i n gW a n g1, Tao Zhu1& Heping Li1
Sika deer ( Cervus nippon hortulorum ) meat is increasingly recognized for its nutritional and culinary
value, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its quality traits remain poorly understood. In this
study, we performed integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic pro ﬁling of six
representative muscle cuts from farmed sika deer (n = 12). Intercostal and trapezius muscles exhibiting
enriched features related to tenderness, marbling, and ﬂavor. Weighted gene co-expression network
analysis identiﬁed two convergent multi-omics regulatory axes, in which transcriptional programs
represented by ME6_trans and ME7_trans were linked to protein modules involved in muscle
structural organization and contractile metabolism (ME3_protein), ultimately re ﬂected in metabolite
clusters associated with lipid utilization and energy homeostasis (ME2_metab). These coordinated
transcription-to-protein-to-metabolite relationships suggest integrated regulation of extracellular
matrix remodeling, muscle ﬁber functional properties, and lipid metabolic adaptation underlying
region-dependent molecular variation in sika deer muscle. In addition, RT –qPCR and Western blot
validation of selected key factors demonstrated expression patterns consistent with the multi-omics
analyses, supporting the robustness of the identiﬁed molecular features. This study represents theﬁrst
integrative multi-omics characterization of molecular variation across major muscle cuts in farmed
sika deer, providing preliminary systems-level insights into coordinated metabolic and structural
features associated with meat quality-related traits.
Sika deer (Cervus nippon hortulorum) is increasingly recognized as a pre-
mium meat source due to its high protein content, low fat, and favorable
amino acid and fatty acid composition 1,2.C h i n a ,a st h ew o r l d’sl a r g e s t
producer of farmed sika deer with an estimated annual population of
700,000, has traditionally prioritized the harvesting of antlers for medicinal3.
In recent years, the growing consumer demand for venison has prompted a
strategic shift in the sika deer industry,transitioning from traditional antler-
oriented practices toward meat-focused production systems4.C o n c u r r e n t l y ,
sika deer meat has entered high-end food markets globally. In addition,
regions such as New Zealand, Europe, and the United States have estab-
lished integrated systems encompassing deer farming, meat quality eva-
luation, and product marketing 5. These developments underscore the
urgent need for systematic research on venison to support industry
advancement and the comprehensive elucidation of meat quality
characteristics.
However, research on deer meat quality remains sparse, particularly at
the molecular level. To date, most studies have focused on macroscopic or
physicochemical parameters, with limited application of high-throughput
omics approaches. For example, a recent study by Jin et al. provided a
comprehensive analysis of the physicochemical and nutritional properties of
meat from twelve sika deer cut parts, highlighting site-speciﬁc differences in
pH, tenderness, amino acid content, and fatty acid composition4. However,
such studies lack insight into the molecular regulatory mechanisms driving
these differences. In recent years, high-throughput omics approaches—
including transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics —have been
widely employed to elucidate meat quality traits in major livestock species
such as cattle, pigs, and poultry6–8. For instance, a 2024 study on beef cattle
undergoing compensatory growth employed RNA-Seq to identify 57 dif-

chilling rate on pork quality, pinpointing several proteins involved in cut

revealing links between oxidative phosphorylation,β-alanine metabolism,

these advances in other livestock, comparable single-omics studies on sika
deer are still absent, and integrated multi-omics investigations in deer meat
have not yet been conducted. This gap underscores the need for a

Transcriptional characteristics across cuts
To explore transcriptional differences among cut regions, we performed
differential gene expression analysis using a “one-vs-rest” comparison
strategy while adjusting for sex, sam pling season, and individual animal
identity. We identi ﬁed a variable number of signi ﬁcantly differentially
expressed genes (DEGs) across six cuts: BB (DEGs = 2), IM (DEGs = 26),
QF (DEGs = 1), T (DEGs = 23), GM (DEGs = 4), and LD (DEGs = 5)
(Fig. 2A and Supplementary Data 2). Subsequent KEGG enrichment ana-
lysis revealed that some DEGs were signiﬁcantly associated with pathways
implicated in meat quality traits (Fig.2B and Supplementary Data 2). For
example, the Protein digestion and ab sorption pathway includes several
genes involved in cellular structure and cytoskeletal organization, such as
collagens and actins, which may affect muscle ﬁber integrity and inter-
muscular tenderness13.A d d i t i o n a l l y ,t h eT G F -β signaling pathway, which is
involved in muscle growth and differentiation, may play a role in regulating
muscle development and tenderness14, and the PPAR signaling pathway,
linked to lipid metabolism, could inﬂuence intramuscular fat deposition and
ﬂavor formation15.I na d d i t i o n ,t h eE C M–receptor interaction pathway,
involving collagens and integrins, may affect tissue stability and shear force,
thereby contributing to meat toughness 16. The IM region exhibited the
greatest number of DEGs, including several upregulated genes closely linked
to meat quality (Fig. 2C). ADIPOQ and PLIN1, key regulators of lipid
metabolism, were signiﬁcantly upregulated and may enhance marbling and
juiciness17,18. Meanwhile, upregulation of ECM-related genes such as
COL11A2, COL12A1, COL22A1, COMP, FMOD,a n d THBS4 suggests
enhanced extracellular matrix stability, potentially improving cut structure
and tenderness19. These results are consistent with Yinshi Sun et al.'s meat
quality studies and highlight the functional relevance of these transcrip-

analysis revealed that male-upregulated genes were predominantly enriched

activity in protein synthesis and lipid regulation. Regarding seasonal effects,

Proteomic proﬁles and functional insights
A total of 5367 proteins were detected (Supplementary Fig. 2A), with
approximately 98% (5271) shared across all cuts (Fig.3A), indicating a high
overlap in protein types among different tissues. Based on this, differential
expression analysis was conducted by comparing each cuts against the
others, revealing differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in each: BB
(DEPs = 40), GM (DEPs = 56), IM (DEPs = 49), LD (DEPs = 60), QF
(DEPs = 128), and T (DEPs = 63) (Fig. 4B and Supplementary Data 4).
Functional enrichment showed region-speciﬁc proteomic patterns asso-
ciated with cuts quality (Fig. 3C and Supplementary Data 3). LD-speciﬁc
proteins were enriched in transcriptional regulation and arginine/proline
metabolism pathways, indicating act ive protein synthesis and turnover,
which may support tenderness and functional integrity 20. In contrast,
downregulated proteins in LD were associated with lipid metabolism and
the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, su ggesting a lower capacity for fat
deposition and stress adaptation21. QF was enriched in glycolysis and pyr-
uvate metabolism, reﬂecting high-energy metabolism that may in ﬂuence
cuts pH and ﬂavor22. IM and GM were associated with lysosomal degra-
dation and glycosaminoglycan metabolism, highlighting their potential role
in maintaining extracellular matrix integrity and improving textural
properties23,24. BB and T showed upregulation in immune-related and
developmental pathways, possibly re ﬂecting stress response or repair
mechanisms with less direct contribution to meat quality.
Regarding sex differences (Supplementary Fig. 2B and Supplementary
Data 3), male samples exhibited upregulation in cAMP signaling and
morphine addiction pathways, suggesting more dynamic responses in
neuromuscular regulation25 (Fig. 3D and Supplementary Data 3). Female
samples were enriched in ribosome biogenesis, basal transcription factors,
and ABC transporters, indicating enhanced capacity for protein synthesis
and metabolic stability26. In terms of seasonal differences (Supplementary
Fig. 2C and Supplementary Data 3), spring samples showed enrichment in
transcriptional regulation and virus-related pathways, suggesting higher
metabolic and renewal activity. In contrast, winter samples were enriched in
carbon ﬁxation, galactose metabolism, and starch/sucrose metabolism
pathways, implying greater capacity for energy storage and sugar accu-
mulation, which may enhance ﬂavor and nutritional quality (Fig. 3Ea n d
Supplementary Data 3). Collectively, proteomic proﬁl e sa c r o s sc u t st y p e s ,
sexes, and seasons highlight functional variations in metabolic regulation,
structural maintenance, and lipid homeostasis, laying the molecular foun-
dation for distinct meat quality traits.

Multi-omics integration reveals key regulatory hubs
To explore multi-level regulatory mechanisms, we constructed a cross-
omics interaction network based on WGCNA module correlations and
identiﬁed several signi ﬁcantly associated module pairs across tran-
scriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic levels (Fig. 6A). Among them,
ME4_metab and ME8_protein exhibited strong negative correlation and
were both highly associated with the IM region, suggesting that this cuts area
features lipid-driven and endocrine-regulated activity, while having lower
energy and structural metabolism—traits consistent with soft texture and
rich ﬂavor. Moreover, ME3_protein and ME2_metab formed two inte-
grated regulatory chains with ME6_trans and ME7_trans
(ME6_trans–ME3_protein-ME2_metab and ME7_trans –ME3_protein-
ME2_metab). ME6_trans was enrichedin oxidative phosphorylation and
glycolysis (Fig. 6B), while ME7_trans focused on carbon metabolism and
lipid biosynthesis (Fig.6C), indicating their roles in energy supply, cutsﬁber
formation, and fat deposition.
We further constructed a tri-omics regulatory network (Fig.6D) and
identiﬁed key hub molecules. Transcriptomic hub genes like COQ9 and
NDUFA8 (energy metabolism) were highly expressed in LD, BB, and GM,
whereas ITGA6 and WWC1 (linked to structural integrity and lipid meta-
bolism) were enriched in IM and QF, reﬂecting their roles in fat accumu-
lation and cuts quality formation (Fig. 6E). In the proteomic level, TBB1,
TNNC1, TNNT1,a n dMYL10 emerged as key hub proteins, showing high
expression in IM and T —cuts regions known for higher fat content and
tender texture—and lower levels in the ﬁrmer BB and QF regions. TBB1
contributes to cytoskeletal integrity, TNNC1 and TNNT1 regulate slow-
twitch ﬁber contraction, and MYL10 inﬂuences cuts ﬂexibility and lipid
metabolism. Their elevated expressionmay support the softness, elasticity,
and marbling features of IM and T, reinforcing their superior tenderness
and ﬂavor (Fig.6F). At the metabolite level, lipid oxidation products such as
Prostaglandin G2 and (±)11-HETE were downregulated in IM and T,
potentially contributing to tenderness and ﬂavor. Conversely, 19(R)-
hydroxy PGE2 was elevated in QF, likely supporting rapid metabolism and
ﬁrmer texture (Fig.6G).
In summary, our multi-omics WGCNA integration identiﬁed a set of
key regulatory modules and hub molecules associated with cuts region-
speciﬁc traits. In particular, the two core interaction chains —
ME6_trans–ME3_protein-ME2_metab and ME7_trans –ME3_protein-
ME2_metab—highlight the coordinated regulation of lipid metabolism,
energy supply, and tissue structure, representing majorﬁndings of this study
and offering valuable targets for meat quality improvement and molecular
breeding.

content, low fat level, and favorable nutritional composition. Although
previous research has reported differences in physicochemical traits among
venison cuts, the molecular mechanismsassociated with these differences
are still not fully understood 1–3. In recent years, omics technologies have
been increasingly applied in cattle, pigs, and poultry to investigate biological

processes associated with tenderness, fat deposition, and ﬂavor
development6–10. Comparable studies in sika deerare still limited, especially
in integrating multiple omics layers. In this study, transcriptomic, pro-
teomic, and metabolomic datasets were analyzed to characterize molecular
variation among six representative muscle cuts from farmed sika deer.
Different muscle cuts exhibited varying degrees of molecular variation
across the transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets. At the
transcriptomic level, IM showed rela tively more differentially expressed
genes, including ADIPOQ and PLIN1, which are associated with lipid
metabolism and intramuscular fat deposition 17,18. Several extracellular
matrix-related genes, including COL11A2, COL12A1, COL22A1, COMP,
FMOD,a n dTHBS4, were also relatively highly expressed in IM. These genes
have been reported to participate in extracellular matrix organization and
structural maintenance in skeletal muscle 19. Pathways including PPAR
signaling, ECM–receptor interaction, and TGF-β signaling were also enri-
ched among different muscle regions. Previous studies have linked PPAR
signaling to lipid metabolism and intramuscular fat deposition, whereas
ECM-related pathways may contribute to tissue structure and tenderness-
associated properties13,19. At the proteomic level, QF was mainly enriched in
glycolysis and pyruvate metabolism pathways, which may inﬂuence muscle
energy metabolism and meat quality characteristics22. In contrast, IM and
GM were associated with lysosomal d egradation and glycosaminoglycan
metabolism, pathways potentially re lated to extracellular matrix main-
tenance and tissue properties 23,24. In addition, proteins such as TNNC1,
TNNT1,a n dMYL10 showed relatively high abundance in IM and T, con-
sistent with their roles in muscle contraction and slow-twitch ﬁber char-
acteristics. Metabolomic analysis identi ﬁed fatty acyls,
glycerophospholipids, and sterol lipids as major differential metabolite
classes among muscle regions 27,28. IM contained relatively high levels of
metabolites such as tiglic acid, oleamide, and propionylcarnitine, which may
be associated with lipid metabolism andﬂavor-related characteristics28.
Cross-omics integration identiﬁed several correlated transcriptomic,
proteomic, and metabolomic modules associated with regional differences
among muscle cuts. Among these, ME3_protein and ME8_protein were
enriched in pathways including glycolysis, amino acid biosynthesis, cytos-
keletal regulation, and PPAR signaling. Previous studies have linked these
processes to tenderness-related traits and intramuscular fat deposition29,30.
Metabolomic modules ME2 and ME4 displayed opposite association pat-
terns between QF and IM/T, suggesting differences in energy metabolism
and lipid-associated processes among muscle regions31,32. Two correlated
module chains, ME6_trans –ME3_protein–ME2_metab and
ME7_trans–ME3_protein–ME2_metab, connected transcriptomic, pro-
teomic, and metabolomic features a ssociated with muscle structure and
metabolism. In addition, hub molecules includingCOQ9, NDUFA8, ITGA6,
TNNC1,a n dTNNT1 displayed region-speciﬁc expression patterns. Finally,
RT–qPCR and Western blot analyses of genes associated with lipid
deposition, extracellular matrix-related characteristics, and muscle con-
traction features (FMOD, THBS4, PLIN1, TNNC1,a n d TNNT1)f u r t h e r
supported the expression patterns observed in the multi-omics analyses.
Several limitations should also be considered. First, this study mainly
focused on molecular proﬁling and did not include direct, detailed histo-
logical analyses of meat quality traits. Second, the relationships identiﬁed by
WGCNA were based on correlation analyses and cannot fully demonstrate
causal regulation among genes, proteins, and metabolites. Although
RT–qPCR and Western blot analyses supported several of the observed
expression patterns, validation was limited to selected targets and repre-
sentative muscle regions.
In conclusion, this study provides an integrative characterization of
molecular differences across six maj or muscle cuts in farmed sika deer.
Integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses revealed
region-dependent molecular differences among muscle regions, with
intercostal and trapezius muscles showing coordinated molecular features
related to lipid metabolism, extracellular matrix organization, muscle con-
traction, and energy utilization. Cross-omics integration further identiﬁed
two correlated module chains, ME6_trans–ME3_protein–ME2_metab and
ME7_trans–ME3_protein–ME2_metab, linking transcriptional variation to
structural and contractile protein modules and downstream metabolic
characteristics. The region-dependent expression patterns of FMOD,
THBS4, PLIN1, TNNC1,a n d TNNT1 were further supported at the tran-
script and protein levels by RT–qPCR and Western blot analyses, providing
independent validation of selected multi-omics ﬁndings. These ﬁndings
provide candidate molecular features associated with variation among sika
deer muscle cuts and establish a reference framework for future studies
integrating direct meat quality measurements and functional validation.
Methods
Sample collection
A total of 72 cuts were obtained from 12 healthy adult sika deer (6 males and
6 females), all raised under standardized feeding and management condi-
tions at Shuangyang Deer Quality Breed Breeding Co., Ltd. (Changchun,
China). All animals were selected with comparable developmental status
and body condition and were maintai ned under standardized intensive
housing conditions with routine health monitoring to minimize biological
heterogeneity. The sample size was determined to ensure sufﬁcient statis-
tical power while adhering to the principles of animal welfare. No animals or
samples were excluded from the analysis. Due to the seasonal reproductive
characteristics of sika deer, estrus generally occurs in autumn, and par-
turition is concentrated mainly between May and June each year. All ani-
mals in the spring group were slaughtered on April 1, 2024, at 22–23 months
of age, whereas all animals in the winter group were slaughtered on
December 23, 2024, at 29–30 months of age. Therefore, when sika deer from
the same birth cohort are slaughtered in different seasons, a difference of
about 6 months in biological age is unavoidable. Within each group, all
animals were slaughtered on the same day under uniform procedures to
maintain consistency in their physiological condition, slaughter handling,
and postmortem treatment. Prior to sample collection, all deer were
transported to the Shilu Deer Industry Group Co., Ltd. in Shuangyang
District, Changchun, Jilin Province, where slaughtering was performed
under uniform protocols. Six distinct cuts—longissimus dorsi (LD), inter-
costal muscles(IM), trapezius (T), b iceps brachii (BB), gluteus maximus
(GM), and quadriceps femoris (QF)—were dissected postmortem. Detailed
sample information is provided in Supplementary Data 1. According to the
speciﬁc requirements of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic
analyses, tissue samples were appropriately processed and preserved,
including storage in RNA-later solution and/or immediate snap-freezing in
liquid nitrogen. All procedures in volving animals were reviewed and
approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Northeast
Forestry University, China (A pproval No. 20220409). This study was
reported in accordance with the ARR IVE guidelines (Animal Research:
Reporting of In Vivo Experiments).
Transcriptomic sequencing and data analysis
Total RNA was extracted from cuts tissue samples collected from different
anatomical regions of sika deer using the Trizol method and quantiﬁed with
the NanoDrop® 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo, USA). Genomic DNA
was removed with RNase-free DNase I and the mRNA libraries were
constructed using the TruSeq Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit (Illumina)
with 5 μg of input RNA. Fragmentation, reverse transcription, adapter
ligation, and ampliﬁcation were conducted following the manufacturer’s
protocol. A 150 bp insert size was selected using AMPure XP beads
(Beckman Coulter), and library quality was validated on the Agilent Bioa-
nalyzer 2100 system. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq
6000 platform.
Raw reads wereﬁltered using FASTP (v0.20.1)33,34 to remove adapters
and low-quality sequences. Clean reads were aligned to the sika deer
reference genome (GCA_040085125.1])12 using HISAT2(v2.0.4)35. Gene-
level counts were generated with HTSeq36, and expression levels were cal-
c u l a t e di nF P K M( f r a g m e n t sp e rk i l o b ase of transcript per million mapped
reads) using the formula: FPKM = (read count × 10 ⁹)/(total mapped
reads × gene length).
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41538-026-01160-4 Article
npj Science of Food Article in Press
Differential gene expression analysis was conducted using the
DESeq237 (v1.42.0) based on read count data obtained from RNA-seq. To
ensure statistical robustness and to avoidpotential pseudoreplication arising
from multiple muscle samples collected from the same animal, sex, sam-
pling season, and individual animal identity were included as covariates in
the design formula. For each cuts type , pairwise comparisons against the
remaining groups were performed, an d differentially expressed genes
(DEGs) were deﬁned using the threshold of adjusted p value (padj) <0.05
and absolute log₂ fold-change (log2FC) > 1. For dimensionality reduction,
transcript per million (TPM) values were calculated by normalizing FPKM
values across genes within each sample38. The top 2000 most variable genes
were selected for principal component analysis (PCA) to assess global
expression patterns across samples.
Proteomic proﬁling and data analysis
Cuts tissue samples from different a natomical regions of sika deer were
ground in liquid nitrogen and lysed using SDT buffer supplemented with
DTT39. After ultrasonication on ice and thermal denaturation at 95 °C,
samples were centrifuged, and supernatants were alkylated with IAM in the
dark. Proteins were precipitated with pre-cooled acetone and washed with
cold acetone before being re-dissolved in dissolution buffer. Protein con-
centrations were measured using a Bradford assay, and protein integrity was
assessed via SDS-PAGE. For digestion, proteins were denatured in 8 M urea
with 100 mM TEAB (pH 8.5), and trypsin was added for a two-step
digestion at 37 °C. After acidi ﬁcation, peptides were desalted using C18
columns and dried under vacuum. Dried peptides were reconstituted,
centrifuged, and subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis using a Vanquish™ Neo
UHPLC system coupled to a Thermo Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer.
Peptides were separated on a PepMap ™ Neo C18 column with a linear
gradient of acetonitrile containing 0.1% formic acid. DIA acquisition was
performed with 300 variable windows (m/z 380–980) and resolution set-
tings of 240,000 (MS1) and 80,000 (MS2).
Raw DIA data were analyzed using DIA-NN software(v2.2.0) in
DirectDIA mode40. A project-speciﬁc protein database was used for spectral
matching, with iRT peptides for reten tion time calibration. Search para-
meters included 10 ppm precursor mass tolerance and 0.02 Da fragment
tolerance. Cysteine residues were carbamidomethylated, and methionine
oxidation and N-terminal modiﬁcations were considered. Up to two missed
cleavages were allowed. Peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) wereﬁltered to
retain only those with ≥99% conﬁdence, and false discovery rate (FDR)
thresholds were set at 1% for both peptides and proteins.
We performed principal component analysis to reduce dimensionality
and visualize the distribution of proteomic expression proﬁles across dif-
ferent cuts regions. Protein abundance data were standardized usingz-score
transformation to ensure comparability across samples. Subsequently, two-
sample t-tests were conducted to identify proteins with signiﬁcant abun-
dance differences between each cuts region and all others. FC was calculated
as the ratio of mean expression levelsbetween groups, providing a quanti-
tative measure of differential expression.
Metabolomic proﬁling and data analysis
Approximately 100 mg of cuts tissue from different anatomical regions of
sika deer was ground in liquid nitrogen and extracted with prechilled 80%
methanol by vortexing. The homogenates were incubated on ice for 5 min
and centrifuged at 15,000 ×g, 4 °C for 20 min. The supernatant was diluted
with LC-MS grade water to a ﬁnal methanol concentration of 53%, then
centrifuged again under the same condi tions. The resulting supernatants
were transferred to autosampler vials for LC-MS/MS analysis41.C h r o m a -
tographic separation was performed on a Hypersil Gold C18 column
(100 × 2.1 mm, 1.9μm) using a Vanquish UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher
Scientiﬁc), coupled with a Q Exactive ™ HF or HF-X Orbitrap mass spec-
trometer (Thermo Fisher Scienti ﬁc). A 12-min linear gradient of 0.1%
formic acid in water (eluent A) and methanol (eluent B) was applied at a
ﬂow rate of 0.2 mL/min. Mass spectrometry was operated in both positive
and negative ion modes, with a spray voltage of 3.5 kV, capillary
temperature of 320 °C, and sheath/auxiliary gas rates of 35 and 10 L/min,
respectively.
Raw MS data were processed using Compound Discoverer 3.3
(Thermo Fisher) for peak detection, alignment, and quantiﬁcation. Main
parameters included a 5 ppm mass tolerance, 30% signal intensity tolerance,
and normalization to total ion intensi ty. Metabolites were annotated by
matching MS/MS spectra against mzCloud, mzVault, and MassList data-
bases. Quality controlﬁltering excluded compounds with a relative standard
deviation >30% in QC samples. Identiﬁed metabolites were annotated using
KEGG42, and LIPIDMaps43 databases.
Metabolite proﬁling data were normalized and analyzed through
Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) using the mixOmics
(v6.26.0)44 in R to identify cuts-speciﬁc metabolic signatures. The PLS-DA
model was used to evaluate the contribution of each metabolite to the
discrimination between cuts types. Metabolites with Variable Importance in
Projection (VIP) scores >1 were selected as discriminant features. Differ-
ential abundance analysis wasconducted with limma (v3.58.1)15,a p p l y i n g
thresholds of 1.5- FC andp value < 0.05, while controlling for sex, sampling
season, and individual animal identity as covariates.
KEGG pathway enrichment analysis
KEGG pathway enrichment analysis was conducted using KOBAS (v2.0)45,
where all differentially expressed genes were ﬁrst annotated to KEGG
Orthology (KO)42 terms using Bos taurus (bta) as the reference species.
Subsequently, enrichment testing via hypergeometric distribution using the
R package clusterProﬁler (v4.19.4) to identify signiﬁcantly overrepresented
biological pathways (adjustedp value < 0.05).
WGCNA-based module identiﬁcation
WGCNA was applied to transcriptom i c ,p r o t e o m i c ,a n dm e t a b o l o m i c
datasets to identify co-expressed mo dules and explore their associations
with cuts regions. WGCNA package (v1.72.5) was applied, we ﬁrst pre-
processed the data and removed ou tlier samples. The optimal soft-
thresholding power was selected using pickSoft-Threshold to construct a
scale-free network. An adjacency matrix was generated and transformed
into a topological overlap matrix (TOM), followed by hierarchical clustering
and dynamic tree cut to identify discrete modules. Each module was sum-
marized by its module eigengene. We then assessed the correlation between
module eigengenes and cuts parts, identifying trait-related modules, which
were further analyzed for KEGG pathway enrichment. Finally, we calculated
pairwise correlations between module eigengenes across the three omics
levels. Module pairs with |r|>0 . 5a n dp < 0.05 were selected to construct a
multi-omics regulatory network, highlighting cross-omics functional links
related to cuts characteristics.
RT-qPCR
RT–qPCR was used to quantify the expression of key genes (FMOD,
TNNC1, TNNT1, THBS4, and PLIN1) across six muscle regions, with three
biological replicates per group. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol
reagent (Takara, Japan), and reverse transcription was conducted using the
PrimeScript™ FAST RT reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (Takara, Japan)
according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Quantitative PCR was carried
out using TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ II (Tli RNaseH Plus) on a SLAN-96S
Real-Time PCR system (Hongshi Medical Technology, China). Each
sample was analyzed with three technical replicates. RPLP0 was used as the
internal reference gene for normalization. Relative gene expression levels
were calculated using the 2 −ΔΔCt method after quality control, where ΔCt
represents the difference between target and reference genes, andΔΔCt is
deﬁned as the difference between experimental and control groups. Primer
sequences were designed using Primer3 and are listed in Supplemen-
tary Data 5.
Western blotting
Western blotting was performed to evaluate the protein abundance of
FMOD, TNNC1, and TNNT1 in representative muscle tissues, including
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41538-026-01160-4 Article
npj Science of Food Article in Press
QF, IM, and T. Detailed information on antibodies is provided in Supple-
mentary Data 6. Samples were rinsed with cold PBS and mechanically
homogenized. Total proteins were e xtracted using RIPA buffer supple-
mented with protease inhibitors, follow e db yi n c u b a t i o no ni c ew i t hi n t e r -
mittent mixing to ensure complete lysis. The lysates were then centrifuged,
and the supernatants were collected for further analysis. Equal amounts of
protein were separated by SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF mem-
branes. After blocking to minimize non-speciﬁc binding, membranes were
incubated with primary antibodies against FMOD, TNNC1, and TNNT1 at
4 °C, followed by incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies at
room temperature. Protein signals were detected using a chemilumines-
cence imaging system. Band intensities were quantiﬁed using image analysis
software, and relative protein levels were calculated by normalization to the
internal reference protein. All experiments were performed with three
independent biological replicates to ensure reproducibility and reliability of
the results.
Statistical analysis and data visualization
All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (v4.3.1). Pearson
correlation was applied to evaluate inter-module relationships across omics
levels, while Spearman correlation was used to assess associations between
WGCNA modules and cuts regions, with p < 0.05 considered signiﬁcant.
Metabolomic pathway activity was assessed using the GSEA function from
t h eRp a c k a g ec l u s t e r P r oﬁler (v4.19.4), based on log2FC values across cuts
groups. All visualizations were generated using R packages, including
ggplot2 (v3.5.1)46, ComplexHeatmap (v2.18.0)14, patchwork (v1.3.0.9)16,a n d
scRNAtoolVis (v0.1.0).
Data availability
The datasets generated and analyzed during this study have been deposited
in the following public repositories and are available upon request from the
corresponding author: Metabolomics data have been deposited in the
MetaboLights database ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metabolights/)u n d e rt h e
accession number MTBLS12900. Proteo mics data are available via the
iProX database (https://www.iprox.cn/) with the ProteomeXchange acces-
sion number PXD067526. Transcriptomics data have been deposited in the
NCBI Sequence Read Archive under the accession number PRJNA1213237.

Chapter 
Introductory Chapter: Water 
Quality – Emerging Concern for 
Sustainable FutureSvetislav 
S. Krstić1.
Water quality in human history and its contemporary stateWater 
quality has not been in focus for a very long period of human history on our 
planet. Most probably, there have been many occasions when humans have learned 
not to drink “dirty” (toxic, polluted, infected) waters due to the impact on health or 
even death, which was firmly embedded in the collective consciousness. As the Bible 
states [1], even God has used toxic waters to punish the Egyptians by turning the 
waters of the River Nile red.
After so many millennia of development and progress, human society has 
unfortunately reached a very grim state regarding global water quality. It is dimly 
expressed [2] as: “In many countries, both developing and developed, current pathways 
for water use are often not sustainable. . . The world faces a worsening series of local and 
regional water quantity and quality problems. . . Water resource constraints and water 
degradation are weakening one of the resource bases on which human society is built.” [ 2] 
The statement is so profoundly corroborated by the newest facts [ 3] based on 
scientific research, which can be summarized as:
(1) Only about 44% of global household wastewater is safely treated before 
being released, leaving a majority that is discharged without adequate 
treatment [4].
(2) Less than half of industrial wastewater is safely treated globally, contributing 
to chemical, nutrient, and pathogen contamination of rivers and lakes [ 4].
(3) By 2030, the health and livelihoods of up to 4.8 billion people could be at risk 
if water quality monitoring and treatment are not improved [ 4].
(4) Roughly half of the world’s population experiences severe water scarcity for 
at least part of the year, and water pollution aggravates these shortages by 
reducing usable freshwater [ 5].
(5) In lower-income countries, poor water quality is mainly due to low levels of 
wastewater treatment, whereas in higher-income countries, agricultural 
runoff is a leading pollution source [ 5].1 
(6)
Emerging water contaminants include pharmaceuticals, hormones, indus-
trial chemicals, detergents, and perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl sub -
stances (PFAS) – substances that are persistent in the environment and 
difficult to remove [ 5].
(7) Wastewater often carries mixtures of pollutants – including microplastics, 
pathogens, heavy metals, and chemicals – that can disrupt aquatic food webs 
and affect wildlife [ 6].
(8) Persistent, toxic “forever chemicals” (PFAS) are increasingly found in US 
tap water and are linked to cancer, immune system harm, and other serious 
health risks [7].
(9) Groundwater contamination from naturally occurring geologic elements – 
like arsenic, fluoride, selenium, and uranium – affects drinking water safety 
around the world. In some regions, a significant share of groundwater 
sources exceeds recommended guidelines [ 8].
(10) Global water quality is declining while water demand increases, requiring 
better wastewater management, pollution reduction, and monitoring to 
protect human and environmental health [ 5].
Many water quality indicators vary with flow conditions and over time. Without 
consistent monitoring, short-duration pollution events may be missed, delaying 
response and increasing impacts on ecosystems and drinking water supplies.2.
The marine environmentMoreover, 
the situation with the marine environment seems to be at least equally 
alarming, if not more so. Academics have already sounded the alarm about the 
destruction of global ecosystems [ 9]. Humanity must immediately and significantly 
alter our harmful trajectory in order to avoid irrevocably damaging our oceans in 
multiple ways that will further affect ocean health for both us and future 
generations. The ocean is the world’s largest realm, housing an astonishing array of 
biodiversity that provides critical ecological functions that ultimately support life on 
Earth [10].
Humanity relies on the ocean for livelihood and wellbeing, including a variety of 
benefits ranging from food production, tourism, pharmaceuticals, energy 
production, shipping, recreation, esthetics, culture, and scientific research. Although 
these services are not always quantifiable, humans heavily depend on an 
immeasurable number of services provided by a healthy ocean, including shoreline 
protection, nutrient and carbon cycling, climate and weather regulation, oxygen 
production, primary productivity, waste detoxification, and biodiversity 
maintenance [11]. Placing a global value on marine ecosystem services is difficult or 
even impossible, likely leading us to make the dangerous mistake of undervaluing the 
ocean despite the large body of evidence that a healthy ocean is critical to the success 
of all life on the planet.2
Water
Quality-AnEmergingConcernforaSustainableFuture
Approximately 
98% of the global ocean is already affected by multiple stressors, 
raising the concerning possibility of large-scale ecological collapse in a number of 
systems. While coastal habitats often experience the most significant damage, even 
remote offshore or deep-water habitats are not immune to increasing threats from 
human activities. Damage to marine habitats has accelerated rapidly around the 
world, with 76% of marine and estuarine species affected, including notable losses of 
50% of coral-reef cover [ 12] and 40% of kelp forests. Simultaneously, extensive 
biodiversity loss is occurring; populations of marine vertebrates decreased by an 
average of 22% from 1970 to 2008, with marine fish experiencing a higher decrease 
of 38%. More than 25 marine species have already been driven extinct, with 
extinction rates expected to increase sharply in the near future. In addition to 
biodiversity and habitat losses, human disruptions render marine ecosystems less 
resilient, considerably increasing their vulnerability to further disturbances [ 13].3.
Selected papers regarding water quality in this bookMany 
interesting works of high quality have been received during the preparation 
of this book. Especially notable are many papers coming from scientists who work in 
developing countries, who have meticulously documented harmful impacts on water 
quality and the consequent deleterious effects on their societies. While these 
attempts are quite commendable for creating awareness of the dangers linked to the 
deterioration of water quality for human health and the environment, this book 
seeks to present some novel aspects in monitoring, new methods, a comprehensive 
approach, or new technologies for the treatment and prevention of water pollution. 
And indeed, this book’s title has attracted some quite interesting research topics like 
contaminants of emerging concern, hydrodynamic cavitation technology for the 
degradation of organic pollutants, or a dual-wavelength continuous-flow 
nephelometer, just to name a few.4.
ConclusionsIt 
is evident that the global scientific community repeatedly and constantly points 
out the dangers of water quality deterioration and the urgent need for rapid, decisive 
actions to reverse the already deleterious effects. The current issue on water quality 
attempts to, once again, initiate the responsibility of the modern human society 
toward sustainable practice regarding water quality, but also overall and global care 
for Planet Earth. Through a modern approach and new insights, we hope to achieve 
strong momentum among decision makers to initiate much more intensive 
rehabilitation, prevention, and restoration activities in order to preserve water 
environments, human health, and biodiversity for future generations.Introductory

title: Breaking barriers: the power of bank competition in driving firms’ new quality productive forces in China
summary: Breaking barriers: the power of bank competition in driving firms’ new quality productive forces in China
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

This study examines how commercial bank competition influences firms’ new quality productive forces (NQPF) in China through a comprehensive composite indicator. Our analysis demonstrates that intensified bank competition significantly enhances firms’ NQPF by mitigating financial constraints, lowering credit costs, and strengthening internal controls. The positive effects are particularly pronounced when digital and green finance initiatives are combined, whereas government intervention negatively moderates this relationship. Heterogeneity analysis reveals stronger impacts for non-state-owned enterprises and high-tech firms. We address endogeneity concerns via an instrumental variable approach, with robustness confirmed through alternative specifications. These findings provide valuable insights into the nexus between banking sector dynamics and firm-level productivity enhancement in China’s evolving financial landscape.

title: From Booking Experience to Impulsive Travel Decisions: Evidence from Vietnam
source: Journal of Quality Assurance in Hospitality & Tourism
summary: From Booking Experience to Impulsive Travel Decisions: Evidence from Vietnam
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

This study investigates how functional and psychological components of the Online Customers’ Travel Booking Experience (OCTBE) influence impulsive travel booking (ITB) behavior. Data were collected from 653 users of online travel booking platforms and analyzed using PLS-SEM with bootstrapping in SmartPLS 3.0. The results reveal that interactivity, informativeness, visual engagement, navigation, search ease, trust, and convenience significantly enhance ITB. However, anticipated travel enjoyment did not directly influence ITB. Booking platform commitment (BPC) partially mediates the links between the experience and ITB, supporting its role as a sequential attitudinal conversion mechanism that transforms booking stimuli into spontaneous travel decisions. Price sensitivity showed a strong negative total effect on ITB but did not significantly moderate the paths between BPC and ITB, reinforcing it as an external impulse-restraint trait rather than an experiential organism component. This study extends customer-experience-based impulsive behavior theory to digital tourism booking and provides actionable insights for designing ethical, customer-centric, and sustainable online travel platforms.

Abstract
Background: Constipation is one of the most common gastrointestinal problems affecting patients with
frailty. Several factors in frail patients contribute to this issue, such as decreased mobility, low oral intake,
comorbidities, polypharmacy, and susceptibility to drug side effects due to exhausted physiologic reserves.
Constipation causes significant morbidity, including abdominal pain, overflow diarrhoea, urinary retention,
delirium, and reduced quality of life; if not managed appropriately, it can lead to increased mortality.
Therefore, timely recognition and a standardised, structured, stepwise approach are critical to preventing
these outcomes. From anecdotal clinical experience in the frailty ward, while emphasis is placed on
managing complex medical conditions, a comprehensive, standardised, and structured approach to
managing constipation is sometimes overlooked, particularly among junior colleagues. This quality
improvement project (QIP) aimed to improve compliance with national guidelines for managing frail
patients with constipation by resident doctors.
Methodology: The QIP was conducted at Fairfield General Hospital in the frailty ward from March 2026 to
August 2026, employing the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) methodology. The objective was to improve
compliance with the national guidelines for the management of constipation in frail patients, focusing on
key gaps identified in the baseline audit, namely the pertinent abdominal and per rectal (PR) exam, review of
constipating medications, and first-line laxative prescribing.
Results: A baseline audit revealed an abdominal exam documentation rate of 33% (n=5); a review of
constipating medications was performed 26% (n=4) of the time, and appropriate first-line laxatives were
prescribed in 46% (n=7) of cases. Following this, targeted interventions such as ward-based teaching
sessions as per national guidelines, drop-in sessions, and a six-point, user-friendly, standardised checklist
were implemented over a period of two months. A retrospective cross-sectional study reviewing 15 case
notes revealed marked improvements across all audited parameters: abdominal exam documentation
improved to 86%, medication review to 80%, and first-line laxative prescribing to 80%.
Conclusion: Compliance with national standards in managing constipation in frail patients among newly
rotated residents can be improved through teaching sessions focused on national best practice guidelines.
Furthermore, the use of a user-friendly, standardised, and accessible checklist in our QIP was associated
with improved compliance with best practices and enhanced quality of care.
Categories:
 Nutrition, Geriatrics, Gastroenterology
Keywords:
 6-point checklist, constipation, frailty syndrome, laxatives, quality improvement project (qip)
Introduction
Constipation is a heterogeneous, symptom-based syndrome with facets of presentation such as infrequent
bowel motions or hard stools, difficulty passing stool, often with associated straining, and a sense of
incomplete emptying 
[1]
. Rome IV criteria require two or more of the following to diagnose
constipation: straining, lumpy or hard stools, sensation of incomplete evacuation and sensation of anorectal
obstruction or blockage in more than 25% of defecations, and fewer than three spontaneous bowel motions
in a week 
[2]
. However, in practice, particularly in the elderly, less frequent bowel motions from the
patient’s normal often make the diagnosis 
[3]
. Furthermore, in geriatric patients, constipation can present as
confusion, overflow diarrhoea, or urinary retention 
[3]
, which necessitates thorough assessment and prompt
management when these are identified. Constipation is quite common in frail patients although large scale
nationwide epidemiologic studies are scarce: a research on constipation in elderly, which enrolled 439
geriatric inpatients, 183 care home residents, and 78 visitors, of a geriatric day hospital showed a
constipation prevalence of 79% (n=347) in geriatric ward inpatients 
[4]
, while a study on the prevalence of
faecal impaction in nursing homes, which sampled 487 residents, revealed a 70.7% (n=486) prevalence of
constipation in care homes 
[5]
. It is a significant contributor to and sequelae of the five aspects of frailty
syndrome, touching on susceptibility to drug side effects, polypharmacy, decreased mobility, delirium,

urinary retention/incontinence, and falls 
[6,7]
. Hence, it is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in
frail patients, resulting in the above aspects of frailty syndrome and, in severe cases, syncopal episodes with
resulting coronary and cerebral ischaemia from excessive straining 
[8]
. To this end, prompt recognition
through a standardised approach and early initiation of management per national guidance are vital for
improving the quality of management of constipation and mitigating the above complications.
Frailty syndrome is a state of compromised physiologic reserve and functional decline due to multiple
factors such as ageing, co-morbidities, and functional impairment, leading to vulnerability to stress, which
otherwise is tolerable in a non-frail population and includes recognised facets of presentation such as falls,
delirium, immobility, incontinence, and susceptibility to drug side effects 
[7]
.
A frailty ward is a medical ward designed to deal with complex medical and end-of-life issues for patients
with frailty and significant comorbidity. Elderly patients are prone to developing constipation for the
following reasons: compromised physiologic reserve increasing susceptibility to drug side effects,
polypharmacy, decreased mobility, low oral intake, and compromised gastrointestinal function 
[9]
. Focusing
on dealing with complex medical issues in frail patients and the widespread prevalence of constipation in
elderly patients sometimes leads to a substandard approach to the management of constipation in frail
patients.
This quality improvement project (QIP) identified key gaps in the approach to frail patients with
constipation and the step-wise management in the frailty ward, devised interventions such as a six-point,
standardised checklist for residents, and demonstrated significant improvement in compliance with national
guidelines 
[3,10]
 following implementation, which later were embedded in the routine processes of
constipation management in the ward. 
Ward-based teaching sessions for resident doctors, informal drop-in sessions, and a six-point, user-friendly,
standardised, national guidelines-aligned checklist were implemented over a period of two months, which
led to the marked improvement.
Materials And Methods
Study design, period, and setting
This QIP employed a Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) methodology with the aim of improving the assessment
and management of constipation in resident doctors in line with national guidelines 
[10,11]
. A special focus
was placed on key gaps identified in the baseline audit, including pertinent abdominal and per rectal (PR)
exams, review of constipating medications, and first-line laxative prescribing for frail patients in the
geriatric ward. The primary objective of the project was to improve compliance with national guidelines
regarding the approach to elderly patients with constipation. Our secondary objective was to evaluate the
effectiveness of the interventions implemented, namely the checklist and teaching sessions. The project was
conducted in the frailty ward at Fairfield General Hospital (Bury, UK) from March 2026 to August 2026, with
the intervention implemented over a two-month period.
Two cycles of retrospective cross-sectional data collection were conducted, reviewing 15 randomly selected
patients with constipation in the frailty ward, using a standardised proforma to assess compliance with each
quality standard. Case notes were randomly selected using a random number generator from the list of
patients with a documented diagnosis of constipation during the study period. The study population
consisted of elderly medical patients (over the age of 65 years) diagnosed with constipation and admitted to
the geriatric ward at Fairfield General Hospital.
Quality standards
The following quality standards were established in accordance with National Institute for Health and Care
Excellence (NICE) guidelines: (i) Adults with constipation should have an assessment that includes a review
of diet and lifestyle, a medication review, and a physical examination 
[10]
. (ii) Adults with constipation
should be offered a first-line laxative appropriate for their clinical situation 
[11]
. The first-line laxative was
defined as an osmotic laxative (e.g., macrogol or lactulose) as per NICE guidance for adults with constipation
[11]
. (iii) Constipating medications should be identified and reviewed at each prescribing encounter 
[11]
.
PDSA
Plan
Our group of three resident doctors convened as part of the 'Plan' to discuss this important aspect of frailty
syndrome. We planned to conduct a baseline audit on parameters drawn from the national guidelines to
identify gaps, and agreed to design interventions in response to the key gaps identified. This was followed by
a baseline audit on 15 patients admitted to a frailty ward of 22 beds, utilising a standardised proforma
developed from the project’s quality standards in accordance with NICE guidance on the assessment and
management of constipation. This proforma included three vital areas: documentation (including the use of
 
2026 Yirdaw et al. Cureus 18(9): e116396. DOI 10.7759/cureus.116396
2
 of 
11
the Bristol Stool Chart 
[12]
 and bowel history documentation), clinical assessment (encompassing
abdominal exams and PR examinations when indicated and constipating medication review), and
management (covering provision of conservative advice and appropriate first-line laxative prescribing).
Randomised sampling through a random number generator from the list of patients with a documented
diagnosis of constipation in the geriatric ward was undertaken during the study period.
Do
This audit revealed key gaps as well as strengths in the management of constipation among elderly patients.
There was a 100% (n=15) rate of daily reviews and use of the Bristol Stool Chart, with an 86% (n=13) rate of
bowel history documentation, which was remarkable. However, there were significant gaps in compliance
with national guidelines: only 33% (n=5) of patients’ notes showed documentation of abdominal exam,
constipating medication review was done in only 26% (n=4) of patients, and appropriate first-line laxatives
were prescribed in 46% (n=7) of the cases.
Following this study, the team met to brainstorm ideas for interventions to improve performance, focusing
particularly on the identified key gap areas. A six-point, user-friendly, standardised checklist aligned with
British Geriatrics Society (BGS) best practice principles and NICE guidance for assessing and managing
constipation was designed, introduced to residents, and implemented for two months 
[10,13-15]
.
Additionally, two ward-based teaching sessions for residents working in the frailty ward were delivered, and
several drop-in sessions regarding the QIP, interventions, and further plans were communicated.
Study
As part of the 'Study', after a couple of months of implementing the interventions, a cross-sectional
retrospective data collection was conducted using the same standardised proforma as in the baseline audit.
This involved reviewing 15 case notes, which revealed marked improvements across all studied parameters.
Notably improved parameters included documentation of abdominal exams, which increased to 86% (n=13)
from 33% (n=5), first-line laxative prescribing, which rose to 80% (n=12) from 46% (n=7), and review of
constipating medications, which improved to 80% (n=12) from 26% (n=4).
Action
Subsequently, to complete the PDSA cycle, the aforementioned interventions, such as the checklist and
drop-in sessions, were embedded in the routine process of addressing constipation in the frailty ward. The
QIP was presented to the newly rotated resident doctors in the geriatric ward and at the hospital’s audit and
governance meeting, and the project was registered with the hospital’s QIP department.

Interventions
Two forms of interventions were implemented, which brought about the desired changes.
Firstly, a six-point, user-friendly, standardised checklist aligned with national guidelines was designed,
posted in the doctor’s office, and implemented during the two-month intervention period. This checklist
was created based on the main points highlighted in national guidance, particularly BGS best practice
principles and NICE guidelines, for the assessment and management of constipation 
[3,10,11,13-15]
, and it
was approved by the geriatricians supervising care in the frailty ward.
The checklist provided quick prompts in the form of questions to assess compliance with national guidelines
in the assessment and management of constipation. Accessibility was ensured by posting checklists on walls
facing doctors as they used ward computers and through drop-in sessions that reminded staff about the
checklist, its content, and where copies are posted on the wall.
Secondly, ward-based teaching sessions and informal drop-in sessions were delivered to resident doctors,
including newly rotated foundation year 1 (FY1) doctors. All resident doctors working in the geriatric ward
attended the two teaching sessions and several drop-in sessions that were planned in advance to ensure
attendance.
The six-point, standardised checklist implemented and embedded in the routine processes of the geriatric
ward is provided in Appendix A.
Strength and limitations
This project demonstrates strengths such as comprehensive coverage of multiple parameters, the use of a
standardised checklist, and successful improvement in process measures, making it a valuable piece of work.
However, limitations such as the small overall sample size (n=15 per cycle), the single-centre design limiting
generalisability, and the absence of checklist fidelity monitoring and sustainability data from further PDSA
cycles are worth acknowledging.
Results
The baseline audit conducted at the start of the project, which studied 15 case notes, revealed key gaps in
the quality standards of the project, such as abdominal exam documentation at 33% (n=5), constipating
medication review at 26% (n=4), and appropriate first-line medication prescribing at 46% (n=7).
Furthermore, conservative advice provision was low, at a rate of 26% (n=4), and digital rectal examination
(DRE) was performed in none of the three patients (0%) where it was indicated. DRE was considered

4

11
indicated in patients with suspected faecal impaction, rectal bleeding, or where a rectal cause of
constipation was suspected based on clinical assessment. Strengths identified from the first audit included a
100% (n=15) rate of Bristol Stool Chart use and daily patient reviews, with 86% (n=13) bowel history
documentation.

advice was provided in 46% (n=7) of cases, and appropriate first-line laxative prescribing improved to 80%
(n=12).

Discussion
Constipation is a significant cause of morbidity in frail patients and can lead to serious complications such
as delirium, falls, urinary retention, acute kidney injury, and, in severe cases, cerebral and coronary
ischaemia from episodes of syncope due to straining if not managed properly 
[6,7]
.
The emphasis on complex medical issues in patients with frailty, the high prevalence of constipation among
elderly inpatients, and the rotation of resident doctors contribute to substandard assessment and
management of constipation in frail patients in geriatric wards. The BGS best practice principles and NICE
guidelines outline the optimal management of constipation, including assessment, appropriate laxative
prescribing, and review of constipating medications.
The baseline audit revealed gaps in documentation, clinical assessment, and management according to
national guidelines. Key gaps identified included abdominal exam documentation at 33% (n=5), review of
constipating medications at 26% (n=4), and appropriate first-line prescribing at 46% (n=7).
Following the implementation of targeted interventions, significant improvement in all studied parameters
was demonstrated. For instance, abdominal exam documentation improved to 86% (n=13), appropriate first-
line laxative prescribing rose to 80% (n=12), and review of constipating medications improved to 80%
(n=12). DRE performance improved to 60% (n=3) from a null performance in the baseline audit. However,
the PR exam findings were based on a very small number of indicated cases (five indicated cases, of which
three were performed), limiting the generalizability of the improvement in this particular parameter. This
project was limited to a single PDSA cycle; further cycles would be valuable to assess the sustainability of
improvements and refine the checklist based on user feedback.
Several QIPs have been published regarding the improvement of assessment and management of
constipation 
[16-20]
. However, these projects focused on only a few parameters, while our QIP covered
about eight important parameters, touching on history documentation, relevant physical examination, and
comprehensive, standardised, and optimal management in line with the BGS best practice principles and
NICE guidelines.
One project conducted in a gastroenterology ward with the aim of improving the recognition of constipation
in predominantly elderly patients revealed a baseline Bristol Stool Chart use of 78.6% (n=19) and
documentation in clinical notes of 17.5% (n=4), which aligns with our baseline audit showing abdominal
exam documentation at 33% (n=5) but 100% Bristol Stool Chart usage (n=15) 
[16]
. In that project, after
 
2026 Yirdaw et al. Cureus 18(9): e116396. DOI 10.7759/cureus.116396
7
 of 
11
several cycles of interventions reminding resident doctors, the stool chart monitoring - as documented in
clinical notes - improved to 66.7% (n=16) from 17.5% (n=4) on the fourth PDSA cycle. Although this project
demonstrated a similar improvement in documentation of bowel history, our project addressed a wider
range of parameters, including relevant examinations, review of constipating medications, appropriate first-
line laxative prescribing, and provision of conservative advice.
Another QIP on constipation management in a geriatric ward concluded that constipation management for
elderly inpatients in that ward was inconsistent and suboptimal 
[17]
. This retrospective data study of 50
patients revealed that documentation of individual bowel habits was 6% (n=3), daily bowel charting was at
53% (n=26), and faecal impaction checked by DRE was at 8.3%. Additionally, there was a 50% (n=25) rate of
appropriate first-line laxative prescribing. The project proposed actions such as advocating for trust-based
guidelines, staff training, flagging patients in board rounds, and promoting timely PR exams; with this, the
project was closed. The results of this project mirror our baseline audit, which showed 0% for PR exams and
46% (n=7) for appropriate first-line laxative prescribing. However, daily bowel charting was quite low
compared to our project, which showed 100% (n=15) use of the Bristol Stool Chart. Moreover, this project
was halted with recommendations to improve identified problems, requiring interventions, and further
study to complete the cycle. However, the project is a remarkable piece of work, which could serve as a
foundation to complete the cycle.
One other project conducted in a geriatrics rehabilitation unit to improve the management of constipation
in elderly inpatients, using a care bundle with a special focus on laxatives such as first-line laxative use,
reducing pro re nata (PRN) laxatives, and using alternative high-fibre and fluid regimens for those who
didn’t tolerate laxatives, revealed improved compliance with hospital-based guidance on laxative
prescribing 
[18]
. This project fine-tuned its focus on laxatives for managing constipation, while our project
covered several parameters. However, this project completed two PDSA cycles and employed devised
prescription guidance, bi-weekly laxative rounds, and the use of a poster, making it valuable work. Similarly,
our project used ward-based teaching sessions, drop-in briefings, and a standardised checklist.
An additional QIP conducted at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust on laxative prescription
monitoring for constipated hospitalised adults identified gaps in appropriate laxative prescriptions and
monitoring. The project designed and introduced a constipation management algorithm and provided
education for staff, after which a marked improvement was noted 
[19]
. This project focused on rationalising
laxative prescriptions, reviewing laxatives once a week, and monitoring outcomes. The baseline study
showed a 17% (n=8) rate of medication reviews once a week, a 28% (n=13) rate of mentions of laxative
reviews at any point in the clinical notes, and a 52% (n=24) rate of documentation of rationale for
prescriptions. Following the interventions, after six months, the review of weekly medication reviews rose to
83% (n=60), the documentation of laxative reviews increased to 81% (n=58), and the documented diagnosis
of constipation reached 97% (n=70). Our project is similar in that a checklist was introduced as an
intervention, laxative prescriptions were audited, and sustained improvement was demonstrated. However,
this project contrasts in that it focused solely on monitoring laxatives and studied a larger sample.
Moreover, the QIP informed the trust's policy, where the introduced algorithm was incorporated.
The final project under consideration was a study conducted in the geriatric ward of Cambridge University
Teaching Hospitals, which focused on improving the recognition of constipation through better use of stool
charts 
[20]
. A baseline audit revealed a stool chart usage rate of 92% (n=25), good quality documentation of
bowel history at 76% (n=19), and a PR exam performance of 0%. Interventions included encouraging staff to
review charts, using smart links to access and import charts, and highlighting incomplete documentation to
ward staff. The third audit, after these interventions, showed stool chart usage of 93% (n=25), good quality
bowel motion tracking at 80% (n=20), and a persistent 0% rate for PR exams. Our project is broader in terms
of covering a wider array of parameters related to documentation, assessment, and management. The PR
exams in this project remained at nil, while our project saw an increase to 60% (n=3) pre-enema following
interventions. This project is useful in identifying both gaps and strengths within the geriatric ward at the
hospital.
This QIP, under discussion, is unique in that it covers a comprehensive set of eight parameters spanning
documentation, clinical examination, and management, whereas most previous QIPs focused on a narrower
set of outcomes, making this project both unique and valuable.
A research article titled "Understanding Constipation as a Geriatric Syndrome" argues for treating
constipation as a geriatric syndrome due to its high prevalence resulting from age-related changes and the
predisposing and precipitating factors in elderly patients 
[21]
. The article recommends inquiring about bowel
movements and constipation symptoms in geriatric patients using a stepwise standardised approach to
managing constipation in this cohort. This research aligns with our QIP in that it includes a literature review
highlighting the high prevalence of constipation in geriatric patients and implements interventions to
improve the approach to constipation in elderly patients according to national guidelines. The project
demonstrated significant improvements in managing constipation through teaching sessions and a
management checklist aligned with national guidelines.
 
2026 Yirdaw et al. Cureus 18(9): e116396. DOI 10.7759/cureus.116396
8
 of 
11
Another study on chronic constipation in the elderly provided a thorough update on evaluating and
managing constipation, detailing a stepwise approach in assessment and management for elderly patients
[2]
. This study emphasised the importance of thorough history-taking that focuses on alarm signs, past
medical history, and medication use. Additionally, examinations including perianal exam, digital rectal
exam, and relevant blood tests such as full blood count (FBC), renal, liver, and thyroid function tests, and
inflammatory markers were emphasised. While specialist physiologic tests such as evacuation proctography,
radiopaque markers, and anorectal manometry with wireless motility capsules are rarely needed in elderly
patients, their use is warranted in refractory cases or when there's suspicion of defecatory disorders
[2]
. Management, as per the study, begins with conservative measures in mild cases, which include increased
oral fluid intake, dietary fibre (starting at 5 grams and titrated up to 25-30 grams), and increased moderate
activity along with appropriate toilet education. The study promotes osmotic laxatives as the first line of
treatment, followed by stimulants if no adequate response is achieved 
[2]
. Lastly, biofeedback sessions were
shown to be effective in elderly patients with pelvic floor dyssynergia 
[2]
. This study aligns with national
guidelines and goes hand-in-hand with the QIP under discussion in that a stepwise approach to managing
constipation is emphasised.
A systematic review on managing constipation in the elderly evaluated 23 randomised controlled trials that
investigated the effectiveness and safety of laxatives in this patient cohort, making comparisons between
laxative use and placebo, among the laxatives within the same group and across different groups 
[22]
. Four
placebo-controlled trials on bulk-forming laxatives did not show a marked increase in bowel movements,
although transit time and stool consistency were demonstrated to improve 
[22]
. Furthermore, these trials
reviewed a limited number of cases, with two covering fewer than 10 patients.
Seven randomised controlled trials on osmotic laxatives were reviewed, four of which compared osmotics
with placebo and three of which contrasted different osmotic laxatives 
[22]
. In the placebo-controlled trials,
a significant increase in bowel movements, a decreased need for laxatives, and improved stool consistency
were demonstrated 
[22]
. Two studies comparing osmotic laxatives (lactulose vs. sorbitol and polyethylene
glycol (PEG) 4000 without and with electrolytes) revealed negligible differences in terms of stool consistency
or bowel movements 
[22]
. These findings concur with national guidelines recommending osmotic laxatives
as the first-line treatment for elderly patients and support the interventions of this project.
Conclusions
Emphasis on complex medical issues in frail patients, the high prevalence of constipation among elderly
inpatients, and the rotation of staffing in the geriatric ward could lead to suboptimal management of
constipation in this cohort. A baseline audit revealed inconsistent documentation and substandard
assessment and management of constipation in the geriatric ward. However, following a two-month period
of intervention that included teaching sessions and the introduction of a standardised checklist, a marked
improvement in the assessment and management of constipation was noted. Further PDSA cycles are
needed to assess the sustainability of these improvements beyond the initial two-month intervention
period. Embedding routine teaching sessions for newly rotated resident doctors and utilising a standardised
checklist aligned with national guidelines in the process of managing constipation is associated with the
improvement of overall assessment and management of constipation in frail patients admitted to
geriatric wards.

title: Performance of Ceramic Pot Filters with Colloidal Silver for Rural Water Treatment
summary: Performance of Ceramic Pot Filters with Colloidal Silver for Rural Water Treatment
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Household ceramic pot filters are promising for rural water treatment, but their performance depends on ceramic composition, pore-former content, and silver application.This study screened 20 physical filters fabricated from red or brown clay at five clay/sawdust ratios (82.5/17.5 to 72.5/27.5),with or without 300 mL of colloidal silver at 80 mg/L.Each filter treated three successive 3-L batches of the same composite rural water.These represented repeated measurements on a single filter rather than independent filter replicates.T1 (red clay, 17.5% sawdust, with silver) removed 81.13% of turbidity, 83.14% of viable mesophilic count (VMC), and 97.22% of fungi; T6 showed comparable performance.In all four clay-by-silver series, mean removal at 17.5% sawdust was greater than that at 27.5% for all three responses.VMC removal was higher in the presence of silver in all 10 matched formulation pairs (mean difference, 5.94 percentage points; median, 4.08; range, 0.26-17.92),whereas differences in turbidity and fungal removal were inconsistent.Because each treatment contained only one physical filter, these patterns are descriptive and do not estimate reproducible treatment effects.Total and thermotolerant coliforms were each not detected in 18 of the 20 filters under the applied conditions.The recorded direct-material subtotal was PEN 26.8-27.1 for filters with silver and PEN 2.8-3.1 for those without silver.In a separate first-filtrate pilot, silver was below the quantification limit of 0.007 mg/L.The 17.5% sawdust formulations require independent replication and long-term validation.

content:

In Gurnah, something irreversible happens to the migrant in going across waters, something in the register of a navigational confusion caused by the untranslatability of experiences between the two worlds. The bug in the existential compass is just as vague as it sounds. Let&s;s put it this way: the migrant knows that they are a stranger, but with some stretch and struggle, they might in time conjure up a somewhat functional, although fragile, affinity with the host society. All the while, they wonder if they have become irrelevant at ‘home’; and who wants to be treated like a foreigner by their kin? Belonging, after all, is a survival instinct, and if we are once beaten by one form of social alienation, it is only natural to be twice shy about throwing ourselves in the bosom of another community, even if it is the one that looks and sounds most like us. This vulnerability must be one of the reasons why out of Gurnah&s;s many characters who leave Zanzibar for English shores only one makes a return home.

summary: Silicon and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi alter biomass partitioning and water-use traits in drought-stressed maize (Zea mays)
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Silicon (Si) and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) have each been reported to improve drought tolerance in maize, yet their comparative effects on biomass allocation and plant water relations remain insufficiently understood. This study evaluated the effects of Si, AMF, and their combined application following a 7-day drought imposed at the vegetative growth stage. Leaf water-status traits were assessed immediately after drought, whereas morphological and biomass traits were evaluated following a 5-day recovery period after re-watering. Silicon significantly increased stem diameter (15.17 mm) and maintained the highest relative water content (88.33%), while AMF significantly increased leaf area (88.41 cm 2 ) and root dry weight (25.12 g). The combined Si + AMF treatment produced the greatest shoot dry weight (99.10 g), although root-to-shoot ratio, water saturation deficit, and water uptake capacity were not significantly affected. Principal component analysis explained 61.5% of the total variation and summarized associations among biomass- and water-related traits. Collectively, the results demonstrate that Si and AMF influenced different aspects of maize performance under drought, supporting their potential as resource-efficient approaches for improving maize production under water-limited conditions.

title: Victoria amazonica (Poepp.) Klotzsch (Amazon Water Lily)
source: Biodiversity and Conservation of Endemic Medicinal Plants
summary: Victoria amazonica (Poepp.) Klotzsch (Amazon Water Lily)
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Victoria amazonica (Poepp.) Klotzsch, also known as the Amazon water lily, is a typical aquatic plant native to the tropical Amazon and Orinoco River basins in South America. The species is known to be one of the most remarkable plant adaptations in an aquatic ecosystem due to its extremely large floating leaves, which can reach up to 3 m in diameter, and its unique thermogenic flowers. It belongs to the Nymphaeaceae family and thrives in the shallow, slowly moving waters of floodplain lakes, oxbow lakes, and riverbanks. This chapter exhaustively describes V. amazonica , including its taxonomy, morphological features, ecological functions, and cultural importance, with a special focus on the structural adaptations that enable its survival in dynamic aquatic environments. Leaf morphology is central to its local ecosystem performance, as it provides hiding spots for fauna and regulates water temperature, while the evolution of its flowers favors nocturnal pollination by beetles. Although its distribution is wide, V. amazonica faces various threats such as habitat loss, water pollution, and climate change, all of which undermine its long-term survival. The chapter further discusses both the traditional and modern applications of the plant in food, medicine, and cosmetics, as well as the socioeconomic impact the plant has on rural populations in the area, highlighting the necessity of conservation efforts to help the species survive in the wild for future generations.

title: Thematic Mapping for Landscape Analysis and Spatial Planning
summary: Thematic Mapping for Landscape Analysis and Spatial Planning
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Thematic cartography is a fundamental tool for quantitative analysis of ecological dynamics, environmental monitoring, and regional planning. The present contribution explores the increasing availability of geo-cartographic information and discusses its relevance in spatial policy analysis. By illustrating their structure, objectives, and applications, we specifically focused on European CORINE Land Cover (CLC) datasets and the Italian “Carta 48 della Natura” project, taken as representative of continental and national geo-spatial databases. The CLC initiative provides harmonized information on land-use and land cover at the continental level, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of territorial dynamics over time − including urbanization, loss of agricultural land, and changes in vegetation cover, among others. The “Carta della Natura” project – developed by a national authority involved in empirical research on environmental monitoring and surveillance – inte grates remote sensing methodologies, image interpretation, field surveys, and geographical analysis with the aim at producing multiscale maps of physiographic units and habitats. The chapter specifically highlights the central role of these operational tools in ecological planning, biodiversity protection, and the definition of spatial policies, through their use in defining environmental quality, landscape fragmentation, ecological sensitivity, and anthropogenic pressure. Finally, the latest innovations and developments in thematic cartography have been illustrated, being regarded not only as cartographic products, but also as a constantly evolving cognitive process.

title: Monitoring Climate—Forest Relationships: The Role of Ecological Networks
summary: Monitoring Climate—Forest Relationships: The Role of Ecological Networks
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

The present work analyses the relationship between climate and Italian forest ecosystems using the International Co-operative Programme on Assessment and Monitoring of Air Pollution Effects on Forests (ICP Forests) monitoring network − active since 1997. Using a historical series of meteorological data collected homogeneously in Italy, selected climatic variables of interest to forestry (such as temperature, precipitation, humidity, and wind) and their seasonal and inter-annual variability have been extensively examined in this contribution. The empirical analysis highlights relevant trends, including recurring patterns and climatic anomalies, with particular attention to 102 extreme events and their potential impact on ecosystems. Another section of our study is dedicated to the quantitative (continuous) assessment of water balance and soil water content at selected sites corresponding with gauging field stations. In brief, the results confirm the importance of continuous monitoring to understand the response of forests to climate change, and to support long-term ecological and physiological analysis of natural ecosystems. The work finally highlights the fundamental contribution of ICP Forests’ network to the detailed characterization of Italian forest (weather and climate) conditions and to the assessment of the future impacts of climate variability on natural habitats.

content:
