BACKGROUND: Practice Leadership is a subset of frontline management in accommodation services for people with intellectual disabilities. Its influence on staff use of Active Support is well established. This study explores Practice Leadership's role in ensuring safe as well as quality support. METHOD: A secondary analysis of qualitative data from a subset of 59 accommodation services that had both strong Practice Leadership and good Active Support, from a large Australian study. RESULTS: The characteristics of strong Practice Leadership mirror many that prevent harm in services: (i) Channelling organisational intent to direct support workers, (ii) Monitoring staff implementation of plans, policies and procedures, (iii) Assessing and improving staff competence, and (iv) Reinforcing a culture of person-centred practice that supports quality of life. CONCLUSION: Seeing Practice Leadership through the lens of safety widens its scope beyond staff use of Active Support to other facets of quality support associated with safe support.

title: Spatial–temporal variability of the Bua River’s physicochemical water quality: a DPSIR-based analysis
source: International Journal of River Basin Management
summary: Spatial–temporal variability of the Bua River’s physicochemical water quality: a DPSIR-based analysis
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Freshwater ecosystems are increasingly threatened by climate variability and catchment degradation, resulting in declining water quality and ecosystem resilience. We assessed spatial and seasonal variability in water quality along the Bua River, Malawi, and applied the Drivers–Pressures–State–Impact–Response (DPSIR) framework to identify degradation pathways and management responses. A stratified sampling design was used across upstream, midstream, and downstream sections during three distinct seasons. Downstream sections consistently exhibited poorer water quality, with turbidity reaching 17.17 ± 0.63 NTU, EC increasing to 183.00 ± 2.80 µS cm−1, ammonium concentrations reaching 120.14 ± 2.00 µg L−1, and chlorophyll-a increasing to 6.70 ± 0.70 µg L−1. Factorial ANOVA revealed significant seasonal effects (F₂,₅₂ = 21.84, p < 0.0001), site (F₂,₅₂ = 6.25, p = 0.0036), and water-quality parameters (F₁₃,₅₂ = 58.80, p < 0.0001). Elevated nutrient concentrations and sediment loads were associated with anthropogenic stressors. Our DPSIR linked these pressures to ecological degradation, declining fisheries productivity and increasing risks to water-dependent livelihoods. Our findings highlight the need for integrated catchment management, riparian restoration, climate-smart agriculture, and strengthened water-quality monitoring to support Malawi’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: Integration of transcriptome and metabolome analyses reveals the mechanism of high-quality formation in Salvia miltiorrhiza
summary: Integration of transcriptome and metabolome analyses reveals the mechanism of high-quality formation in Salvia miltiorrhiza
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Salvia miltiorrhiza is an important medicinal plant, and its medicinal value is largely associated with specialized metabolites such as tanshinones and salvianolic acids. However, systematic evaluation of high-performing candidate germplasms and the molecular features associated with favorable quality-related traits remains limited. Here, we established an integrated quality–efficiency evaluation framework to assess S. miltiorrhiza germplasms and explore transcriptome–metabolome associations potentially related to metabolite accumulation. Five cultivars (Danza No.1, Danza No.2, Jidan No.4, Danza No.5, and Anguo S. miltiorrhiza ) were evaluated by integrating phenotypic traits, quantitative determination of major active components, preliminary comparative enzyme-inhibition data, and non-targeted metabolite profiling. UHPLC–Q-Orbitrap-MS/MS annotated 95 constituents, and JD4 exhibited the most distinct metabolomic profile and the best overall performance in the integrated quality–efficiency evaluation, indicating it as a high-performing candidate germplasm. Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 2,851 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in JD4, which were significantly enriched in plant hormone signaling, MAPK signaling, and plant–pathogen interaction pathways. Integrated metabolome–transcriptome analysis identified significant associations between tanshinone-related metabolites and defense- or hormone-responsive genes. In particular, cryptotanshinone was negatively associated with the calcium signaling component CML, whereas tanshinone IIA showed positive associations with the transcription factors PIF4 and ABF, suggesting that defense- and hormone-related regulatory pathways may contribute to tanshinone accumulation in JD4. This study provides a multi-dimensional framework for evaluating S. miltiorrhiza germplasms by integrating anatomical traits, chemical composition, preliminary bioactivity screening, metabolomics, and transcriptomics. The results highlight JD4 as a promising candidate germplasm that warrants further field and functional validation under the present experimental conditions, and provide candidate metabolites, genes, and pathways for future functional validation and molecular breeding of S. miltiorrhiza .

title: Assessing Landscape Quality With Quali-quantitative Measures
summary: Assessing Landscape Quality With Quali-quantitative Measures
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Monitoring environmental quality and landscape characteristics has taken on a central role in land-use planning, natural resources, protected areas, and habitat conservation in general. Interest in these topics is shared by several disciplines, such as ecology, nature conservation, environmental sciences, forestry, economics, spatial planning, landscape architecture, and sociology, among others. For this reason, since the 1970s, many authors have developed methodologies to estimate the quality and naturalness of places, districts, and 16 regions based on land-use and soil consumption data. Two main approaches estimating environmental quality can be envisaged, namely based on ecosystem functions for human society (i.e. environmental value) or on the intrinsic value of ecosystems (i.e. naturalness). Use of these dimensions as proxies for environmental quality (both in the field of nature conservation and land-use planning) is a widely accepted concept.

summary: Evaluation of the impact of body mass index and mid-upper arm circumference on the quality of cardiopulmonary resuscitation
content:

Evaluation of the impact of body mass index and 
mid-upper arm circumference on the quality of 
cardiopulmonary resuscitation
Sinan Önder · İlter Ağaçkıran · Elif Öztürk İnce · Gülseren Ace · Bektaş Can Balkız · 
Bülent Erbil · Mehmet Ali Karaca
Received: 11 April 2025 / Accepted: 28 August 2026
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
High survival rates in cases of cardiac arrest can only be achieved through high-quality and effective chest 
compressions. The muscle strength and physical characteristics of the practitioners are among the factors that 
influence effective chest compressions. This study aims to investigate the relationship between the measure -
ment of mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), a surrogate anthropometric marker of muscle mass in the 
body, and the effectiveness of CPR. A total of 142 final-year medical students were selected as participants. 
The study examined the impact of the participants’ physical characteristics, body mass index (BMI), and 
MUAC measurements on CPR quality. Of the participants, 78 were male, and the rate of achieving appropri -
ate chest compression depth was found to be 99%. MUAC measurements of participants achieving appropriate 
compression depth ranged between 24 and 28 cm for women and 30–34 cm for men. While most participants 
with normal BMI achieved the ideal compression rate, no significant correlation was observed between BMI 
and CPR quality (n = 51, p = 0.812). Among women with a MUAC of 24 cm or more, 92.3% (n = 12) achieved 
appropriate chest compression depth, whereas this rate was 76.7% (n = 33) for men. Participants classified as 
underweight based on BMI had a compression success rate of 8% (n = 7), compared to 58% (n = 51) for those 
with normal BMI. In this study, CPR quality did not differ significantly by MUAC for both genders. Although 
participants within optimal MUAC ranges achieved adequate compression depth more frequently, these dif -
ferences were not statistically significant. Participants with a normal BMI were more successful in achieving 
the ideal compression rate. On the other hand, underweight participants could not maintain adequate chest 
compression depth.
Keywords Cardiopulmonary resuscitation · Mid-upper arm circumference · Body mass index

Introduction
International CPR guidelines emphasize the importance of high-quality chest compressions to improve survival 
rates1–3. Effective CPR can maximize coronary perfusion and the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) in 
patients1. For effective, uninterrupted, and prolonged chest compressions, it is recommended that practitioners 
position themselves perpendicular to the patient’s body and use their own body weight, thus preventing early 
muscle fatigue in the practitioner. Besides training and the application of quality CPR, the personal and physical 
characteristics of the rescuer also influence the effectiveness of CPR. Previous studies have noted that factors 
such as the rescuer’s weight, height, physical fitness, and muscle strength affect the quality of CPR. However, 
there are limited practitioner-based studies on CPR quality, and existing research is insufficient in this regard4–6.
With technological advancements, various devices have been developed to monitor and improve CPR quality. 
These include metronomes and feedback devices. CPR feedback devices analyze the quality of resuscitation by 
providing information on parameters such as compression rate, compression fraction, the ratio of adequate chest 
compressions, and appropriate chest recoil1.
While previous studies have demonstrated that higher body weight and BMI are positively associated with 
achieving adequate chest compression depth, BMI cannot differentiate between muscle and fat mass7. Mid-Upper 
Arm Circumference (MUAC) is a validated, well-established surrogate marker for appendicular skeletal muscle 
mass in both nutritional and clinical assessments8,9. Therefore, evaluating MUAC as a rapidly obtainable surro -
gate for muscle mass could offer new insights beyond BMI. Although a recent study has explored arm circumfer-
ence in relation to CPR10, comprehensive data combining BMI and MUAC to evaluate their distinct impacts on 
CPR quality remains scarce.
This study aims to investigate the impact of physiological parameters, including the gender, height, weight, 
mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and Body Mass Index (BMI) of chest compression practitioners, as well 
as their exercise habits, on the quality of chest compressions.
Methods
Study design
This prospective descriptive observational study was approved by the Non-Interventional Clinical Research Eth-
ics Committee of Hacettepe University, with approval number GO 21/1270, dated December 7, 2021, and deci -
sion number 2021/20-28. Consent was obtained from each participant in the study. In the study, training was 
conducted according to and evaluated according to the American Heart Association's Adult Advance Cardiac Life 
Support guidelines3.
Between May 1 and August 31, 2022, 6th-year medical students at Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine 
who agreed to participate were included in the study conducted at the Department of Emergency Medicine. A 
post-hoc power analysis indicated that the sample size provided sufficient statistical power to detect moderate 
effect sizes for the primary outcomes regarding BMI and MUAC. Participants performed uninterrupted chest 
compressions for 2 min on an adult PRESTAN CPR manikin, used for educational purposes, with a True CPR™ 
device (Physio-Control®, Redmond, WA, USA), also employed for training purposes.
Data on CPR quality obtained from the True CPR™ device, including chest compression depth, rate, count, 
compression fraction, and the percentage of compressions achieving proper chest recoil, were recorded in a study 
form for each volunteer. Chest compression fraction (CCF) was automatically calculated by the True CPR™ 
device's proprietary software, which continuously logs the exact duration of active chest compressions relative 
to the total 2-min scenario time.
Each participant’s height and weight were measured to calculate their BMI, and their MUAC was also measured.

BMI was calculated using the formula “BMI = kg/m2” and classified according to the criteria set by the World 
Health Organization11. MUAC measurements were taken by a single designated researcher using a standard -
ized measuring tape to minimize inter-rater variability. MUAC measurements were taken while participants 
were seated, with the forearm flexed at a 90-degree angle and resting on a table, focusing on the midpoint of the 
humerus bone. Additionally, participants’ age, gender, and exercise habits were recorded in the data form.
Inclusion criteria
To be eligible for the study, participants needed to:
 ● Be 6th-year students at Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine.
 ● Consent to participate in the study.
 ● Have attended the “Basic Life Support and Advanced Cardiac Life Support” course in the 5th-year Emergency 
Medicine curriculum.
 ● Have participated in the “Basic Life Support and Advanced Life Support Algorithms” course and its practical 
application in the 6th-year Emergency Medicine Internship program.
 ● Have observed or participated in cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the emergency department at least once.
Exclusion criteria
Exclusion criteria included:
 ● Failure to provide consent for participation.
 ● Having physical or chronic conditions that restrict physical activity.
Statistical analysis
All data were analyzed using SPSS Statistics 23 and Jamovi version 2.3.24.0, with a significance level set at 
p < 0.05. Categorical variables were presented as frequency (n) and percentage (%) and compared using χ 2 tests 
or Fisher’s exact test as appropriate. Normally distributed data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), 
while non-normally distributed data were presented as median (IQR). Comparisons between two groups were 
made using the Student’s t-test or Mann–Whitney U test, as appropriate.
Results
Between May 1 and August 31, 2022, a total of 142 medical students participating in their emergency medicine 
internship at Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine were included in the study. Of the 142 participants, 54.9% 
(n = 78) were male. The median age of the participants was 24 years (IQR: 2). The average height was 173 cm 
(SD ± 10.2; minimum 150 cm, maximum 200 cm). The median weight was 70.5 kg (IQR: 26), the median BMI 
was 23.2 kg/m2 (IQR: 4.95), and the median MUAC was 30 cm (IQR: 7). The mean compression rate was 104 
compressions per minute (range: 79–135), and the compression fraction was calculated as 100%. Since compres-
sion fraction was 100% across all groups, it was not included in statistical analyses. The median percentage of 
adequate chest compressions was 99% (IQR: 8), and the median rate of adequate chest recoil was 88.5% (IQR: 
43.5) (Table 1).
Additionally, when the participants’ physical characteristics were examined, those in the group achieving the 
ideal compression rate had an average height of 174 cm, median weight of 72.5 kg, median BMI of 23.4 kg/m2, 
and median MUAC of 30 cm. None of these physical characteristics yielded a statistically significant difference

between those who achieved the ideal compression rate and those who did not (Table 2). No significant correla-
tion was found between compression rate and variables such as height, age, weight, BMI, MUAC, or weekly 
exercise time (Table 3).
When the impact of BMI on achieving the ideal compression rate was examined, 58% (n = 51) of those who 
achieved the ideal compression rate had a normal BMI, 27.3% (n = 24) were overweight, 8% (n = 7) were under-
weight, and 6.8% (n = 6) were obese. No statistically significant difference was found among these groups based 
on BMI classification (p = 0.812) (Table 4).

For women, the MUAC of those who achieved adequate compression depth (5–6 cm) ranged from 24 to 
28 cm. Based on MUAC measurements, female participants were divided into three groups. Among women 
with MUAC < 24 cm, the proportion achieving adequate compression depth was 7.7%, compared to 84.6% in the 
24–28 cm group and 7.7% in the > 28 cm group. Although the group with MUAC measurements between 24 and 
28 cm was the most successful in achieving adequate compression depth, no statistically significant difference 
was observed among the groups (p = 0.410) (Table 5).
For men, the MUAC of those who achieved adequate compression depth (5–6 cm) ranged from 30 to 34 cm. 
Among men with MUAC < 30 cm, the proportion achieving adequate compression depth was 23.3%, compared 
to 53.5% in the 30–34 cm group and 23.3% in the > 34 cm group. Although the group with MUAC measurements 
between 30 and 34 cm was the most successful in achieving adequate compression depth, no statistically signifi-
cant difference was observed among the groups (p = 0.499) (Table 6).
Discussion
The performance of effective chest compressions has been recognized as a key determinant of successful out -
comes in cardiac arrest for over 40 years12. Both the American Heart Association (AHA) and the European 
Resuscitation Council (ERC) emphasize the importance of high-quality chest compressions as the cornerstone of 
resuscitation care1,2. In this study, the effects of BMI and MUAC on chest compression quality were investigated 
within the framework of the AHA’s core criteria.
It has been shown in earlier research that the mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a reliable indicator 
of muscle mass in the body 8,13. Recent studies have demonstrated a positive correlation between arm muscle 
thickness and overall muscle mass14,15. Since MUAC is practical and does not require specialized equipment, it 
is highly accessible. Aygun et al.10 reported significant positive correlations between maximum biceps circumfer-
ence and both compression quality and overall CPR quality, whereas no significant association between MUAC 
and compression depth was observed in our cohort; this discrepancy may reflect differences in anthropometric 
measurement methods and participant characteristics. However, few studies have examined the specific effect of 
MUAC on CPR performance, making this study one of the rarely to evaluate MUAC in conjunction with BMI as 
a determinant of CPR quality.

In our study, the average MUAC was found to be 26 cm in women and 32.5 cm in men. The highest proportion 
of adequate compression depth was observed in participants with MUAC values of 24–28 cm among women and 
30–34 cm among men; however, these differences were not statistically significant. Although participants within 
these specific MUAC ranges achieved higher rates of adequate depth, the study found no significant correlation 
between MUAC and the ability to achieve the ideal compression rate or adequate compression depth for either 
gender (p = 0.410 for women, p = 0.499 for men). Conversely, participants who achieved adequate chest recoil 
had specific MUAC ranges, with women being more successful in achieving complete chest recoil during CPR 
compared to men.
When examining CPR quality indicators by gender, this study found that both genders had similar compression 
rates. However, the percentage of compressions performed at an adequate depth (5–6 cm) was 96% for women 
and 100% for men, with men achieving higher rates of adequate compression depth. Previous studies by Ok et 
al., Kim et al., Zhang et al., Mayrand et al., and Russo et al. have similarly reported better compression depth 
performance in men6,16–19. According to these findings, female participants tend to perform faster but shallower 
chest compressions compared to their male counterparts. Consistent with the literature, our study also found that 
male participants achieved higher rates of adequate compression depth, likely due to their greater muscle mass. 
Muscle size and overall CPR performance can be influenced by various potential confounding factors, including 
training history, sex, age, and nutritional status. Although we focused on MUAC, it is essential to recognize that 
repeated CPR training may build muscle memory and technique that can compensate for differences in baseline 
muscle mass.
When examining the relationship between BMI and adequate compression depth, a weak positive correlation 
was found. Mayrand et al. reported a positive correlation between chest compression depth and increases in 
weight and height19. On the other hand, Ock et al. found no significant relationship between adequate compression 
depth and variables such as gender, height, or weight 20. Krikščionaitienė et al. found that participants classified 
as underweight were less likely to perform adequate chest compressions 21. Sánchez et al. noted that individuals 
with a BMI ≥ 23 kg/m2 maintained an adequate compression depth for 2 min, while those with a BMI < 23 kg/m2 
performed effectively only 80% of the time in the first minute, dropping to 30% by the second minute 22. Simi-
larly, Wang et al. found that individuals with above-average BMI (mean BMI 21.6 ± 2.3 kg/m2) performed better 
in CPR quality parameters23. Oh et al. showed that rescuers with higher BMI were more successful in achieving 
adequate compression depth24. Similarly, Eyupoglu et al. 7 found that participants who performed optimal CPR 
had significantly higher BMI values than those with suboptimal CPR, while BMI was not significantly associated 
with CPR performance in our study, possibly due to differences in study populations, training backgrounds, and 
CPR assessment protocols.
The general conclusion from previous studies is that anthropometric variables like height and weight can influ-
ence chest compression quality to some extent24–26. Higher BMI increases the likelihood of success in achieving 
adequate compression depth, but it may inversely affect chest recoil rates. Additionally, the greater muscle mass 
in men contributes to higher rates of adequate compression. Conversely, individuals with lower BMI face greater 
challenges in achieving adequate chest compression depth on CPR manikins27,28. Although previous studies have 
suggested that gender and BMI may influence CPR performance, our findings did not demonstrate statistically 
significant associations between BMI or MUAC and the CPR quality parameters evaluated.
Limitations
This study has several limitations. First, the single-center design and the specific cohort of 6th-year medical stu-
dents limit generalizability. By the time students reach the sixth year, they have already received BLS training 
in their fifth year; this prior exposure and repeated training likely homogenized their skill levels, which could 
have masked the isolated impact of physical characteristics like MUAC on CPR quality. Although quantitative 
CPR quality data from their 5th-year training were not recorded, all participants had successfully passed their

practical and theoretical internship examinations, ensuring a uniform baseline level of competence. Second, the 
2-min CPR sessions on a manikin cannot fully evaluate the "real" quality of CPR at the scene, as a brief simula-
tion fails to replicate the physical fatigue and dynamic challenges of a prolonged clinical cardiac arrest scenario. 
Furthermore, BMI cannot differentiate between muscle mass and fat mass, and the relatively narrow range of 
MUAC within our specific, young cohort of medical students may have limited our ability to detect statistically 
significant differences.
Conclusion
In conclusion, this study found no statistically significant difference in CPR quality based on MUAC for both 
genders. While an increase in MUAC showed a tendency towards better compression depth, it did not reach 
statistical significance. In contrast, higher MUAC was associated with lower rates of adequate chest recoil. Fur -
thermore, CPR practitioners with a normal BMI were more successful in achieving the ideal compression rate, 
while underweight practitioners struggled to perform adequate chest compressions.

source: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

A family relationship involves interaction and emotional bond between all members in a family. It usually involves living under one roof, communicating, taking care of oneself, solving challenges, continuing family traditions and giving each member a sense of belonging. Happiness is an emotional state of well-being, narrowly defined as good things that happen to a person at a given moment, or more broadly, a positive evaluation of his life and achievements, i.e. a subjective feeling. Quality of Life as the subjective evaluation of one's perception of their reality relative to their goals as observed through the lens of the culture and value system. 150 young adults of age ranging from 17 to 23 were selected by using Convenience Sampling method. The scales used were Brief Family Relationship scale (1994) by Ting Fok C C. et.al, Subjective Happiness Scale (1999) by Lyubomirsky, S. and Lepper, H.S. and Quality of Life Scale (2003) by Burchkardt, C.S and Anderson, K.L. Pearson correlation, independent sample t test and Multivariate Analysis of Variance were used to analyse the data. Results showed that Family relationship, Subjective happiness and Quality of life have significant relationship. Also, it was found that there is no significant difference between Family relationship, Subjective happiness and Quality of life based on gender and birth order.

Those who tire easily of saltwater struggle with Abdulrazak Gurnah&s;s writing too. Not that the briny matter is visible everywhere in Gurnah necessarily; it is easy, in fact, to lose sight of it in the compulsive meanders of his raconteurs. But the dampness follows us around every bend, muddies the dust of the East African interior and the concrete of urban England on every page, until it errs its way back into colonial and migrational environments. The saltwater builds houses, fills up rooms and exposes its furniture to mould, evokes and erodes memories of the slave trade, drifts the migrant across the seas and enters their worst nightmares in the pang of mob violence, like a mirage that strangles the horizon of arrival. It is, maybe, for this ubiquitousness that water lingers on as the one unreadable element in Gurnah&s;s imagination. This book follows this somewhat counterintuitive logic, for it aims to de-emphasise a state of alterity in Abdulrazak Gurnah&s;s writing as part of the Indian Ocean&s;s cultural politics and instead approach his literary geographies as sites of material porosity, where history is understood in the dynamic interface of human and nonhuman matters. The rationale of this project is to untie literary analysis from a predictable system of meaning-making of the Indian Ocean as if it is a series of material and cultural codes somewhere out there. Gurnah&s;s work helps achieve this liquescent critique by weaving oceanic geopolitics with something closest to a liquid style of storytelling and a solvent imagination. During a prolific literary career that spans more than three decades and eleven novels, Gurnah has maintained an abiding interest in the imbrication of littoral and land zones and the effect of proliferation of biopolitical technologies associated with various iterations of colonial and postcolonial bordering, including partitioning, arbitrary detention, deportation and expulsion. The continuum of coasts and interiors in Gurnah&s;s work undermines the racist-military imaginary that conceived of coasts as places of civilisation, however secondary to European culture, and the interior as the deep, dark heart of the African continent.

title: Associations of physical activity, dietary quality, and their changes with all-cause mortality in older Chinese adults: a prospective study
summary: Associations of physical activity, dietary quality, and their changes with all-cause mortality in older Chinese adults: a prospective study
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Physical activity (PA) and dietary quality are important modifiable behaviors in later life, but evidence on the association between their changes and all-cause mortality remains limited, particularly among older Chinese adults. We examined the associations of PA, dietary quality, and their joint changes over time with all-cause mortality. This study included 11,528 older adults aged ≥ 65 years from the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (2002–2018). Physical activity (PA) was assessed using self-reported activity frequency, and dietary quality was evaluated using the Simplified Healthy Eating Index (SHE) and Dietary Diversity Score (DDS). Separate exposure measures included baseline levels and annualized changes in PA, SHE, and DDS. Joint changes in PA and dietary quality were assessed using 16 prespecified patterns derived from two assessments. In a secondary analysis, group-based multi-trajectory modeling (GBMTM) identified joint trajectories of PA and dietary quality among 6,008 participants with at least three assessments. Multivariable Cox regression models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all-cause mortality. During 69,288 person-years of follow-up (median follow-up of 6 years), 7,168 participants died. Each 1-point/year increase in ∆PA, ∆SHE, and ∆DDS was associated with lower all-cause mortality risk, with HRs of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.76–0.80), 0.95 (95% CI: 0.92–0.97), and 0.91 (95% CI: 0.88–0.95), respectively. Among the joint change patterns, improvement in either behavior was generally associated with a lower mortality hazard than persistently low levels of both. Persistently high PA and dietary quality were associated with the lowest hazards in the PA-SHE and PA-DDS analyses (HRs, 0.55–0.57; both P < 0.01). GBMTM showed directionally consistent associations. No significant multiplicative or additive interaction between PA and diet quality was observed. These findings suggested that sustained high PA and diet quality in were associated with reduced all-cause mortality risk among Chinese adults aged 65 years and older, highlighting the importance of maintaining regular PA and healthy dietary habits for extending lifespan.

Background: Unsafe abortion remains an important public health concern in Nigeria, particularly among adolescent girls and young women living in underserved communities. This study assessed experiences of self-managed medication abortion delivered through trained clinical and non-clinical providers and examined perceived quality of care. Methods: Implementation research was conducted among 510 adolescent girls and young women aged 15 to 30 years who accessed medication abortion in selected urban slums of the Federal Capital Territory and Nasarawa State. Participants completed a semi-structured exit questionnaire, and descriptive statistics were used for analysis. In addition, 120 clinical and non-clinical providers underwent pre- and post-training assessment, including assessment of attitudes toward abortion. Results: Participants had a mean age of 24.7 years. Contraceptive use following medication abortion reached 83.2%, while 87.2% of respondents had a positive abortion-perception score. Participants generally reported favourable experiences of confidentiality, respectful treatment, counselling, medication information, and referral support. Mean satisfaction with services was 9.2 out of 10. Provider assessments also indicated improvements in abortion-related knowledge and attitudes following training. Conclusion: The findings suggest that a community-based model involving trained clinical and non-clinical providers is feasible and acceptable for expanding access to medication abortion and related reproductive health services in underserved communities. Further evaluation during scale-up would help establish effectiveness and sustainability.

If water can make its way in and out of the sovereign imaginary and its primitive technology, if it can wet the map&s;s function as the most abstract construct in political geography, could it be that it carries the agency to dampen conditions of (post-)colonial life too? Could we conceive a material consistency in technologies that curtail access to air for the Black migrant, an element to disrupt the human lung&s;s primary function to inhale oxygen? As I was reading Gurnah&s;s 1980s novels, Pilgrims Way (1988) and Dottie (1990) , I felt a very subtle change in my breathing pattern that I had not noticed before, almost as imperceptible as breathing itself, but I had a hard time placing it in the order of an empathic response. It was not that I was choking for Gurnah&s;s characters, or that I had identified with the migrant, drowning once in water and once in the socio-bureaucratic antagonisms long after arriving on land; it felt more like the reading body was attuning itself to the gasping for air in the confinement of possibilities of flourishing after the ship docks.

summary: Under-water ignition and combustion of PDMS processed Al/CuO nanoparticle composite
content:

Under-water ignition and combustion of PDMS 
processed Al/CuO nanoparticle composite
Z. B. Wang · A. Q. Wang · J. Ehling  · C. J. MacRobbie · S. Kim · L. Saini · S. Deng  · 
J. Z. Wen  · M. Y . Shen
Received: 15 April 2026 / Accepted: 24 August 2026
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
This study investigates the fabrication and performance of hydrophobic nanothermite powders prepared by 
combining liquid polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) prepolymers with thermite powders in a dispersion medium. 
The resulting composite remained dry when submerged underwater and could be ignited by laser irradiation. 
High-speed imaging measurements showed an ignition delay of 2.3 ms under underwater conditions. Finite-
element simulations based on a two-phase flow model revealed rapid cooling and condensation of water vapor 
during ignition. Preliminary analysis of the bubble composition suggests the evolution of gaseous products 
from the thermite reactions. These results demonstrate the feasibility of underwater laser ignition of ther -
mite–PDMS composites and provide insights into the complex physical and chemical processes involved in 
underwater combustion.
Keywords Thermite reactions · Hydrophobic nanothermite · PDMS · Contact angle · Underwater 
combustion · Heat transport · Laser-induced ignition
Introduction
Thermite formulations represent a category of highly energetic materials with characteristic exothermic reac -
tions, generating substantial heat upon ignition. Nanothermite refers to a solid mixture of nano-sized reactive 
particles. These compositions are commonly referred to as metastable intermolecular composites, denoting their 
distinctive reactive properties1. The resulting high temperatures, combined with their ease of use and portabil -
ity, have earned thermite great interest across various applications, including propulsion systems, controlled 
demolitions, welding and metal cutting, and firework displays. An easy way to initiate and sustain underwater 
combustion could offer significant potential for various marine and aquatic applications, including welding 2,3, 
cutting, and propulsion. However, the hydrophilic nature of aluminum 4 and copper oxide5 causes wetting when 
submerged in water, leading to heat loss that hinders ignition and flame propagation. Consequently, research in 
underwater combustion is limited, with a lack of understanding of reaction propagation and energy release from 
nanothermite reactions underwater.
Article in Press
Scientific Reports
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68857-0
They are most commonly composed of metal powder as a reducing agent and an oxidizer such as metal oxides, 
while fluoropolymers6 or iodine oxides7 can also be used. In this study, aluminum and copper oxide are used, and 
the reaction can be described as:
 2Al + 3CuO → Al2O3 + 3Cu (1)
The initiation of thermite combustion typically requires a high-temperature heat source, such as spark or flame. 
Once activated, the reaction between the metal powder and metal oxide can reach temperature up to 2843 K for 
Al/CuO composites8,9. This characteristic imparts thermite with remarkable effectiveness as a potent heat source.
The aluminum thermite system has been well studied, revealing two main modes of aluminum oxidation: one 
occurring in the condensed phase, where oxygen ions traverse the Al/CuO interface, and the other in the gas 
phase, involving the dissociation of CuO before O2 gas engages with aluminum, resembling the oxidation process 
in an oxygen-rich environment10. Upon ignition of the Al/CuO mixture, the flame propagates through mass and 
heat transfer processes such as thermal conduction and mass convection. Experimental observations using electri-
cally heated nanothermite coatings have indicated that CuO decomposition precedes ignition when the heating 
rate exceeds 2,000 K/s11.
Additionally, lightly packed Al/CuO powders were observed to have three modes of combustion with increas-
ing surrounding inert gas pressure, with combustion velocity decreasing from 1,000 to 2 m/s 12. Convection 
dominates at low pressures, and thermal conduction dominants at high pressures, suggesting a gas-solid reaction 
mechanism13.
In addition to these mechanisms, when the particle sizes drop to the nanoscale, nanothermites behave slightly 
differently from traditional ones, as the thickness of the oxidation layer on the aluminum powder can no longer 
be neglected, forming a shell of alumina, which not only reduces the effective aluminum weight fraction, but 
also inhibits the reaction. At this scale, Al/CuO nanothermite can also react through reactive sintering 14, where 
reaction initiation occurs at the Al/CuO interface, and capillary forces sustain the process by delivering unreacted 
material to the reaction site. Reactive sintering occurs much faster than the burning time, typically within 10 µs.
Nevertheless, efforts on underwater combustion have been made. Meir et al. initiated combustion in a naturally 
hydrophobic iron thermite using microwaves. The sample was confined underwater within a bubble by a magnet 
using the bubble-marble effect15. Yu et al. employed a different approach by igniting superhydrophobic Co 3O4/
Al core-shell nano-wires with a nanosecond Nd/YAG laser. The fabrication involved vacuum-coating aluminum 
onto Co3O4 nanowires, before applying a hydrophobic fluoroalkylsilane layer. While these pioneering methods 
show promise, they exhibit limitations, the iron thermite is not easily generalized to other components, and the 
nanowires involve a complicated fabrication that is slow and expensive and are limited to two-dimensional 
structures.
This paper presents a simple method to achieve underwater combustion of thermites by introducing a novel 
approach for crafting hydrophobic nanothermite powders. The sample is made by mixing liquid PDMS prepoly-
mers with thermite powders within a dispersion liquid. The resultant composite remained dry when submerged 
underwater and could be readily ignited by laser irradiation. Furthermore, the concept of creating a hydrophobic 
coating using pre-curing polymers could be applied to materials beyond CuO/Al thermite or PDMS.
Beyond demonstrating underwater ignition and combustion, this research investigates the mechanisms in Al/
CuO nanothermite when immersed underwater with PDMS as an additional reagent, to deepen the understanding 
of heat dissipation channels, water phase change with rapid heating, and potential gas generation.

Sample preparation and characterization
To prepare a thermite sample with an equivalence ratio of 1(ER = 1), 0.8 g CuO and 0.27 g Al nano-powder 
(~ 50 nm diameter, SkySpring Nanomaterials, Inc.) were used. The excess aluminum compensates for the oxi -
dation layer on the Al nano-powders. The prepolymer and catalyst (Dow Corning Sylgard 184 kit) were mixed 
thoroughly at 10:1 mass ratio. The powders and about 60 mg of the prepolymer were added to a beaker followed 
by the addition of approximately 5 ml acetone to fully immerse the powders. The mixture was ultrasonicated 
and thoroughly mixed then dried and cured for 2 days in a wide container under well-ventilated conditions. The 
sample dried and naturally cracked into ~ 3 mm pieces.
The SEM images were taken by a JEOL JSM 7401 F unit and the results are shown in Fig. 1. The raw thermite 
sample is presented in Fig. 1a, while the 5% PDMS composite is shown in Fig. 1b. Compared to the raw ther -
mite sample, the morphology does not change significantly, although the size of the particles may have increased 
slightly. If the PDMS is assumed to be evenly coated on each particle, the thickness is estimated to be less than 
2 nm for a 5% PDMS mass ratio.
By submerging the sample with 5% PDMS ratio in 1% hydrochloric (HCl) acid for several days, the acid slowly 
dissolves the CuO and Al particles, leaving behind the PDMS framework that binds these nanoparticles, and its 
SEM image is shown in Fig. 1f. The spherical cavities visible in the green box in Fig. 1f suggest that PDMS acts 
as a binding agent, clustering the nanoparticles into distinct clumps rather than uniformly coating each individual 
particle. This indicates that the CuO/Al nanoparticles are still in contact with each other, and existing combustion 
mechanism, such as reactive sintering may still be valid with the introduction of the PDMS coating. The smaller 
bright spots within the green box in Fig. 1f are sputter-coated gold particles for better imaging.
The coated sample exhibits visual similarity to the original sample, and the evaluation of its hydrophobic -
ity was conducted through contact angle measurements 16. Upon gently pressing the powder into a 5-mm flake, 
the contact angle is measured to be approximately 150° for an 11.7% PDMS mass ratio, as illustrated in Fig. 2. 
This value is greater than the typical contact angle of PDMS, which is around 110° 17. Sabbah et al. have previ -
ously reported an increase in the contact angle for PDMS with wrinkles, attributed to surface roughness 18. The 
observed superhydrophobic effect in our study can be explained by the surface roughness induced by the thermite 
nanoparticles. Li et al. have also documented the fabrication of a superhydrophobic surface by coating PDMS on 
aluminum, aligning with the observed hydrophobic behavior in our coated thermite sample19.
The reported values correspond to static contact angles measured under ambient conditions. Dynamic contact 
angles (advancing/receding) and hysteresis were not measured, but are expected to influence wetting transitions 
and long-term stability of the hydrophobic state, as discussed by Butt et al. 20. These effects will be investigated 
in future work.
The optical reflection spectra (250–2500 nm) of Al nanoparticles, CuO nanoparticles, and their composite 
mixtures were measured using a UV–Vis–NIR spectrophotometer equipped with an integrating sphere attach -
ment, designed specifically for rough pellet surfaces. Kramers–Kronig (KK) analysis typically assumes specular 
reflectance at a well-defined interface, such as the surface of a bulk solid. Nevertheless, it has been successfully 
applied to porous and nanostructured films, where the surfaces are rough, but the reflectance remains predomi -
nantly specular. Using KK analysis, we obtained the corresponding extinction spectra and found that the extinc-
tion coefficient of the Al–CuO nanocomposite is lower than the value predicted by a simple linear combination 
of the individual components. Furthermore, the characteristic absorption bands in the spectra shift to lower ener-
gies relative to those of the individual components [support data]. These spectral changes suggest that the close 
contact between Al and CuO nanoparticles influences the optical response of the composite. However, the optical 
measurements alone do not provide direct evidence of electronic coupling, charge transfer, or carrier-mediated 
interactions.

Experiments and results
Experimental setup and ignition conditions
As shown in Fig. 3, a piece of the flake (about 3 mg) was placed into a container before water was added. The 
sample was then placed in a combustion chamber and a 5 W continuous laser with 532 nm wavelength was used 
to ignite the sample. The laser spot diameter was approximately 200 μm, corresponding to a power density of 
approximately 1.6 × 10 4 W/cm
2
. The 532 nm wavelength was chosen due to the strong absorption by CuO and the 
Al/CuO composite, enabling efficient photothermal heating and rapid ignition. A function generator triggered the 
laser and the camera simultaneously.
To avoid ambiguity, the definitions of ignition and combustion used in this study are clarified as follows. 
Ignition is defined as the onset of a self-sustained exothermic reaction, identified by a sudden increase in emis -
sion intensity together with rapid gas generation. Combustion refers to the subsequent sustained reaction phase

flake was placed in a container 
and water was added slowly. The 
laser and the camera were triggered 
simultaneously when the reaction 
started in the combustion chamber.
 
Fig. 2 The PDMS coating can make the thermite super-hydrophobic. Thermite with 11.7% PDMS ratio has a contact angle 
of 148.5° ± 4.7°.

involving continued heat release and product formation. It should be noted that bubble formation alone is not 
considered sufficient evidence of ignition but is instead interpreted in conjunction with optical/emission signa -
tures observed in high-speed imaging.
Ignition behavior and delay time
Selected frames from the high-speed video are shown in Fig. 4. The complete video is provided in the Support -
ing Information. Figure 4b, c show that ignition occurred about 2.2 ms after the laser onset, delivering 11 mJ 
of energy to the sample. This is comparable to another experiment using a 1040 nm, 100-fs pulsed laser with a 
10-MHz repetition rate and 4 W average power, which also ignited the sample in 2 ms. At a lower equivalence 
ratio (ER = 0.6), insufficient fuel significantly delayed the ignition to around 30 ms for both the green laser and 
the infrared laser. This trend is consistent with previous studies on Al/CuO nanothermites, where fuel-lean mix-
tures exhibit longer ignition delays compared to fuel-rich compositions due to reduced heat release and slower 
reaction kinetics. Additionally, ignition delay is known to strongly depend on equivalence ratio, with lean mix -
tures generally increasing ignition delay because of reduced reactive species concentration and slower chain-
branching processes1.
Bubble growth and dynamic evolution
To better analyze the reaction, Fig. 5 illustrates the temporal evolution of the bubble’s size, where the horizontal 
size is indicated by the dashed arrow in Fig. 4g, and the vertical size is indicated by the solid arrow in Fig. 4h.
The bubble first appeared at 2.3 ms, as shown in Fig. 4c, initiating a slow-expansion stage at a speed of about 
0.29 m/s, forming a 5-mm bubble by 5.3 ms, as shown in Fig. 4e. The bubble then expanded rapidly and reached a 
Fig. 4 High-speed images of the underwater ignition. Time in milliseconds after the laser onset is labeled. The horizontal size 
is indicated by the dashed arrow, and the vertical size is indicated by the solid arrow.

diameter of 20 mm at a rate of 1.54 m/s. As discussed later, this slow expansion stage may be attributed to PDMS 
decomposition and vaporization while the fast expansion stage may be driven by the thermite reaction.
Following this fast-expanding phase, the bubble entered a pulsing stage characterized by size oscillations with 
a decelerating expansion, followed by fragmentation into smaller bubbles at the surface before completely col -
lapsing. A more detailed discussion of this bubble generation process will be provided in the later discussion.
After the expansion stage, the bubble entered a pulsation stage where its volume oscillates around a baseline, 
as shown in Fig. 5 from 10 ms to about 25 ms. The oscillation frequency was determined to be approximately 
600 Hz, which will be discussed later.

Analysis and discussion
Role of PDMS in underwater ignition
The role of PDMS in the present system is multifaceted. Experimentally, its primary function is to provide a 
hydrophobic coating that facilitates underwater ignition by reducing direct contact between water and the ther -
mite particles. However, additional effects may also contribute, including thermal insulation, interfacial modifi -
cation, and possible gas generation during decomposition. The relative importance of these mechanisms cannot 
be resolved based on the current data, and their contributions are coupled under the transient high-temperature 
conditions of ignition. A more detailed understanding of the role of the polymer coating would require systematic 
studies, such as comparisons with non-reactive hydrophobic coatings, systematic variations in coating thickness 
and composition, and direct characterization of thermal and gas-generation behavior. These investigations are 
beyond the scope of the present work and will be addressed in future studies.
Bubble dynamics modeling
During the nanothermite reaction, the initial nanoparticles are rapidly transformed into Al₂O₃ and Cu products, 
which are generated in a highly transient and expanding environment. A significant portion of these particles is 
entrained within the bubble or concentrated near its interface rather than uniformly dispersed in the surrounding 
liquid. While studies have shown that clustered nanoparticles can significantly modify local rheological behavior 
even at low concentrations23,24, in the present system such effects are expected to be localized. Consequently, the 
bulk liquid may still be approximated as Newtonian to first order, while localized particle–fluid interactions near 
the interface may enhance viscous dissipation, damping, and deviations from idealized bubble dynamics. These 
effects are not explicitly included in the current model and represent a source of uncertainty.
The effect of ambient pressure was not explicitly investigated in this work. At increased water depth, higher 
pressure is expected to enhance gas solubility and suppress bubble formation and persistence. This may reduce 
the effectiveness of the hydrophobic air layer and increase heat loss to the surrounding liquid, potentially inhib -
iting ignition and sustained combustion. Therefore, the present approach may have limited applicability under 
high-pressure underwater conditions.
The Rayleigh–Plesset equation describes the radial dynamics of a gas bubble in a liquid by balancing inertial, 
viscous, surface tension, and pressure forces acting on a spherical interface. It is derived under the assumptions 
of a perfectly spherical bubble in an infinite, incompressible liquid, with symmetric radial motion. In the present 
study, the observed bubble is not perfectly spherical but rather approximately hemispherical and attached to a 
solid surface, which introduces geometric asymmetry and boundary effects. These conditions violate the strict

distribution around the bubble. In particular, the presence of the solid boundary reduces the amount of liquid that 
must be displaced during expansion and can lead to higher oscillation frequencies and altered collapse dynamics.
Despite these limitations, the Rayleigh–Plesset equation is employed here as a first-order, reduced-order model 
to capture the dominant features of bubble growth and oscillation. Previous studies 25,26 have shown that, even 
under non-ideal conditions, it can provide reasonable order-of-magnitude estimates of bubble dynamics when 
interpreted qualitatively. Accordingly, any gas temperatures, pressures, or gas quantities inferred from the model 
should be interpreted as approximate estimates subject to the assumptions of the analysis rather than directly 
measured quantities.

Oscillation behavior and frequency analysis
To further characterize the oscillatory behavior of the bubble, the natural frequency can be estimated using Min-
naert’s formulation. It should be noted, however, that this model is derived under the assumptions of a spherical 
bubble undergoing small-amplitude oscillations in an infinite, incompressible, and Newtonian liquid. In contrast, 
the bubbles observed in the present study are millimeter-scale, approximately hemispherical, and attached to a 
solid boundary, and they undergo large-amplitude oscillations with continuous gas generation and heat transfer. 
These conditions deviate from the assumptions of the Minnaert model and can affect the effective inertia, damp-
ing, and restoring forces governing the oscillation.
Therefore, the Minnaert equation is employed here only as a first-order, order-of-magnitude estimate of the 
oscillation frequency. Deviations between predicted and observed frequencies are expected due to geometric 
asymmetry, boundary effects, and nonlinear oscillation dynamics. The natural bubble frequency could be esti -
mated by a formula proposed by Minnaert in adiabatic conditions27:

Analyzer (Netzsch STA 449 F1 Jupiter®). For each experiment, about 5 mg sample was placed in an alumina pan

lower measured energy release10. Additionally, the incorporation of PDMS may further contribute to incomplete

Bubble evolution mechanism
Based on the energy properties of the reagents and the simulations, a more detailed analysis on the evolution of 
the bubble could be made as follows:
Before the bubble appeared at 2.3 ms, the sample remained nearly motionless, undergoing continuous heating 
with only negligible movements observed in the air pocket.
While the bubble that emerged at 2.3 ms could be water vapor, observations by Akhatov et al. revealed that a 
millimeter-sized bubble induced in water by a laser pulse collapses within a microsecond, and experiments by 
Kim et al. suggests that it takes seconds for focused continuous laser to induce a bubble in water 36. Considering 
the rapid heat transfer at the liquid/vapor interface summarized by Kim 37, it is suggested that the bubble com -
prised other gases. Considering that PDMS can decompose at approximately 170 ℃35, CuO starts to decompose 
at above 700–800 ℃38, and our DSG results demonstrated weight loss in the Al/CuO-PDMS composite starting 
at about 300 ℃, the initial slow-expansion stage may be attributed to PDMS decomposition at this temperature. 
This endothermic decomposition was sustained by the external laser, and with the gas generated in this process, 
heat loss to the water was greatly reduced.
When the sample reached approximately 550 ℃ in Fig. 4d, the nanothermite reaction started. This exothermic 
reaction became self-sustaining, resulting in the rapid expansion of the bubble. Numerous events, including ther-
mal expansion, water evaporation, release of dissolved gasses, PDMS decomposition into smaller molecules, and 
CuO decomposition into O2, together pushing the bubble to its maximum size.
Despite the nanothermite reaction lasted until 28 ms as shown in Fig. 4n, o and completely ended in Fig. 4p, 
the average bubble size started to decrease 10 ms before the reaction ended. The bubble then underwent approxi-
mately 6 pulsations following this general trend, as discussed earlier. Furthermore, the bubble experiences desta-
bilization, the spherical surface fractured into smaller pieces over time.
This pulsation is quite different from the typical dynamics of other underwater bubbles, which contract to a 
much smaller size before rebounding, and maintaining a spherical form in the first cycle 39–42. This may suggest 
that gas generation occurs throughout the entire reaction, distinguishing it from the free expansion of the bubble.
Analyzing the bubble evolution and the sources of gas generation clarifies the chemical reactions occurring in 
the millisecond-scale regime. These observations also point toward the need to investigate the potential electronic 
interactions that happen on much shorter timescales that may help initiate the chemical reactions.
Interfacial considerations and conceptual energy-band alignment
The optical measurements presented in the Supplementary Material indicate that the optical response of the Al/
CuO nanothermite differs from that of its individual constituents. Specifically, changes in the measured optical 
spectra were observed after Al and CuO nanoparticles were combined to form the nanothermite system. These 
observations demonstrate that the nanothermite exhibits distinct optical behavior compared with the separate 
materials. However, the optical measurements alone do not provide direct evidence of electronic coupling, charge 
transfer, carrier transport, or other interfacial electronic processes.
CuO semiconductors can exhibit either p-type or n-type conductivity, as discussed by Aleksandar Živković 
and Nora H. de Leeuw43. Previous investigations have predominantly reported p-type conduction in CuO, which 
is attributed to the presence of copper vacancies and interstitial oxygen in the solid 44,45. The work function of

Proposed mechanism of laser-induced bubble evolution
Figure 10 summarizes the proposed bubble evolution mechanism derived from the experimental observations and 
the preceding discussion, highlighting the coupled effects of nanothermite heat release, PDMS decomposition, 
and interfacial water vaporization that govern bubble nucleation, growth, oscillation, fragmentation, and col -
lapse. Upon laser irradiation, the incident energy is primarily absorbed by the embedded Al/CuO nanothermite 
particle, triggering a highly exothermic reaction that rapidly heats the surrounding PDMS matrix and initiates 
gas generation. The combined effects of PDMS pyrolysis and interfacial water vaporization lead to the formation 
and expansion of a hemispherical bubble, whose subsequent evolution is governed by the interplay among heat 
release, gas production, vapor condensation, and the inertia of the surrounding liquid.
The proposed mechanism consists of eight stages. First, the incident laser energy passes through the water 
and PDMS with negligible absorption and is predominantly absorbed by the Al/CuO nanothermite core. Second, 
localized heating initiates the thermite reaction, releasing a substantial amount of heat. Third, the surrounding 
PDMS undergoes rapid pyrolysis, generating gaseous decomposition products and forming a hemispherical gas 
dome at the water–PDMS interface. Fourth, heat transfer from the reaction zone to the adjacent water causes 
intense vaporization, and the generated water vapor mixes with the pyrolysis gases, resulting in further bubble 
inflation. Fifth, continued heat release and gas generation rapidly increase the internal pressure, driving dramatic 
hemispherical bubble expansion. Sixth, the bubble undergoes oscillatory motion due to the competition between 
internal pressure and the inertia of the surrounding liquid. Seventh, as the reaction subsides and heat dissipates,

nanothermite embedded in PDMS at a water–solid interface. (1) Incident laser irradiation passes through the water and 
PDMS with negligible absorption and is primarily absorbed by the Al/CuO core. (2) Localized heating initiates ignition of 
the Al/CuO nanothermite reaction, releasing substantial thermal energy. (3) The surrounding PDMS undergoes rapid pyroly-
sis, producing gaseous decomposition products and forming an initial hemispherical gas bubble at the interface. (4) Heat 
transfer from the reaction zone to the adjacent water causes intense vaporization, and the generated water vapor mixes with 
the pyrolysis gases, further inflating the bubble. (5) Continued heat release and gas generation rapidly increase the internal 
pressure, driving dramatic bubble expansion into a large hemispherical cavity. (6) The bubble undergoes oscillatory motion 
due to the balance between internal pressure and the inertia of the surrounding liquid. (7) As the reaction weakens and cool-
ing progresses, gas generation decreases and vapor condensation lowers the internal pressure, causing bubble instability and 
fragmentation into smaller daughter bubbles. (8) Continued heat dissipation and gas loss lead to bubble collapse, followed 
by the gradual dissolution of the remaining microbubbles into the surrounding liquid.

unstable and fragment into smaller daughter bubbles. Finally, continued cooling and gas loss lead to bubble col-

Limitations and future work
Introducing PDMS and the surrounding water environment further increases the complexity of the system by add-
ing additional thermal, chemical, and transport processes, including potential gas generation. Although unlikely 
to dominate under the present conditions, it is theoretically possible for aluminum to react with water vapor to 
form hydrogen50, and such secondary pathways cannot be completely excluded.
Overall, a more definitive understanding of the underlying mechanisms would require additional experimental 
investigation, such as in-situ spectroscopic diagnostics, emission measurements, or direct analysis of reaction 
intermediates and products. Future work incorporating such techniques would help clarify the respective roles of 
interfacial processes, thermal effects, and gas generation in the ignition and combustion behavior.
The present study focuses on demonstrating underwater ignition feasibility and characterizing the associ -
ated bubble dynamics, which are markedly different from combustion behavior in air or vacuum. While these 
observations provide important insight into the ignition process, a comprehensive assessment of combustion 
performance—including ignition-energy thresholds, reaction duration statistics, propagation behavior, pressure 
generation, and energy efficiency—remains beyond the scope of the current work. Such quantitative characteriza-
tion is an important direction for future research and will be pursued to provide a more complete understanding 
of underwater nanothermite combustion.
Summary
By dispersing PDMS prepolymers and Al/CuO nanothermite powders in a solvent such as acetone, a hydrophobic 
PDMS coating was formed around the nanothermite particles, enabling laser ignition underwater. The hydropho-
bic coating plays a critical role by reducing heat loss to the surrounding water and facilitating energy accumula-
tion for ignition. The water contact angle increased from 115° to 150° as the PDMS content increased from 1% to 
12%; however, only samples containing 2–9% PDMS could be successfully ignited underwater.
This study further investigated the heat-transfer and ignition mechanisms of the Al/CuO nanothermite system. 
Analysis based on the Rayleigh–Plesset equation, together with experimental observations and thermodynamic 
considerations, suggests rapid cooling and condensation of water vapor during bubble evolution, indicating that 
the bubble likely contains both water vapor and reaction-generated gases.
These findings improve the understanding of heat transport and ignition processes in nanothermite systems and 
demonstrate an effective strategy for achieving underwater ignition through hydrophobic surface modification. 
The coating approach may be extended to other energetic materials and hydrophobic polymers. In addition, the 
observed optical behavior and large interfacial area of the Al/CuO nanothermite suggest that interfacial effects 
may influence energy absorption and localization during laser ignition, although the detailed underlying mecha-
nisms require further experimental investigation.

source: International Journal of Environmental Analytical Chemistry
summary:
Tea-assisted CeO
                    <sub>2</sub>
                    nanoparticles as electrode modifiers for electrochemical detection of nitrite in environmental water samples
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Here, we report a tea-assisted synthesis of cerium oxide nanoparticles (CeO2 NPs) and their evaluation as a simple, noble-metal-free electrode modifier for electrochemical nitrite (NO2−) detection under neutral conditions. Oxygen-rich phytochemicals in Camellia sinensis extract promoted precursor formation with Ce3+ ions, followed by thermal conversion to crystalline CeO2 NPs. Spectroscopic, diffraction and microscopic analyses supported the formation of CeO2 NPs. When drop-cast onto a glassy carbon electrode, the CeO2 NP layer increased the electrochemically accessible interface and improved the apparent current-density response towards NO2− oxidation compared with bare GCE under identical conditions. This improvement is attributed to the beneficial contribution of the CeO2 NP-modified interface. Using current density at 1.10 V vs Ag/AgCl as the analytical signal, CeO2 NPs/GCE exhibited a linear response towards NO2− over 0.039–10 mM, with a sensitivity of 1.3255 µA cm−2 µM−1 and a calculated LOD of 2.80 µM. The sensor exhibited good cycling repeatability, electrode-to-electrode reproducibility, 28-day storage stability and selectivity against inorganic and electroactive interferents. Application to river and tap water samples yielded recoveries of 97.24–109.51%, with RSD values of 1.36–2.81%. These results support tea-derived CeO2 NPs/GCE as a stable and practical platform for NO2− determination in aqueous environmental matrices.

title: Exploring Travel Intention of Vietnamese Gen Z Travelers to Dark Tourism Sites
source: Journal of Quality Assurance in Hospitality & Tourism
summary: Exploring Travel Intention of Vietnamese Gen Z Travelers to Dark Tourism Sites
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

This study explores the travel intentions of Vietnamese Generation Z toward dark tourism using the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). Based on 342 valid survey responses, the research examines how superstition and psychological constraints influence attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and behavioral intention. The findings indicate that superstition positively affects all three core TPB components. Furthermore, psychological constraints also positively influence these constructs. This demonstrates that in the context of dark tourism, internal psychological barriers act as motivators rather than deterrents, as young travelers actively seek emotional challenges and thrills. Practically, this study recommends using peer-based social influence and emotional preparation to encourage youth participation in dark tourism. Ultimately, this research provides theoretical updates and practical guidance for responsible tourism marketing in Southeast Asia and similar cultural settings.

Abstract
Honey is one of the most widely consumed natural food materials in the world due to its nutritional, medicinal, and
economic importance. However, adulteration of honey with cheap sweeteners such as invert sugar, high fructose corn
syrup, and sugar syrups, has become a major global concern. Adulteration not only aﬀects honey quality and authenticity
but also poses serious health and economic risks to consumers and producers. Adulteration can elevate consumers’
blood glucose levels, potentially contributing to diabetes, obesity, abdominal weight gain, hypertension, and higher
blood lipid levels. The various analytical techniques, including liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, nuclear
magnetic resonance, and isotope ratio mass spectrometry, have been employed for the detection of adulterants.
Strengthening of food regulatory systems and awareness among consumers and beekeepers are vital to ensure the
purity of honey and protect the global honey market. A review is essential to consolidate information on the extent of
adulteration and techniques employed for its detection across regions and markets. This paper reviews honey
adulteration practices, detection methods, and tools used for their detection, and outlines their impacts on human
health, trade, and consumer trust and summarizes analytical methods for detection, improves monitoring protocols and
discusses emerging technologies such as UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy and Artificial Intelligence (AI), Thermal Imaging and AI,
Hyperspectral Imaging and Chemometrics.
Categories: Food processing, Food quality, Food security and sustainability
Keywords: honey, adulteration, sugar syrup, authenticity, detection, health impact
Introduction And Background
Honey is a natural substance produced by honeybees (Apis spp.) that contains a complex mixture of carbohydrates,
enzymes, amino acids, minerals, antioxidants and vitamins [1,2]. Due to its nutritional and therapeutic value and wide
availability, honey has been consumed since ancient times and is an important economic product for
beekeepers.  However, increasing market demand and high commercial value have led to widespread adulteration
activities [3].
Adulteration of honey is defined as the intentional addition of foreign material into honey, such as sugar syrups or
artificial sweeteners, to increase volume and reduce cost [4]. However, honey is frequently adulterated for economic gain.
Adulteration includes the addition of cheaper sweeteners, dilution with water, use of industrial-grade sugars, or
manipulation of bees’ feeding to increase yield [5]. Such adulteration aﬀects honey’s authenticity, therapeutic properties,
and market value. The high demand for honey, combined with financial incentives, makes it highly vulnerable to fraud

[6]. Hence, detection and prevention of honey adulteration have become global priorities in food safety. This fraudulent
practice compromises the authenticity, safety and worldwide, consumption of honey as a natural sweetener, a spread,
and a key ingredient in baking and processed foods and the dietary pleasure and medicinal eﬃcacy of honey [7].
Moreover, adulterated honey can have long-term health implications, including metabolic disorders and allergies [8].
Thus, understanding the nature, detection, and impact of honey adulteration is significant to ensure safe food and
customer protection. Honey adulteration is not merely a food fraud issue. It is a multilayered supply chain problem
involving chemical mimicry, technological evasion, and regulatory gaps. To detect these, various honey adulterations
detection techniques are available, which include physicochemical Tests, isotope analysis, Spectroscopic and
Chromatographic Techniques, Melissopalynology, and DNA Analysis. These methods have significantly improved
adulteration traceability; however, eﬀective enforcement and increased awareness are equally important for combating
honey adulteration. Traditional food safety approaches are not adequate for evaluating Economically Motivated
Adulteration (EMA) or for preventing deliberate food adulteration. Therefore, avoidance of EMA requires a holistic and
systems-based approach that takes advantage of multiple data sources and disciplines [9]. These techniques have many
limitations, and fraudsters are constantly adapting to existing revealing methods. The methodology used is focused on a
limited number of indicators, which are insuﬃcient to detect the purity of honey. It is no longer possible to focus on one
indicator only, but a wide range of quality indicators need to be determined in order to detect honey adulteration [5]. To
overcome these issues, new generation technologies such as UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy and Artificial Intelligence (AI),
Thermal Imaging, and Hyperspectral Imaging and Chemometrics have been utilized. But these advanced methods are
much costlier, diﬃcult to access, and lack universal detection protocols.
This manuscript summarizes current knowledge of how adulteration impacts quality, highlights health concerns
associated with adulterated honey, describes analytical techniques along with their limitations, economic consequences,
and new emerging technologies used in the detection of adulterated honey. Understanding the economic consequences
can motivate stricter regulations and support policies to protect authentic honey markets.
Review
Types and sources of honey adulteration
Honey adulteration occurs at diﬀerent stages of production and marketing. Direct adulteration, indirect adulteration,
mislabeling fraud, and ultra-processing practices exploit the chemical similarity between natural honey sugars (fructose,
glucose) and industrial syrups, making detection increasingly complex. Each honey type has a unique isotopic signature,
pollen profile, and spectral fingerprint. Adulteration disrupts this fingerprint, reducing traceability and authenticity
verification. The sources of honey adulteration are given in Figure 1 and further details of this diagram are discussed in
the text below.

Direct Adulteration
It is the addition of exogenous sugars (corn, rice, cane syrups rich in C4 sugars). Adulterants are often added to honey
because of their low cost and similar composition. While these substances can mimic honey, they are harmful to bee
colonies, as they can negatively impact factors like the formation of hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), pH levels, and overall
colony health. Additionally, the quality of the honey is compromised. It involves adding of cane sugar syrup, corn syrup,
glucose, or invert sugar after honey extraction. These adulterants mimic natural honey sugars, making detection diﬃcult.
The common adulteration activities are adding high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS), rice syrup, cane sugar syrup, beet sugar
syrup, and invert sugar syrup [10]. These syrups imitate honey’s carbohydrate composition and are often diﬃcult to
detect using basic tests.
Water addition reduces viscosity and increases the potential for fermentation, degradation, and microbial growth. Honey
with moisture above 20% is generally considered adulterated or improperly processed [11]. Artificial sweeteners such as
aspartame, saccharin, or acesulfame-K are used to enhance sweetness while reducing cost. These compounds do not

physicochemical properties, they can be accurately identified and quantified through chromatographic analysis [12].
Colorants (caramel), thickeners (starch, gelatin), and artificial flavors may be added to mimic the sensory characteristics of
natural honey [5].
Indirect Adulteration
This form of adulteration occurs when honeybees are fed sugar syrups or molasses during nectar flow or periods of
nectar scarcity, resulting in alterations to the intrinsic composition of honey. Consequently, the produced honey becomes
compositionally similar to honey adulterated with exogenous sugars, making its detection particularly challenging. Such
feeding practices can modify the natural sugar profile and other quality attributes of honey, especially when artificial
syrups are provided without appropriate management practices [13].
Processing
Adulteration is not limited to the addition of foreign substances; it also includes processing and labeling practices that
misrepresent the quality or identity of honey. Excessive heating, often employed to delay crystallization and improve
visual appearance, can degrade the natural quality of honey by reducing enzyme activity, increasing HMF content, and
diminishing heat-sensitive bioactive compounds. Similarly, mislabeling the botanical or floral origin of honey (e.g.,
marketing multifloral honey as monofloral honey) constitutes economic adulteration because it provides false
information regarding the product's identity and origin. Such practices violate food regulatory standards, as they deceive
consumers and compromise the authenticity, traceability, and quality of honey [14,15]. 
Methods for detection of adulteration
Detection of honey adulteration requires robust, sensitive, and reliable analytical methods because adulteration practices
have become increasingly advanced. Advances in analytical chemistry have led to several reliable techniques for
detecting honey adulteration:
Physicochemical Tests
Detecting honey adulteration relies heavily on physicochemical parameters that reflect honey’s natural composition.
Adulterants such as sugar syrups, molasses, invert sugar, jaggery syrup, and starch-based additives alter these parameters
in measurable ways.
Tests such as moisture content, electrical conductivity, HMF level, diastase activity, sucrose level, and acidity provide
preliminary indications of honey purity [11,16]. The following physicochemical tests are widely used to evaluate honey
authenticity.
Moisture Content: It indicates dilution of honey with water or early harvesting. Pure honey typically contains <20%
moisture, depending on botanical origin. Adulterated or immature honey contains >20% moisture levels. Increased
moisture levels are associated with sugar syrup addition and improper processing. It can be measured using a digital
refractometer or Abbe refractometer, based on the refractive index. Low moisture (<15%) can also occur when honey is
heated excessively [1].
pH and Free Acidity: Natural honey is mildly acidic (pH 3.2-4.5) due to organic acids like gluconic acid, which is produced
through the enzymatic oxidation of glucose by glucose oxidase. This acidic environment contributes to the characteristic
flavor, microbial stability, and extended shelf life of honey by inhibiting the growth of spoilage microorganisms.
Adulteration disrupts acidity levels. Lower acidity suggests sugar or rice syrup adulteration while abnormally high acidity
may occur due to fermentation. pH can be checked with a pH meter and free acidity with titration with NaOH
[17]. Although pH and free acidity are valuable physicochemical indicators of honey quality, they should be interpreted
alongside other analytical parameters because natural variations in botanical origin and geographical source can also
influence these characteristics.
