Electrical Conductivity (EC): EC reflects ash and mineral content. Addition of plant syrups or sugar solutions alters EC
values. Pure honey typically shows conductivity 0.2-0.8 mS/cm while adulteration of honey with honeydew possess
higher EC. Lower value of EC significantly indicates adulteration with sugar syrup. It is measured using a conductivity
meter in a 20% honey solution [18].
Ash Content: Ash represents the mineral content, and its normal range in pure honey is generally 0.02-0.3%. Higher ash
content indicates honey rich in honeydew, mineral-rich adulterants, molasses, or jaggery syrup. The presence of lower
ash content reflects diluted or artificially inverted or refined sugar syrup. It is a supporting indicator when combined with
sugar profile (sucrose/reducing sugars), HMF levels, and enzyme activity. It is detected by dry ashing at 600°C in a muﬄe
furnace [3].
Reducing Sugars (Glucose + Fructose): Pure honey contains >65% reducing sugars. Adulteration alters sugar ratios. Low
reducing sugar indicates addition of sucrose syrup. These can be detected with Lane-Eynon titration or high-performance
liquid chromatography (HPLC) [19].
Sucrose Content: Pure honey has <5% sucrose. Increased sucrose suggests addition of cane sugar or incomplete natural
inversion. High sucrose (>5%) indicates cane sugar or jaggery adulteration. It is detected with polarimetry or HPLC [20].
HMF Content: It is an indicator of heat treatment and storage. HMF forms when fructose degrades during heating or
prolonged storage. HMF >40 mg/kg indicates overheating or addition of inverted sugar. Very low HMF may also indicate
fresh adulteration. The Winkler method and spectrophotometry are used to detect HMF [11].
Diastase Activity (Enzymatic Index): Diastase (amylase) naturally present in honey and decreases with heating or
adulteration. Diastase number <8 indicates adulteration or thermal degradation. The Schade or Phadebas method is used
for its detection [21].
Proline: Proline is the major amino acid in pure honey. Pure honey usually contains >180 mg/kg. High proline content
indicates natural, unadulterated honey while low proline content in honey indicates sugar syrup adulteration and
immature/uncapped honey. In the proline test, deep red color detects pure honey, while a faint color indicates
adulterated honey. The proline test is usually combined with other tests (like sucrose content and the HMF test) for
confirmation. It is detected with a spectrophotometric ninhydrin assay [22].
Specific Optical Rotation: Monofloral honey typically shows negative optical rotation (usually around −20° to −30°).
Natural honey possesses high fructose content (normal composition). Positive rotation suggests sugar or starch syrup
adulteration. The addition of cane sugar-based syrups alters optical behavior. A polarimeter reading on a honey solution
detects optical behavior [23].
Color Measurement (Pfund Scale): Honey color (dark, amber, light) depends on floral source, mineral content, storage,
and processing floral source but also changes when adulterated. The Pfund Scale expresses color in millimeters (mm
Pfund) and confirms the color grade. It is helpful along with other physicochemical test to detect the purity of honey.
Irregular color changes may signal caramel addition, molasses mixing, and excessive heating. Reading the absorbance at
560 nm and converting to Pfund values [24].
Viscosity: It is the thickness or resistance to flow of honey. Honey viscosity depends on moisture, sugar composition, and
temperature. Lower viscosity indicates dilution with syrup while higher viscosity may indicate adulterants like jaggery
syrup. Pure honey has a thick, slow-flowing consistency, forms a continuous thread when poured, and does not spread
quickly. Adulterated honey has a thin, watery consistency, flows rapidly, breaks easily while pouring and indicates low
viscosity. It can be detected with a Brookfield viscometer [24].
Density and Specific Gravity: In pure honey, normal specific gravity (SG) range is 1.35-1.40 g/mL. A lower value of SG in
honey indicates dilution with water, addition of sugar syrup, or high moisture content. It must be observed at a
standardized usually 20°C; otherwise, it aﬀects readings. Density decreases when adulterated with water or sugar syrups
[25].

Its normal range is 0.1-0.5%. Abnormal alkalinity indicates mineral-rich adulterants or contamination. Below the normal

These various physicochemical methods are significant to analyze the purity of honey. The limitations of these include
low specificity and they are easily bypassed by sophisticated adulterants. This review shows that these physicochemical
tests may overlap between natural and adulterated honey because natural variation (botanical origin, processing,
storage) can produce the same parameter ranges as mild adulteration.
Isotope Analysis
Isotope ratio mass spectrometry (IRMS) distinguishes between C₃ plant-based nectar and C₄ sugar adulterants. Stable
isotope analysis especially stable carbon isotope ratio analysis is an important scientific method used to verify honey
authenticity and identify adulteration, including the addition of C4 plant-derived syrups such as corn or sugarcane
[27,28]. IRMS distinguishes authentic honey from cane- or corn-syrup-adulterated honey based on δ13C isotopic ratios.
The δ¹³C value of authentic honey ranges from −23.5% to −25.5% [6]. Isotope analysis is highly reliable for cane and corn
syrup detection but cannot detect C3 adulterants such as rice syrup.
Spectroscopic and Chromatographic Techniques
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), HPLC, and liquid chromatography-mass
spectrometry are powerful tools for identifying sugar adulterants at trace levels [29]. NMR is highly eﬀective for detecting
C3 and C4 plant-derived syrups [6].  Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry  is used to detect  volatile profiles and
additives such as artificial flavorings [12]. Raman Spectroscopy is useful for identifying specific functional groups in
adulterants [30]. HPLC is used for profiling sugars, organic acids, and identifying adulterants [31]. The chromatographic
techniques have high sensitivity and specificity but are expensive, time-consuming, and require skilled personnel. The
spectroscopic techniques create a “spectral fingerprint” of honey. They are rapid and non-destructive and can detect
subtle compositional deviations. The limitation of these techniques is that they require chemometric models and large
reference databases.
Melissopalynology and DNA Analysis
Melissopalynology and DNA barcoding are used to confirm floral and geographical origin of honey [32,33]. DNA
barcoding is emerging as a reliable authentication tool.
Emerging Technologies include: chemometric modeling, machine learning-based spectral analysis, electrochemical
sensors, and metabolomic fingerprinting [30]. These approaches are promising for rapid and field-level detection.
Implications of Honey Adulteration
Honey adulteration directly aﬀects honey’s chemical, physical, and sensory properties. It reduces nutritional value (loss of
bioactive compounds, phenolic compounds, enzymes, antioxidants), alters physicochemical parameters such as sugar
profile, viscosity, moisture content, and HMF  levels, and diminishes authenticity markers critical for labeling and
consumer trust. Altered sugar ratios aﬀect crystallization and viscosity while elevated HMF levels indicate overheating or
sugar addition.

Impact on Quality and Authenticity
Adulteration alters honey’s natural composition, reducing enzymatic activity (e.g., invertase, diastase) and antioxidant
capacity [34]. It also distorts flavor, aroma, and color characteristics. It reduces therapeutic value (wound healing,
antimicrobial eﬀects). Adulterated honey demonstrates  decreased enzyme activity, reduced antioxidant and
antimicrobial properties, and altered sensory qualities [13]. Proline, pH, and moisture content levels decline  with
increasing amounts of molasses, sugar, banana adulterants, and melted candy. Overall, sugar composition serves as an
important indicator for identifying honey adulteration [35].
Health Implications
Consuming adulterated honey may pose several health risks. High levels of added sugars contribute to obesity, diabetes,
and cardiovascular issues. Industrial syrups may introduce contaminants, pesticide residues, or harmful additives. Infants,
immunocompromised individuals, and people with specific metabolic conditions are particularly at risk. Natural honey
oﬀers several health benefits, including reducing low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and total cholesterol levels in healthy
individuals. In contrast, consuming 3-20% dietary fructose has been shown to increase LDL and total cholesterol by 11%
and 9%, respectively. Therefore, adding sugar to honey can pose significant health concerns [36]. Adulteration poses
serious health risks to consumers, which can contribute to high blood pressure and an altered lipid profile, higher blood
sugar concentrations, obesity, and abdominal weight gain. The utilization of adulterated honey potentially causes
obesity, diabetes, and gastrointestinal disorders due to excess refined sugar intake [37]. In addition, chemical residues
from processing may cause allergic or toxic reactions. Although many added syrups are food-grade, chronic consumption
of adulterated honey increases glycemic load, enhances the risk of obesity and metabolic disorders, and reduces
medicinal benefits [12]. Industrial-grade syrups may contain chemical contaminants harmful to health. Certain
adulterants (e.g., syrups, contaminants) can cause liver and kidney damage. Histological studies link adulterated honey to
organ toxicity and renal dysfunction.

Economic and Trade Impact
Honey adulteration undermines the beekeeping and food industry. It imposes regulatory and trade burdens on
beekeepers and farmers by increasing costs for testing and  certification and causing trade disputes due to failed
authenticity checks. It causes a loss of consumer confidence and market value of authentic honey. Unfair competition for
genuine producers aﬀects livelihoods and rural economies. It strains regulatory agencies due to testing and enforcement
costs. Understanding these economic consequences can motivate stricter regulations and support policies to protect
authentic honey markets.
Honey and bee products improve sustainable incomes for farmers [38]. Adulteration undermines the integrity of the
honey market, leading to financial losses for genuine producers and loss of consumer trust [39]. International honey trade
has faced multiple rejections due to regulatory violations of purity principles, aﬀecting export revenues. Adulteration
causes significant losses to genuine beekeepers, distorts market competition, and aﬀects export standards [2]. Today,
honey adulteration causes significant economic losses, not only by reducing the quality of honey but also by making it
more challenging to market genuine honey. The majority of the honey available in the market consists of caramelized
sucrose lacking nutritional value. As a result, the widespread presence of such adulterated products has led consumers to
lose confidence in the true nutritional benefits of genuine honey [37]. It impacts the beekeeping sector by reducing
profitability, discouraging apiculture, and threatening pollination services and biodiversity indirectly
Regulatory Standards and Prevention
Honey adulteration creates a negative feedback loop aﬀecting producers, regulators, and consumers. Agencies like Food
Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and the Codex Alimentarius Commission [11] define quality parameters
for authentic honey. These include limits for HMF (<40 mg/kg), a minimum diastase number (8), and the absence of
added sugars. The Codex Alimentarius Standard (CODEX STAN 12-1981) specifies acceptable limits for major honey
quality parameters such as moisture, HMF, sucrose, and enzyme activity [11]. National standards like FSSAI (India) also
regulate honey purity. Preventive strategies include promoting traceability through QR-coded packaging, third-party
testing using advanced analytical tools, beekeeper training on ethical honey production, and consumer awareness
campaigns on identifying pure honey.
Emerging Technologies and Future Scope
Emerging analytical technologies combined with AI are expected to revolutionize honey authentication by enabling
rapid, accurate, and non-destructive detection of adulteration. Future research should focus on developing portable and
cost-eﬀective spectroscopic devices integrated with machine learning algorithms for real-time, on-site honey
authentication throughout the supply chain. UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy and AI: Researchers in Bangladesh have developed
a rapid, non-destructive method to detect honey adulteration using UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy paired with machine
learning. Their findings could protect consumers and support food quality enforcement. The method captures absorption
spectra across 200-900 nm, allowing detailed chemical profiling and identification of adulterants like corn syrup and
caramel color [40]. Thermal imaging and AI: It is a novel approach for classifying levels of honey adulteration. It detects
adulteration based on heat signatures and composition diﬀerences. It provides high classification accuracy even at low
adulteration levels [41]. Hyperspectral Imaging and Chemometrics: It uses spatial and spectral data. It enables
quantification of adulteration levels. Detection of adulteration is based on hyperspectral imaging technology,
LIBSVM, and PLSR models for qualitative and quantitative analysis [42]. 
Another important research direction is the establishment of comprehensive global spectral and chemical fingerprint
databases representing authentic honey from diﬀerent botanical and geographical origins. Such databases would
enhance the robustness and generalizability of AI-based authentication models while minimizing false-positive and false-
negative classifications. The development of multimodal analytical platforms that combine spectroscopic,
chromatographic, isotopic, and metabolomic data is expected to provide higher sensitivity and specificity than individual
techniques. Future studies should also emphasize the standardization and validation of AI-assisted analytical methods
according to international regulatory guidelines to facilitate their routine adoption by food testing laboratories and
regulatory agencies. In addition, cloud-based platforms and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensors could enable

Conclusions
Honey adulteration remains a significant challenge to food authenticity, consumer safety, and global trade. Increasingly
sophisticated adulteration practices highlight the need for advanced analytical methods and strict regulatory
monitoring. Modern detection techniques have improved adulteration traceability, but enforcement and awareness are
equally crucial. Fraudsters are continuously adapting to existing detection methods. Collaborative eﬀorts among
researchers, regulatory bodies, and honey producers are essential to ensure that honey reaching consumers remains
pure, natural, and beneficial to health. Adoption of combined physicochemical, spectroscopic, chromatographic, and
isotope-based techniques is essential to ensure honey authenticity. Consumer awareness, quality enforcement, and
improved traceability can significantly reduce adulteration and protect the apiculture industry. Therefore, it is
emphasized that periodic training sessions for stakeholders on detecting adulteration should be conducted to help
prevent the presence of adulterated honey in the market. Although there are various techniques available to analyze the
quality of honey, these have their own limitations. Further advanced methods are much costlier, diﬃcult to access, and
lack of universal detection protocols. Therefore, more research is needed to overcome the negative loop, develop quality
evaluation techniques, and also understand the functioning of new emerging technologies. Thus, future research must
focus on global authentication databases and multi-method approaches, consumer protection, and industry
sustainability.

Abstract
Dry matter percentage (DM) is a critical physiological trait in sugar beet, functioning 
not only as a quantitative measure but also as an integrative marker of carbon 
assimilation, assimilate partitioning, and ionic regulation. We hypothesized that 
variation in DM across genotypes arises from differences in photosynthetic efficiency, 
sucrose allocation to storage roots, and mineral ion homeostasis. To test this, we 
evaluated 66 sugar beet cultivars across 47 field trials (2019–2024) and assessed the 
relationships between DM and key agronomic, quality, and physicochemical traits. 
DM ranged from 15.8 to 27.1%, reflecting substantial genotypic diversity together 
with interannual environmental variation. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis 
revealed strong positive associations between DM and sucrose content ( r = 0.88), 
white sugar content ( r = 0.87), and extraction coefficient of sugar ( r = 0.78), whereas 
moderate positive correlations were observed with sugar yield ( r = 0.34) and white 
sugar yield ( r = 0.54). Conversely, DM was negatively correlated with root yield ( r = 
− 0.22), sodium ( r = − 0.75), nitrogen ( r = − 0.31), and molasses sugar ( r = − 0.71). 
Multivariate regression confirmed that DM significantly improves quality-related traits 
while reducing impurity-related traits, with no significant influence on potassium or 
alkalinity. Year-specific correlation analyses further demonstrated that the positive 
associations of dry matter with sugar content, white sugar content, and extractable 
sugar coefficient, together with its negative association with sodium concentration, 
remained consistent across growing seasons, whereas relationships with yield-related 
traits were more variable. These findings support the role of DM as a mechanistic 
marker of source-sink dynamics and ion regulation in sugar beet physiology. By 
linking DM to underlying physiological processes, this study provides a framework 
for selecting genotypes with enhanced sucrose accumulation and extractable sugar 
quality. DM thus emerges as a reliable indicator for breeding programs aiming to 
improve sugar quality and processing efficiency while maintaining acceptable field 
performance.
Keywords Association, Dry matter, Sugar beet
 1 Introduction
Sugar beet ( Beta vulgaris L.) is a fundamental industrial crop whose economic value 
depends on both root biomass and extractable sucrose. Among root quality traits, dry 
matter percentage is of particular importance because it reflects the non-water fraction 
Page 2 of 9
Fasahat et al. Discover Plants (2026) 3:402 
of biomass, largely composed of sugars, and strongly influences sugar yield and process -
ing quality. Dry matter content integrates physiological processes including photosyn -
thetic carbon gain, assimilate partitioning into storage roots, and regulation of mineral 
ion uptake. While correlations between dry matter and sucrose concentration have long 
been reported, the physiological mechanisms underlying these associations remain 
poorly understood [1].
Carbon assimilation and source–sink dynamics play a central role in dry matter for -
mation. High- dry matter genotypes may exhibit greater activity of sucrose-phosphate 
synthase, invertases, or sucrose synthase, which enhance sucrose loading and storage in 
root vacuoles [ 2]. Similarly, efficient phloem transport and assimilate unloading to root 
parenchyma promote dry matter accumulation. Ion balance is also critical: excess Na + 
and NO3
− not only reduce sucrose purity but also alter osmotic status, thereby diluting 
dry matter content [3]. Thus, variation in dry matter across genotypes may reflect funda-
mental physiological differences in carbon metabolism and ionic regulation.
The accumulation of dry matter and sucrose is also influenced by environmental and 
agronomic factors such as growth duration, climatic conditions, irrigation, and nutri -
ent management. Drought and salinity stress, for instance, can increase dry matter by 
reducing water content, but simultaneously decrease juice volume and processing qual -
ity. Adaptations such as increased root-to-shoot ratios under drought [ 4–6] highlight 
the dual role of dry matter in stress tolerance and product quality. Improved irrigation 
and balanced nitrogen application significantly enhance dry matter, sucrose content, and 
yield [7]. Long growth duration and optimal planting density further promote dry matter 
and sucrose accumulation, while continuous monoculture negatively impacts photosyn -
thetic capacity and dry matter partitioning [8].
Genotypic variation also plays a major role. Although total dry matter production 
may be similar among cultivars, differences in allocation between root and shoot tissues 
account for much of the observed variation [ 9]. Breeding strategies aimed at improv -
ing root-to-shoot partitioning or enhancing sink strength are therefore promising 
approaches for increasing dry matter and sugar yield. Recent genomic studies have con -
firmed extensive genetic diversity underlying dry matter and sucrose-related traits, with 
complex marker-trait associations emphasizing the multifactorial control of these traits 
[10].
Despite extensive breeding for yield and sucrose concentration, relatively few stud -
ies have addressed dry matter as an integrative physiological trait. Most reports have 
remained descriptive, focusing on correlations rather than mechanisms. We hypothesize 
that variation in dry matter reflects differences in carbon partitioning efficiency and ion 
regulation, and that this integrative trait can predict sugar yield and purity. The objec -
tives of this study were therefore to: (i) quantify variation in dry matter across cultivars 
and years, (ii) assess associations between dry matter and agronomic/quality traits, and 
(iii) interpret these associations within a physiological framework to identify mechanis -
tic drivers of sucrose accumulation and root quality.

Fasahat et al. Discover Plants (2026) 3:402 
2 Materials and methods
This study utilized data obtained from 47 field trials conducted between 2019 and 2024 
at the Motahari Research Station in Karaj, Iran. The trials involved 66 registered mono -
germ diploid sugar beet cultivars (Supplementary Table S1). The physicochemical prop-
erties of the experimental soil during multi-year field trials are presented in Table 1.
Monthly meteorological data, including relative humidity, maximum temperature, 
minimum temperature, and temperature range are provided in Supplementary Table S2.
In autumn, agricultural operations including plowing, fertilizer application, and sup -
plementary tillage for seedbed preparation (shallow plowing, disking, and harrowing) 
were performed. Seeds were sown each year in a randomized complete block design 
with four replications in late April. Each experimental plot consisted of three rows, 
with intra-row spacing of 20 cm and inter-row spacing of 50 cm. Agronomic practices, 
including fertilizer application, irrigation, planting depth, and crop management, were 
kept as uniform as possible across years to minimize management-related variation. Pest 
control involved chemical pesticides, while weed management was conducted manu -
ally and mechanically. During the harvest stage, roots from each plot were harvested, 
weighed, and homogenized into pulp samples. These samples were then transferred to 
specialized trays and stored at −20 °C for one day to one week before being sent to the 
Sugar Technology Laboratory at the Sugar Beet Seed Institute for qualitative analysis. 
The qualitative evaluation of pulp samples was performed using an automated beet labo-
ratory system (Betalyser, Anton Paar, Germany), adhering to ICUMSA standard proto -
cols [11].
Root yield and white sugar yield traits were measured. White sugar yield was calcu -
lated using Eq. (1) [12]:
 WSY = RY × WSC (1)
Where WSY represents white sugar yield, RY denotes root yield, and WSC signifies the 
white sugar content. T o evaluate the effect of dry matter on multiple agronomic and 
quality traits including root yield, sugar yield, white sugar yield, sugar content (SC), 
sodium (Na), potassium (K), alkalinity (Alc), white sugar content, extraction coefficient 
of sugar (ECS), and molasses sugar (Ms), separate linear mixed-effects models were fit -
ted. The general model was:

Models were fitted using the Maximum Likelihood (ML) method in PROC MIXED of 
SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA). The significance of the fixed effect of 
dry matter was evaluated using Type III tests of fixed effects, with statistical significance 
declared at P < 0.05. Model adequacy was assessed using Akaike’s Information Crite -
rion (AIC), corrected AIC (AICC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and graphical 
examination of residuals, including residual-versus-fitted plots, normal Q–Q plots, and 
histograms with fitted normal density curves.
Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients were calculated using the pooled multi-year 
dataset to quantify associations between dry matter and agronomic and technological 
traits. In addition, Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated separately for each 
growing season to evaluate the consistency of trait relationships under different annual 
environmental conditions. Correlation heatmaps were generated in R (version 4.5.1). 
Monthly meteorological summaries used to characterize seasonal environmental varia -
tion are presented in Supplementary Table S2, and the year-specific Pearson correlation 
matrices are provided in Supplementary Table S3.
All statistical analyses were conducted using SAS software version 9.4 (SAS Institute, 
Cary, NC, USA). Additional analyses and visualizations were performed in R to explore 
relationships among variables. Residual diagnostics including marginal and conditional 
residual plots, Q–Q plots, and histograms with overlaid normal density curves were 
used to verify assumptions of normality and homoscedasticity for each trait [13].
3 Results
The analysis of dry matter percentage across a diverse set of sugar beet genotypes 
revealed a considerable range, varying from 15.8 to 27.1%. This wide variation reflects 
substantial genetic diversity as well as the sensitivity of dry matter formation to environ -
mental and management factors. The mean dry matter percentage was approximately 
21.7%, consistent with earlier reports, and highlights the pivotal role of dry matter in 
determining sugar yield, processing quality, and tolerance to environmental stresses. 
Such variability presents an opportunity for targeted breeding programs aimed at select-
ing superior genotypes with enhanced dry matter traits.
Meteorological conditions varied among years (Supplementary Table S2). Annual pre-
cipitation ranged from 0.94 mm day −1 in 2022 to 1.75 mm day −1 in 2019, while maxi -
mum summer temperatures consistently exceeded 36  °C. Relative humidity showed 
considerable seasonal fluctuations, declining during summer months and increasing 
during autumn and winter.
Root yield also showed large variation, ranging from 49.7 to 140.8 t ha −1, with an aver-
age of 91.5 t ha −1, comparable to commercial production levels. The mean sugar con -
tent was 15.2%, while white sugar content averaged 13.4%. Mineral nutrients were highly 
variable: sodium (Na) ranged from 0.7 to 11.9 meq.100 g−1, potassium (K) from 2.2 to 7.2 
meq.100 g−1, and nitrogen (N) from 0.3 to 7.1 meq.100 g −1. This variability likely reflects 
differences in soil characteristics, environmental conditions, and fertilization practices. 
Importantly, such fluctuations directly affect plant physiology, as excess Na+ may induce 
Page 5 of 9
Fasahat et al. Discover Plants (2026) 3:402 
salinity stress, elevated N may alter assimilate partitioning toward amino compounds, 
and variable K levels influence osmotic adjustment and sugar translocation.
3.1 Correlation analysis
Spearman’s rank correlation revealed significant associations between dry matter and 
key agronomic and quality traits at the 1% probability level (Table  2). A weak negative 
correlation was observed between dry matter and root yield ( r = − 0.22), suggesting a 
tendency for increased dry matter to coincide with reduced fresh biomass; a trade-off 
between yield and quality frequently reported in sugar beet. Conversely, dry matter 
exhibited significant positive correlations with sugar yield ( r = 0.34), white sugar yield 
(r = 0.54), sucrose content ( r = 0.88), and white sugar content ( r = 0.87). These strong 
coefficients emphasize that genotypes with higher dry matter not only possess denser 
roots but also show superior sucrose accumulation and recoverable sugar.
The extraction coefficient of sugar also correlated strongly with dry matter ( r = 0.78), 
supporting the hypothesis that higher dry matter enhances the efficiency of sucrose 
recovery during processing. Mineral composition showed contrasting patterns: Na ( r 
= − 0.75) and N ( r = − 0.31) were negatively associated with dry matter, implying that 
higher- dry matter roots maintain tighter control over ion uptake or compartmentaliza -
tion, leading to fewer impurities and improved quality. Potassium ( r = − 0.05) and alka -
linity (r = − 0.09) showed weak, nonsignificant correlations, suggesting limited influence 
on dry matter variability. Molasses sugar content displayed a strong negative correla -
tion with dry matter ( r = − 0.71), indicating that higher dry matter reduces by-products 
that hinder sugar crystallization. To evaluate whether these relationships were stable 
under contrasting environmental conditions, Pearson correlation coefficients between 
dry matter and the measured traits were calculated separately for each experimental 
year (Supplementary Table S3). Despite considerable interannual variation in weather 
conditions (Supplementary Table S2), the positive associations of dry matter with sugar 
content, white sugar content, and extraction coefficient of sugar remained consistently 
strong across all six years. Likewise, dry matter maintained a stable negative relationship 
with sodium concentration and, in most years, with molasses sugar content. In contrast, 
correlations between dry matter and root yield, sugar yield, and white sugar yield var -
ied substantially among years, indicating a stronger environmental influence on these 
productivity-related traits than on the technological quality attributes.
The Pearson correlation heatmap revealed clear clusters of strongly associated traits in 
sugar beet roots. A pronounced positive correlation was detected among SC, WSC, and 
ECS ( r > 0.9), indicating that these quality-related traits are tightly interlinked (Fig.  1). 
Similarly, Sy and Wsy were highly correlated with each other (r = 0.95). These strong pos-
itive linkages suggest that improvement in one of these traits is likely to be accompanied

In contrast, several strong negative correlations highlight potential trade-offs. Sugar

3.2 Regression analysis
Complementing the correlation analysis, multivariate regression was performed to 
evaluate the independent effects of measured traits on DM percentage and to develop 
predictive models for DM. The mixed-effects regression model revealed that DM 
exerted a significant negative influence on root yield and sodium content, confirming 
Fig. 1 Correlation heatmap of physiological and technological traits in sugar beet roots in multi-year field assess-
ment. Ry: root yield, Sy: sugar yield; Wsy: white sugar yield; Sc: sugar content; Wsc: white sugar content; ECS: extrac-
tion coefficient of sugar; Na: sodium; K: potassium; N: nitrogen; Alc: alkalinity; Ms: molasses sugar
 
Page 7 of 9
Fasahat et al. Discover Plants (2026) 3:402 
that increases in DM are associated with reductions in these variables. In contrast, DM 
had a highly significant positive effect on sugar yield, white sugar yield, sucrose content, 
white sugar content, and extraction coefficient of sugar, indicating that these quality and 
efficiency traits improve with higher DM values. Additionally, molasses sugar content 
was negatively and significantly affected by DM, while potassium and alkalinity showed 
nonsignificant effects, highlighting a lower sensitivity of these traits to variations in DM 
(Table 3).
Together, these results confirm that dry matter is not merely a descriptive trait but an 
integrative marker of physiological efficiency, capturing both carbon allocation and ion 
regulation in sugar beet roots.
4 Discussion
Our study investigates the physiological basis of dry matter variation in sugar beet by 
integrating large-scale phenotypic data with agronomic and quality traits. We hypoth -
esize that dry matter is not merely a descriptive agronomic parameter but a mechanistic 
integrator of carbon assimilation, assimilate partitioning, and ion regulation, governed 
by complex physiological and molecular processes. Although all experiments were con -
ducted at the same location, interannual variation in rainfall, air temperature, and rela -
tive humidity was evident. Such seasonal differences may partly explain the observed 
variability among years and should be considered when interpreting the relationships 
between dry matter and quality traits. Nevertheless, because the objective of the pres -
ent study was to investigate overall associations across a large multi-year dataset rather 
than to quantify genotype × environment interaction, the analyses were performed using 
pooled data.
The observed strong positive correlations between dry matter and sucrose content, 
white sugar yield, and extraction coefficient of sugar suggest that high-dry matter gen -
otypes allocate a greater proportion of photosynthates toward carbohydrate storage in 
roots. This allocation likely involves enhanced phloem loading and unloading mecha -
nisms, mediated by sucrose transporter proteins, which regulate source-to-sink carbon 
flux [14–15]. Such genotypes may exhibit increased activity or expression of these trans-
porters, facilitating sucrose accumulation and contributing to improved sugar yield and 
quality.

Conversely, the significant negative correlations between dry matter and sodium and 
nitrogen contents point toward active ion homeostasis mechanisms in high-dry matter 
genotypes. Efficient exclusion or compartmentalization of Na + through ion transport -
ers family members may reduce ion toxicity and maintain osmotic balance [ 16–17]. 
Similarly, lower nitrogen content suggests a metabolic shift favoring carbon allocation to 
sucrose synthesis over amino acid biosynthesis, reflecting alterations in carbon-nitrogen 
metabolism that optimize sugar accumulation. These physiological adjustments likely 
confer enhanced tolerance to environmental stresses and improved extract purity.
While these correlations align with prior agronomic observations, our study advances 
the field by providing a comprehensive, multi-environment dataset supporting dry mat -
ter as a robust integrative trait linking carbon and ion dynamics in sugar beet roots. 
This insight opens new avenues for molecular and biochemical investigations, such as 
transcriptomic profiling of sucrose transporter and ion channel genes, enzyme activity 
assays related to carbon metabolism, and ionomic analyses to unravel genotype-specific 
regulatory networks.
The year-specific correlation analysis further supported the robustness of the over -
all relationships observed in the pooled dataset (Supplementary Table S3). Despite the 
interannual differences in temperature, and relative humidity (Supplementary Table 
S2), the positive associations of dry matter with sugar content, white sugar content, and 
extraction coefficient of sugar remained consistently strong across all growing seasons. 
Likewise, the negative relationship between dry matter and sodium concentration was 
maintained throughout the study period. By contrast, the relationships between dry 
matter and yield-related traits (root yield, sugar yield, and white sugar yield) showed 
greater year-to-year variation, indicating that these traits are more sensitive to seasonal 
environmental conditions than technological quality traits. These findings suggest that 
dry matter is more closely linked to the physiological processes governing sugar accu -
mulation and impurity regulation than to biomass production per se.
Furthermore, understanding the genetic architecture underlying dry matter varia -
tion will be critical for marker-assisted breeding. Recent genomic studies [ 10] indicate 
substantial genetic diversity associated with dry matter and sucrose traits, suggesting 
that targeted selection for transporter and ion regulation genes could enhance breeding 
efficiency.
In conclusion, dry matter content emerges as a physiologically meaningful marker 
reflecting the interplay between carbon assimilation and ion regulation, rather than a 
simple correlative trait. Incorporating mechanistic insights into dry matter variation will 
facilitate development of superior sugar beet cultivars with optimized yield, quality, and 
stress resilience.

In March 2023, Freie Universität Berlin held a funeral for human remains belonging to 54 individuals which had been uncovered on the previous site of the notorious Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Anthropology, Human Heredity, and Eugenics. These bones were found independently from many hundreds of skulls housed in the Museum für Völkerkunde (Ethnological Museum), in the Königliche Museen zu Berlin (Royal Museums of Berlin) and in the Rasseschädelsammlung (racial type skull collection). Suspecting that the fragments were study items collected from victims of genocides by the German colonial empire in South West Africa, East Africa and the Holocaust by Nazi Germany, the University decided not to investigate their origins, citing the necessity of avoiding what Nazi scientists did in separating people according to a fiction of race (‘ Bone Fragments ,’). Now meshed and indistinct, the bones carry a story back to the provenance of extermination techniques and the longer-running thread in the sinister history of scientific racism in Europe.

title: Liquid Objects
summary: Liquid Objects
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Liquid Objects: Abdulrazak Gurnah and the Material Ecologies of Water offers a consistent reading of Gurnah’s work as oceanic constellations that stretch our dualistic assumptions of human and nonhuman matter. The book attempts to make better sense of these worlds in motion by closely observing the flow of four objects—namely map, breath, border and bone. Each object moves us on a journey into Gurnah’s Indian Ocean worlds and attunes us to the multiplicity of flows that exceed the familiar framework of interpreting them. Keyvan Allahyari shows that Gurnah’s capacious imagination resists our habitual handles of inquiry, and that reading itself always migrates across currents of matter and memory that we can only hope to partially grasp. This book will be an enriching reading for scholars and researchers of literature, cultural studies, Indian Ocean studies and African studies.

Введение 
В современных условиях развития промышленного производства вопросы 
экологической безопасности приобретают все большую значимость. Рост требований к 
качеству промышленной продукции связан не только с ее функциональными и 
эксплуатационными характеристиками, но и с необходимостью контроля параметров, 
оказывающих влияние на безопасность человека, производственной среды и 
окружающей среды. В связи с этим возрастает роль средств измерения, обеспечивающих 
оперативный и достоверный контроль экологически значимых показателей продукции 
[1-4]. 
Традиционные измерительные приборы, применяемые в промышленности и 
лабораторной практике, во многих случаях обеспечивают требуемую точность, однако 
не всегда отличаются достат очной гибкостью, удобством модернизации и широкими 
возможностями визуализации результатов. При изменении состава контролируемых 
параметров, ужесточении требований к качеству продукции или необходимости 
интеграции прибора в цифровую среду возникает потребно сть в более адаптивных 
решениях [5-7]. 
Одним из таких решений являются виртуальные приборы. Виртуальный прибор 
представляет собой программно -аппаратную измерительную систему, в которой 
функции традиционного средства измерения реализуются за счет совмещения 
датчиков, модулей ввода-вывода, вычислительной платформы и специализированного 
программного обеспечения [8 -10]. В отличие от классических приборов, виртуальные 
системы позволяют изменять структуру интерфейса, алгоритмы обработки, форму 
визуализации и сост ав выполняемых функций преимущественно программными 
средствами [11-13]. 
Целью статьи является разработка и обоснование методов построения 
виртуальных приборов экологического контроля качества промышленной продукции. 
Для достижения поставленной цели определ ены требования к виртуальным приборам 
экологического контроля, выделены основные этапы их построения, предложена 
функциональная структура виртуального прибора и определен состав контролируемых 
параметров. 
Постановка задачи 
При экологическом контроле качества промышленной продукции важное 
значение имеют параметры, позволяющие оценивать соответствие продукции и 
условий ее производства установленным требованиям безопасности. В зависимости от 
вида продукции к таким параметрам могут относиться температура, влажность, уровень

запыленности, концентрация газовых примесей, наличие вредных включений и 
стабильность технологического режима [14-16]. 
В рамках настоящей работы предложено рассматривать виртуальный прибор как 
средство измерения и анализа четырех основных экологически значимых параметров: 
температуры, влажности, запылённости и концентрации газовых примесей. Выбор 
именно этих параметров обусловлен тем, что они позволяют оценивать состояние 
производственной среды и косвенно харак теризовать условия обеспечения качества 
промышленной продукции. Температура и влажность влияют на стабильность 
технологических процессов и условия хранения продукции. Запылённость отражает 
уровень загрязнения рабочей зоны и может быть связана с экологической и санитарной 
безопасностью. Концентрация газовых примесей позволяет оценивать состояние 
воздушной среды и наличие вредных выбросов или испарений. Таким образом, 
постановка задачи заключается в разработке методов построения виртуального 
прибора, обеспечи вающего экологический контроль качества промышленной 
продукции за счет интеграции измерительных каналов, программной обработки 
данных, графической визуализации и алгоритмов оценки соответствия 
контролируемых параметров нормативным требованиям. 
Методы исследования 
Для решения поставленной задачи использован комплекс взаимосвязанных 
методов исследования. Системный анализ применен для рассмотрения виртуального 
прибора как целостной системы, включающей измерительный, вычислительный, 
визуализирующий и оценочный уровни. Структурное моделирование использовано для 
разработки функциональной структуры прибора. Сравнительный анализ применялся 
для сопоставления традиционных и виртуальных приборов по критериям гибкости, 
масштабируемости, удобства модернизации и визуализации [17-19].

Методика построения виртуального прибора включает следующие этапы: выбор 
контролируемых параметров; подбор датчиков и каналов ввода; формирование 
структуры виртуального прибора; разработку алгоритмов обработки информации; 
проектирование интерфейса пользователя; оценку результатов контроля (рис.1). На 
этапе проектирования интерфейса формируются цифровые индикаторы, шкалы, 
графики, таблицы, сигналы состояния, кнопки управле ния и средства формирования 
отчета. Предлагаемая методика носит воспроизводимый характер и может быть 
использована при создании виртуальных приборов различного назначения [20]. 
Результаты и их анализ 
В результате исследования была предложена функциональная структура 
виртуального прибора экологического контроля качества промышленной продукции. 
Основу такой структуры составляют взаимосвязанные модули, каждый из которых 
выполняет строго определенную функцию в общем процессе контроля. На первом 
уровне располага ются датчики температуры, влажности, запылённости и 
концентрации газовых примесей. На втором уровне располагается модуль ввода 
данных, обеспечивающий прием сигналов от датчиков и передачу их на дальнейшую 
цифровую обработку (рис.2).

Практический анализ показывает, что виртуальные приборы особенно

title: Life quality and depression in mothers of children with spina bifida: A cross-sectional study
summary: Life quality and depression in mothers of children with spina bifida: A cross-sectional study
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Spina Bifida (SB) frequently manifests with neurological, orthopedic, and urological complications in children, which severely restrict the activities of daily living (ADL) for both the affected children and their families. This cross-sectional study aimed to evaluate how specific functional independence domains, multidimensional quality of life (QoL), and socioeconomic factors in children with Spina Bifida correlate with maternal depression and maternal QoL dimensions. The study sample consisted of 30 children with SB, aged between 2 and 18 years, and their mothers. Children’s functional independence and QoL were assessed using the Pediatric Functional Independence Measure (WeeFIM) and the Children’s Quality of Life Scale (CQLS), respectively. Maternal QoL was evaluated using the Nottingham Health Profile (NHP), and maternal depression levels were assessed via the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). Children’s functional independence demonstrated a moderate and statistically significant negative correlation with maternal QoL ( r =-0.421, p = 0.023; indicating that higher child independence is associated with better maternal QoL) and maternal depression levels ( r =-0.412, p = 0.024). A high, statistically significant negative correlation was found between maternal NHP scores and pediatric QoL ( r =-0.561, p = 0.008; indicating that greater maternal health distress is associated with lower pediatric QoL). Furthermore, a moderate, statistically significant negative correlation was identified between family income level and maternal depression ( r =-0.380, p = 0.03). The study suggests that the compromised quality of life and limited functional independence of children with SB show significant correlations with maternal depression and mothers’ health-related quality of life. Particularly, children’s challenges in self-care, communication, and social interaction, alongside lower family income levels, are closely linked to maternal psychological well-being. These findings underscore the need for integrated, multidisciplinary rehabilitation programs that not only target the child’s functional status but also actively incorporate psychosocial support services to promote overall family health.

title: Fine-scale habitat quality drives isotopic niche variation in a didelphid opossum in fragmented semideciduous dry forests of central Brazil
source: Isotopes in Environmental and Health Studies
summary: Fine-scale habitat quality drives isotopic niche variation in a didelphid opossum in fragmented semideciduous dry forests of central Brazil
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Studies on the effects of habitat fragmentation on animal trophic ecology have traditionally emphasised patch size or habitat loss, while the role of habitat quality has been comparatively overlooked. We investigated how habitat quality – assessed through as fine-scale variation of forest structure and food resource availability within patches – alongside patch attributes and landscape configuration, shapes the isotopic niche of the opossum Gracilinanus agilis in fragmented semideciduous dry forests of the central Brazilian Cerrado. Using a multiscale approach, we investigated the trophic responses of the species to environmental variation across 36 forest patches during two field campaigns conducted in 2018. Small mammals were live-trapped, habitat quality descriptors were quantified, and patch- and landscape-scale metrics (1-km buffer) were measured. Isotopic niche metrics were estimated from δ13C and δ15N values obtained from hair samples. Regression analyses showed that variation in δ¹⁵N range (NR) increased with patch core area, indicating a broader range of trophic levels in larger and better-preserved patches. At the habitat-quality scale, the evenness of niche packing (SDNND) decreased with increasing vine abundance, suggesting that preferential understory use in more degraded forests may increase microhabitat overlap among individuals and leads to a more homogeneous trophic structure in isotopic space, with individuals more evenly packed within a narrower isotopic niche. SDNND also declined with higher termite abundance, indicating increased isotopic similarity among individuals as this resource became more intensively exploited. At the patch scale, SDNND increased with patch core area, suggesting greater trophic differentiation among individuals in larger patches with more pristine vegetation. Overall, trophic responses varied across spatial scales, with patch characteristics and habitat quality exerting stronger effects than landscape-level structure. Our findings highlight the importance of fine-scale environmental conditions in shaping the trophic niche structure and reinforce the need to incorporate habitat quality into fragmentation research.

title: Student internships within higher education institutions: an emergent conceptual typology
summary: Student internships within higher education institutions: an emergent conceptual typology
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Student internships are recognised in scholarly discourse as important, useful opportunities for developing skills, building experience, and aiding employability. However, there are barriers to accessing student internships and inequity of experience. Whilst there is an increasing body of literature on internships facilitated by Higher Education Institutions (HEIs), little literature focuses on internships within HEIs (i.e. with HEIs as internship hosts). In particular, student and staff accounts of their own experiences are under-represented, and there is little consensus on the types of internships offered, responsibilities involved, and factors supporting success. This lack of clarity constitutes a significant barrier to offering opportunities to students in accessible and clear ways, heightening inequities. Therefore, the purpose of this project was to gain insight into the types of internships on offer within HEIs. The project used an applied qualitative approach and a grounded theoretical methodology to analyse the perceptions of student interns and HEI staff within a Scottish university. Key findings indicate a wide range of internship types, responsibilities and experiences. This has informed the creation of a new theoretical conceptualisation of HEI internships: a hierarchical typology of internship types. This will be useful for any HEI offering internships, aiding clear communication about internships offered.

title: No-reference image quality assessment via multihead cross-scale attention fusion and contrastive ranking loss
source: Fourth Asia Conference on Advances in Image Processing (AAIP 2026)
summary: No-reference image quality assessment via multihead cross-scale attention fusion and contrastive ranking loss
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

No-Reference Image Quality Assessment (NR-IQA) must predict perceptual quality scores directly from distorted images without access to any pristine reference, making it substantially more challenging than full-reference approaches. While Transformer-based frameworks have recently advanced the state of the art, existing methods still leave room for improvement in cross-layer multi-scale feature interaction, the density of ranking supervision extracted from each training batch, and the spatial adaptability of the attention mechanism. Taking a code-reproduced TReS as the baseline, this paper introduces three targeted enhancements. First, a Multi-Head Cross-Scale Attention Fusion (MCSAF) module applies multihead self-attention to the concatenated feature sequences from different ResNet-50 layers, allowing each scale’s contribution to adapt to the input content instead of being determined by naive concatenation. Second, an Advanced Contrastive Ranking Loss extends TReS’s triplet loss—which exploits only the extreme-quality sample pair within each batch—into a joint formulation comprising all-pair dynamic-margin ranking, hard negative mining, and temperature-scaled InfoNCE contrastive learning; this raises the effective supervision density from 𝑂(1) to 𝑂(𝐵 2 ) with no additional inference cost. Third, a Deformable Attention mechanism with Learnable Position Encoding replaces fixed sinusoidal codes with end-to-end optimizable row-column embeddings and uses a lightweight offset MLP to predict 𝐾 sampling points per query, reducing attention complexity from 𝑂(𝑁2 ) to 𝑂(𝑁𝑀𝐾). Experiments on LIVE, CSIQ, TID2013, LIVEC, and KonIQ-10K show state-of-the-art results on all three synthetic benchmarks (CSIQ SROCC/PLCC: 0.9465/0.9593, +4.0%/+2.8% over baseline) and reveal configuration-dependent patterns on authentic-distortion data. Ablation studies consistently identify the Advanced Contrastive Ranking Loss as the most universally effective component.

title: Dynamic adaptive fusion and adversarial alignment model for robust multimodal affective perception in industrial IoT social robots
summary: Dynamic adaptive fusion and adversarial alignment model for robust multimodal affective perception in industrial IoT social robots
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

To achieve natural and robust human–robot interaction, social robots are increasingly serving as key platforms for perception and interaction in smart application scenarios driven by the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), such as collaborative smart manufacturing environments, human–robot co-working production lines, and assistive decision-making tasks in complex, open environments. However, within dynamic, open physical environments, a robot's perceptual modalities are frequently partially compromised due to factors such as sensor occlusion, environmental background noise, lighting variations, or non-cooperative user behaviour. A marked decline has been observed in the subject's emotional intelligence, which is indicative of a significant deterioration. The core challenge of deploying robotic affective intelligence is addressed in this paper through the proposal of a dynamic adaptive multimodal affective perception model for social robots. The model combines the Transformer architecture with adversarial feature alignment techniques, enhancing robustness by simulating uncertain omissions in robotic perception. The model's core is designed to capture intermodal dependencies through a multi-granularity cross-modal interaction module. The model employs an adversarial domain alignment module to reduce feature distribution discrepancies between complete and incomplete perception states. Furthermore, a dynamic feature integration mechanism adaptively assesses the reliability of each modality and adjusts fusion weights. The experimental findings, derived from three publicly available datasets (namely, CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and IEMOCAP), demonstrate that the model attains sentiment recognition accuracies of 84.2%, 83.7%, and 85.1%, respectively, under conditions of modality deficiency. This performance surpasses that of prevailing mainstream approaches, including early fusion, late fusion, tensor fusion, and multimodal transformers. This provides an effective solution for incomplete multimodal affective analysis in practical applications. Furthermore, this study presents a robust and reliable multimodal affective computing framework for intelligent human–robot interaction within IIoT environments, while also offering an effective approach to affective modeling under conditions of incomplete multimodal perception.

title: Age-specific neutralizing antibody levels against human metapneumovirus during the post-COVID-19 pandemic period: a cross-sectional seroepidemiological study in Taizhou city, Eastern China
summary: Age-specific neutralizing antibody levels against human metapneumovirus during the post-COVID-19 pandemic period: a cross-sectional seroepidemiological study in Taizhou city, Eastern China
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

The COVID-19 pandemic has altered the epidemic patterns of human metapneumovirus (hMPV) globally. As no licensed prophylactic products currently exist for hMPV, understanding population immunity is essential for identifying susceptible groups and informing prevention strategies. This study aimed to quantify age-specific hMPV neutralizing antibody (NAb) levels and seroprevalence in the postpandemic period. We analyzed serum samples collected in a previously published community-based cross-sectional sero-epidemiological survey conducted in Taizhou city, eastern China, from June 2 to June 30, 2024, using a multistage, age-stratified sampling design with additional oversampling of children aged < 5 years. Serum samples were tested for hMPV NAb levels via a fluorescence-based microneutralization assay, with seropositivity defined as a titer of 1:30. We estimated geometric mean titers (GMTs) and seroprevalence rates across age groups. Factors associated with the NAb titer were examined using generalized linear models. We also examined the relationship between RSV- and hMPV-specific antibody responses, given their potential cross-reactivity. A total of 1303 participants aged 16 months to 93 years were included. Antibody levels were lowest among children aged 16 to < 36 months (GMT: 217, 95% CI: 159–295). The GMTs increased to 331 among children aged 3–4 years and exceeded 1000 among those aged 5–11 years, remaining elevated throughout life. The highest GMTs were observed in adults aged 65 years and older (1829, 95% CI: 1620–2064). Among children aged < 5 years, NAb titers increased by 74.7% (95% CI: 14.4%–167.0%) for each additional year of age. Approximately 67.8% (137/202) of the participants were seropositive in the age groups of 16 to < 36 months. From 6 years onward, the seroprevalence was close to or reached 100%. Higher RSV prefusion F IgG antibody titers were significantly associated with higher hMPV NAb titers (Spearman’s ρ: 0.302, P < 0.001), which may reflect shared epidemiological exposures, individual differences in immune responses, or possible cross-reactive immunity between the two viruses. This study provides population-based evidence of age-specific hMPV NAb patterns in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period. The relatively low seroprevalence in children aged 16 to < 36 months highlights the importance of continued hMPV surveillance in this potentially susceptible population.

title: Clinically integrated breastfeeding peer counseling to promote breastfeeding equity: Research protocol for patient-centered costs of infant feeding and lactation care
summary: Clinically integrated breastfeeding peer counseling to promote breastfeeding equity: Research protocol for patient-centered costs of infant feeding and lactation care
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Despite national and international recommendations for exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months of age, 44% of infants receive no breastmilk at this important milestone, imposing a significant cost on the US economy vis a vis elevated cardiovascular, infectious, and metabolic disease burden for the mother and infant. However, interventions to increase breastfeeding also come with individual costs that may disproportionately impact parent-infant dyads with lower incomes. These costs may partially explain why dyads who are publicly insured are less likely to meet these breastfeeding recommendations. This paper describes the research protocol to calculate out-of-pocket and opportunity costs related to infant feeding in the Furthering Equity through infant feeding EDucation and S upport (FEEDS) study, a randomized controlled trial of clinically-integrated breastfeeding peer counseling (ci-BPC). We will recruit 990 pregnant individuals delivering across three hospital sites. This protocol will leverage the pragmatic randomized controlled trial of FEEDS. Detailed patient out-of-pocket and opportunity costs will be compared by feeding type (exclusive breastmilk, exclusive formula, mixed feeding). The large, racially and economically diverse sample will permit stratified analyses of patient costs by race and ethnicity, insurance status, and birth delivery site. title: A neighborhood prediction-based quality enhancement method for CRT progressive image reconstruction
source: Fourth Asia Conference on Advances in Image Processing (AAIP 2026)
summary: A neighborhood prediction-based quality enhancement method for CRT progressive image reconstruction
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) represents a grayscale image as multiple residue shadow images and enables progressive reconstruction by introducing moduli step by step. When the available moduli are insufficient and their product is less than 256, the CRT result determines only each pixel’s congruence class rather than a unique grayscale value. Thus, one residue may correspond to several candidates within the range of 0 to 255, and directly rendering the residue can cause structural artifacts. To address this underdetermined reconstruction problem, we propose a pixel-domain neighborhood prediction method. For each pixel, feasible candidates are enumerated from the current CRT residue using the current modulus product as the step size. A lightweight predictor based on the already reconstructed left and upper neighbors then estimates a plausible pixel value, and the candidate closest to this prediction is selected as the output. Experiments using PSNR and SSIM compare conventional CRT progressive reconstruction with the proposed method at different reconstruction levels. Results show that when the modulus product is below 256, the proposed method consistently improves objective quality and visual structural consistency without additional transmitted information. As more moduli are introduced, reconstruction ambiguity decreases and the recovered image becomes more accurate.

title: Assessment of Nomophobia and Its Correlation with Sleep Quality in Medical Students of North-western Region of Uttar Pradesh: A Cross-sectional Study
summary: Assessment of Nomophobia and Its Correlation with Sleep Quality in Medical Students of North-western Region of Uttar Pradesh: A Cross-sectional Study
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Background: Nomophobia, or the fear of being without a mobile phone, is an emerging psychological condition that raises concerns among medical students.Medical students show a high dependency on smartphones for academic and social purposes, which may expose them to sleep deprivation.To assess its significance, this study examines the relationship between nomophobia and sleep quality among medical students.Objective:• To estimate the prevalence of nomophobia among medical students.• To evaluate the sleep quality of medical students.• To investigate the association and correlation between the nomophobia questionnaire (NMP-Q) score and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI score). Materials and methods:A cross-sectional study was conducted among 100 1st-year medical students at Government Medical College in the North-Western Uttar Pradesh region.The severity of nomophobia and the sleep quality of all participants were assessed using the NMP-Q and the PSQI, respectively.Informed consent was obtained from the participants before data collection began.Later, this data was collected and analyzed using Excel to determine the correlation between nomophobia scores and sleep quality indices for each student.Results: Out of the 100 participants, 54% were men and 46% were women, with the majority belonging to the 18-20 years age-group (55%).Moderate nomophobia was observed in 66% of students and severe nomophobia in 20%.Poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5) was observed in 62% of the participants.Although a higher proportion of poor sleep quality was observed among students with moderate and severe nomophobia, the association was not statistically significant (χ 2 = 2.53, p = 0.11).However, a weak positive correlation was observed between nomophobia and PSQI scores (Spearman's r s = 0.20, p = 0.03).Conclusion: Nomophobia and poor sleep quality were commonly observed among medical students.A weak positive correlation was found between nomophobia and sleep quality; however, no statistically significant association was observed in the categorical analysis.These findings suggest a possible relationship but do not establish causation.Further studies are required to explore this relationship and its implications for mental well-being and academic performance.

title: Multi-task CNN–LSTM architecture with hybrid PSO–GWO optimization and SHAP explainability for joint prediction of urban air quality and health impact
source: International Journal of Computers and Applications
summary: Multi-task CNN–LSTM architecture with hybrid PSO–GWO optimization and SHAP explainability for joint prediction of urban air quality and health impact
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Health risks and accurate air quality prediction play a crucial role in the environmental surveillance and protection of the public health. Current methods are limited to single task classification of Air Quality Index (AQI) with few features and do not consider estimating the health impacts or multi-modal environmental data. The study proposes a new multi-task CNN-LSTM deep learning model, which simultaneously predicts the category of AQI and the health impact scale score with two output heads. The three different data modalities, including pollution indicators, meteorological variables, and anthropogenic activity factors, are combined into one multi-modal data type in the framework. The branches of the CNN are used to draw the interactions between spatial features of each mode, whereas the LSTM layers simulate the temporal environmental relationship. A hybrid PSO-GWO algorithm is dynamically adjusting model hyperparameters, and SHAP is multi-level explainable. The proposed model shows AQI classification accuracy of 95.30%, macro ROC-AUC of 0.9919, and health impact prediction R2 = 0.8945. SHAP indicates CO, proximity to industries, and NO2 as main drivers of AQI, whereas PM10, industrial proximity, and CO are predominant for health risk. The suggested framework presents an explainable, and implementable resolution to smart environmental monitoring and population health decision-making.

Atmospheric water harvesting (AWH) is limited by the high energy demand for
sorbent regeneration, while batterythermal management dissipates sub-
stantial low-grade heat unused. Here, we propose a thermally symbiotic
architecture integrating these systems. Battery discharge waste heat regen-
erates a MOF-303 sorbent layer via desorption, while the sorption process
passively stabilizes battery temperature. The sorbent’s regeneration enthalpy
aligns with the battery’s thermal output, triggering desorption under−12 to
−20 A discharge. Within 46 min, the MOF exceeds 50 °C, releasing vapor for
condensation in a sealed setup. Concurrently, sorption extracts heat from the
battery, reducing peak temperatures by ~10 °C. Notably, this integrated system
achieves a water production rate of 1.39 g g−1 day−1, a 117% increase over solar-
driven counterparts. Finite-element simulations validate the heat transfer
dynamics and identify key thermal efﬁciency parameters. This work estab-
lishes a closed-loop thermal cycle that repurposes energy-storage waste heat
to power AWH, enabling sorbent regeneration without solar heating. The
strategy offers a pathway to enhance thermal efﬁciency across various energy
and environmental systems through internal heat recovery.
In nature, symbiotic relationships represent ﬁnely tuned mutualistic
interactions, wherein two distinct organisms co-evolve to establish
interdependent systems that improve survival, resilience, and ecolo-
gical ﬁtness. For example, the human gastrointestinal tract hosts
trillions of microorganisms that facilitate nutrient breakdown, syn-
thesize essential vitamins, and provide a protective barrier against
pathogens. In return, these microbes inhabit a nutrient-rich, stable
environment supported by the host 1,2. A similarly interdependent

In engineered thermal systems, symbiotic coupling of compo-
nents with opposing thermal requirements offers an opportunity to
enable efﬁcient energy utilization. Lithium-ion batteries—compared to
traditional battery chemistries such as nickel–cadmium, nickel–metal
hydride, and lead –acid—provide a superior combination of high
energy density, long cycle life, minimal self-discharge, high voltage,
low maintenance, and rapid charging 7,8. However, lithium batteries
generate signiﬁcant heat during discharge due to internal resistance
and electrochemical reactions, which can lead to thermal runaway
once it rises to overtemperature 9–11. In this hazardous condition, the
battery’s temperature increases uncontrollably, potentially causing
ﬁres or explosions12,13. To mitigate this risk, battery thermal manage-
ment (BTM) is widely employed to enhance the battery ’s heat dis-
sipation capabilities, which is crucial for maintaining optimal operating
temperatures below 55 °C and ensuring safety, performance, and
longevity13,14. Based on the cooling medium, BTM can be classiﬁed into
air cooling, liquid cooling, and composite phase change material
(CPCM) cooling BTMs15,16. While effective in limiting thermal buildup,
these cooling strategies are inherently dissipative, discarding the bat-
tery’s thermal energy into the environment without functional recov-
ery, thus representing a major limitation in thermal resource
utilization.
In contrast to BTM systems that require heat extraction, certain
emerging environmental technologies depend on continuous heat
input to function. One such application is sorption-based AWH, which
has gained attention for its ability to extract water vapor from ambient
air and convert it into liquid water 17–19. This technology captures
atmospheric moisture even at low relative humidity (RH) and converts
it into potable water, typically using solar irradiance for desorption20,21.
A key advantage of sorption-based AWH is its geographical adapt-
ability and scalability. The performance of these systems hinges on the
properties of the sorbent materials, primarily MOFs, covalent organic
frameworks (COFs) 22, zeolites 23,s i l i c ag e l24, hygroscopic salts 25,
hydrogels26,27,a n dt h e i rh y b r i d s28–31. Among these, MOFs such as MOF-
30332,M O F - 8 0 133, Al-Fum31,M I L - 1 6 034,a n dU i O - 6 635 stand out due to
their high surface area, tunability, low regeneration temperature, and
exceptional selectivity, enabling adsorption at sub-30% RH
conditions36,37. Recent advances in continuous-operation AWH devices
have enabled multiple adsorption–desorption cycles per day, drama-
tically improving water output. 33,38,39 However, in regions lacking
consistent sunlight or where solar irradiance is insufﬁcient, such sys-
tems struggle to maintain continuous regeneration, prompting alter-
native strategies that require externally paid thermal input 40,41.T h i s
approach may not be viable in resource-limited arid environments,
where both water scarcity and energy access are major constraints37.
Interestingly, the thermal demands of BTM and AWH systems are
inherently complementary: BTM produces low-grade heat that is
typically dissipated, while AWH systems require precisely such low-
grade thermal energy for desorption. The operating temperature
range of lithium batteries during high-rate discharge42 coincides well
with the initial regeneration temperatures of water-saturated MOFs
used in AWH43, creating a thermodynamic basis for coupling the two.
In a conceptual BTM–AWH hybrid system, thermal energy generated
during battery discharge can be redirected to regenerate the sorbent
through passive heat transfer. In an integrated BTM –AWH system,
thermal energy released during battery discharge is harnessed to drive
desorption in the sorbent layer, while the sorbent simultaneously acts
as a thermal sink, which absorbs latent and sensible heat during
moisture uptake, reducing peak b attery temperature and enabling
passive regeneration. This bidirectional exchange, in which the ther-
mal output of one subsystem drives the operation of the other while
simultaneously receiving stabilizing feedback, establishes a closed-
loop, self-regulating partnership. This integrated approach is termed
“Thermal symbiosis ”. It extends beyond traditional unidirectional
waste-heat recovery by forming a mutually reinforcing system that
enhances thermal management and functional output without a
dedicated external heat source for sorbent regeneration.
Despite this conceptual promise, there have been no prior
demonstrations of such a thermally symbiotic strategy, nor estab-
lished frameworks for integrating AWH and BTM subsystems through
direct thermal coupling. To address this gap, we developed a proto-
type system that couples a lithium battery pack with a passive
sorption-based atmospheric water generator (AWG) containing a
MOF-303 layer. This architecture enables bidirectional thermal inter-
action: waste heat from battery discharge is transferred through a
thermally conductive copper-based interface to drive MOF regenera-
tion, while the sorbent layer simultaneously buffers temperature
spikes during cycling. Experimental results show that at a discharge
current of −16 A, the MOF layer passively reaches temperatures above
50 °C within 46 min, initiating effective desorption and moisture
release. Concurrently, the sorption module extracts both latent and
sensible heat, reducing the battery ’s peak temperature by approxi-
mately 10 °C and allowing safe operation under elevated current loads.
To overcome the mismatch in temporal operating pro ﬁles between
battery discharge and sorbent regeneration, we implement an asyn-
chronous strategy in which three battery modules alternately supply
heat to a common AWG unit, enabling up to 15 regeneration cycles
per day without relying on solar heating. Notably, the 24 h continuous
operation enabled a water production rate of 1.39 g(water) g(MOF)
−1 day−1,
a 117% increase over the solar-driven system. This enhancement,
stemming from the doubled operational time and a steady, weather-
independent heat source, establishes the method as a more ef ﬁcient
and reliable strategy, particularly for sun-limited regions.
To elucidate the internal therma l behavior governing this ther-
mally symbiotic system, we performedﬁnite-element thermal simula-
tions that trace spatiotemporal heat-transfer pathways within the
coupled modules. The simulations reveal critical design parameters—
including interface thermal conductivity and battery discharge proﬁles
—that in ﬂuence thermal transport ef ﬁciency and desorption perfor-
mance. Together, our experimental and computational analyses
demonstrate a self-regulating, closed-loop thermal integration strat-
egy that refunctionalizes waste heat from energy storage systems to
drive decentralized water harvesting. This is a report to realize AWH
and BTM as a single thermally symbiotic design. By harmonizing dis-
parate thermal requirements through shared heat infrastructure, this
framework offers a versatile blueprint for integrating heat-intensive
and heat-generating subsystems. The broader principle of “thermal
symbiosis” introduced here can be extended to a wide range of energy
and environmental technologies seeking improved thermal efﬁciency
through intra-system heat circulation.
Results
A thermally symbiotic BTM–AWH architecture
As illustrated in Fig. 1a, AWH with MOFs typically involves a two-step
cycle: adsorption and desorption. Initially, at lower ambient tempera-
tures, the MOF adsorbs water vapour, reaching a hydrated state.
Subsequently, during the regeneration phase, the temperature is ele-
vated—typically above 40 °C—inducing desorption and returning the
MOF to a dehydrated state 39,44. This desorption step is energy-inten-
sive, often requiring an external heat source. Interestingly, this heat
demand aligns with the thermal management characteristics of
lithium-ion batteries. During operation, batteries generate signiﬁcant
