waste heat, which must be dissipated to maintain temperatures below
a safe operating threshold of 55 °C. This creates a complementary
supply-demand relationship: the AWH system requires heat for deso-
rption, while the battery produces excess heat that must be removed.
We captured infrared images of battery packs with and without an
integrated MOF-based AWH system. Under identical discharge condi-
tions, the battery pack with the B TM-AWH system exhibited a lower
temperature. This temperature reduction indicates that a portion of
the battery’s waste heat was transferred to drive the AWH process,
thereby supporting the concept of thermal symbiosis.
The system comprised two main components, as depicted in
Fig. 1b. The ﬁrst component, referred to as the sorption unit, consisted
of a 2.5 × 6.5 × 7.5 cm copper container housing a 5 g MOF-303 layer for
water absorption and desorption processes (Suppl. Fig. 1). MOF-
30332,43, which has superior adsorption kinetics compared to other
benchmark MOFs or salts under arid conditions (Suppl. Table 5), was
characterized in terms of its crystal structure, microstructure, and
pore size distribution (Suppl. Figs. 2–4 and Suppl. Table 1). The MOF
layer reaches adsorption equilibrium within 30–40 min across 20–60%
RH (Suppl. Fig. 40a). Fitted with a pseudo‑ﬁrst‑order kinetic model, the
adsorption rate constant (k1, Suppl. Equation 6) at 30% RH and 25 °C
was determined to be 0.14 min−1 (Suppl. Fig. 40b, Suppl. Table 4). This
copper container with high thermal conductivity facilitated heat
transfer between the two components, reducing interfacial thermal
resistance. The second component was a 14 Ah battery pack, assem-
bled with four 3.5 Ah lithium cells in parallel using nickel sheets, which
was further encased in plastic support for shape stabilization and
partial heat insulation (Suppl. Fig. 5). To ensure optimal contact within
the system, silicone thermal grease with a high thermal conductivity of
approximately 5 W m−1 K−1 was utilized to ﬁll the air gaps between the
sorption unit and battery pack (Suppl. Figs. 6 and 7). The silicone layer
is relatively thick and non‑uniform, as illustrated in Suppl. Fig. 43. This
promoted efﬁcient heat transfer by conduction through the silicone
thermal grease, which replaces the air gaps.
In operation, the sorption unit ﬁrst adsorbs atmospheric water
before being coupled with the discharging battery pack to achieve
thermal symbiosis, involving the sorption unit recycling heat from the
battery pack for water desorption, while the battery pack simulta-
neously dissipates heat to the sorption unit. This reciprocal heat
exchange helped maintain the battery pack within a safer temperature
range while concurrently facilitating water production by the
MOF layer.

Across the tested discharge currents, the incorporation of the

the battery pack and MOF. In subsequent discussions, the discharge

Battery waste heat drives sorbent regeneration
The sorption behavior of the sorption unit was examined as follows.
MOF-303 exhibits relatively high desorption energy due to its hydro-
philic functional groups, which strongly interact with water
molecules32,43. In Fig. 3a, MOF-303’s desorption activation energy was
ﬁtted and calculated based on its desorption performance under var-
ious heating rates (Suppl. Fig. 9), using the Kissinger equation 47,48
(Suppl. Equation 1), amounting to approximately 40 kJ mol-1. This value
aligned with the reported literature, indicating its high capacity to
absorb heat generated by the battery pack.
In Fig. 3b, we compared the desorption process to traditional
solar-driven desorption, with MOF layers pre-adsorbing water at 30%
RH and 25 °C for 30 min (Suppl. Fig. 10). Under a 1.0 kW m −2 light
irradiance, the MOF layer was heated to 39 °C in roughly 20 min, due to
limited light absorbance (Suppl. Fig. 11). The solar-driven MOF layer’s
temperature exceeded the battery pack-driven counterpart around
20 min. However, after 20 min, the battery pack-driven MOF layer
displayed a higher temperature, which may lead to a superior
desorption rate.

Cling ﬁlm was employed to seal the sorption element to simulate
an actual AWG, creating a simple closed system as depicted in Fig.3c.
Before desorption (discharge), there was no water vapor condensation
on the inner cling ﬁlm (Suppl. Fig. 12). During discharge, heat was
transferred from the battery pack to the MOFs for desorption, leading
to a closed cavity with high water vapor partial pressure due to the
abundance of desorbed water. Concurrently, the copper container ’s
temperature increased due to its high thermal conductivity. This
temperature rise increased the air temperature within the cavity due to
heat transfer from the heated copper container, accompanied by
convective air mixing. The temperature gradient led to cooling of the
inner cling ﬁlm surface, facilitating condensation of water vapor, as
illustrated in Fig.3d. This lab-scale AWG experiment demonstrated the
potential for water production facilitated by the battery pack.
Battery pack-driven water production can be achieved without
sunlight, broadening the application of sorbents in regions with lim-
ited sunlight and extending their daily production time to increase
water yield. In this study, we initially employed an isochronous and
one-to-one mapping approach, pairing one sorption unit with one
battery pack during the thermal symbiosis process. To preserve bat-
tery life, the charging current was limited to 0.5 C (7 A), resulting in a
charging time of approximately 133 min (Suppl. Fig. 13). As illustrated
in Fig. 3e (the clearer schematic diagram is shown in Suppl. Fig. 39),
one cycle consisted of a 62 min desorption and water generation
period (during this period, the battery pack completed the discharge
process), followed by a 30 min adsorption period at 30% RH and 25 °C
(Supplementary Fig. 10), allowing the sorption to equalize. Con-
currently, the battery pack began recharging for 133 min. However, the
battery pack’s charging time exceeded the sorption unit’s adsorption
time, creating a timing mismatch in which the battery pack required
more time before initiating the next sorption cycle. Consequently, one
cycling time of the sorption unit was extended to approximately
195 min, including a 62 min water generation and a 133 min sorption
unit’s charge time, which reduced the daily (24 h) theoretical cycle
number to only 7 times.
In contrast to the isochronous battery-to-sorbent pairing, we
adopted an asynchronous con ﬁguration that eliminates downtime
associated with the battery ’s prolonged charging period. By coordi-
nating three battery packs (Packs 1, 2, and 3) with a single sorption unit,
the system enables continuous regeneration cycles —eliminating the
need to wait for the same pack to recharge. As shown in Fig. 3e, the
sorption unit can complete one cycle in 92 min using a single battery
pack. The three battery packs contributed to water generation during
the 0 –92, 92 –184, and 184 –276 min intervals, respectively. After
completing its ﬁrst discharge, Pack 1 had enough time to charge,
preparing for its second water generation cycle at 276 min. This
asynchronous design reduced the sorption unit’s cycle time to 92 min,
increasing its theoretical daily cycle count to 15, representing a 114%
improvement over the isochronous con ﬁguration. The increased
production frequency of the BTM-AWH system resulted in a higher
daily water yield than that achievable under standard 1.0 kW m−2 solar
irradiance, the typical condition for AWH, as conclusively demon-
strated in Fig. 5.
MOF-303 is well recognized for its exceptional stability. To eval-
uate its cycling stability, we tested the adsorption behavior of MOF-
303 after 50 sorption cycles; the detailed procedure is provided in the
Supporting Information (Supplem entary Fig. 14). Notably, the
adsorption kinetics of MOF ‑303 showed minimal change over 50
cycles, as supported by nearly identical pore ‑size distributions, pre-
served crystalline frameworks, and stable granular morphology
(Suppl. Figs. 2–4). This structural and performance consistency high-
lights the material’s robustness and strongly indicates the long ‑term
operational stability potential of the BTM‑AWH system. Moreover, the
introduction of the AWH module enhances the long‑term performance
of the battery pack, manifesting as superior electrochemical char-
acteristics (Suppl. Fig. 45).

body consisted of a transparent acrylic plate (Suppl. Fig. 34), inside
which the BTM-AWH unit was housed. A semiconductor cooler was

The bottom of the chamber was insulated to minimize heat loss,

Under dynamic conditions (e.g., vibration or tilting), liquid con-
densate may leak or accumulate near electrical contacts, thereby
posing a risk of short circuits or insulation failure. To mitigate this risk
in future practical designs, the following safety measures are pro-
posed: First, electrical contacts should be insulated and physically
separated from the condensate pathway to reduce the risk of moisture
exposure. Second, structural optimization of the prototype is sug-
gested: as illustrated in Suppl. Fig. 44, securing the BTM-AWH assem-
bly with a ﬁxed cover can help mitigate vibration and tilting while also
shielding the assembly from dripping water. Furthermore, elevating
the assembly on a platform would allow any condensate toﬂow safely
beneath it, ensuring no direct contact between water and electrical
components.
Discussion
This study introduces a thermo-symbiotic system in which waste heat
generated during battery discharge drives MOF-based atmospheric
water harvesting, while the sorption unit concurrently moderates the
battery temperature. The coupled system effectively utilizes battery
waste heat to drive MOF desorption, maintaining safe operating tem-
peratures (below 55 °C) under high discharge currents while simulta-
neously achieving a substantial enhancement in water yield compared
to solar-driven analogues. The implementation of an asynchronous
operational mode further enables continuous operation without solar
heating for sorbent regeneration. These results collectively demon-
strate a scalable strategy for synergistic energy and water manage-
ment. Beyond the speci ﬁcc o n ﬁguration presented, the “thermo-
symbiosis” framework is generalizable. Its core principle—repurposing
low-grade waste heat for a useful thermal demand—c a nb ee x t e n d e dt o
larger battery systems (e.g., in electric vehicles or stationary storage)
and is compatible with other sorbents featuring low regeneration
temperatures. This design offers a practical solution for off-grid or
resource-constrained environments, such as telecommunication sta-
tions or remote facilities, where concurrent thermal management and
water supply are critical. Looking forward, this work opens promising
avenues for material innovation (e.g., composites with enhanced
thermal properties) and system-level integration with renewable
energy sources, paving the way toward fully autonomous, sustainable
water-energy systems. Thus, the present study not only establishes a
functional prototype but also provides a versatile blueprint for
synergistic resource recovery in a wide range of applications.

Materials
Aluminum nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO)3·9H2O, AR) and sodium acet-

Preparation of MOF-303
Dissolve 1.88 g Al(NO) 3·9H2O in 10 mL deionized water, denoted as
Solution-1. Dissolve 0.78 g C5H4N2O4·H2Oa n d0 . 6 gN a O Hi n t o1 5 m L
deionized water, denoted as Solution-2. Mix two solutions by pouring
Solution-2 drop-by-drop into Solution-1. Stir the mixture and place it at
100 °C for 24 h, and clean the residue with deionized water twice. Dry
the residue in a 120 °C vacuum oven for 24 h.
Preparation of the CPCM
A PCM solution was prepared by dissolving 7.2 g Na 2S2O3·5H2O, 2.8 g
CH3COONa·3H2O, and 0.2 g SrCl 2·6H2O in a sealed glass bottle. The
mixture was stirred at 70 °C for 3 h. Subsequently, 8.5 g of the resulting
liquid PCM was added dropwise to 1.5 g of EG under physical stirring to
form the CPCM.
Program setting of the battery pack
The battery pack discharges at constant currents of −12, −1 4 ,- 1 6 ,- 1 8 ,
and -20 A until the voltage decreases to 2.7 V. The battery pack is then
charged at a constant current of 7 A until the voltage reaches 4.25 V,
followed by constant-voltage charging at 4.25 V until the current
decreases to 0.7 A.

title: Peripheral pachymetry, eccentricity, and composite tomographic-biomechanical indices for screening forme fruste/suspect keratoconus
summary: Peripheral pachymetry, eccentricity, and composite tomographic-biomechanical indices for screening forme fruste/suspect keratoconus
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Early identification of forme fruste or suspect keratoconus is challenging because curvature-based parameters may remain near normal. This study evaluated Pentacam HR- and Corvis ST-derived parameters across normal, forme fruste/suspect keratoconus, and clinical keratoconus eyes. This single-center retrospective cross-sectional study included eyes examined at Beijing Tongren Hospital from January 2020 to December 2022. Eyes were classified as normal (NOR), forme fruste/suspect keratoconus (DUN), or clinical keratoconus (KCN). Pentacam-derived structural parameters and Corvis ST-derived composite indices were compared among groups. Generalized estimating equations and one-eye-per-patient analyses were used to assess inter-eye correlation. Receiver operating characteristic curves with 95% confidence intervals and DeLong comparisons were generated for NOR-versus-DUN discrimination. The study included 600 eyes: 272 NOR eyes from 136 patients, 51 DUN eyes from 51 patients, and 277 KCN eyes from 168 patients. Kmax was similar between NOR and DUN eyes (45.14 ± 1.64 D vs. 45.24 ± 1.79 D, P = 0.994), but higher in KCN eyes (55.47 ± 9.20 D; both P < 0.001). PachyMin decreased stepwise from NOR to DUN and KCN eyes (533.16 ± 29.42, 506.45 ± 26.49, and 461.88 ± 46.54 μm; all pairwise P < 0.001). For NOR-versus-DUN discrimination, EccInf had an AUC of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.727–0.902), followed by Cor.Vol (0.770; 95% CI, 0.695–0.844). Among composite indices, TBI had the numerically highest AUC (0.759; 95% CI, 0.680–0.839), followed by BAD-D (0.751; 95% CI, 0.677–0.824), CBI (0.668; 95% CI, 0.583–0.753), and SSI (0.666; 95% CI, 0.588–0.744). Sensitivity analyses did not materially change the interpretation. Pentacam HR and Corvis ST parameters showed distinct patterns across the NOR-DUN-KCN spectrum. Peripheral structural parameters and composite indices helped distinguish clinically defined NOR from DUN eyes, supporting layered screening interpretation rather than parameter superiority or longitudinal disease staging.

title: Quality 4.0 Frameworks in Smart Cities
summary: Quality 4.0 Frameworks in Smart Cities
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Quality 4.0 is conceptualized as an integrative governance approach for smart cities within the present chapter. Quality 4.0 is positioned here as an enabling layer that reframes the set of known quality governance standards in the context of digitalization, data availability, and multi-stakeholder governance. It critically reviews the application of traditional standards and approaches—ISO management system approaches, Six Sigma methodologies, and Total Quality Management approaches—as its architectural, analytical, and cultural constituents that can be enhanced by Internet of Things (IoT)–based digital enablement of artificial intelligence (AI) for the purpose of converting static quality compliance approaches into dynamic learning-driven operation architectures. It also reviews the principal challenges of smart cities that require holistic data availability with institutional fragmentation, long time scales of operation, regulatory restrictiveness, and social differentiation. Quality 4.0 is outlined as providing the aforementioned necessary enabling infrastructure for smart cities without obstructing the need for politics in smart decision-making. It also presents the complete Smart City Quality 4.0 Framework with its constituents of multidimensional quality of cities, architectural governance through processes, and domain architectures in modularity with feedback loops in connectivity with social resilience through risk management. It concludes by affirming that Quality 4.0 offers the long-awaited enabling infrastructure in smart city policy for energizing strategic governance of smart cities with real-time processes in its learning organizational capacities in decision-making.

Abstract
Developing cost-effective bifunctional electrocatalysts is important for sustainable and clean energy production. 
Herein, a hierarchical NiFe layered double hydroxide integrated with MnO 2 nanorods and single-walled car -
bon nanotubes (NiFe-LDH@MnO2/SWCNT) was synthesized to enhance bifunctional catalytic activity toward 
oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). The synergistic coupling between 
Ni and Fe promotes high-valent Ni active sites that facilitate OH⁻ adsorption and accelerate OER kinetics, 
whereas synergistic adsorption of hydrogen and hydroxyl intermediates facilitates improved HER performance. 
The incorporation of multivalent MnO2 introduces redox-active centers that enhance electron transfer and inter-
mediate formation, whereas the conductive SWCNT framework provides rapid charge transport and increased 
electrochemically active surface area. Among the synthesized catalysts, NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT exhibits 
superior electrocatalytic performance, with low overpotentials of 206 mV for OER and 198 mV for HER at 
10 mA cm-2 with a small OER Tafel slope of 33 mV dec -1. Comparative analyses demonstrate that the catalyst 
outperforms several previously reported NiFe-LDH and MnO 2-based systems, exhibiting faster reaction kinet -
ics and improved efficiency. The enhanced activity achieved from hierarchical architecture, improved electro -
lyte diffusion, and strong interfacial electronic coupling. These results reveal that NiFe-LDH@MnO 2/SWCNT 
is a promising electrocatalyst for efficient overall water splitting.

Introduction
Water electrolysis via electrocatalysis is emerging as a leading method for producing hydrogen (H2) and oxygen 
(O2) from water, offering a clean, sustainable pathway for energy production. As an environmentally friendly 
technology, it avoids greenhouse gas emissions and offers a viable alternative to fossil-fuel–based energy sources. 
Moreover, its scalability makes it attractive for industrial applications 1,2. The minimum theoretical cell voltage 
required for water splitting is 1.23 V , corresponding to a Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) of 237.1 kJ mol -1. In 
practice, the required voltage exceeds this value due to sluggish kinetics of the hydrogen evolution reaction

(HER) and the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), which significantly reduce energy conversion efficiency. 
Reducing the overpotential associated with these reactions is therefore critical, and the development of efficient 
electrocatalysts plays a central role in improving overall performance. While noble-metal-based catalysts, such as 
Pt (for HER) and Ru/Ir oxides (for OER), remain the benchmarks, their high cost and limited availability hinder 
their widespread deployment. As a result, considerable research has focused on discovering cost-effective and 
durable alternatives3. Among these, transition–metal–based materials, including phosphides4, sulfides5, oxides6, 
nitrides1,7, and hydroxides8, have shown great potential for enhancing both HER and OER activities.
Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) have attracted considerable interest as bifunctional catalysts for both HER 
and OER 9. In these two-dimensional materials, transition-metal cations occupy octahedral sites within MO 6, 
while charge-compensating anions reside between stacked layers. LDHs composed of Fe, Co, and Ni are particu-
larly effective under alkaline conditions: incorporation of trace Fe into Ni(OH) 2 markedly improves OER activ-
ity by enhancing interfacial conductivity 10,11. Among them, NiFe-LDH stands out due to its unique electronic 
structure, large specific surface area, and tunable interlayer chemistry, which together confer excellent catalytic 
performance. Indeed, the identity of the intercalated anion can modulate the electron density at active sites and 
thus strongly influence OER kinetics12–14. In particular, Reevesite-type NiFe-LDH, a naturally occurring hydro-
talcite-phase mineral, showed enhanced OER activity compared to conventional NiFe-LDH. This improvement 
is attributed to potential-induced contraction of the M–O bond at Ni and Fe centers, which optimizes the adsorp-
tion energies of oxygen intermediates and lowers overpotentials. Moreover, the strong electronic interactions 
between Ni and Fe facilitate efficient redox transitions and accelerate charge-transfer processes15.
The intrinsic activity of NiFe-LDH can be further boosted through hybridization with conductive carbon nano-
materials such as carbon nanotubes, graphitic carbon nitride, and graphene 16,17. These carbonaceous scaffolds 
(i) provide rapid electron pathways, (ii) supply additional catalytic sites, (iii) suppress nanosheet agglomeration, 
and (iv) facilitate mass transport of reactants and products18,19. For example, coupling NiFe-LDH with graphene 
oxide yields a highly percolated network that accelerates both charge transfer and mass diffusion 20. Likewise, 
single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT)–In2O3 heterostructures promote electron transfer through the metallic 
nanotube backbone while In 2O3 enhances the adsorption of water and reaction intermediates 21. Uniform wrap-
ping of MnO2 around multiwalled CNTs has been shown to increase catalytic activity dramatically, and SWCNTs 
themselves afford high conductivity, a large surface area, and favorable hydrogen-adsorption energetics 22–24. 
MnO2 is an earth-abundant material, making it an attractive co-catalyst. Mixed-valent Mn4+/Mn3+ centres facili-
tate rapid redox cycling, significantly enhancing the electrocatalytic performance of OER and HER. Furthermore, 
the unique crystallographic structure of MnO2, arising from the arrangement of MnO6 octahedra, improves elec-
trocatalytic efficiency25,26. These structural features translate into low charge-transfer resistance and strong O 2 
adsorption, resulting in superior OER performance for MnO2 relative to many other first-row oxides MnO2 com-
pared with many conventional first-row transition-metal oxides27,28. Incorporating Mn into NiFe-LDH has been 
shown to modulate its electronic structure and catalytic behavior further. Mn doping introduces hybrid energy 
levels between the Ni 3d and O 2p orbitals, effectively narrowing the band gap and improving electrical conduc-
tivity. This modification also reduces the Gibbs free energy required for the adsorption and conversion of oxygen 
intermediates, thereby facilitating the Ni2+ → Ni3+/Ni4+ transition, which is important for efficient OER kinetics. 
Moreover, Mn incorporation optimizes the electron density distribution around Ni and Fe centers, enhancing 
their ability to adsorb and activate reaction intermediates and thereby improving the overall catalytic efficiency 
of NiFe-LDH-based catalysts29,30.
Despite extensive studies on NiFe-LDH-based electrocatalysts, achieving low overpotentials and rapid OER 
kinetics remains a key challenge. Previously reported systems such as Ni 2Fe1-LDH/rGO/NF (228 mV , 37.9 mV 
dec− 1)31, NiMoO4/NiFe-LDH/rGO (270 mV , 76.2 mV dec− 1)32, and NiFe-LDH/Ti3C2Tx–rGO (~ 235 mV , ~ 40 
mV dec− 1)33 highlight the need for further enhancement in catalytic efficiency. The present NiFe-LDH integrated 
with SWCNT and MnO 2 exhibited a lower Tafel slope (~ 33 mV dec − 1) and reduced overpotential, indicating 
faster kinetics and improved charge-transfer efficiency. This enhanced performance is attributed to the synergistic

transport and increases active site accessibility. Notably, the exploration of the Reevesite phase combined with 
such a ternary architecture provides a unique strategy that remains largely unexplored for overall water splitting

Experimental section
Materials and chemicals
All chemicals used, such as ferric nitrate nonahydrate, nickel (II) nitrate hexahydrate, and urea, were obtained 
from SRL, India. Super black and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) were sourced from Sigma-Aldrich, while 
single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) and potassium permanganate were supplied by Nano Research Ele -
ments and Merck, respectively. Deionized water purified through a Milli-Q system was used in all procedures. 
All chemicals were of high purity and used without further purification, with specifications as provided by the 
respective suppliers.
Synthesis of NiFe-LDH
A solution was prepared by dissolving 1 mmol of nickel nitrate hexahydrate and 0.5 mmol of ferric nitrate 
nonahydrate in a mixture of 50 mL of water and 30 mL of ethanol. To this, 4 mmol of urea was introduced, and 
the mixture was stirred until fully mixed. The homogeneous solution was poured into a stainless steel autoclave 
lined with Teflon and subjected to hydrothermal treatment at 120 °C for 16 h. The resulting solid was separated 
by filtration, thoroughly washed with both deionized water and ethanol, and then dried under vacuum at 80 °C.
Synthesis of MnO2/SWCNT
A dispersion of 20 mg of SWCNTs was prepared in 100 mL of deionized water via ultrasonication. To this 
homogeneous suspension, 200 mg of KMnO4 was added, and the mixture was stirred continuously for 1 h. Sub-
sequently, concentrated hydrochloric acid was slowly introduced to reduce the permanganate ions, and stirring 
was continued for an additional hour. The resulting mixture was transferred to a Teflon-lined stainless steel auto-
clave and subjected to hydrothermal treatment at 140 °C for 1 h. After naturally cooling to room temperature, the 
product was washed thoroughly with deionized water and ethanol to remove residual reactants and impurities, 
followed by drying at 70 °C.
Synthesis of NiFe-LDH@MnO2/SWCNT
MnO2/SWCNT (1, 3, 5 mg) was dispersed in a 1:1 mixture of DI water and ethanol for 1 h, and then the NiFe-
LDH synthesis procedure was followed for the synthesis of NiFe-LDH@MnO 2/SWCNT. The 1, 3, and 5 mg 
MnO2/SWCNT samples with NiFe-LDH are named NiFe-LDH@1-MnO 2/SWCNT, NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/
SWCNT, and NiFe-LDH@5-MnO2/SWCNT, respectively. The schematic representation of the synthesis proce-
dure is given in Fig. 1.

Material characterization
The samples were characterized using various techniques, including XRD on a PANalytical EMPYREAN instru-
ment, SEM on a Carl Zeiss EVO 10 microscope, HR-TEM on a JEOL JEM-2100 Plus microscope, and XPS on 
a ThermoScientific K-Alpha instrument.
Electrochemical measurements
The electrochemical tests were performed using a Squidstat™ Plus electrochemical workstation in a three-elec -
trode setup with Hg/HgO reference electrode and graphite rod counter electrode. The graphite rod counter elec -
trode was used to avoid possible interference from Pt-based counter electrodes during HER measurements, while 
Hg/HgO was selected as a pH-compatible reference electrode for alkaline electrolyte, providing a stable refer -
ence potential in 1.0 M KOH34,35. The working electrode was prepared by coating a nickel foam piece (1 cm x1 
cm) with a catalyst slurry, comprising the catalyst, carbon black, and PVDF in a 9:0.5:0.5 mass ratio, and drying 
it in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 12 h. The deposited coating mass was approximately 3.5 mg on a 1 cm x 1 cm 
electrode, corresponding to a total loading of ∼3.5 mg cm− 2. Carbon black was used as a conductive additive to 
improve electron transport within the catalyst layer, while PVDF was used as a binder to enhance the adhesion of 
the catalyst on the nickel foam substrate. Control experiments showed that direct coating of the catalyst on nickel 
foam without binder led to poor adhesion and delamination during electrochemical testing. For comparison, bare 
nickel foam and PVDF/CB-coated nickel foam were also evaluated as control electrodes under identical condi -
tions, and the corresponding LSV curves are provided in Fig. S1 and Fig. S2. The electrochemical tests were 
conducted in 1.0 M KOH solution, involving linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) at a scan rate of 5 mV s − 1 and 
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The results were referenced to the reversible hydrogen electrode 
(RHE) using the equation: ERHE = EHg/HgO + 0.059 pH + 0.098. Both the LSV curves and chronopotentiometric 
stability measurements were corrected for solution resistance using iR compensation.

Results and discussion
Structural and morphological analysis of NiFe-LDH@MnO2/SWCNT nanocomposite
XRD analysis revealed the crystal structure of the electrocatalysts, as shown in Fig. 2a and b. The diffraction 
peaks at 11.7°, 19.5°, 34.4°, 39°, and 46.6° for NiFe-LDH and NiFe-LDH@MnO 2/SWCNT correspond to the 
Reevesite crystal phase, indicating the formation of a (Ni, Fe) hydrotalcite structure with carbonate anions in 
the interlayer space. This confirms the formation of NiFe-LDH with carbonate interlayer anions36. The observed 
low-angle reflection at 11.7° corresponds to the basal reflection of the layered hydroxide structure. While the 
relative peak intensities differ slightly from the standard reference pattern (JCPDS No. 26-1286), such varia -
tions are attributed to stacking disorder and imperfect layer alignment, which are commonly observed in layered 
hydroxide materials37. Furthermore, the successful in-situ growth of MnO 2 on SWCNT in MnO 2/SWCNT was 
verified by the appearance of MnO 2 peaks at 22.3°, 34.7°, 37°, 43°, 56.7°, and 62.5° (JCPDS No. 14–0644) in 
Fig. 2b. The peaks corresponding to MnO2 are not distinguishable in the NiFe-LDH@MnO2/SWCNT composite, 
likely due to its low concentration. Therefore, the presence of MnO2 was confirmed by further characterization.
The morphology of the synthesized materials was studied using HR-TEM and SEM analysis. As shown in 
Fig. 3a, the synthesized NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT exhibits a flower-like architecture comprising ultrathin 
nanosheets with expanded interlayer spacing. Notably, Fig. 3a (inset) also reveals separated sheets, indicating 
the presence of both stacked and individual nanosheets. The hierarchical nanosheet structures were developed 
via a two-step process: an initial oxidation reaction followed by crystallization. The nanosheets are stacked into 
a flower-like structure to reduce surface energy. The hierarchical, flower-like morphology of NiFe-LDH provides 
a greater number of surface-active sites, thereby enhancing adsorption and electrochemical performance38. When 
NiFe-LDH is grown in situ on MnO2/SWCNT, the hydrolysis of urea releases OH⁻ ions that react with Ni2+ and 
Fe3+ ions to nucleate into nanosheets on the MnO2/SWCNT surface. As the reaction progresses, these nanosheets 
stack and form a flower-like structure. The SWCNT serves as a conducting network that connects nanosheets and 
microflowers. MnO2 nanorods are evenly distributed between the layers, as inferred from Fig. 3b39. The micro-
graphs of NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT composite further confirmed the sheet-like morphology of NiFe-LDH. 
The images reveal the formation of defect-rich hexagonal nanosheets that interconnect and stack upon each other. 
The characteristic hexagonal shape of LDH is evident in Fig. 3c and d, where MnO2 and SWCNT are embedded 
between the NiFe-LDH sheets. Figure 3e shows the particle size distribution curve, indicating an average MnO2

The Tafel slopes (Fig. 5b) were evaluated to investigate the electrocatalytic reaction kinetics using the equation 
η = b log j + a, where η is the overpotential, b is the Tafel slope, j is the current density, and a is the Tafel constant. 
This analysis provides insight into the rate-determining step and efficiency of the catalyst. The Tafel slope was 
evaluated following the standard recommendations for electrocatalytic water-splitting analysis reported by Anan-
tharaj et al.45. The NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT (33 mV dec− 1) possessed a smaller Tafel slope when compared 
to other catalysts NiFe-LDH (62 mV dec− 1), NiFe-LDH@1-MnO2/SWCNT (46 mV dec− 1), and NiFe-LDH@5-
MnO2/SWCNT (41 mV dec− 1). This implies rapid electron transfer and intrinsic activity of the hybrid structure 
in NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT. The observed Tafel slope of less than 40 mV dec− 1 suggests an efficient four-
electron transfer process. Additionally, the oxidation of hydroxide species, oxygen-oxygen bond formation, and 
oxygen evolution co-occur. The electrocatalyst with closely spaced active sites will exhibit a similar mechanism, 
as shown in Fig. 5c46. The chronopotentiometry technique (Fig. 5d) was applied to assess the stability of NiFe-
LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT. The NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT was tested for 48 h at a constant current density of 
50 mA cm− 2. The NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT showed excellent stability of about 98.04%. The observed post-
OER morphology in Fig. 5e and f indicates electrochemical reconstruction of NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT. 
This morphological changes can be attributed to OER-induced surface reconstruction and structural degradation 
of the NiFe-LDH-based composite under alkaline medium. During OER, the surface and edge sites of NiFe-LDH 
actively participate in the reaction, and continuous interaction with OH⁻ species can induce structural changes 
within the layered framework, leading to partial dissolution and reconstruction of the catalyst during prolonged 
OER operation47.

LDH@1-MnO2/SWCNT, and NiFe-LDH@5-MnO2/SWCNT, as shown in Fig. 6a. From the result, it is evident

Table 1 presents the electrocatalytic activity of the synthesized electrocatalysts. The synthesized NiFe-LDH 
composites have shown excellent OER performance and reasonable HER performance. The 3d transition metal 
hydroxide is more active in an alkaline medium. In an alkaline medium, Fe 3+ can induce a high-valency state in 
Ni, facilitating bonding with OH⁻ and promoting water dissociation during the OER. The selective adsorption 
of OH− on Ni-sites forms OH–Niδ+ intermediates, then decomposes to form O2. The synergy between Ni and Fe 
species facilitates water dissociation for HER, with hydrogen adsorption on Ni sites and OH − adsorption on Fe 
sites from Had–Niδ+ and FeOOH intermediates. Additionally, the presence of Fe inhibits the self-oxidation of Ni 
and promotes the dissociation of water into H2 during the HER process49,50. The dispersion of MnO2 nanorods on 
NiFe-LDH and SWCNT increases the electrochemically active sites and conductivity of the composite material, 
NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT. This synergistic combination enhances the inherent OER and HER activity of 
NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT51,52.
A comparative analysis of the electrocatalytic performance of NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT with other 
reported NiFe-LDH composites reveals its superior OER activity, as evident from Fig. 8a. MnO 2 played an 
important role in enhancing the OER performance of the NiFe-LDH. Since MnO 2 enables reversible transitions 
between the Mn 2+, Mn 3+, and Mn 4+ oxidation states, it promotes OER. Additionally, the Mn n+ increases the 
electron transfer from the electrolyte and forms OOH intermediates, which subsequently undergo deprotonation. 
Also, the presence of Mn3+ ions in MnO2 enhances the adsorption of OH− and accelerates the reaction intermedi-
ates. A comparative analysis of MnO 2-based composites for OER revealed that NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT 
outperforms other materials, as evident from Fig. 8b. Notably, the Tafel slope of NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT 
(33 mV/dec) is less than that of other MnO 2-based materials, including CoTe/MnO 2/BN (81 mV/dec) 53, Ni/
MnO2/CC (45 mV/dec)54, and MnO2 anchored N–Ti3C2 MXene (73.2 mV/dec)55. This superior performance is 
attributed to the MnO2 nanorods grown on conductive SWCNTs, which enhance the high-conductivity pathway, 
facilitating high electrolyte diffusion into the LDH layers and thereby reducing the liquid sealing effect. The 
hierarchical structure of NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT composite further enhances the electrocatalytic surface 
area and high electrical conductivity. Although the HER activity of NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT is lower when

compared to other catalysts, as shown in Fig. 8c, optimizing HER performance is important for overall water 
splitting. A slow HER process can increase the overpotential and decrease system efficiency. Future modifica -
tions, such as incorporating HER-active materials or surface engineering, can enhance performance. Overall, the 
use of earth-abundant transition metals, such as Ni, Fe, and Mn, reduces production costs, making large-scale 
applications more economically viable. With its improved electrocatalytic efficiency, stability, and durability, the 
NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT is a promising candidate for electrochemical water splitting.
Conclusion
To summarize, this study successfully synthesized the hierarchical NiFe-LDH with intercalated CO 3
2− and its 
composites via a simple hydrothermal method. The morphological studies of the synthesized electrocatalysts 
were investigated using SEM and HR-TEM analysis. The results revealed that NiFe-LDH exhibited nanosheet 
and micro-flower morphologies. Furthermore, the in-situ growth of NiFe-LDH on MnO 2/SWCNT led to the 
uniform dispersion of MnO 2 nanorods and effective integration of SWCNT within the NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/
SWCNT composite. Electrochemical studies revealed that the optimized NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT exhib-
ited low overpotentials of 206 and 198 mV at 10 mA cm− 2 for OER and HER, respectively. Additionally, the stud-
ies revealed that the heterojunction formed between NiFe-LDH, MnO2, and SWCNT enhanced the conductivity 
and mass-transfer properties of NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT. Notably, the NiFe-LDH@3-MnO 2/SWCNT 
showed enhanced OER performance compared to HER, which can be attributed to the role of MnO2 in enhancing 
the OER performance of NiFe-LDH. MnO 2 facilitates a reversible transition among the Mn 2+, Mn3+, and Mn4+ 
oxidation states, catalyzing the OER and achieving better performance than most reported NiFe-LDH-based 
electrocatalysts. Moreover, the fabricated two-electrode system retained approximately 98.63% of its initial per-
formance after 48 h of continuous operation. The enhanced electrocatalytic activity is attributed to the hierarchi-
cal morphology and hetero-interfaces formed between NiFe-LDH, MnO2, and SWCNT. Our work suggests that 
the NiFe-LDH@3-MnO2/SWCNT can be a cost-effective and efficient catalyst for water-splitting applications.

title: How Equity and Quality Are Considered by Cancer Centers Offering Practice-Integrated Telehealth Visits: A Qualitative Study
summary: How Equity and Quality Are Considered by Cancer Centers Offering Practice-Integrated Telehealth Visits: A Qualitative Study
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

INTRODUCTION: The COVID-19 pandemic forever changed health care delivery and led to a rapid uptake in telehealth visits. However, the quality and equity of these visits compared to in-person visits are unknown. This analysis interviewed oncology practitioners to understand how US-based cancer centers considered care quality and equity in the implementation and sustainability of telehealth programs. METHODS: This qualitative study employed semistructured interviews to explore practitioners' experiences and perceptions regarding care equity and quality within integrated telehealth services. Primary data collection occurred through interviews conducted between October 2021 and January 2023. These interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using qualitative thematic analysis. RESULTS: Four main themes, representing interviews with 39 professionals from 16 organizations, were identified: 1) organization-level diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) efforts remained conceptual and disconnected from oncology telehealth services, 2) equity and quality-related actions were predominately reactive rather than proactive, 3) equity was misinterpreted as providing equal care to all patients, and 4) telehealth quality and equity were not systematically measured or prioritized. DISCUSSION: These findings highlight how organizational DEI efforts did not translate to tangible operational practices in oncology telehealth care. These results suggest limited organization DEI maturity and practice-level accountability for equity and quality and a lack of understanding of equity. CONCLUSION: To deliver high-quality and equitable oncology telehealth, cancer centers and other health care organizations must progress beyond awareness of equity issues. They need to implement concrete resources, support systems, and policies that facilitate effective strategy execution.

title: Quality 4.0 in Smart City Management
summary: Quality 4.0 in Smart City Management
content:
Quality 4.0 in Smart City 
Management
This work introduces Quality 4.0 as an era of advanced quality management 
principles applied in the context of smart cities, blending classical and new 
approaches incorporating digital technologies, data analytics, artificial intel ‑
ligence, and participatory system of governance. The authors define Quality 
4.0 in the smart city as a complex socio‑technical system where high‑quality 
public services emerge from the interplay of data, institutions, and infrastruc‑
ture in relation to citizens and accountability mechanisms.
This book proposes a new interpretative framework for Quality 4.0, target‑
ing its usefulness to operationalizing urban strategies, enabling decision‑mak‑
ing and adaptive systems of public management. The focus areas include 
system interoperability, security and data quality, public confidence and trust 
in the delivery systems, digital inclusion, urban resilience, and institutional 
adaptation and continuous learning. Its main contribution is in the framing of 
citizens as co‑creators of quality public service. In the smart city ecosystem, 
urban user experience, social participation, digital justice, and transparency of 
decision‑making are placed in the middle of the quality management process. 
From this perspective, Quality 4.0 is an instrument of correlation between 
operational efficiency and social responsibility, sustainable development, and 
democratic legitimacy.
The work represents an important contribution to the field of quality man‑
agement, digital transformation in public administration, and smart city devel‑
opment. Due to its interdisciplinary nature, it will find a wide audience among 
researchers, public decision‑makers, urban practitioners, and quality manag‑
ers, as well as all those interested in the future of sustainable and responsible 
urban governance.
Radosław Wolniak is a Full Professor at the Department of Economics and 
Informatics at the Silesian University of Technology (Poland). For over two 
decades, he has been dealing with the issues of quality management, Industry 
4.0, and smart city. He has been listed in Stanford University’s ranking of the 
world’s top 2% scientists.
Joanna Rosak‑Szyrocka, PhD, is an Assistant Professor at the Faculty of 
Management at Częstochowa University of Technology. Her research interests 
focus on quality management and process improvement, increasingly linked 
to digital transformation in Industry 4.0 and Quality 4.0 concepts, as well 
as sustainability‑oriented management topics such as ESG (Environmental, 
Social, and Governance) and responsible innovation. In her scientific output, 
she addresses organizational and technological determinants of efficiency 
and quality in manufacturing and service settings, often emphasizing how 
data‑driven tools (e.g., digital quality systems, analytics, and AI‑related 
solutions) can support continuous improvement and sustainable performance. 
She has been listed in Stanford University’s ranking of the World’s Top 2% 
Scientists.

Introduction
Today modern smart city is complex socio‑technical system, where technol‑
ogy, data, infrastructure, public institutions, and citizens coexist together to 
ensure the growing impact of these digital transformation initiatives on qual‑
ity of urban services. It includes such solutions as the Internet of Things (IoT), 
artificial intelligence (AI), big data, digital twins, management dashboards, 
and predictive analytics that enhance monitoring, assessment, and optimiza ‑
tion of urban processes. Using standards, accountability, data security, re‑
silience, and social participation to ensure a coherent quality management 
system particularly demonstrates the value of these capabilities.
This monograph presents Quality 4.0 in Smart City Management as an 
integrated approach to the quality management process in smart cities. Qual‑
ity 4.0 is perceived as a modern decision‑making paradigm that integrates 
traditional quality tools with advanced digital technologies and the continuous 
learning logic of the urban system. This methodology lays the grounds for a 
process‑oriented and systemic rationale of quality based on ISO standards, 
Total Quality Management, Six Sigma, and Plan–Do–Check–Act (PDCA) 
cycles while reinforcing the city altogether with IoT, AI, big data, digital 
twins, and dashboards to be monitored adaptively in real time with predictive 
analytics.
The discussion begins with the premise that developing smart cities re‑
quires a holistic quality management model that links urban strategy and 
operational processes, metrics, data security and resilience, and citizen ex‑
perience development. Cities create more data and build digital public ser ‑
vices and smart infrastructure; hence, they need systems to integrate multiple 
complex areas as well as mechanisms for continued institutional coordina‑
tion, privacy protection, trust‑building, and public value creation. The areas 
outlined in connection with it are organized by Quality 4.0, enabling quality to 
be perceived as a multilevel and dynamic category involved across the urban 
management processes. The monograph consists of seven 
chapters. Chapter 
1 proposes Quality 4.0 as a smart city management framework, where tradi‑
tional quality standards fit into a digital multi‑stakeholder dynamic urban en‑
vironment. Chapter 2 outlines the major motivating conditions for Quality 4.0

like data privacy, cybersecurity, financial resources, interoperability, and 
technological complexity. 
Chapter 3 emphasizes citizens, trust, participation, 
inclusiveness, and digital equity as essential aspects of the quality of public 
services. Chapter 4 analyzes the articulation between KPIs (Key Performance 
Indicators), models of evaluation, data quality, and digital security. Chapter 5 
describes practical cases of various smart city governance models around the 
world from Eastern Europe and the Global South. Future Trends such as AI, 
digital twins, edge computing, autonomous systems, resilience, and sustain‑
ability are covered in Chapter 6. In Chapter 7 authors sum up key conclusions 
and provide recommendations on the future development of Quality 4.0 as a 
framework for management of smart cities. The monograph recommends an 
innovative Smart City Quality 4.0 Continuous Learning Model presented in 
Figure 0.1.
Quality 
4.0 in smart city management is defined in the model as a con‑
sequence of data, quality‑oriented ecosystems, cybersecurity and privacy, 
resilience and sustainability, interoperability, and citizen experience. And at 
the same time, it suggests urban quality as continuous system learning behav‑
ior that requires not only constant monitoring and analysis but also feedback 
loops, adaptation, and therefore also improvement of public services.
The proposed approach conceives a smart city as one that scores highly 
on quality through its capacity to reconcile the technological efficiency 
of institutions with institutional responsibility concerning social value.

Introduction 3
The components of smart city quality include process efficiency, security and 
privacy, transparency in decision‑making, service accessibility and affordabil‑
ity, infrastructure resilience, environmental sustainability, digital equity, and 
citizen trust. Quality, understood in this latter sense, is not just a matter of 
measuring individual outcomes but rather the ability of the city to learn and 
respond to changes in social, technological, or environmental conditions and 
adjust its services accordingly.
The importance of gathering lessons from cities is also emphasized by the 
monograph. The analyzed cases show that Quality 4.0 evolves in response to 
local institutional, technological, social, and financial factors. For this reason, 
particular importance shall be given to build up the data capacity of the city 
for the responsible use of data, strengthen inter‑organizational coordination 
capacities, enhance citizen engagement, and systematically improve public 
services. Therefore, Quality 4.0 may be perceived as a remedy to the chal ‑
lenges of the real‑time city where data, digital technologies, institutions, and 
citizen co‑generate an ecosystem of urban governance.
As Calabrese, Kloeckl and Ratti (2008) noted, “The real‑time city is now 
reality.” Hence, Quality 4.0 provides a scaffolding for shaping the real‑time 
city into an urban system that learns, cares, secures, and responds to its 
citizens.
We hope that this book becomes a relevant resource where the reader can 
gather knowledge to build alternative understanding and progress in Quality 
4.0 for managing smart cities.

Abstract
Purpose To investigate the clinical application value of multi-parameter imaging with 
dual-layer detector spectral CT (DLCT) for GTH visualization.
Methods A total of 61 patients who underwent abdominal portal venous phase-
enhanced SLCT were retrospectively enrolled. The raw image data were reconstructed 
into 120 kVp conventional images (CI120 kVp) and virtual monoenergetic images 
(VMIs) at 40, 50, 60, and 70 keV (VMI 40−70 keV). Regions of interest (ROIs) were placed 
on the main trunk of GTH and the erector spinae muscle at the corresponding level 
to measure CT values and standard deviations (SD, indicative of image noise). The CT 
values, image noise, signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), and contrast-to-noise ratios (CNRs) 
of VMI and CI120 kVp were analyzed. The image quality and anatomical information 
of each group were subjectively evaluated by integrating three-dimensional (3D) 
reconstruction technology, iodine density map, and effective atomic number (Zeff ) 
map.
Results For GTH visualized on VMI40 keV, the CT value (530.56 ± 82.33 HU), SNR 
(25.34 ± 5.63), and CNR (57.85 ± 12.43) was significantly higher than those of the 
remaining groups (all P < 0.001). Subjective scoring indicated that VMI40 keV achieved 
the optimal image quality and vascular visualization performance. The iodine density 
map demonstrates relatively high density in vascular regions, the Zeff map shows 
distinct coloration between vascular regions and non-vascular areas.
Conclusion VMI 40 keV using DLCT provides better GTH image quality compared with 
CI120 kVp, which may offer valuable support for clinical practice and preoperative surgical 
planning.
Keywords Dual-layer detector spectral CT (DLCT), Gastrocolic trunk of Henle, Virtual 
monoenergetic image
1 Introduction
GTH typically arises from the confluence of multiple tributaries, including the right gas -
troepiploic vein (RGEV), right colic vein (RCV), and anterior superior pancreaticoduo -
denal vein (ASPDV), occasionally, the superior right colic vein (SRCV) and middle colic 
Page 2 of 9
He et al. Discover Imaging (2026) 3:10 
vein (MCV) may also be incorporated. Characterized by a high rate of anatomical varia -
tion and a predisposition to intraoperative bleeding, the GTH serves as a critical con -
trol point in procedures such as laparoscopic right hemicolectomy [ 1]. Thus, accurate 
characterization and diagnosis of GTH variations are crucial for preventing iatrogenic 
vascular injury and ensuring radical tumor resection. To date, most GTH-related stud -
ies have relied on intraoperative observations and cadaveric dissections [ 2–4]. CT, one 
of the most widely used diagnostic modalities in clinical practice, enables clear, accu -
rate, and non-invasive visualization of human vascular anatomy [ 5], thereby facilitating 
large-scale in vivo studies of the GTH. However, the dilution of intravascular contrast 
agent concentration during systemic circulation impairs the clear visualization of small 
branches (e.g., ASPDV) [ 6, 7], limiting the anatomical assessment of the GTH via CT 
venography. DLCT can optimize the contrast between vessels and surrounding tissues 
by extracting VMI, while enhancing the CT values of target tissues to achieve optimal 
image quality. While this technique has been applied in arterial imaging [ 8, 9], its appli-
cation in GTH imaging remains unreported. In this study, we evaluated the imaging 
quality of the GTH using multi-parameter DLCT images combined with 3D reconstruc -
tion technology, with the aim of identifying the optimal VMI for GTH visualization. In 
summary, this is a novel imaging method that significantly improves the image quality of 
GTH. Our findings are expected to provide a theoretical basis and reference for clinical 
practice and precision surgery in abdominal surgery.
2 Materials and methods
2.1 Patients
A total of 94 patients who underwent abdominal enhanced spectral CT scans between 
August 2025 and September 2025 were retrospectively reviewed, with 61 patients ulti -
mately included after meeting the study eligibility criteria. Among the included patients, 
there were 35 males and 26 females, aged 36–81 years, with a mean age of (60.91 ± 12.82) 
years. Inclusion criteria were defined as follows: (1) Visualization of the GTH in the por -
tal venous phase of abdominal enhanced CT; (2) No prior gastrointestinal surgery before 
CT examination; (3) Without respiratory artifacts. Exclusion criteria included: (1) Severe 
CT image artifacts precluding diagnostic adequacy; (2) History of abdominal or vascular 
surgery; (3) Obscured GTH visualization due to adjacent tumors; (4) Severe hepatic or 
renal dysfunction (Fig. 1).
2.2 Computed tomography protocols and scanner
All patients underwent enhanced abdominal CT scan with SLCT (Spectral CT 7500, 
Philips Healthcare, the Netherlands). The patients were positioned in the supine posi -
tion for scanning. The scanning range spanned from the hepatic dome level to the ischial 
tuberosity level. Bolus Tracking technology was employed for contrast agent monitor -
ing, with the tracking plane set at the descending aorta and a trigger threshold of 110 
HU. Arterial phase and portal venous phase scans were acquired at 10 s and 36 s post-
threshold triggering, respectively. Scanning parameters were as follows: tube voltage: 
120 kV, tube current: adaptive, pitch: 0.85, gantry rotation time: 0.75 s, matrix: 512 × 512, 
slice thickness: 1 mm, slice interval: 1 mm. A non-ionic iodinated contrast agent, iopam-
idol (370 mgI/mL, Beijing Northland Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.), was administered via 
the antecubital vein using a high-pressure injector (MEDRAD® Centargo CT Injection 
Page 3 of 9
He et al. Discover Imaging (2026) 3:10 
System, Bayer AG, Germany) at an infusion rate of 3.0 mL/s, with a total dose ranging 
from 1.5 to 2.0 mL/kg of body weight. A spectral-based imaging (SBI) dataset was auto -
matically generated post-acquisition.
2.3 Image reconstruction and analysis
The SBI data were transferred to the Philips IntelliSpace Portal workstation, CI 120 kVp, 
VMI40−70 keV, iodine density maps, and Zeff maps were reconstructed. Subsequently, vol -
ume rendering (VR) images were generated based on the CI120 kVp and VMI40−70 keV. ROIs 
were placed on the main trunk of GTH and the left erector spinae muscle at the same 
axial level. The CT values and SD were measured, followed by the calculation of SNR 
and CNR. To ensure consistency, the diameter of each ROI was set to two-thirds of the 
GTH lumen diameter, and vascular walls were carefully avoided. All measurements were 
performed independently by two senior radiologists, and the mean values were adopted 
for subsequent analyses. A schematic illustration of the measurement protocol is pro -
vided in Fig. 2.
The calculation formulas for SNR and CNR are as follows:
 SNR = CT value(GTH)/SD(GTH)
 
 CNR = [CT value(GTH) − CT value(erector spinae muscle)] /SD(erector spinae muscle)
Fig. 1 Patient enrollment, inclusion, and exclusion
 
Page 4 of 9
He et al. Discover Imaging (2026) 3:10 
Subjective evaluation of VR images were independently performed by two senior radiol -
ogists, with the scoring criteria defined as follows: 5 points: excellent vessel signal inten -
sity with very sharp edge of vessels; 4 points: good signal intensity with sharp edge of 
vessels; 3 points: fair signal intensity with fairly sharp edge of vessels; 2 points: bad signal 
intensity with unclear vessel edge; 1 points: worse signal intensity with blurred edge of 
vessels [10].
2.4 Statistical analysis
The SPSS 22.0 software (SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA) was used for all statistical analyses. 
All parameter values were tested for normality and homogeneity of variance. Data 
conforming to a normal distribution were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation. 
Inter-group comparisons were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), 
followed by Tukey’s test for post-hoc pairwise comparisons. For data deviating from a 
normal distribution, values were expressed as median (first quartile, third quartile) 
[M (Q1, Q3)], with inter-group comparisons conducted via the Kruskal-Wallis H test 
and Bonferroni correction applied for pairwise comparisons. The inter-rater reliability 
of subjective image quality scores between the two radiologists was assessed using the 
Kappa test. P < 0.05 was set as the statistical significance threshold.
3 Results
The CT values: No statistically significant differences were observed between the 
CI120 kVp and VMI70 keV groups (P > 0.05), whereas statistically significant differences were 
noted among all other groups ( P < 0.001). The CT value of VMI 40 keV was the highest, 
with increasing energy levels, the CT values of the vessels gradually decreased.
Image noise: No statistically significant differences were observed between the 
CI120 kVp and VMI70 keV groups (P > 0.05), whereas statistically significant differences were 
noted among all other groups (P < 0.001). The VMI40 keV group demonstrated the highest

In 1868, anatomist Henle first described the common trunk structure formed by RGEV 
and RCV, which was subsequently termed the GTH [ 11]. With the widespread adop -
tion of radical resection for right-sided colon cancer, the GTH has emerged as a core

landmark for delineating the surgical plane, guiding vascular manipulation, and assess -
ing the radicality of resection. Owing to its deep anatomical location, variable tribu -
tary patterns, and short, robust main trunk, iatrogenic injury during surgery frequently 
results in refractory venous hemorrhage. In recent years, advances in three-dimensional 
(3D) imaging have facilitated the maturation of anatomical insights, preoperative evalua-
tion protocols, and surgical management strategies for the GTH [12].
Conventional CT exhibits limitations in visualizing small venous vessels, primarily 
attributed to the reduced contrast agent concentration within the portal vein. DLCT 
employs a stacked dual-detector configuration: the upper detector layer absorbs low-
energy X-ray photons, while the lower layer captures high-energy photons. This design 
enables simultaneous dual-energy data acquisition and decoupling in a single scan, elim-
inating the need for repeated scanning or voltage switching. Retrospective generation of 
multimodal parameters, including VMI 40–200 keV, iodine density map, and Zeff map—is 
feasible without additional radiation exposure [13, 14].
In this study, the CT values of GTH were compared across VMI 40−70 keV and CI 120 kVp 
group. The results demonstrated that, with the exception of VMI 70 keV, the CT values

of GTH in all other VMI groups were significantly higher than those in the CI 120 kVp 
group—indicating that spectral CT can enhance vascular enhancement. Among these 
groups, the VMI 40 keV yielded the most pronounced elevation in CT value of GTH, 
which is consistent with related vascular studies [ 15, 16]. Low-energy VMI (40–60 keV) 
approximates the K-edge of iodine (33.2  keV), markedly amplifying the photoelectric 
effect, this leads to a significant increase in the CT values of iodine-containing vessels 
and facilitates the visualization of distal small vessels [17].
Image noise exhibited a downward trend with increasing energy levels. Among the 
groups, VMI40 keV showed the highest noise, while CI 120 kVp had the lowest noise—con -
sistent with prior reports [ 18]. This phenomenon can be attributed to two key factors: 
first, low-energy X-rays have limited penetration, leading to insufficient photon flux 
detected by the detector and thus marked amplification of quantum noise; second, 
VMI40 keV yield the highest venous CT values, which increases the degree of inhomoge -
neity and further contributes to elevated noise levels [ 19, 20]. Studies focusing on lower 
extremity veins have reported that the image noise of VMI 40 keV is lower than that of 
CI120kVp [21], which is inconsistent with this study. This discrepancy can be attributed to 
the relatively small caliber of GTH, which renders it more susceptible to partial volume 
effects and uneven contrast agent filling, consequently, the image noise of GTH is higher 
than that of large-caliber vessels such as the portal vein, aorta, and lower extremity ves -
sels [ 22–24]. Nonetheless, the noise level of VMI 40 keV remains less than twice that of 
CI120 kVp, this outcome is facilitated by the anti-correlation noise suppression technology 
integrated into SLCT, which not only mitigates noise but also fully preserves the high-
contrast advantage of VMI40 keV. In contrast, no significant difference in image noise was 
observed between VMI 70 keV and CI 120 kVp. This indicates that VMI 70 keV benefits from a 
higher photon flux and more uniform enhancement, leading to inherently reduced noise 
and greater similarity to CI 120 kVp. Despite exhibiting the highest noise level, VMI 40 keV 
achieved the optimal SNR and CNR, with statistically significant differences compared 
to VMI 50–70 keV and CI 120 kVp. Additionally, VMI 40 keV received the highest subjective 
image quality scores, confirming it as the optimal imaging approach for visualizing the 
GTH. Prior studies have established that low-energy VMI enhances the imaging quality 
of the common hepatic artery, portal vein, and hepatic vein [ 25], further, VMI40 keV has 
been shown to deliver the highest diagnostic performance for characterizing portal vein 
thrombosis and to provide the most favorable visualization of the adrenal vein [ 26, 27], 
which is consistent with this study. Regarding clinical workflow, Yoshida et al. compared 
VMI40eV of the portal vein with CI in the late venous phase [ 27], which is more refined. 
However, it is impractical to intentionally scan the late venous phase in enhanced 
abdominal CT. Furthermore, adrenal veins are tributaries of the inferior vena cava, while 
GTH is a tributary of the portal vein, so they are not comparable. Some studies have 
placed the ROI on the psoas major muscle as background noise [ 28, 29], yet using the 
erector spinae muscle as background noise is more common in academic research [ 15, 
22, 30]. Notably, neither approach has been shown to exert a significant impact on the 
study outcomes.
In iodine density map, iodine-free voxels are calibrated to 0 mg/ml (displayed as black), 
while iodine-containing tissues are visualized in grayscale corresponding to their iodine 
concentrations [31]. Iodine density map [mg/ml] hold the potential to quantify iodine 
enhancement and improve the visualization of iodine within contrast-enhanced tissues, 
Page 8 of 9
He et al. Discover Imaging (2026) 3:10 
thereby enhancing the detectability of microvessels. Zeff map facilitate more promi -
nent vessel visualization through pseudocolor staining of distinct substances. However, 
iodine density map and Zeff map cannot be subjected to 3D reconstruction, precluding 
stereoscopic assessment of vessels. As such, they can serve as a robust complement to 
VMI40 keV.
This study has several limitations. First, as a retrospective single-center study, it is sus -
ceptible to selection bias, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Second, 
the anatomical classification of GTH based on VMI40 keV requires validation with a larger 
sample size to enhance the robustness of the results. Third, further investigations are 
warranted to explore whether optimizing contrast agent parameters (e.g., concentration, 
dose, and injection rate) can further improve the imaging quality of GTH, as well as to 
determine whether low-voltage, low-radiation-dose scanning protocols can serve as a 
viable alternative to CI120 kVp.
In conclusion, VMI40 keV with DLCT exhibits the optimal vascular optimization effect 
for the GTH, significantly enhancing vascular imaging quality. When combined with 
iodine density map and Zeff map, the branching patterns of the GTH can be visualized 
more comprehensively. With the continuous advancement of CT and scanning technol -
ogies, as well as the deepening of research on the GTH, it is believed that DLCT venous 
imaging technology will be increasingly widely applied in clinical practice in the future.

title: Addressing educational quality in nursing home placements: exploring nurse educators’ time-commitments. A qualitative study
summary: Addressing educational quality in nursing home placements: exploring nurse educators’ time-commitments. A qualitative study
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Nurse educators play a critical role in maintaining educational quality by supervising first-year student nurses during their initial clinical placements in nursing education. Nurse educators’ time-commitments, defined as the time dedicated to fulfilling educational responsibilities, can either enhance or hinder the efficiency of supervision. Hence, addressing educators’ time-commitments is essential in aiming for high-quality education. This study aimed to explore nurse educators’ experiences with time-commitments while supervising first-year student nurses during their initial clinical placements. A qualitative, exploratory and descriptive research design was used, based on five focus group interviews with 22 nurse educators, conducted in spring 2019. The data were analysed using Malterud’s framework for systematic text condensation. The study found that nurse educators experienced important time-related pressure caused by fragmented placement structures, extensive travel between sites and the need to balance physical and digital supervision. Additionally, educators reported a high demand for continuous availability for both students and registered nurse mentors, often extending beyond contracted hours. The results highlight a need for organisational strategies that acknowledge educators’ workload and support sustainable supervision practices.

title: Indicators, Evaluation, and Digital Security in Quality 4.0 for Smart Cities
summary: Indicators, Evaluation, and Digital Security in Quality 4.0 for Smart Cities
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

This chapter discusses performance indicators, evaluation models, and digital security functions influencing quality in smart city-centered systems from a Quality 4.0 viewpoint. It discusses how the traditional static, compliance-focused quality metrics are being supplanted by data-driven dynamic systems. This chapter contributes to a systemic narrative where evaluation is framed as a dynamic, data-intensive activity that connects monitoring, predictive analytics, and adaptive governance mechanisms. Special emphasis is put on the importance of data governance, digital security, and transparency as essential determinants of systemic performance and public trust in urban settings relying heavily on data. This analysis highlights a crucial interdependence among data quality, decision-making processes, and general smart city system efficacy in an increasingly complex world. The uniqueness of this chapter can be found in framing smart city technologies as a support system for data-driven quality management, where reliability, quality, and governance of data directly affect the quality of management. Results indicate that the effectiveness of Quality 4.0 systems is contingent not only on technological capabilities but also on structural features concerning security, transparency, and trust within urban governance generally.

title: Synergistic Effects of Potassium and Autoclaved Azotobacter Lysate on Yield and Fruit Quality of Physalis peruviana L. in Hydroponics
summary: Synergistic Effects of Potassium and Autoclaved Azotobacter Lysate on Yield and Fruit Quality of Physalis peruviana L. in Hydroponics
content:

To limited water and soil resources, hydroponic cultivation systems are expanding rapidly worldwide. In the present study, the growth characteristics and fruit yield of Physalis peruviana were evaluated under soilless cultivation conditions. The seeds of the Indian Asian giant variety were prepared, and after planting, the produced seedlings were cultivated in a culture medium of cocopeat and perlite in a ratio of 60:40. The treatments included Hoagland nutrient solution with four levels of potassium (235, 185, 285, 335 mg L−1 of potassium) and Azotobacter lysate at two levels (Without Azotobacter lysate (AZ0) and autoclaved Azotobacter lysate (AZ1)). Vegetative, reproductive, and chemical characteristics were investigated. The results showed that the effect of Azotobacter lysate alone on leaf chlorophyll, total leaf chlorophyll, fruit carotenoids, fruit vitamin C and fruit potassium was significant at 5% level. The effect of different potassium concentrations alone on fruit numbers, average fruit weight, yield and total phenols was significant at the 5% level. The interaction effect of Azotobacter lysate and different potassium concentrations on flower number, fruit formation percentage, chlorophyll b, fruit nitrate content and fruit pH was significant at the 5% level. Briefly the lysate enhanced sink strength, necessitating higher K levels for optimal yield.

Abstract
As a critical component of China’s national park system, the Yellow River Estuary National Park exhibits a 
unique habitat evolution mechanism shaped by the interplay between anthropogenic disturbances and ecologi -
cal restoration within a land–sea interaction zone. This study simulates land use and land cover change and 
assesses habitat quality dynamics from 2003 to 2023, with scenario projections for 2033, by integrating the 
InVEST and PLUS models. The results reveal a dual-process mechanism underlying habitat change: urbaniza -
tion drives the expansion of construction land, which encroaches upon cropland and barren land, leading to 
widespread habitat degradation and fragmentation; concurrently, wetland restoration and water body expansion, 
driven by ecological policies, partially offset these losses by locally enhancing habitat quality in coastal zones. 
This coexistence of degradation and restoration shapes a spatially heterogeneous pattern, where low-quality 
habitat expands and consolidates around urban agglomerations, while high-quality habitat becomes increasingly 
fragmented and confined to remnant wetland patches. Scenario projections indicate a continuation of these 
trends, with further expansion of low-quality habitat and sustained fragmentation of high-quality areas, suggest-
ing limited ecological resilience under current land use trajectories. By uncovering the process-based linkages 
between land use transformation and habitat quality response, this study provides a mechanistic understanding 
of estuarine habitat evolution and offers a scientific foundation for spatial planning and ecological governance 
in integrated land–sea national parks. These insights contribute to broader discourses on land quality and eco -
system service sustainability in deltaic social-ecological systems.

Introduction
The establishment of a nature reserve system with national parks as the main body in China is an important insti-
tutional innovation in the construction of global ecological civilization construction and a key practice to realize 
the harmonious coexistence between man and nature1. At present, China has established a national park system to 
protect the authenticity and integrity of the natural ecosystem and build a national ecological security barrier 2,3. 
Yellow River Estuary National Park is the first Marine land integrated national park in China. It undertakes the 
important mission of ecological protection and high-quality development in the Yellow River Basin 4. It is an 
important practice to fully implement the concept that “lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets”, 
adhere to harmonious coexistence between man and nature, and promote all-round, all-round, and all-round eco-
logical protection5,6. As a key indicator of ecosystem health, habitat quality directly reflects the capacity of land-
scapes to provide essential ecosystem services, such as biodiversity maintenance, water purification, and climate 
regulation. Moreover, land use changes not only alter habitat patterns but also affect land quality which in turn 
influences the delivery of these services. Therefore, assessing habitat quality dynamics within the framework of 
land quality and ecosystem services is critical for guiding national park management and regional sustainability. 
In 2021, the Chinese government formulated the outline of the Yellow River Basin ecological protection and 
high-quality development plan, indicating that the high-quality ecological protection and high-quality develop -
ment of Yellow River Estuary National Park have been incorporated into the national strategic plan.
Although previous studies have extensively examined the spatial and temporal variation of habitat quality 
under land-use change, most have emphasized changes in habitat quality patterns and future trends. Less atten -
tion has been paid to the relationship between specific land-use transitions and their corresponding habitat quality 
responses. In estuarine wetlands, where human activities and ecological restoration jointly influence land-use 
change, overall habitat quality trends may conceal spatially differentiated processes of degradation and improve-
ment. Clarifying this relationship is therefore important for understanding habitat quality evolution in estuarine 
protected areas.
Against this background, this study examines the spatio-temporal relationship between land-use change and 
habitat quality in the Yellow River Estuary National Park. The PLUS model is employed to characterize and 
simulate land-use dynamics, while the InVEST model is used to evaluate habitat quality under observed and 
projected land-use patterns. (Fig. 1). At the level of land use simulation, the multi-factor driven land use change 
simulation prediction is constructed based on the PLUS model to identify the leading driving mechanism of land 
use spatial evolution in the study area. The land use pattern in 2023 was simulated by using the land use data in 
2003 and 2013, and compared with the actual land use results in 2023 to evaluate the accuracy and applicability 
of the model. On the premise that the reliability of the model has been verified, further use the land use change 
from 2013 to 2023 to predict the Scenario prediction of land use pattern in 2033, providing a spatial basis for 
habitat quality analysis. Finally, based on the land use data at different stages, the simulation results of the PLUS 
model are used as an important input of the InVEST model to quantitatively evaluate the temporal and spatial 
distribution characteristics of habitat quality in the study area in 2003, 2013, 2023 and 2033. The system reveals 
the potential ecological risk of land use change on habitat quality, so as to realize the comprehensive analysis of 
the evolution process of habitat quality evolution in Yellow River Estuary National Park.
Accordingly, the central scientific question of this study is how different land-use transitions are associated 
with spatially differentiated changes in habitat quality within a dynamic estuarine landscape. The research results 
can not only provide a scientific basis for the space control, ecological restoration and adaptive management of 
Yellow River Estuary National Park, but also provide a theoretical basis and typical cases for the research and 
practice of similar land and sea integrated protected areas in the world.
