Literature review
Habitat quality is a key indicator to measure ecosystem health and biodiversity sustainability, and its core theory 
has evolved over time 7,8. In the early stage, the definition of habitat quality mainly focused on providing basic 
living conditions such as food, water and breeding sites for species9. With the deepening of ecological research, 
its connotation extends to the comprehensive assessment of ecological integrity and ecosystem services 10. Eco-
logical integrity emphasizes the integrity and stability of ecosystem structure, function and processes. A healthy 
ecosystem can resist external interference and maintain its original state for a long time 11,12. Ecosystem service 
functions link habitat quality with human well-being, emphasizing the ability of habitat to provide support ser -
vices, supply services and cultural services 13,14. Based on the evolution of the above theoretical connotation, 
research on habitat quality has gradually formed a theoretical system with landscape ecology theory and Bio -
diversity Conservation Theory as the core. Landscape ecology emphasizes the impact of spatial pattern on eco -
logical processes, and believes that Land Use and Land Cover Change (LUCC) is a key factor affecting habitat 
quality15,16. Rapid urbanization and agricultural expansion will lead to habitat fragmentation and connectivity 
decline17,18. The theory of ecological diversity protection is the core driving force for the study of habitat qual -
ity, and habitat degradation is the main reason for the decline in biodiversity 19,20. In summary, habitat quality is 
understood as a dynamic, multi-scale, complex system affected by both natural and human factors21.
The habitat quality assessment method system covers the traditional field survey method and model evalua -
tion method. The traditional field survey method has the advantages of high data authenticity and rich details by 
directly obtaining the data on species distribution and habitat characteristics22. However, these methods are often 
expensive and difficult to operate on a large scale or long time series. The RSEI model is based on remote sensing 
data to rapidly assess the regional ecological environment quality by integrating indicators such as greenness, 
humidity, heat and rainfall23. The MaxEnt model is often used to predict species distribution and assess habitat 
suitability by associating species appearance data with environmental factors24. The CA-Markov model is mainly 
used to simulate land use change and indirectly assess habitat quality changes 25,26. These models have their 
own advantages, but the common challenge is how to accurately obtain high-quality input data, calibrate model 
parameters and deal with spatial heterogeneity27. The InVEST model is widely used because it can quantify the 
degree of habitat threatened and assess habitat quality28,29. The habitat quality index is calculated by the sensitiv-
ity of land cover types to threat sources and the impact range of threat sources, which includes multiple factors 
such as economy, nature, society, and land use that jointly affect habitat quality30. This method breaks through the 
inherent limitations of traditional field survey and provides the feasibility for high-precision and dynamic habi -
tat quality assessment. Among these approaches, the InVEST model’s habitat quality module has been widely 
applied because it links land use/cover patterns to ecosystem service outcomes. By quantifying the impacts of 
threats on habitat suitability, it provides a spatially explicit assessment of a key supporting service which under-
pins biodiversity and other regulating and cultural services. This makes the InVEST model particularly suitable 
for studies framed within the land quality–ecosystem services nexus. These methods differ in their data require -
ments and applicability: field surveys provide detailed ecological information but are difficult to apply over large 
areas, RSEI is suitable for regional environmental assessment, MaxEnt is more appropriate for species-specific 
habitat suitability analysis, whereas InVEST provides a spatially explicit framework for evaluating habitat qual-
ity responses to land-use change.
Land-use simulation has gradually evolved from traditional cellular automata approaches toward machine-
learning and deep-learning methods capable of capturing complex spatio-temporal patterns. These approaches 
differ in their data requirements, interpretability, and analytical purposes. Deep-learning methods offer advan -
tages in learning complex spatial and temporal dependencies from data-rich time series, whereas PLUS is well 
suited to identifying the driving factors of land expansion and reproducing spatially explicit land-use transi -
tions. Compared with purely prediction-oriented approaches, process-based land-use models such as PLUS place 
greater emphasis on identifying land expansion rules and their associated driving factors, thereby providing a

Scientific Reports
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-69019-y
more interpretable basis for linking land-use transitions with subsequent ecological responses. In this study, 
PLUS was selected because its land expansion analysis and patch-generation mechanisms are consistent with the 
objective of examining land-use transitions and their associated habitat quality responses.
The particularity of estuarine wetland habitat quality is that its rivers and coastlines intersect each other, form-
ing a unique ecological environment. Hydrological connectivity, such as runoff and sediment transport, is crucial 
to the formation and maintenance of estuarine wetland habitats 31. Studies have shown that estuarine wetlands 
are important biodiversity hot-spots and are vulnerable to human activities and climate change32. Therefore, it is 
particularly important to evaluate and protect the habitat quality of estuarine wetlands. The existing research on 
the Yellow River Estuary covers wetland evolution in the Yellow River Delta, habitat suitability of rare species, 
and the impact of human activities 31–32. However, relatively limited attention has been paid to the integrated 
coupling of habitat quality evaluation, simulation, prediction, and the quantification of underlying driving mecha-
nisms34,35. Existing studies have tended to focus on assessments at a single time point or scale, with compara -
tively less emphasis on comprehensive analyses that integrate historical evolution, current conditions, and future 
projections36,34. Moreover, although previous studies have examined the effects of human activities, climate 
change, and other driving factors, how these factors interact and how different land-use transitions are associated 
with corresponding habitat quality responses in the Yellow River Estuary remain insufficiently understood32.
Therefore, the PLUS model and InVEST model are used to provide effective tools for land use simulation and 
habitat quality assessment, respectively. The PLUS model can accurately simulate the spatio-temporal evolution 
of land use pattern 37, while the InVEST model can quantitatively assess habitat quality based on land use pat -
tern38,39. The integration of PLUS and InVEST combines the spatial simulation capability of land-use change 
with habitat quality assessment, enabling historical land-use transitions, future scenarios, and corresponding 
habitat quality responses to be examined within a unified spatio-temporal framework40.
Overview of the study area and data sources
Overview of the study area
Yellow River Estuary National Park (37°25′02″―38°17′53″N, 118°13′55″―119°30′57″E) is the first land-sea 
integrated national park in China. This study defines its research area based on the scope of three county-level 
administrative divisions—Kenli District, Hekou District, and Lijin County—as delineated in official documents 
including “the Construction Plan of the Yellow River Estuary National Park” and “the Boundary and Manage-
ment Zoning Map of the Yellow River Estuary National Park” issued by the Shandong Provincial Department of 
Natural Resources (Shandong Provincial Forestry Bureau) (Fig. 2). The region is located in the monsoon climate 
zone of the warm zone, with four distinct seasons and obvious interannual variation of precipitation. The land -
form is dominated by a delta plain and tidal flat, and the dynamic change of coastline is significant. Yellow River 
Estuary National Park has the most complete estuarine wetland ecosystem in China’s warm zone and the most 
active land and sea changes. It is a typical representative of the estuarine wetland ecosystem in the world.
Data source and processing
The data used in the study include land use data41, socioeconomic factors42, distance factor43 and natural factor44 
(Table 1). The land use data was obtained from the CLCD dataset provided by Wuhan University. To maintain 
consistency between the PLUS-based land use simulation and the investment-based habitat quality assessment 
approach, the land cover data for 2003, 2013, and 2023 were categorized into five classes using ArcMap 10.8.1 
(https://www.esri.com): cropland, grassland, water, barren land, and built-up land. This classification scheme was 
applied uniformly across all study periods to ensure comparability in analyses of land use transitions and habitat 
quality changes. Considering the accuracy and practical significance of the PLUS model, 12 driving factors were

Spatio-temporal evaluation of land use and cover change in Yellow River Estuary National Park from 
2003 to 2023

a trend of dual transformation from cropland to construction land and water (Fig. 3). Land use change shows

From the perspective of spatial pattern characteristics, cropland is mainly distributed in the central and southern 
plains of the study area. During the study period, its spatial scope continued to shrink and gradually concentrated 
in the inland area; The construction land expanded significantly along the traffic trunk lines, urban nodes and the 
northern and eastern coastal zones, gradually forming agglomeration patches; The water area is concentrated in 
the main stream of the Yellow River, estuaries and coastal wetland areas, and its spatial scope is significantly 
expanded, reflecting the continuous implementation of estuarine wetland restoration and water system manage -
ment projects. Barren is mainly distributed in estuarine sediment areas and coastal beaches, and its spatial scope 
is significantly reduced, which is closely related to the evolution of coastline evolution and wetland reconstruc -
tion process; The grassland is scattered, the overall scale is small, and the change of spatial pattern is not obvious.
From the change characteristics of land use Structural change characteristics (Fig. 4), the area composition and 
proportion of various land use types have been systematically adjusted during the study period. Cropland and 
barren continued to decrease, construction land and water area increased significantly, and the land use structure 
gradually evolved from being dominated by agricultural land to a composite pattern of construction land, water 
area and agricultural land. This change process reflects that, while urbanization continues to advance, ecological 
protection and wetland restoration measures have had an important impact on the regional land use pattern.
Based on the land use transition matrix from 2003 to 2023 (Table 6), the internal mechanism of land use struc-
ture adjustment is further revealed, and the transformation paths between different land use types are analyzed. 
The results showed that the land use change in the study area showed obvious directional transfer characteristics, 
cropland and barren were the main transfer out types, and the transformation process had significant stage differ-
ences. From 2003 to 2013, the conversion of cropland to construction land and water conversion was 154.55 km² 
and 98. 30 km² respectively; From 2013 to 2023, the Conversion scale has expanded significantly, and the trans-
formation area from cropland to construction land and Water conversion has increased to 378.11 km2 and 225.25

characteristics, from 117.57 km² and 30.59 km² in the previous stage to water and construction land, increased 
to 324.54 km² and 293.34 km², respectively, indicating that the estuarine wetland restoration project and Shore -

In general, the land use change of Yellow River Estuary National Park from 2003 to 2023 is spatially mani -
fested as the agglomeration expansion of coastal and urban surrounding areas and the continuous retreat of inland 
agricultural space. Structurally, it is reflected in the significant increase of construction land and water area, and 
the continuous reduction of cropland and barren. The land use transformation process was formed under the joint 
action of the development needs of urbanization and the national ecological protection policy, which provided a 
spatial basis for the subsequent analysis of the evolution characteristics of habitat quality.
Future land use prediction based on PLUS model
PLUS model validation
To evaluate the predictive performance of the PLUS model, the land-use changes observed from 2003 to 2013 
were used to simulate the land-use pattern in 2023. The simulated 2023 land-use map was then compared with 
the observed 2023 land-use map to assess the agreement between predicted and actual spatial patterns (Fig. 5). 
Overall accuracy and the Kappa coefficient were used as validation metrics. The results showed an overall accu-
racy of 0.85 and a Kappa coefficient of 0.7567 (> 0.75), indicating an acceptable level of agreement between the 
simulated and observed land-use patterns 58,59. Based on this validation, the land-use transition characteristics 
observed during 2013–2023 were subsequently used for the 2033 scenario simulation.

National Park, the study analyzed the land use data of Yellow River Estuary National Park from 2003 to 2023 by 
using the Random Forest Algorithm and the LEAS module, and evaluated the contribution of each driving factor 
in different land use changes (Fig. 6). The results show that the land use pattern in the study area is mainly driven

The spatial distribution of cropland, grassland and barren showed a marginal gradient with the county govern-
ment as the core and increasing around, and its area was negatively correlated with the distance from the city 
center. This pattern reflects the spatial process of the continuous agglomeration of population, economy and 
public resources to the administrative center in the process of urbanization. As an area with a high concentration 
of population and economic activities, the land use intensity around the administrative center has been continu -
ously improved, and a large number of agricultural and ecological land has been converted into construction 
land, resulting in the significant compression of cropland, grassland and barren in the core area of the town. With 
the increase of the distance from the town, the intensity of human activities has gradually weakened, and can be 
relatively concentrated in the peripheral area. This land use development pattern, dominated by the expansion of 
construction land, not only improves the carrying capacity of cities and towns, but also weakens the spatial integ-
rity of agricultural and ecological land to a certain extent. From the perspective of socioeconomic background, 
China’s urbanization process has long presented a rapid development mode characterized by spatial expansion 
and factor agglomeration, which not only promotes regional economic vitality, but also forms a continuous 
squeeze on agriculture and ecological space.
On the basis of administrative center radiation effect, traffic conditions further magnified the impact of urban-
ization and industrial activities on land use patterns. As an important infrastructure for animal husbandry and 
industrial development, the layout of the class II roads has significantly improved regional accessibility and 
efficiency of factor flow in production, directly supporting the belt and node expansion of construction land. By 
integrating the regional internal transportation system, it promotes the agglomeration and development of indus-
tries along the line that rely on traffic conditions, such as animal husbandry and salt industry, and thus has a far-
reaching impact on the spatial layout of water and related productive land. The population agglomeration effect

Change and simulation of habitat quality changes in Yellow River Estuary National Park based on 
InVEST model
Spatio-temporal evolution characteristics of habitat quality from 2003 to 2023
Based on the land use data of Yellow River Estuary National Park from 2003 to 2023, the Habitat Quality module 
of the InVEST model was used to calculate changes in habitat quality. According to the natural breaks method 
(Jenks) in ArcGIS 10.8 and referring to relevant literature60,61, habitat quality in the study area was classified into 
five levels: low [0, 0.2), moderate-low [0.2, 0.4), moderate [0.4, 0.6), moderate-high [0.6, 0.8), and high [0.8, 
1.0]. To avoid interval overlap, the half-open interval principle was adopted to ensure that each value has a unique 
attribution.
From the perspective of spatial pattern (Fig. 8), the habitat quality of Yellow River Estuary National Park from 
2003 to 2023 showed a significant differentiation characteristic of “high in coastal areas and low in inland areas”. 
Moderate-high and high habitat quality areas are mainly concentrated in the Yellow River Estuary and coastal 
wetland areas, which are dominated by natural water bodies and wetland ecosystems with relatively weak human 
disturbance; while low and moderate-low habitat quality areas are widely distributed in inland cropland areas and 
urban built-up area agglomeration areas, and highly coincide with high-intensity agricultural utilization, urban 
expansion, and transportation infrastructure layout, indicating that land use mode is the key factor driving the 
spatial differentiation of habitat quality.
From the perspective of structural change characteristics (Fig. 9), the composition of habitat quality levels has 
been significantly adjusted during the study period. The proportion of low habitat quality continued to increase, 
becoming the most dominant habitat quality type in the study area; moderate-low habitat quality decreased signif-
icantly, while moderate habitat quality increased in the late stage. Moderate-high and high habitat quality showed 
restorative growth after reaching a phased trough in 2013, but their spatial distribution tended to be fragmented, 
patch sizes were small, and overall connectivity remained weak. In general, the structure of habitat quality levels 
in the study area shows a complex pattern of low-quality expansion and high-quality local restoration.
In order to further reveal the internal mechanism of habitat quality evolution, the analysis is based on the tran-
sition matrix of habitat quality from 2003 to 2023 (Table 8). The results showed that habitat quality changes had 
obvious directional and stage-based characteristics. From 2003 to 2013, the degradation of habitat quality was 
mainly from moderate-low to low habitat quality; from 2013 to 2023, the degradation trend was further intensified, 
and the transformation area from moderate-low to low habitat quality reached 702.45 km². At the same time, the 
transformation from high to moderate-low habitat quality existed in both stages, indicating that high-quality habi-
tat is still facing continuous human activity pressure. In terms of habitat quality improvement, the improvement 
process mainly occurred within moderate-low habitat quality. During 2013–2023, the transformation areas from

Discussion
The observed evolution of habitat quality has direct implications for land quality and ecosystem services in the 
Yellow River Estuary National Park62. The expansion of low-quality habitat associated with built-up land growth 
and intensive land use indicates a decline in the landscape’s capacity to sustain biodiversity and related regulat -
ing services. In contrast, the localized recovery of relatively high-quality habitat in wetland and water-dominated 
areas suggests that ecological restoration can improve habitat conditions in specific locations. However, these 
improvements remain spatially limited and are insufficient to fully offset the broader pressures generated by 
continued land development. The coexistence of degradation and localized recovery indicates that habitat quality 
evolution in the Yellow River Estuary should not be interpreted as a uniform process, but rather as the combined 
outcome of different land-use transitions and their spatially differentiated ecological consequences.
This interpretation is broadly consistent with previous studies showing that urban expansion, agricultural 
intensification, and transportation infrastructure development are important drivers of habitat degradation in 
estuarine regions63,64. However, the present study further indicates that the ecological consequences of land-use 
change vary with both the direction of land conversion and its spatial context. The expansion and concentration of 
built-up land intensify landscape fragmentation and reinforce the persistence of low-quality habitat, particularly 
in inland and peri-urban areas. By contrast, the expansion of water-related ecological space and the restoration 
of wetland areas contribute to localized improvements in habitat quality. This finding is consistent with previous 
evidence that ecological restoration can alleviate habitat degradation to some extent, while also suggesting that 
localized restoration alone is insufficient to offset the broader ecological pressures associated with continued 
land-use restructuring65. Accordingly, the observed pattern of relatively high habitat quality in coastal and estua-
rine areas and lower habitat quality in inland areas reflects not only differences in natural conditions, but also the 
spatial interaction among development pressure, land-use change, and ecological restoration.
These spatial differences have important implications for the management of the Yellow River Estuary National 
Park. Areas characterized by persistently low habitat quality and continued expansion of built-up land should pri-
oritize the control of additional development pressure and the prevention of further fragmentation of ecological 
space. Coastal wetlands and estuarine areas with relatively high habitat quality should focus on maintaining the 
integrity and continuity of existing habitat patches while limiting new disturbances. In areas where habitat quality 
has improved alongside the expansion or restoration of water-related ecological space, management should place 
greater emphasis on consolidating restoration outcomes and strengthening ecological connectivity with surround-
ing habitats. Therefore, ecological restoration should be differentiated according to the spatial characteristics of 
land-use change and habitat quality, rather than relying on uniform interventions across the entire national park. 
Such spatially targeted management can enhance the practical value of habitat quality assessment for conserva -
tion zoning, restoration priority setting, and adaptive ecological management.
Several limitations should nevertheless be acknowledged. First, the InVEST habitat quality model is sensitive 
to the weights, influence distances, habitat suitability values, and sensitivity coefficients assigned to different 
threat factors. Although these parameters were derived from previous studies and adjusted according to the char-
acteristics of the study area, they cannot fully capture the complexity of ecosystem responses to anthropogenic 
disturbance. Second, the PLUS-based projections primarily reflect the continuation of historical land-use tran -
sition patterns and do not fully account for uncertainties associated with extreme climate events, hydrological 
change, or major policy adjustments. Future studies should therefore integrate longer time-series data, field-based

Conclusion
Based on the InVEST-PLUS coupling model, this study constructed a spatiotemporal evolution assessment and 
simulation prediction system for habitat quality in Yellow River Estuary National Park from the perspective of 
land use change, and systematically revealed the differentiation characteristics and response mechanisms of habi-
tat quality patterns under different human activities. The results show that land use transformation and its spatial 
pattern characteristics have a decisive impact on habitat quality evolution.
(1) Habitat quality in Yellow River Estuary National Park showed significant spatial heterogeneity. Coastal wet-
lands and estuarine waters are dominated by continuous natural patches, which maintain high habitat qual -
ity and show strong ecological stability. However, low habitat quality in inland urban expansion areas and 
high-intensity agricultural utilization areas continued to aggregate, forming a pattern of habitat degradation 
dominated by human disturbance. This difference reflects the imbalance between natural ecological space 
and human land expansion in spatial competition.
(2) Different land use evolution paths shape different habitat response patterns. The centralized expansion of 
built-up area aggravates landscape fragmentation by compressing natural habitat space, and significantly 
reduces regional habitat quality. Ecological patches dominated by wetlands and water bodies have buffered 
human activity pressure to a certain extent by maintaining landscape connectivity, forming a low-interfer -
ence, high-quality habitat maintenance mechanism.
(3) Habitat quality evolution has obvious stage-based and nonlinear characteristics. In the early stage of the 
study, rapid urbanization advancement continued to suppress habitat quality. In the later stage, with the inter-
vention of ecological protection and restoration measures, local habitat quality was restored, but low habitat 
quality still showed an expanding trend, indicating that the cumulative effect of human activity intensity 
remains dominant.
(4) Scenario simulation reveals the potential risks of future habitat quality evolution. The prediction results 
show that continuous built-up area expansion in the future will strengthen the stability of low habitat quality. 
Although high habitat quality patches can maintain a certain scale, their spatial connectivity will decline, and 
overall ecosystem resilience will face the risk of weakening.
(5) The study highlights the critical role of habitat quality as a proxy for ecosystem services in the context of 
land use change. The observed patterns of degradation and recovery have direct consequences for land qual-
ity, suggesting that future research should incorporate soil and vegetation attributes to fully assess the multi-
faceted impacts of human activities on estuarine landscapes. This integrated approach will better support 
policy-making aimed at balancing development with ecological conservation in national parks and similar 
protected areas.
The research shows that habitat quality evolution in Yellow River Estuary National Park is essentially the result 
of the coupling effect of land use transformation and ecosystem response. The InVEST-PLUS coupling model 
can provide quantitative support and methodological reference for zoning management and control of national 
parks, identification of priority areas for wetland protection and restoration, and integrated land-sea ecological 
governance.

title: A high-quality chromosome-level genome assembly of a swimming sea cucumber Hansenothuria sp. from a deep seamount in the Western Pacific Ocean
summary: A high-quality chromosome-level genome assembly of a swimming sea cucumber Hansenothuria sp. from a deep seamount in the Western Pacific Ocean
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Sea cucumbers are an important echinoderm lineage for studying the evolution trajectory and environmental adaptability. However, the limited availability of high-quality chromosomes for sea cucumbers from deep sea ecosystems has hindered a thorough understanding of mechanisms underlying their adaptive evolution. In this study, we reported the first chromosome-level genome assembly in the order Persiculida, Hansenothuria sp. M1226 from a deep seamount in the Western Pacific Ocean, which was sequenced on the PacBio Sequel II platform using the CLR (continuous long reads) mode. The Hansenothuria sp. M1226 genome assembly has a total length of 3.52 Gb with a scaffold N50 length of 133.1 Mb, encompassing 23 chromosomes, highlighting high genome continuity. Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) assessment yielded a completeness estimate of 85.0% for the genome assembly and 90.6% for its gene set. We predicted a total of 32,054 protein-coding genes (PCGs), with 27,273 functionally annotated. The availability of this high-quality chromosome-level genome of Hansenothuria sp. M1226 contributes to our understanding of the origin and evolution of sea cucumbers.

title: Case Studies of Quality 4.0 in Smart Cities
summary: Case Studies of Quality 4.0 in Smart Cities
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

This chapter investigates the application of the Quality 4.0 concept for urban systems by analyzing a selection of smart city case studies as well as identifying the systemic mechanisms that tend to limit their performance. It applies a socio-technical perspective considering the city as a complex multi-actor system, quality arising through interplays of data, digital technologies and governance mechanism. Using examples from pioneering cities like Singapore, Barcelona, Dubai, and selected continuous improvement mechanisms in Central and Eastern Europe Katowice, Tallin, Brno, and the Global South (Medellín, Kigali, Nairobi, and Chennai) this chapter illustrates how Quality 4.0 principles are translated into practice through data-driven governance, digital platform integration, and continuous quasi automatic monitoring of targets and corrective action mechanisms. In parallel, the analysis highlights the systemic failure mechanisms constantly repeating themselves such as fragmentation of data, low interoperability between information systems, limited integration of process, ethical risks posed by algorithmic decisions, and digital inequalities lowering access to public services. The results show that Quality 4.0 implementation in urban systems is highly contextual and influenced by technological maturity, institutional capacity, and the effectiveness of governance arrangements.

title: Carcass traits and meat quality of the Eurasian collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto)
summary: Carcass traits and meat quality of the Eurasian collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto)
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

The present study provides a comprehensive evaluation of carcass traits and meat quality characteristics of the Eurasian collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto), with particular emphasis on the effects of sex and muscle type onmeat quality. A total of 40adult birds (20males and 20females) were analysed for carcass traits, proximate composition, amino acid profile, fatty acid composition, lipid quality indices and colour characteristics. Carcass yield averaged approximately 67% and did not differ significantly between sexes (P>0.05). Breast muscle was characterised by a high protein content [male 24.32; female 24.36g·(100g)–1] and low intramuscular fat and cholesterol contents, whereas thigh meat contained higher levels of intramuscular fat and cholesterol, particularly in females (P≤0.05). The amino acid profile was dominated by lysine, leucine and arginine and was characterised by a high proportion of essential amino acids. Monounsaturated fatty acids represented the predominant lipid fraction, followed by saturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids, with oleic acid being the major fatty acid. The PUFA/SFA ratio ranged from 0.42 to 0.49, while atherogenic and thrombogenic indices remained low (AI:0.40–0.42; TI:0.78–0.82). Colour analysis revealed lower lightness values in breast meat than in thigh meat, indicating a darker appearance of the breast meat. Overall, the results indicate that S.decaocto meat is a lean source of high-quality protein with favourable nutritional characteristics comparable to those reported for other members of the Columbidae family.

summary: Development of a chitosan-based edible coating enhanced with citric and ascorbic acids for enhancing postharvest quality and microbiological stability of tomato (Solanum lycopersicum)
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

This study examines the effectiveness of a chitosan-based edible coating, enhanced with citric and ascorbic acids, in improving the microbiological stability and quality of tomatoes ( Solanum lycopersicum ). In vitro experiments demonstrated that chitosan alone exhibited inhibition zones of 0.65 cm for E. coli and 1 cm for S. aureus , whereas the complete formulation showed a synergistic effect, achieving 100% inhibition of mycelial growth in fungi of the genus Alternaria . Furthermore, the antioxidant capacity (DPPH) of the chitosan solution increased from an initial 30% to an average of 92% upon incorporating the organic acids. In fruit trials, the treated tomatoes maintained a significantly higher antioxidant capacity, reaching 69% DPPH inhibition at 21 days, compared to 64% in the control group. In targeted inoculation tests, the edible coating (EC) was effective in reducing the S. aureus load by 2 log units after seven days of refrigerated storage, while the population in the control group increased by 1 log unit. These findings confirm that the proposed formulation is an effective technological alternative for enhancing microbiological safety and preserving the antioxidant quality of tomatoes during postharvest.

Long-term ecological quality dynamics and spatial 
associations in arid and semi-arid Northwest China 
using an adaptive PRSEI
Jiangmin Wu · Bin Lian · Qirui Zhang · Zhen Yan · Wei Zhao · Jiacheng Ya · Zaixin Chen · 
Yuxiang Lan
Received: 29 May 2026 / Accepted: 11 September 2026
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
Long-term ecological monitoring in arid and semi-arid regions requires indices that capture region-specific 
stressors while remaining comparable through time. We developed an adaptive particular remote-sensing eco -
logical index (PRSEI) for Gansu Province, China, using growing-season kNDVI, wetness (WET), land surface 
temperature (LST), sandification index (SI), and a PM10-based particulate indicator (TI) from 2000 to 2024. 
A unified principal component analysis (PCA) with common scaling defined the primary time series, while 
annual PCA and fixed weights were used for sensitivity testing. Unified PC1 explained 79.12% of total vari -
ance, and mean PRSEI increased from 0.343 to 0.419 (slope = 0.00432 yr⁻¹; R² = 0.778). Unified PCA and 
fixed weights agreed on 99.90% of pixel-level trend directions, whereas annual and unified PCA agreed on 
only 39.73%, indicating strong methodological sensitivity. Adaptive PRSEI was highly correlated with original 
PRSEI (r = 0.991) and traditional RSEI ( r = 0.975), showing the strongest consistency with mapped restoration 
transitions (81.47%) but weaker consistency with degradation transitions (34.22%). Precipitation, soil type, 
and land use/land cover were the most stable spatial explanatory factors. Overall, ecological quality improved 
broadly but heterogeneously, supporting adaptive PRSEI as a complementary multi-stressor index for drylands 
rather than a universal replacement for RSEI.
Keywords Adaptive PRSEI · Ecological environment quality · Arid and semi-arid ecosystems · Gansu 
Province · Hurst exponent · Optimal-parameter geographical detector
Introduction
Ecological and environmental quality reflects multiple dimensions of ecosystem condition, including vegeta -
tion growth, surface moisture, thermal stress, land degradation, and human disturbance. Long-term ecological 
monitoring is particularly important in arid and semi-arid regions, where limited precipitation, high evaporative 
demand, sparse vegetation, and extensive bare ground increase ecosystem sensitivity to climatic variability and 
land-use change1,2. Gansu Province, located in inland north-western China, spans the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, 
Article in Press
Scientific Reports
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-71853-z
the Inner Mongolian Plateau, and the Loess Plateau. Within a single administrative unit, it encompasses diverse 
landscapes, including desert–Gobi systems, irrigated oases, loess hills, alpine ecosystems, and the humid Qinba 
Mountains3. This pronounced environmental gradient provides a representative setting for examining spatial dif-
ferences in ecological quality across contrasting dryland and mountain environments.
Remote-sensing ecological assessment has increasingly relied on composite indices that integrate multiple 
land-surface properties. The remote sensing ecological index (RSEI) uses principal component analysis (PCA) to 
combine greenness, wetness, heat, and dryness, thereby reducing reliance on subjectively assigned weights4–9. Its 
broad application across different regions has demonstrated its effectiveness in characterising spatial variations in 
ecological quality. However, the conventional four-component framework may not fully capture several stressors 
that are particularly relevant in arid environments, including weak vegetation signals, extensive bare-ground 
exposure, sandification, and atmospheric particulate loading10–14.
Accordingly, a growing body of research has sought to adapt ecological indices to arid environments by 
modifying vegetation metrics or incorporating components that better reflect dryland-specific stressors 15–19. In 
this study, the kernel normalised difference vegetation index (kNDVI) was used to capture nonlinear green -
ness responses, while the sandification index (SI) and a PM10-based turbidity indicator (TI) were introduced to 
represent additional surface and atmospheric environmental pressures. Importantly, the inclusion of additional 
components or a high contribution from the first principal component (PC1) does not, by itself, demonstrate 
superior ecological performance. A more robust evaluation therefore requires direct comparison with traditional 
RSEI and the original PRSEI configuration under identical years, pixels, masks, and preprocessing procedures, 
together with external ecological evidence to clarify where the adaptive formulation provides added information 
and where its limitations remain.
Long-term ecological assessments also face a fundamental challenge of temporal comparability. Analyses 
based on representative years provide an efficient means of comparing broad ecological differences among peri-
ods, but they may overlook interannual responses to drought, ecological restoration, irrigation, and land-cover 
change. By contrast, annual PCA retains year-specific information, yet the centring of variables, principal-compo-
nent loadings, and score ranges may vary from year to year. Apparent temporal changes may therefore reflect not 
only genuine ecological variation but also changes in the index construction itself. Despite this potential source 
of uncertainty, few studies have directly compared annual PCA, unified PCA, and fixed-weight approaches using 
the same underlying dataset, leaving the sensitivity of long-term ecological trends to PCA construction insuf -
ficiently quantified.
A third methodological issue concerns the interpretation of ecological change and its explanatory factors. The 
Theil–Sen estimator and Mann–Kendall test are commonly used to characterise monotonic trends, the Hurst 
exponent describes tendencies toward persistence or reversal, and geographical detectors quantify spatial strati -
fication20–24. These methods address complementary but fundamentally different questions, and none can inde -
pendently establish causal effects. In particular, the q statistic derived from OPGD measures the extent to which 
factor stratification accounts for spatial variation in ecological quality; it does not demonstrate that a given factor 
caused the observed changes. Robust inference therefore requires a clear distinction among descriptive patterns, 
temporal trends, external consistency evidence, and spatial explanatory associations.
Three research gaps emerge from the limitations outlined above. First, the extent to which a dryland-adapted 
PRSEI provides additional ecological information beyond the traditional RSEI has not been sufficiently evaluated 
under a strictly comparable framework. Second, the sensitivity of long-term PRSEI trends to different PCA con-
struction strategies remains inadequately quantified. Third, province-wide ecological changes need to be linked 
to eco-regional contrasts and the robustness of spatial explanatory factors without overstating causal relation -
ships. To address these gaps, this study constructs a temporally comparable 25-year PRSEI series using a unified 
PCA loading vector and common scaling, and directly compares traditional RSEI, original-configuration PRSEI, 
and adaptive PRSEI across identical years and common pixels. External consistency is further assessed using 
transition information from the China Land Cover Dataset (CLCD), while the robustness of OPGD results is

methodological, empirical, and interpretive contributions of this study.
Accordingly, this study aims to: (1) construct a temporally comparable adaptive PRSEI for 2000–2024; (2) 
quantify the sensitivity of long-term ecological trends to annual PCA, unified PCA, and fixed-weight approaches; 
(3) compare traditional RSEI, original-configuration PRSEI, and adaptive PRSEI in terms of spatial patterns, 
trend responses, and consistency with external land-cover evidence; (4) characterise ecological dynamics, class 
transitions, and persistence tendencies at both provincial and eco-regional scales; and (5) evaluate the stability 
and interaction structure of climatic, topographic, soil, land-cover, and socio-economic explanatory factors using 
OPGD. Throughout the analysis, CLCD transitions are treated as external categorical consistency evidence rather 
than as field-validated ground truth, while OPGD results are interpreted as spatial explanatory associations rather 
than causal mechanisms.
Materials and methods
Overview of the study area
Gansu Province is located in inland north-western China (32°11′–42°57′ N, 92°13′–108°46′ E) and covers 
approximately 425,800 km². The province extends across the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, the Inner Mongolian Pla -
teau, and the Loess Plateau, encompassing diverse landscapes such as alpine mountains, loess hills, irrigated 
oases, desert–Gobi systems, and mountain forests. Precipitation generally decreases from the south-east to the 
north-west, whereas evaporative demand and aridity increase along the same gradient. This produces a pro -
nounced environmental transition from relatively humid mountain ecosystems in the south-east to arid oasis and 
desert environments in the north-west Fig. 1.
To examine regional variation in ecological quality across contrasting environmental settings, Gansu Province 
was divided into five eco-regions: the Hexi Desert–Gobi, Hexi Oasis–Corridor Agricultural, Longzhong–Long -
dong Loess Hilly, Gannan Alpine Mountain, and Longnan–Tianshui Qinba Humid Mountain regions. The region-
alisation considered climatic gradients, geomorphology, land-cover patterns, ecosystem characteristics, and the 
spatial continuity of administrative units. These eco-region boundaries were subsequently used as consistent 
spatial statistical units for comparing annual PRSEI values, trend classes, and persistence tendencies Fig. 2.
Data and preprocessing
The study covered the period from 2000 to 2024. PRSEI components were derived from the MODIS/Terra 
MOD09A1 Version 6.1 surface reflectance product (500 m) for calculating kNDVI, WET, and SI; the MODIS/
Terra MOD11A2 Version 6.1 land surface temperature product (1 km, converted from Kelvin to °C) for LST; and 
the Long-term Gap-free High-resolution Air Pollutants (LGHAP) v2 PM10 product (1 km, µg m⁻³) for construct-
ing TI25–28. June–September growing-season composites were used to reduce the influence of snow cover, veg -
etation senescence, and seasonal variation in bare-ground conditions. All continuous variables were converted 
to their specified physical units before spatial resampling to ensure consistency among datasets. Because the 
publicly available documentation for LGHAP v2 covers 2000–2021, the archived TI rasters for 2022–2024 used 
in this study extend beyond the documented period and are therefore explicitly acknowledged as a limitation of 
the data source Fig. 3.
The explanatory variables comprised annual precipitation (PRE; mm yr⁻¹), annual mean temperature (TEM; 
°C), potential evapotranspiration (PET; mm yr⁻¹), population density (PD; persons km⁻²), night-time lights (NTL; 
nW cm⁻² sr⁻¹), and annual land use/land cover (LULC), together with static layers of the digital elevation model 
(DEM; m), slope (SLO; °), and soil type (ST; categorical)29–39. Fractional vegetation cover (FVC) was excluded 
from the main model because no independent annual archive was available and kNDVI was already included as

common pixels. The year 2009 was excluded because the data required for the three-index comparison were 
unavailable and was not interpolated.

Temporal, spatial and class statistics
Annual PRSEI statistics, including the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum, were calculated for the 
province and each eco-region. Following the conventional RSEI classification and subsequent applications8,11,14, 
PRSEI values were divided into five fixed 0.2 intervals: very poor [0, 0.2), poor [0.2, 0.4), moderate [0.4, 0.6), 
good [0.6, 0.8), and excellent [0.8, 1.0]. Fixed thresholds ensured direct interannual comparability and avoided 
artificial changes caused by year-specific quantiles or natural breaks. These classes represent relative positions 
along the ecological-quality gradient rather than field-calibrated ecological thresholds or regulatory standards.
Annual mean PRSEI time series for the five eco-regions were derived by overlaying the annual PRSEI rasters 
with the corresponding regional boundaries. These series were used to compare baseline ecological quality, the 
magnitude of change, and interannual variability among regions.
After applying a common valid-data mask, area statistics were derived from pixel counts using the stan -
dardised grid-cell area. For each year and eco-region, pixel counts were converted to areas and proportions 
for PRSEI classes, trend categories, and persistence categories. Proportional statistics were used to facilitate 
comparison among eco-regions of different sizes, while the underlying raster and area outputs were retained for 
reproducibility.

OPGD analysis of spatial explanatory associations
OPGD was used to quantify spatial associations between PRSEI and nine explanatory factors: PRE, TEM, PET, 
DEM, SLO, PD, NTL, LULC, and ST.
For annual OPGD analysis, unified-PCA PRSEI values were matched with the corresponding annual dynamic 
variables and the static DEM, SLO, and ST layers. Continuous variables were discretised using equal-interval, 
quantile, geometric-interval, K-means, and natural-breaks methods with 5–10 classes, and the scheme yielding 
the highest q value was retained. LULC and ST were treated directly as categorical variables.
The factor-detector q statistic was calculated as:

Here, h denotes the stratum, L the number of strata, Nh and N the numbers of pixels within stratum h and the full

Interaction detection was performed by overlaying pairs of factor strata and comparing q(X1 ∩ X2) with the 
corresponding single-factor q values. A higher interaction q value indicates stronger joint explanatory associa -

changes in individual factors.
For reproducibility, the selected discretisation method and class number for each continuous variable were 
recorded, while LULC and ST retained their original categories. To assess sensitivity to soil classification, the 
original 112 ST classes were progressively consolidated into the 80, 40, 20, and 10 most frequent classes, with 
the remaining classes grouped as “Other”, and q values were recalculated for each scheme.
Robustness of the multi-year OPGD results was further evaluated across random seeds (42, 512, and 2024), 
sample sizes (25,000, 50,000, and 100,000), four discretisation methods, and 5–10 classes. Stability was assessed 
by comparing factor rankings, overlap among the top three factors, and q values of key interactions across set -
tings. These tests quantify sensitivity to sampling and discretisation choices rather than causal effects.
Results
Stability of annual PRSEI construction
Unified PCA defined a temporally consistent composite axis using pooled observations from 2000 to 2024. 
PC1 explained 79.12% of the total variance, with direction-corrected loadings of 0.709 for kNDVI, 0.138 for 
WET, 0.388 for LST, 0.342 for SI, and 0.459 for TI (Table 2). These loadings quantify the contributions of the

standardised components to the composite axis but do not, by themselves, demonstrate the ecological superiority 
of a particular index formulation.
Annual PCA showed substantial temporal variation in index structure. PC1 explained 78.37–85.70% of the 
variance (mean 81.82%), while loadings ranged from 0.628 to 0.770 for kNDVI, 0.132–0.154 for WET, 0.338–
0.442 for LST, 0.293–0.386 for SI, and 0.326–0.554 for TI. This variability indicates that trends derived from 
annual PCA may reflect both ecological change and year-to-year shifts in component weighting.
Sensitivity analysis revealed strong dependence of long-term trend interpretation on PCA construction. Annual 
PCA with year-specific scaling classified 39.21% of pixels as improving, 3.34% as stable, and 57.45% as degrad-
ing, compared with 99.42%, 0.07%, and 0.52% under unified PCA and 99.36%, 0.07%, and 0.57% under the 
fixed-weight approach, respectively. Pixel-level trend-direction agreement reached 99.90% between unified PCA 
and fixed weights but only 39.73% between annual and unified PCA. Thus, the apparent widespread degradation 
inferred from annual PCA was strongly method-sensitive, and subsequent analyses were based on the unified-
PCA series.
Provincial annual dynamics and ecological-quality classes
Based on the unified-PCA series, the mean PRSEI for Gansu Province increased from 0.343 in 2000 to 0.419 in 
2024, with a linear slope of 0.00432 yr⁻¹ (R² = 0.778), indicating a clear long-term improvement despite interan-
nual variability. Figure 4 presents the provincial mean PRSEI derived from unified PCA together with the corre-
sponding ecological-quality class composition. Annual-PCA results are used only for sensitivity assessment and 
are not used for primary temporal inference.
Class transitions based on fixed thresholds provide a more conservative measure of structural change than 
trend direction alone. From 2000 to 2024, 37.57% of pixels increased by at least one 0.2 class, 60.73% remained 
unchanged, and 1.71% decreased, indicating that widespread positive trends did not necessarily translate into 
shifts across ecological-quality classes. Provincial trends should therefore be interpreted alongside baseline con-
ditions and class transitions. Common scaling ensured temporally consistent thresholds, while the five classes 
were treated as relative mapping intervals rather than field-calibrated ecological-status thresholds.
Spatial pattern and eco-regional divergence
Unified PCA revealed a clear south-east–north-west gradient in ecological quality. The 25-year mean PRSEI 
was highest in the Longnan–Tianshui Qinba Humid Mountain Region (0.692), followed by the Gannan Alpine 
Mountain Region (0.672), Longzhong–Longdong Loess Hilly Region (0.440), Hexi Oasis–Corridor Agricultural 
Region (0.343), and Hexi Desert–Gobi Region (0.225). This spatial ranking remained consistent across repre -

Residual degradation was highest in the Hexi Oasis–Corridor Agricultural Region (2.062%), followed by 
the Longnan–Tianshui Qinba Humid Mountain Region (0.328%), Longzhong–Longdong Loess Hilly Region

proportions were small, their occurrence across eco-regions with contrasting baseline conditions warrants tar -
geted monitoring. Accordingly, the Hurst analysis is used here as a monitoring indicator of historical persistence 
rather than a predictive tool; a positive trend combined with H > 0.5 indicates persistence in past trajectories but 
does not guarantee continued improvement under future climatic, water-use, or land-cover change.

Discussion
Comparative performance and trade-offs of adaptive PRSEI
Direct comparison among the three indices provides a more robust basis for evaluating adaptive PRSEI than PC1 
variance contribution alone. Adaptive PRSEI remained highly consistent with original PRSEI in both spatial pat-
tern (r = 0.991) and trend direction (99.00% agreement), indicating that replacing NDVI with kNDVI modified

RSEI was also high (r = 0.975), but trend-direction agreement was much lower (51.15%), highlighting the sensi-
tivity of long-term change trajectories to index composition.
CLCD-based external consistency further revealed a trade-off rather than universal superiority. Adaptive 
PRSEI showed the highest consistency with restoration transitions (81.47%) but the lowest with degradation 
transitions (34.22%), compared with 78.97% and 44.53% for original PRSEI and 55.58% and 70.36% for RSEI, 
respectively. All three indices also distinguished stable natural vegetation from stable bare land. These results 
support adaptive PRSEI as a complementary multi-stressor index for drylands, particularly for capturing recov -
ery-related responses, while degradation assessment should be corroborated using RSEI, land-cover transitions, 
or independent field evidence.
Two component-level findings further refine interpretation of the adaptive PRSEI. First, the difference between 
adaptive and original PRSEI was not greatest in the lowest-NDVI group, providing no evidence that kNDVI 
improves sparse-vegetation discrimination; it is therefore interpreted here only as a nonlinear greenness trans -
formation. Second, excluding TI reduced the provincial trend slope from 0.00432 to 0.00248 yr⁻¹, while spatial 
correlation remained high ( r = 0.988) and trend-direction agreement was 75.97%, indicating that TI materially 
affects temporal trend inference. However, PM10 is treated as a general particulate-matter proxy rather than a 
dust-specific indicator, and dust-related mechanisms require further validation using independent evidence such 
as AOD, dust-event frequency, or deposition data.

Temporal comparability reshapes long-term trend interpretation
The contrast between annual and unified PCA demonstrates that long-term ecological trend inference is highly 
sensitive to index construction. Because annual PCA allows component loadings, centring parameters, and scal-
ing ranges to vary among years, apparent temporal changes may partly reflect changes in the composite index 
itself. The high trend-direction agreement between unified PCA and fixed weights (99.90%), compared with only 
39.73% between annual and unified PCA, supports the use of a fixed index framework for long-term temporal 
inference. Under this framework, positive trends were widespread, although only 37.57% of pixels crossed at 
least one fixed PRSEI class. This distinction indicates that trend direction and class transition capture different 
aspects of ecological change and should therefore be interpreted jointly.
Eco-regional divergence in ecological quality and trends
Eco-regional analysis further identified areas where positive trends coexist with persistent ecological constraints. 
The Hexi Desert–Gobi Region had the lowest 25-year mean PRSEI (0.225) and the slowest improvement rate 
(0.00270 yr⁻¹), while the Hexi Oasis–Corridor Agricultural Region retained the highest proportion of residual 
negative trends (2.07%). These patterns are consistent with persistent constraints related to water limitation, high 
evaporative demand, wind erosion, sandification, and intensive water use, indicating that positive trends do not 
necessarily imply the removal of ecological risks. By contrast, the Longnan–Tianshui Qinba Humid Mountain, 
Longzhong–Longdong Loess Hilly, and Gannan Alpine Mountain regions showed higher ecological baselines 
and/or faster improvement. Although these patterns are broadly consistent with more favourable hydrothermal 
conditions and previously reported restoration or soil-conservation processes, the available evidence does not 
permit attribution to specific policies or engineering interventions.
Management interpretation should jointly consider PRSEI baseline levels, class transitions, trend direction, and 
persistence tendencies. Low-value areas may still require continued protection despite positive trends, whereas 
small residual degradation patches are better suited to targeted monitoring and should not be interpreted as evi -
dence of province-wide ecological decline.
Coupled spatial associations among water availability, soil, and land cover
The most robust OPGD finding was the consistent hierarchy of spatial associations across annual models. PRE, 
ST, and LULC remained the top three factors, with their principal pairwise interactions yielding q values of 
0.889–0.907. This stable pattern supports a joint interpretation involving water availability, soil background, and 
land-cover configuration, while remaining insufficient to establish causal mechanisms.
A plausible ecological interpretation is that precipitation influences vegetation growth, surface moisture, and 
bare-ground exposure, while soil properties such as texture, water-holding capacity, salinity, and erodibility mod-
ulate responses to climatic inputs. LULC further differentiates major surface types, including cropland, grassland, 
forest, bare land, water bodies, and built-up areas 41–46. Although these pathways are consistent with previous 
studies, they should be regarded as mechanistic hypotheses because OPGD cannot resolve temporal mediation 
or intervention effects.
Interaction effects can be interpreted as context-dependent spatial associations: the relationship between PRE 
and PRSEI may vary across soil and LULC categories, and similar land-cover types may exhibit different PRSEI 
levels under contrasting moisture conditions. However, these interactions do not imply that changing a given 
factor will produce a specific PRSEI response. Soil-classification sensitivity further showed that ST q values 
remained similar after moderate aggregation but declined under coarser classifications. Thus, soil background is 
a robust contributor to spatial stratification, while the magnitude of its q value remains dependent on classifica -
tion resolution.

Implications for ecological management across contrasting eco-regions
Management priorities should integrate PRSEI baseline conditions, class transitions, trend direction, and per -
sistence tendencies. In the arid Hexi region, the results support continued protection of desert vegetation and 
oasis margins, targeted monitoring of residual degradation patches, and closer consideration of ecological water 
requirements in irrigation and groundwater management. Because this study did not quantify the effects of spe -
cific interventions, these measures should be viewed as evidence-based management priorities rather than pre -
scriptive recommendations for particular engineering actions.
In the Loess Hilly, alpine, and humid mountain regions, relatively rapid ecological improvement suggests that 
restoration and conservation gains should be consolidated rather than assumed complete. Continued priorities 
include soil and water conservation, grassland and wetland protection, forest conservation, and monitoring of 
localised degradation. However, project-specific recommendations require independent information on restora -
tion intensity, grazing pressure, water use, and protected-area management.
The enhanced joint associations among water availability, soil conditions, and LULC further suggest that 
ecological monitoring and intervention assessment should be stratified by environmental context. Such context-
specific evaluation is better supported by the present evidence than uniform province-wide recommendations and 
provides a practical basis for prioritising future field validation and process-based research.
Limitations and future work
First, the 474.751 m grid is appropriate for long-term provincial-scale monitoring but may not resolve narrow 
valley oases, urban fringes, or small restoration patches. Higher-resolution Landsat, Sentinel, or Chinese satellite 
data should therefore be used for local validation while retaining the temporal continuity of the MODIS-based 
analysis.
Second, OPGD q values and interaction terms represent spatial associations rather than causal effects and can-
not resolve temporal ordering, mediating pathways, or intervention responses. Future causal attribution should 
therefore integrate OPGD with process-based models, quasi-experimental designs, field observations, or matched 
restoration controls.
Third, the PM10-based TI is not dust-specific because PM10 includes both dust and non-dust sources. In addi-
tion, the archived TI grids for 2022–2024 extend beyond the period documented for LGHAP v2. Dust-specific 
interpretation therefore requires further validation using independent evidence such as AOD, dust-event fre -
quency, or deposition records.
In addition, annual data on ecological engineering intensity, grazing pressure, groundwater abstraction, and 
irrigation water use were unavailable. Consequently, the low q value of NTL should not be interpreted as evi -
dence that human activities exert little influence on ecological quality.
Finally, although unified PCA improves temporal comparability, it remains sensitive to global minimum–
maximum extremes. The five fixed 0.2 classes should be interpreted as comparable mapping intervals rather than 
universal ecological thresholds, and CLCD provides external categorical consistency rather than field validation. 
Future work should therefore assess more robust scaling approaches, field-calibrated thresholds, and independent 
ecological datasets.
Conclusion
This study constructed a temporally comparable adaptive PRSEI for Gansu Province (2000–2024) using uni -
fied PCA and common scaling. The unified PC1 explained 79.12% of the total variance. Sensitivity analysis 
showed that long-term trend inference was highly dependent on PCA construction: pixel-level trend-direction 
agreement was only 39.73% between annual and unified PCA, but reached 99.90% between unified PCA and the

fixed-weight approach. These results highlight the importance of maintaining a consistent index framework in 
long-term ecological time-series analysis.
Under the unified-PCA framework, mean provincial PRSEI increased from 0.343 to 0.419 (slope = 0.00432 
yr⁻¹; R² = 0.778). Positive trends covered 99.42% of the common-mask area, although only 37.57% of pixels 
increased by at least one fixed PRSEI class. Ecological improvement was therefore widespread but spatially het-
erogeneous: all five eco-regions showed positive trends, while the Hexi Desert–Gobi Region retained the lowest 
baseline and the Hexi Oasis–Corridor Agricultural Region the highest proportion of residual negative trends.
Index comparison showed that adaptive PRSEI remained highly consistent with original PRSEI spatially and 
showed greater consistency with mapped restoration transitions, but weaker consistency with degradation transi-
tions than traditional RSEI. It should therefore be viewed as a complementary multi-stressor index for drylands 
rather than a universally superior replacement for RSEI. OPGD further identified PRE, ST, and LULC as the most 
stable spatial explanatory factors, although their q values indicate association rather than causality. Remaining 
uncertainties in TI interpretation, degradation detection, class calibration, and process attribution require further 
validation using independent atmospheric, field, and management data.

Abstract
Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs) must provide reliable, low-latency, and 
energy-efficient communication despite rapid changes in physiological urgency, 
body-induced channel variation, and heterogeneous sensor quality. Existing adaptive-
rate and QoS-aware schemes often optimize only a subset of these factors and 
may induce unstable rate switching when link or physiological states fluctuate. This 
study proposes HALA-DR, a health- and link-aware adaptive data-rate mechanism 
that jointly integrates physiological urgency, recent link quality, residual energy, 
and node quality. A four-level controller with an emergency override and hysteresis 
maps the fused state to low, medium, high, or emergency transmission rates. The 
per-interval time complexity is O(NM), which reduces to O(N) when the number 
of monitored physiological variables M is fixed. A reproducible MATLAB evaluation 
was conducted using an IEEE 802.15.6-compatible star topology, identical baseline 
settings, 30 independent runs, confidence intervals, and paired statistical tests. In the 
15-node scenario, HALA-DR achieved 236 kbps throughput, a 95.1% packet delivery 
ratio, 45 ms end-to-end latency, 0.94 mJ per successfully delivered packet, and 118 h 
network lifetime. Scalability, mobility, interference, and ablation analyses show that 
the link-quality term contributes most strongly to reliability and latency, whereas the 
energy term contributes most strongly to lifetime. These results indicate that HALA-
DR provides a reproducible and balanced improvement in WBAN communication 
efficiency and QoS.
Clinical trial registration
Not applicable.
Keywords Wireless body area network, Adaptive data rate, Physiological urgency, Link 
quality, Quality of service, Energy efficiency, IEEE 802.15.6
 1 Introduction
Wireless Body Area Networks integrate wearable or implanted sensors with a body 
coordinator to support continuous physiological monitoring, remote healthcare, reha -
bilitation, and context-aware assistance [ 1]. Unlike conventional wireless sensor net -
works, a WBAN operates close to or inside the human body and must satisfy stringent 
Page 2 of 17
Ye et al. Discover Computing (2026) 29:635 
requirements for low power consumption, bounded latency, reliability, and coexistence 
[2, 3]. IEEE 802.15.6–2026 explicitly recognizes heterogeneous traffic, quality-of-ser -
vice requirements, extremely low-power operation, multiple data rates, body-induced 
antenna effects, and user motion as central design considerations [ 1]. These characteris-
tics make static transmission settings unsuitable for sustained operation under variable 
physiological and radio conditions.
A fixed-rate sensor transmits at the same rate during both stable and abnormal physi -
ological periods. A high fixed rate can reduce response time but wastes energy and 
channel capacity when signals are stable, whereas a low fixed rate conserves energy but 
may delay urgent information. Adaptive-rate control is therefore attractive, but the deci-
sion is challenging because physiological urgency, link quality, residual battery energy, 
and sensor reliability evolve on different time scales. A controller that reacts too strongly 
to a single noisy indicator may also oscillate between rates, increase control traffic, and 
shorten network lifetime.
Recent real-time WBAN monitoring has emphasized selective signal restoration and 
physiological trend prediction in resource-constrained health-monitoring systems [ 4]. 
Communication-focused research spans discrete utility-based rate adaptation [ 5], meta-
heuristic transmission-rate optimization [ 6], route-stability-aware communication [ 7], 
multi-path QoS routing [8], and learning-based or multi-objective routing [ 9, 10]. These 
studies show that adaptive communication can improve reliability or energy efficiency, 
but they operate at different decision layers and usually optimize only a subset of physi -
ological urgency, channel state, residual energy, sensor quality, and switching stability. 
A lightweight controller that directly couples these factors for sensor data-rate selection 
remains comparatively underexplored.
The research question is therefore: how can a body coordinator select a transmission 
rate that prioritizes urgent physiological data, remains robust to channel and mobility 
variation, protects battery life, and avoids unstable switching on resource-constrained 
WBAN devices? To address this question, we propose HALA-DR, a health- and link-
aware adaptive data-rate controller.
The main contributions are:
 • A normalized physiological-urgency function with explicit normal and emergency 
bounds, together with an emergency override that elevates critical traffic without 
requiring a computationally expensive classifier.
 • A transparent composite state score that jointly considers urgency, link quality, 
residual energy, and node quality, followed by four-level rate mapping and a 
hysteresis/dwell-time constraint that suppresses unnecessary switching.
 • A reproducible and fair evaluation protocol in which fixed-rate, DDRA, GABAT, 
and EPRS baselines are reconstructed under the same topology, channel, traffic, run 
duration, random seeds, and metrics; newer learning-based and link-adaptation 
methods are additionally positioned qualitatively because they optimize different 
decision layers.
 • A broader evaluation using standard WBAN indicators, repeated-run confidence 
intervals, scalability, mobility, interference, ablation, decision-time, communication-
overhead, and complexity analyses.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section  2 reviews related adap -
tive-rate and QoS-aware WBAN methods. Section  3 presents the system model and 
HALA-DR algorithm. Section  4 specifies the reproducible evaluation protocol. Section  
5 reports the experimental comparison results and discusses robustness, ablation, limi -
tations, and practical deployment. Section  6 concludes the paper.
2 Related work
2.1 Adaptive transmission-rate control
Rate adaptation addresses the mismatch between time-varying network capacity and 
heterogeneous sensor streams. Szkaliczki [ 5] formulates discrete data-rate selection as 
a multiple-choice multidimensional knapsack problem and shows that a greedy strategy 
can approximate the optimum with short execution time. This treatment is useful when 
each stream has a finite set of quality levels, but physiological urgency and node health 
are not primary decision variables. Goyal et al. [ 6] combine genetic and BAT optimi -
zation to adjust transmission rates under QoS and posture-dependent link constraints; 
the approach improves optimization quality but requires iterative search and parameter 
tuning.
2.2 QoS-, route-, and energy-aware WBAN communication
QoS-aware routing complements rate control by selecting reliable forwarding paths. 
EPRS estimates route stability and residual energy to improve packet delivery and net -
work lifetime [ 7]. Mehmood et al. [ 8] distinguish normal and emergency traffic and 
reserve the best path for critical data. IM-QRP [9] focuses on QoS-aware next-hop selec-
tion, while Aryai et al. [ 10] combine metaheuristic optimization with machine learning 
for adaptive real-time routing. Cooperative fault-tolerant communication [ 11], lifetime-
oriented routing [ 12], ZITA [ 13], cooperative RF energy-harvesting transmission [ 14], 
relay-placement optimization [15], two-tier lightweight forwarding [ 16], multi-objective 
routing [ 17], and link-quality-aware clustering [ 18] similarly seek reliable and energy-
conscious delivery. These protocols establish the importance of traffic priority, link 
condition, and residual energy, but routing decisions are not equivalent to selecting a 
sensor’s transmission rate, and they do not directly address rate oscillation.
Recent WBAN research also addresses edge collection [ 19], compressed sensing and 
security [20, 21], encryption [ 22, 23], antennas [24], interference management [25], and 
congestion control [26]. Broader WBAN reviews and energy-efficient healthcare frame -
works [27, 28], together with Markov decision process-based inter-WBAN transmission 
schemes [ 29], further illustrate the diversity of communication objectives and deploy -
ment settings. More recent work extends adaptation toward learning and lower-layer 
control: Chen [ 30] shifts model-driven transmission-power control and link adapta -
tion to the hub, Arafat et al. [ 31] use Q-learning for QoS-aware routing, and Chen [ 32] 
applies Gaussian Thompson sampling to energy-efficient MCS selection under non-sta -
tionary channels. These methods strengthen the recent comparison landscape, but they 
optimize routing, transmit power, or PHY/MCS selection rather than application-level 
health-aware sensor data rates. Table 1 therefore distinguishes direct data-rate control 
from these adjacent decision layers. Only methods that can be reconstructed under the 
same topology, traffic, and metric definitions are used as quantitative baselines; newer

2.3 Research gap and positioning
Table 1 summarizes the closest methods. The remaining gap is narrower than the general 
problem of adaptive WBAN communication: application-facing sensor data-rate control 
still lacks a transparent, low-complexity mechanism that (i) treats physiological urgency 
as an explicit decision variable, (ii) combines urgency with measured link, energy, and 
sensor-health states, (iii) supports a fail-safe emergency override, (iv) suppresses ping-
pong switching through hysteresis and dwell time, and (v) is evaluated with repeated-
run statistical evidence under identical conditions. HALA-DR is designed to address this 
specific and testable gap rather than to replace routing or PHY-level link adaptation.
3 Proposed HALA-DR method
3.1 System model and assumptions
The WBAN contains N sensor nodes and one body coordinator. Each node measures 
one or more physiological variables and periodically reports data to the coordinator 
through an IEEE 802.15.6-compatible wireless link. The coordinator maintains recent 
link statistics, residual-energy reports, node-quality status, and configured urgency 
thresholds, and it selects one of four transmission rates for each node. Routine traffic 
uses the low or medium rate, elevated traffic uses the high rate when resources permit, 
and emergency traffic receives the maximum rate and priority access. Figure 1 shows the 
architecture and the location of the adaptive controller. Because the topology contains 
a single coordinator, the coordinator index j is fixed; after the distance definition below, 
the controller notation omits j and uses Li and Si for clarity.
The design assumes that the coordinator can obtain short-window RSSI, SNR, and 
packet-delivery statistics from acknowledgments and can receive periodic residual-
energy and sensor-health reports. Physiological thresholds are application-specific

emergency response while reducing ping-pong switching and its associated control and 
queueing overhead (Table 2).
3.5 Algorithm workflow and packet scheduling
Figure 2 summarizes the complete workflow. At each decision interval, the coordina -
tor acquires physiological, link, energy, and node-quality states; normalizes the required 
inputs; computes Ui, Li, Ei, and Qi; forms Si; selects a candidate rate; applies emergency, 
capacity, energy, hysteresis, and dwell-time constraints; schedules packets; and updates 
the short-window statistics after acknowledgments or timeouts. Emergency packets 
enter a strict-priority queue, whereas routine classes use weighted round-robin schedul -
ing to prevent starvation.
Algorithm 1 HALA-DR decision procedure executed at the body coordinator
3.6 Computational complexity and communication overhead
Urgency estimation requires O(M) operations per node, whereas link, energy, quality, 
and rate mapping require constant time. The overall per-interval decision complexity is 
therefore O(NM), which becomes O(N) when the physiological feature set M is fixed. 
The coordinator stores a short state window for each node, giving O(NW) memory for 
history length W. The proposed packet format adds a 4-byte state report and a 1-byte 
rate command per decision interval. In the 15-node scenario, this corresponds to an 
estimated 1.8% control overhead for HALA-DR, lower than the multi-path signaling 
of EPRS but higher than that of a fixed-rate system. The overhead is reported explicitly 
rather than being absorbed into payload throughput.

3.7 Practical safety and security considerations
HALA-DR controls communication resources; it does not diagnose disease or replace 
medical alarms. Clinical thresholds must be configured and validated for the intended 
application. Rate-control messages should be authenticated to prevent false emergency 
escalation, battery-drain attacks, or forced rate suppression. Sensor failures are repre -
sented through Q i and timeout rules, but secure key management, privacy protection, 
and formal fail-safe behavior remain deployment requirements [20, 22].
4 Experimental methodology
4.1 Simulation environment and network configuration
The evaluation protocol was specified to support reproducibility. All methods use the 
same MATLAB release, topology, channel, traffic, energy model, simulation time, and 
random seeds. The body coordinator is located near the waist, and nodes are placed at 
anatomically plausible chest, arm, wrist, waist, finger, and ankle positions with small 
random perturbations. The main comparison uses 15 nodes, whereas scalability tests 
vary the network from 5 to 25 nodes. A 100 s warm-up precedes the 1200 s evaluation 
period and populates the 10 s state-history window before reported metrics are accumu-
lated. Table 3 lists the complete configuration.
4.2 Baselines and fairness controls
Four quantitative baselines are considered: (i) a fixed-rate controller using the medium 
rate; (ii) DDRA, reconstructed from the discrete utility-based adaptation strategy in [ 5]; 
(iii) GABAT, reconstructed from the QoS-supported optimized transmission-rate design 
in [ 6]; and (iv) EPRS, reconstructed as a route-stability-aware QoS baseline from [ 7].

described by its source, while the PHY, traffic, topology, random seeds, and evaluation

and PHY/routing assumptions are not directly equivalent to application-level sensor
