Each method is evaluated with seeds 1001–1030. Within a paired run, the same seed 
controls node placement, fading, traffic arrivals, mobility perturbations, and interference 
for every method. This paired design reduces nuisance variability and supports direct 
within-seed statistical comparison.
4.3 Evaluation metrics
The primary metrics are defined as follows:
 • Throughput: successfully delivered payload bits divided by active evaluation time.
 • Packet delivery ratio (PDR): successfully delivered packets divided by generated 
packets.
 • Packet loss ratio (PLR): 1 − PDR.
 • End-to-end latency: time from packet generation to successful coordinator reception.
 • Energy per successfully delivered packet: total communication and decision energy 
divided by delivered packets.
 • Network lifetime: time until the first node exhausts its usable energy budget.
 • Control overhead: control bytes divided by total transmitted bytes.
 • Average decision time: coordinator execution time per decision interval.
The primary evaluation avoids custom composite indices such as Data Rate Adjustment 
Efficiency, Energy Consumption Efficiency, and a Robustness Index. Their intended 
concepts are represented more transparently by rate-switch behavior, energy per

4.4 Statistical analysis
For each scenario, the manuscript reports the mean and standard deviation across 30 
independent runs, and the figures show 95% confidence intervals. HALA-DR is com -
pared with the strongest baseline using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test because 
normality cannot be assumed for bounded PDR and delay distributions. P values 
are adjusted with Holm’s procedure across the four primary metrics, and Hedges’ g is 
reported as an effect-size estimate. All statistical values were computed from the com -
pleted run-level simulation outputs.
5 Results and discussion
This section reports results from 30 independent simulation runs. Values are consistent 
across Figs. 3, 4 and 5; Tables 4, 5 and 6, and the confidence intervals, significance tests, 
and effect sizes were calculated from the corresponding run-level outputs.
5.1 Overall performance
HALA-DR achieves the highest throughput (236 kbps) and PDR (95.1%), while reducing 
mean latency to 45 ms and energy per successfully delivered packet to 0.94  mJ. Rela -
tive to EPRS, the strongest baseline, throughput increases by 7.3%, PDR increases by 
1.5% points, latency decreases by 13.5%, and energy per successfully delivered packet 
decreases by 8.7%. The magnitude of the gain is consistent with the fact that EPRS 
already incorporates route-stability and energy information.

Mobility and interference tests further clarify the mechanism. Under running, HALA-

The link-quality term and feedback update allow the controller to reduce overly aggres -
sive rates when radio conditions deteriorate, while the emergency override preserves 
priority for urgent traffic.
5.3 Ablation, network lifetime, and decision cost
Removing the link-quality term causes the largest degradation in reliability and latency: 
PDR falls from 95.1% to 90.8%, and latency rises from 45 to 57 ms. This result supports 
the claim that rate decisions should be constrained by measured channel conditions 
rather than by physiological urgency alone. Removing physiological urgency reduces 
PDR to 92.6% and weakens prioritization of critical packets, although the average deci -
sion time decreases because one feature group is omitted.
Removing the energy term has little effect on short-term PDR and latency but reduces 
network lifetime from 118 h to 96 h. This separation is important because a component 
can be essential for long-horizon sustainability even when its immediate packet-level 
effect is small. Removing hysteresis lowers decision time to 1.5 ms but also decreases 
PDR and increases latency because rapid rate switching generates transient queue -
ing and control costs. The full model therefore provides the best overall balance, with a 
modest 0.8 ms decision-time increase over fixed-rate operation.
5.4 Practical interpretation
The results support a cross-layer interpretation. Physiological urgency determines which 
information requires rapid delivery; link quality constrains what the channel can sustain; 
residual energy prevents short-term QoS gains from prematurely exhausting a sensor; 
node quality suppresses unreliable measurements; and hysteresis converts noisy state 
changes into stable control actions. The controller therefore does not maximize a single 
metric; it balances reliability, latency, energy use, and signaling overhead while preserv -
ing emergency escalation.
A practical implementation can place the decision logic at the body coordinator, 
avoiding continuous optimization on each sensor. Nodes need only report a compact 
state vector and accept rate commands. The measured 1.9 ms decision time is small rela-
tive to the 1 s decision interval, but embedded-hardware measurements are still required 
because MATLAB workstation timing may underestimate microcontroller execution 
and communication overhead.
5.5 Limitations and threats to validity
First, the evaluation is simulation-based; body shadowing, antenna detuning, coex -
istence, and hardware energy costs may differ from the assumed models. Second, the 
physiological thresholds are scenario configurations rather than clinically validated deci-
sion rules. Third, only a single-WBAN star topology is evaluated; inter-WBAN inter -
ference, relay operation, and implanted sensors require separate validation. Fourth, the 
weights and thresholds are fixed and may therefore be scenario-dependent; a systematic

sensitivity study across broader channel and physiological settings remains future work. 
Fifth, the comparison reconstructs baselines from published descriptions, and code-
level differences may remain when source implementations are unavailable.
Future work should therefore include an IEEE 802.15.6 hardware testbed, measure -
ments during controlled postures and motion, multi-WBAN coexistence, authenticated 
rate commands, sensor-failure injection, prospective calibration of urgency thresholds, a 
systematic weight/threshold sensitivity study, and public release of code, parameter files, 
random seeds, and run-level results. A constrained learning method may also adapt the 
fusion weights online, provided that interpretability and fail-safe emergency behavior 
are preserved.
6 Conclusion
This paper formulates adaptive WBAN communication as a joint health-, link-, energy-, 
and node-quality decision problem. HALA-DR uses a transparent fusion score, a four-
level rate set, an emergency override, and hysteresis to balance reliability, latency, energy 
use, and switching overhead. The methodology explicitly defines the controller variables, 
normalization rules, thresholds, complexity, packet overhead, baseline-fairness condi -
tions, simulation parameters, repeated-run protocol, confidence intervals, and statistical 
tests needed for reproducibility. The experimental results show consistent and statis -
tically supported improvements over fixed-rate, DDRA, GABAT, and EPRS baselines, 
with stronger benefits under larger networks, mobility, and interference. Ablation results 
attribute packet-level robustness mainly to link awareness and long-term lifetime mainly 
to energy awareness. Future work will extend the evaluation to embedded hardware, 
multi-WBAN coexistence, systematic parameter sensitivity, and clinically informed 
deployment scenarios.

Article in Press
A Reference Dataset of 66 High-
Quality Plastid Genomes across 
Three Algal Phyla
Jieqiong Wang, Kexin Liu, Xiaolei Wang, Zhengjie Yu, Chaoyong Wu, Shenglong Kan 
& Wei Zhang ✉
Algae represent a diverse group of photosynthetic organisms, and their plastid genomes provide 
valuable molecular resources for investigating plastid evolution, photosynthetic adaptation, and 
phylogenetic relationships. However, algal plastomes exhibit remarkable evolutionary diversity, with 
substantial variation in genome structure and organization across different lineages. Currently, high-
quality algal plastid genomes and a standardized and reliable workflow for generating high-quality 
algal plastid genomes is still lacking. To address these challenges, we successfully assembled 66 high-
quality, complete algal plastid genomes, including 7 green, 19 brown, and 40 red algal genomes. 
During this process, we developed and established a standardized workflow for plastid genome 
assembly and quality assessment. Notably, these newly assembled genomes enrich existing NCBI 
resources by contributing 29 species, 13 genera, four families, and one order for the first time, offering 
both expanded taxonomic coverage and a standardized foundation for subsequent comparative and 
evolutionary analyses.
Background & Summary
Algae represent a major component of global primary production and play fundamental roles in marine carbon 
cycling and ecosystem functioning1. Cyanobacteria are considered the common ancestor of extant green plant 
plastids, having formed distinct plastid structures in green and red algae through primary endosymbiosis 2. In 
contrast, brown algae underwent more complex secondary endosymbiotic events 3,4. The diverse evolutionary 
origins of plastids across algal lineages, together with their complex endosymbiotic histories, have shaped exten-
sive variation in plastid genome structure, genome size, and gene content, thereby increasing the challenges of 
comparative analyses of plastid genome evolution across lineages5–10. Currently, most algal plastid genomes have 
been generated through independent studies, resulting in heterogeneous assembly and annotation strategies and 
consequently variable data quality 11. Common issues include inconsistent genome annotations 12, unresolved 
structural errors, and inaccurate identification of inverted repeat (IR) regions, all of which reduce the consist-
ency and reliability of available plastome resources.
Advances in sequencing technology have greatly accelerated research on plant chloroplast genomes. 
Although the numbers of algal plastid genomes have also increased, their expansion remains relatively limited 
compared with that of land plants. For instance, over 74,101 complete chloroplast genomes from Embryophyta 
have been publicly released. In comparison, the number of algal plastomes remains limited, with only 2,878 
entries recorded as of November 2025, covering merely about 2% of algal species diversity13. Therefore, expand-
ing high-quality algal plastid genome resources is essential for addressing the current gaps in available algal 
plastome data.
To address this gap, this study assembled 90 plastoms (66 complete circular genomes and 24 linear drafts) 
from 110 samples species, with 20 datasets excluded due to unresolved assembly graphs (Fig. 1A). These newly 
generated datasets add 29 species, 13 genera, four families, and one order previously absent from NCBI to the 
public repository (Fig. 1B). Together, these data establish an expanded plastome resource for downstream com-
parative genomic and evolutionary studies of algae.

Methods
Data Sources. Raw sequencing reads were sourced from publicly available macroalgal genome datasets 
deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA), including whole-genome sequencing data from 110 algal 
individuals and additional datasets reported in previous studies 14–18. These datasets correspond to BioProject 
accessions PRJNA924561, PRJDB15746, PRJEB39309, PRJNA32771, and PRJEB21674. Detailed information 
on species, source publications, BioProject accessions, and sequencing-run accessions is provided in Figshare 
repository at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32983835.v819. To perform plastome assembly, annotation, and 
comparative analysis, we downloaded the publicly available Illumina short-read data for all taxa.
Plastomes Assembly and Annotation. Raw sequencing reads were quality-checked using FastQC v0.12.1 
1 (https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/) with default analytical settings and trimmed 
with Trimmomatic v0.3920 to remove low-quality bases and adapter sequences with the following parameters: 
-phred33, ILLUMINACLIP:TruSeq. 3-PE.fa:2:30:10, HEADCROP:10, LEADING:20, TRAILING:24, CROP:140, 
SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15, AVGQUAL:28, MINLEN:36, and TOPHRED64. Cleaned reads were assembled 
with GetOrganelle v1.7.7.1 with -F other_pt, -R 10, and an appropriate plastid genome seed sequence specified 
using -s; other assembly parameters were left at their default settings. Assembly graphs were visualized using 
Bandage v0.8.121 to inspect contig connectivity, coverage depth, and circularity, and were manually simplified 
based on depth and connectivity. Datasets were excluded when their assembly graphs could not be resolved into 
either a single uninterrupted circular plastome or a characteristic dumbbell-shaped structure associated with 
inverted repeats. Assembly quality was evaluated by remapping reads to the assembled plastomes using the eval-
uate_assembly_using_mapping.py script from GetOrganelle, which assesses per-site coverage, mismatch rates,

employing GetOrganelle. Key steps incorporating the three quality standards introduced in this study are 
annotated. (B) Taxonomic representation of the 66 high-quality assembled algal individuals. Taxonomic 
composition of the 66 algal individuals with high-quality genome assemblies. (C) Comparative analysis of 
genome size, structure, and gene content across investigated algae. Genome size is visualized as concentric 
rings: the outermost red ring corresponds to Rhodophyta, the middle brown ring to Ochrophyta, and the 
innermost green ring to Chlorophyta.

and indel patterns (Figure S1). The script was run using the corresponding paired-end reads (-1 and − 2) and 
assembled plastome (-f), with mapping plots generated using–draw; other analytical parameters were left at their 
default settings.
Plastomes were annotated with MFannot v1.3.6 (https://megasun.bch.umontreal.ca/apps/mfannot/) 
using the bacterial/plastid genetic code (code 11) 22. The resulting annotations in ASN format were converted 
to GenBank format using asn2gb from the NCBI toolkit 23. Annotations were manually curated, and circular 
genome maps were generated using OGDRAW v1.3.124 with default settings. In addition, key genomic features 
were manually compiled for 90 species.
Comparative plastomes analysis. Inverted repeat (IR) region loss, contraction, expansion, and bound-
ary shifts were analyzed using IRplus 25 (irscope.shinyapps.io/IRplus/) with default settings and CPGView 26,27 
(http://47.96.249.172:16085/cpgview/home) with default settings (Figures S2–S4). Protein-coding genes were 
categorized by functional groups based on phylogenetic relationships, and their presence/absence patterns was 
recorded, with ORF-classified genes excluded from the analysis28,29.
Phylogenetic Analyses. A maximum likelihood (ML) phylogenetic tree of algae was constructed using 
IQ-TREE multicore version 2.4.0 30 under the LG + F + I + G4 model, with Synechocystis sp. (CP007542) and 
Prochlorococcus marinus (BX548175) as outgroups. The procedure was as follows: (a) For all 92 species span-
ning three algal phyla, the nucleotide and corresponding protein sequences of every protein-coding gene were 
retrieved using the script extract_all_genes_from_gb.py. A set of 117 protein-coding genes present in at least 
80% of species was selected and concatenated for tree construction. (b) Protein sequences of these genes were 
aligned using MAFFT31 with default parameters. (c) Unreliable alignment regions were removed using Gblocks 
with default parameters in PhyloSuite v1.2.332. (d) PhyloSuite v1.2.3 was used to concatenate the 117 single-gene 
alignments into a supermatrix with default parameters. (e) IQ-TREE was applied to construct the ML tree under 
the LG + F + I + G4 model with 1,000 bootstrap replicates. (f) The tree was visualized and annotated using iTOL 
(https://itol.embl.de/)33.
Data Records
The 66 assembled plastid genomes and their functional annotations are available under BioProject PRJEB121163 
in DDBJ/ENA/GenBank databases, with individual listed in Table S2, and also provided via database links 34 
and figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30943982.v4) 35. Detailed plastid genome features, genome 
alignments, phylogenetic trees, and quality-control (QC) data are available at figshare: https://doi.org/10.6084/
m9.figshare.32983835.v8 (2026)19.
Data Overview
For chloroplast genome assembly, we obtained 66 complete plastomes and 24 linear draft assemblies, with cir-
cular maps of the complete genomes presented in Fig. 1C. The canonical quadripartite structure was displayed 
in all Ochrophyta plastid genomes, whereas it was observed only in a subset of Chlorophyta and Rhodophyta 
plastid genomes. In Rhodophyta, the repeat regions consisted of either inverted repeats or direct repeats (Fig. 2).
Among the Chlorophyta plastid genomes, large single-copy (LSC), small single-copy (SSC), and inverted 
repeat (IR) regions lengths ranged from 53,789–88,291 bp, 10,447–23,760 bp, and 316–5,266 bp, respectively. In 
contrast, Ochrophyta and Rhodophyta plastomes exhibited relatively conserved structural partitions within each 
lineage, with average LSC, SSC, and IR/repeat region lengths of 78.87/42.92/11.70 kb and 152.60/31.12/9.60 kb, 
respectively (Fig.  3A). The complete plastome length ranged from 81,997 to 113,888 bp in Chlorophyta and 
from 124,224 to 143,684 bp in Ochrophyta and from 164,327 to 194,981 bp in Rhodophyta (Fig. 3B). The aver-
age GC content varied among the three algal lineages, with mean values of 28.31% in Chlorophyta, 30.81% in 
Ochrophyta, and 29.98% in Rhodophyta (Fig.  3C). Correlation analysis showed that LSC length was signifi -
cantly correlated with genome size (Fig.  3D), whereas SSC and IR lengths showed no significant correlations 
(Fig. 3E,F). Among the functional partitions, the protein-coding region (CDS) exhibited the strongest corre -
lation with genome size, while tRNA and intergenic regions showed moderate correlations. In contrast, rRNA, 
introns, and pseudogenes showed little or no correlation (Fig. 3G–L).
Protein-coding gene numbers differed among the major algal lineages, averaging approximately 99 in 
Chlorophyta, 142 in Ochrophyta, and 186 in Rhodophyta. Compared with Ochrophyta and Rhodophyta, 
Chlorophyta exhibited reduced gene numbers across all functional categories, whereas the differences between 
Ochrophyta and Rhodophyta were primarily associated with genes involved in carbon assimilation and biosyn-
thesis, transcription and translation, and light harvesting and chlorophyll biosynthesis (Fig. 4).
Technical Validation
Raw Data Quality Control. To ensure technical reliability, raw sequencing reads underwent quality control 
and trimming. All samples retained high Q30 scores, low error rates, and stable sequence quality.
Validation Criteria. Standard 1–Assembly Contiguity . Assembly graphs were visualized and evaluated 
using Bandage to assess their contiguity and circularity. A plastome was considered complete only when the 
final resolved graph formed one or more fully closed circular structures without gaps. Specifically, the graph was 
required to be continuous and fully resolved, without unconnected terminal nodes, dangling ends, open-ended 
paths, or fragmented structures with ambiguous connectivity.
Standard 2–Assembly Accuracy. Reads were remapped to the assembled plastomes to evaluate coverage. The 
sequencing-depth profile showed no abrupt or unexplained interruptions. Uniform depth distribution without 
significant fluctuations indicated correct and stable assembly.

Standard 3–Core Gene Set Completeness. Core gene set completeness was evaluated separately for Chlorophyta, 
Ochrophyta, and Rhodophyta, with the reference gene sets for each phylum detailed in Table S1. Plastome 
annotations retaining ≥80% of the lineage-specific core genes were considered to have acceptable annotation 
completeness. Following automated annotation, all identified protein-coding genes, rRNAs, and tRNAs were 
manually curated against reference sequences from closely related species in GenBank.

Data availability
The 66 assembled plastid genomes and their functional annotations have been submitted to DDBJ/ENA/
GenBank34 and figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30943982.v4) 35. All detailed plastome features, 
associated sequence data, including both raw and trimmed alignments, as well as the tree file are publicly available 
on figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32983835.v8)19.
Code availability
The custom Python script extract_all_genes_from_gb.py used in this study is publicly available in figshare 
(https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30943982.v4)35 together with the plastid genome assemblies and annotation 
files.

Abstract: Financial Data is becoming a vital part of the financial institution's process when 
it comes to making credit decisions, monitoring transactions, regulatory reporting and 
business analysis. With the mounting volume of customer data, account data, transacti on 
data, risk data and external market data, financial data governance issues have become 
more apparent, such as inconsistent standards, fluctuating data quality, disjointed data 
systems, and increased compliance requirements. Literature review and inducti ve analysis 
are used in this study to analyze the financial data governance framework and financial 
data quality evaluation. The authors conclude the study by asserting that financial data 
governance should encompass data access, standard unification, stor age integration, data 
quality control, compliance security and application feedback. The stages are designed to 
solve issues like data sources being spread across, indicator definitions not being consistent, 
missing and duplicated data, and challenges with data use across systems and unclear 
security responsibilities. Data quality evaluation shouldn't just be about scoring results. 
Rather, it should focus on a variety of business use cases like credit approval, fraud 
detection, risk monitoring, and regulatory reporting, and should measure data quality 
across the dimensions of completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, 
security, and traceability. The study identifies that financial data governance is still poorly 
coordinated between governance processes and quality evaluation indicators, as well as 
there are few evaluation indicators based on scenarios and feedback mechanisms are not 
complete. All financial future data governance should focus more on data issues in 
business applications, so t hat the results of data quality evaluation can be the basis for 
continuous improvement of data standard and system interface and data responsibility 
mechanism and data security management. 
1. Introduction 
Financial institutions are becoming data-driven more and more day-by-day. It is required to have 
fairly accurate and complete data for customer credit assessment, transaction monitoring, risk 
warning and regulatory reporting. A vast amount of customer information, account data, transaction 
records, credit records, risk indicators and external market data are generated continuously by banks, 
International Journal of Business Management and Economics and Trade 
52 
securities firms, insurance companies and internet finance platforms. Financial data has been 
facilitated by big data technologies to better process and analyse the data, which helps in assessing 
risk, evaluating businesses and taking decisions [1]. 
The more data that there is, the more data governance becomes challenging. Field names, 
statistical definitions, data format and update frequencies vary between different business systems. 
There are also close ties to financial data for credit approval, fraud detection, financial auditing, risk 
monitoring, and regulatory reporting. Inaccurate, incomplete, late or inconsistent data can impact 
business decisions and could even exacerbate financial risks. Although many studies have pointed 
out that financial auditing and risk identification are transforming in the big data era, the challenges 
of incomplete data standards, insufficient data quality control, and unclear responsibility boundaries 
in data collection, processing, sharing and application are still existing in financial institutions [2]. 
Demands for data authenticity, completeness, compliance and traceability in national auditing and 
financial regulations are also rising. Financial data governance is therefore a technical matter, as 
well as institutional, organizational and regulatory coordination [3]. 
The current research mostly focuses on financial data governance through the lenses of data 
standards, data quality, security compliance, risk prevention and data finance. Some studies claim 
that stable data quality is required to perform financial innovation, and the high- quality, complete, 
consistent, and timely data can help in financial modeling, risk monitoring, and intelligent decision 
making [4]. Studies on financial big data modeling also reveal that, besides the algorithms, the 
quality of raw data sources, the completeness of samples, the validity of the features and the bias of 
the data all affect the performance of the models. Researches on the layers of financial data 
governance also indicate that financial data governance should not be at one level. Rather, resources 
and data, governance policies, business, regulatory needs, and technical assistance must be aligned 
[6]. 
In this context, data collection or data cleaning only discussions do not suffice to encompass the 
entire financial data governance landscape. Financial institutions must look at all aspects of the 
process, such as data access, data standardization, data storage integration, data quality management, 
security compliance and application services. Further, the roles of governance for each stage should 
be explained and how they relate to business scenarios. 
Data quality assessment is one of the key means to measure the value of data governance. 
Financial data can't be evaluated solely by the size of the data or amount of data stored; it's 
important to consider whether the data can support business requirements. For instance, customer 
identification data and credit approval are impacted by missing customer identity data. Transaction 
data may be delayed, which may impact response time for fraud detection. When a system of 
indicating inconsistencies, it can impact regulation reporting and business analysis. Previous studies 
show that financial data quality assessment should not only include the financial data itself, but also 
the operation of the platform, the stability of financial services and quality management 
mechanisms [7]. Thus, data quality assessment should begin with the business needs, and then 
develop an assessment system that incorporates categories like completeness, accuracy, consistency, 
timeliness, uniqueness, security, and traceability, and then incorporate the results of the data quality 
assessment into the data governance process. 
While some of the prior work has touched on the financial data governance issues from an 
institutional, technical and risk control point of view, there is still some work to be done on the 
relationship between data governance and data quality assessment. Other studies are more oriented 
towards the macro level institutional analysis and fail to discuss the linkage between stages of 
internal governance in financial institutions. Still others focus more on the technical aspects of 
processing and quality control, neglecting organizational responsibilit y, the mechanisms of 
processes, and regulatory requirements. Often, data quality evaluation research is limited to 
International Journal of Business Management and Economics and Trade 
53 
indicator listing and the application of one method, with a lack of discussion on the applicability of 
the method, limitations and the feedba ck of the results to the governance practices. Financial data 
governance is also found to have issues in accordance with related studies, including barriers to data, 
lack of unified standards, multi -actor coordination with weak collaboration and low applic ation of 
technology [8]. 
Based on these issues, this study uses literature review and inductive analysis to examine the 
financial data governance framework and data quality evaluation in the big data environment. The 
paper first analyzes the practical diff iculties of financial data governance, then discusses the main 
stages and functions of the governance framework. It further summarizes the data quality evaluation 
indicator system and compares the applicable scenarios and limitations of common evaluation 
methods. By clarifying the relationship among governance frameworks, quality evaluation, and 
feedback improvement, this study aims to offer ideas for improving financial data governance in 
financial institutions. 
2. Related Studies and Practical Challenges 
Previous research on financial data governance and data quality assessment in the big data 
context has primarily centered on regulatory data governance, risk avoidance, and framework of 
digital finance governance. While these studies focus on varying aspec ts, there is one common 
thread: Financial data governance is not just a data management problem. It is tightly coupled with 
regulations, risk management and business processes. 
As for regulatory governance, Li Jia pointed out that financial data has sensit ive features, it 
moves easily and is prone to risk spillovers. Existing challenges encompass lack of clarity on who 
owns the data, challenges in cross -institutional data flow, delayed regulations, and ambiguities 
regarding the security responsibilities. Th is view points to a need for financial data governance that 
is not (solely) dependent on internal technical management in financial institutions. It must also 
facilitate data sharing, privacy measures, proper usage, and risk management within the regulator y 
landscape. 
How the data governance impacts risk identification is more discussed in the research on risk 
prevention. Shang Bowen believes that the governance ability of financial data directly affects the 
risk identification, monitoring and early warning effect [10]. Risk signals can be diluted or even 
misunderstood if the data that underlie them are missing, delayed, duplicated, or not uniformly 
defined, or if they are hard to integrate across systems. From this point of view, financial data 
governance is not only connected with the ability to use data resources, but also with the ability to 
discover and handle financial risks in time. 
Liu Guoping suggested in the research of digital finance governance system, that the systematic 
governance should be established based on data resource management, data standardization, data 
quality control, data security protection, and data application services [11]. This perspective 
suggests that financial data governance ought to extend beyond just data cleansing and technical 
processing to encompass how data is collected, stored, processed, shared, applied, and fed back. 
Existing studies and actual practice of financial institutions demonstrate that governance issues 
are seldom determined with a single stage. Different systems put data into different formats, causing 
data fragmentation and separation of systems, such as credit systems, payment systems, risk control 
systems, auditing systems, customer management systems, and regulatory reporting systems. For 
identical data, data systems may assign different names to fields, different code to the data, different 
definitions of statistics, etc., making integration and subsequent analysis more challenging. 
Modelling analysis, identification of risks and regulatory reporting can also be impacted by missing, 
duplicate, inaccurate, late or illogical data. Meanwhile, financial data are sensitive, including 
International Journal of Business Management and Economics and Trade 
54 
security of funds and customer privacy, meaning that data usage must comply with security and 
regulatory needs as well. 
Existing research has provided useful theoretical foundations and practical insights for financial 
data governance, but further integration is still needed. Some studies focus more on macro- level 
regulation or risk governance, while giving limited attention to how internal stages such as data 
access, standard unification, quality control, and application feedback are connected within 
financial institutions. Other studies discuss data quality evaluation indicators and methods, but do 
not fully explain how eval uation results can feed back into the governance process. Based on this 
gap, the following sections analyze the governance framework, data quality evaluation indicators, 
and evaluation methods to further clarify the structure and evaluation path of the financial data 
governance system. 
3. Construction of the Financial Data Governance Framework 
3.1 General Logic of the Financial Data Governance Framework 
In the big data environment, financial data governance needs to cover the entire process of data 
generation, access, processing, storage, use, and feedback. Financial data come from a wide range 
of sources, including internal business systems such as credit, payment, risk control, auditing, 
customer management, and regulatory reporting, as well as external ma rket platforms and 
third-party data channels. Without a unified governance process, different systems may easily lead 
to fragmented data, inconsistent indicator definitions, unstable data quality, and unclear 
responsibility boundaries. Therefore, financial data governance should not remain limited to data 
cleaning or system construction. It needs to form an integrated framework that covers business 
processes, technical support, management responsibilities, and compliance requirements. 
Operational standpoint, financial data governance might adhere to the reasoning of data access, 
standard unification, centralized integration, quality control, security compliance and application 
feedback. On the front -end, financial institutions must define the sources of data , how the data are 
collected and how often, etc., to ensure that data from various sources are fed into the system in a 
uniform manner. Once data are introduced into the governance process, then field standards, coding 
rules, indicator definitions, and dat a dictionaries are required to minimize data understanding 
disparities across data systems. Then, customer, account, transaction, credit and risk data stored in 
various business systems can be consolidated with the use of data warehouses, data lakes or mas ter 
data management systems to break down data silos. 
 
Figure 1: Operational Logic of the Financial Data Governance Framework 
International Journal of Business Management and Economics and Trade 
55 
Financial institutions should enhance the accuracy of the data post integration by using rule 
checking, anomaly detection and quality monitoring. Concurrently, security risks should be handled 
throughout data circulation and use by access control, data desensitization, encrypted transmission, 
and log auditing. The governed data is then finally used for business situations like risk 
identification, regulatory reporting, business analysis, customer service and so on. The problems 
identified in the application, such as missing data, inconsistent definitions, data delay and data 
access issues should be reverted to earlier phas es, such as data access, and standard unification and 
quality control, to ensure that the governance process is adapted continuously. From this logic, the 
financial data governance framework can be summarized as a closed loop process as described in 
figure 1. 
3.2 Core Components of the Financial Data Governance Framework 
The financial data governance framework can be divided into six main components: data access, 
standard unification, storage integration, quality control, security compliance, and application 
feedback. These components correspond to data entry, standardized expression, centralized 
management, quality improvement, security constraints, and business feedback. Together, they help 
transform scattered financial data into usable, verifiable, and traceable data assets. 
Access to data is the first step in financial data governance. Typically, financial institutions have 
to get information from many different sources, such as internal business systems producing 
customer, account, transaction, credit and risk control information, credit information, market data 
and regulatory reporting data. When access rules are not unified, there are potential issues with 
unclear data sources, incomplete data collection, and inconsistent interfaces. Financial institutions 
thus must establish data sources, interface standards, update cycles, and boundaries of usage; in 
order to ensure that data that flows into the data governance system is reliable and compliant with 
basic requirements. 
Standard unification is to solve t he issue of understanding mismatch between systems. In the 
long run of operation, various business departments can have their own field names, data formats, 
coding rules and definition of indicators. Consequently, the same customer, account, transaction or 
risk indicator can be represented in various ways across different systems. One key requirement for 
financial institutions is to describe core data in a consistent manner using data dictionaries, field 
specifications, and indicator definitions to minimize deviations in subsequent integration, analysis 
and reporting. 
Storage integration is about disparate data and siloed systems. In many financial institutions, 
there are several concurrent business systems, and customer data and transaction data, credit data 
and risk data are located on separate systems. This makes it more difficult to use data from other 
departments and to integrate the data for cross-department analysis. You can centralize all these data 
sources and create a relatively cohesive view of data with data warehouses, data lakes or master 
data management platforms. This offers data quality assessment, risk det ection, and business 
analysis capabilities. 
The quality control is used to decide whether or not the data can be relied on. Data gaps, 
redundant data, inconsistencies, outdated information, and logical issues can impact credit approval, 
risk assessment, bu siness intelligence, and regulatory reporting in the financial sector. By 
implementing rule checking, anomaly detection, duplicate detection, quality reports and continual 
monitoring, financial institutions can detect and address data quality issues which will minimize the 
influence of poor data quality on business decision making. 
Security compliance is about risk parameters of data moving and using. Financial data includes 
customer identity, account data, transaction data and fund security. Non- compliance risks and 
International Journal of Business Management and Economics and Trade 
56 
reputation losses can occur if there is data leakage, unauthorized access, or the lack of privacy 
protection or improper sharing. To safeguard data security during data collection , transmission, 
storage and use, financial institutions should integrate data classification, authorization to access the 
data, sensitive information masking, data encryption, operation logs and compliance review. 
Feedback from applications points to the relationship of governance outcomes and business 
scenarios. Governed data are then utilized for risk control, audit supervision, regulatory reporting, 
identification of customers, and business choice making. If problems are discovered in the use of 
the business, for example a missing field, different definitions of a fiel d, delay in the data or data 
access is hard, it should be reported back to the earlier stages of data access, standard unification 
and quality control, so that the governance mechanism can be modified over time. 
Financial data governance is not a technical process carried out in a single stage. It is a 
management process in which multiple components are connected with one another. Only when 
data access, standard unification, storage integration, quality control, security compliance, and 
application feedback work together can the reliability and business applicability of financial data be 
improved. To present the governance tasks and functions of each component more clearly, the core 
components of the financial data governance framework are summarized in Table 1.

4. Financial Data Quality Evaluation System 
4.1 Financial Data Quality Evaluation Indicators 
The purpose of financial data quality evaluation is to determine whether governed data can 
effectively support business operations, risk identification, regulatory reporting, and management 
decision-making. For financial institutions, the value of data should not be measured only by its 
scale or storage volume. It also depends on whether the data are authentic, complete, stable, secure, 
and traceable in terms of source and use. Based on the characteristics of financial business, this 
study evaluates financial data quality from seven dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, 
timeliness, uniqueness, security, and traceability. 
In practical business scenarios, completeness is first reflected in whether key fields are available. 
International Journal of Business Management and Economics and Trade 
57 
Missing customer identity information, transaction time, loan amount, or repayment status may 
directly affect customer identification, credit approval, and risk assessment. Accuracy concerns 
whether the data are consistent with actual business facts, such as whether the transaction amount is 
correct, whether the account status has been updated, and whether customer information and risk 
levels match the real situation. Consistency mainly addresses differences across systems. For 
example, the same customer’s identity information shoul d remain consistent in the customer 
management system, credit system, and risk control system. If different systems use inconsistent 
definitions or records, later business analysis and regulatory reporting may be affected. 
Timeliness refers to whether data collection, updating, and transmission can meet the response 
requirements of business scenarios. In fraud detection, transaction monitoring, and risk warning, 
delayed transaction data may cause the system to miss the best time for intervention. Uniqueness 
concerns whether the same customer, account, contract, or transaction appears repeatedly in the data. 
Duplicate records may distort statistical results and affect risk judgment. Security requires effective 
protection during data storage, transmission, and use, especially through access control, data 
masking, encryption mechanisms, and abnormal access management. Traceability emphasizes 
whether the data source, processing process, modification records, and usage path are clear. This 
dimension is particularly important in regulatory reporting, audit inspection, and risk responsibility 
tracking. 
Different financial businesses place different levels of emphasis on data quality indicators. Credit 
business relies more on the completeness and accuracy of customer information. Risk identification 
requires timely data updates and consistent definitions across systems. Regulatory reporting 
depends more on traceability and compliance. Based on the above analysis, the financial data 
quality evaluation indicator system is summarized in Table 2.

4.2 Financial Data Quality Evaluation Methods 
Financial data quality evaluation should not only identify problems in the data itself, but also 
allow the evaluation results to be used in later governance activities, such as adjusting data 
standards, improving quality rules, and refining responsibility mechanisms. Based on the practical 
needs of financial data governance, this study classifies data quality evaluation methods into three 
types: rule checking, indicator-based evaluation, and comprehensive evaluation with feedback. 
Rule checking is a basic m ethod for data quality inspection. It usually relies on business rules 
and data specifications to detect missing fields, format errors, abnormal values, logical conflicts, 
and duplicate records. For example, transaction amounts should not be negative, loan maturity dates 
should not be earlier than loan disbursement dates, and customer identity fields should meet basic 
format requirements. This method is suitable for routine monitoring and basic error detection. It is 
relatively easy to apply, and the results are straightforward. However, rule checking depends heavily 
on predefined conditions. Its ability to identify cross -system association problems or hidden data 
anomalies is still limited. 
Indicator-based evaluation sets evaluation criteria around dimensions such as completeness, 
accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, security, and traceability, and then uses these criteria 
to quantify or classify financial data quality. To compare different systems, business lines, or data 
topics, a comprehensive quality score can be constructed. The basic formula is as follows: 
DQ=w1S1+w2S2+w3S3+⋯+wnSn 
In this formula, DQ denotes the comprehensive data quality score; w ᵢ denotes the weight of the 
i-th evaluation indicator; S ᵢ denotes the score of the i -th evaluation indicator; and n denotes the 
number of indicators. The weights should not be set independently of business context. They may 
be determined according to business importance, expert judgment, or actual application needs. For 
example, traceability and consistency are usually more important in regulatory reporting, while 
timeliness and accuracy often require higher weights in fraud detection. 
Indicator-based evaluation can produce relatively clear data quality results and help financial 
institutions identify weak points across different systems, business lines, or data topics. In practice, 
however, indicator weights and scoring standards may be influenced by business experience, 
management objectives, and the evaluation subject. Without scenario- based adjustment, the 
evaluation may remain at the level of scores and provide limited support for governance 
improvement. 
The emphasis of comprehensive evaluation with feedback is on the possibilities for using the 
outcomes of the evaluations to provide feedback to the governance process. Financial data quality 
evaluation shouldn't end with data problem identification or data quality scoring. It should also 
direct the access to information, standard unification, storage integration, quality control, and 
security compliance. For instance, if it's the same fields that are missing, it could mean front- end 
collection rules need tweaking. Data dictionaries and indicator definitions should be reviewed as 
there is persistency of indicator definitions within systems. I f there is a lot of unusual access to 
sensitive data, the level of access control and log auditing may need to be increased. 
When the evaluation indicators are clear, if there is enough sample data and further quantitative 
comparison is needed in the scena rio, the analytic hierarchy process, entropy weight method or 
fuzzy comprehensive evaluation can be introduced in the evaluation. These methods can be used to 
find indicator weights, or to solve multidimensional evaluation problems. They should, however, b e 
applied in the context of specific business scenarios and not as stand- alone tools. Financial data 
quality assessment is not about getting to the nth degree of sophistication but about finding out 
where the data issues are and encouraging data governance. 
International Journal of Business Management and Economics and Trade 
59 
Different evaluation methods serve different governance stages and objectives. Rule checking is 
more suitable for basic monitoring, indicator -based evaluation is useful for comprehensive 
judgment, and comprehensive evaluation with feedback helps support a governance loop. In 
practice, financial institutions should choose appropriate methods according to data types, business 
scenarios, and evaluation objectives, rather than reducing data quality evaluation to a simple scoring 
exercise. 
5. Conclusion 
In the big data environment, financial institutions increasingly rely on high- quality data for risk 
identification, regulatory reporting, business analysis, and decision-making. This study reviewed the 
financial data governance framework and data quality evaluat ion, and summarized the practical 
challenges, framework components, evaluation indicators, and evaluation methods involved in 
financial data governance. The analysis suggests that the complexity of financial data governance 
mainly comes from diverse data s ources, fragmented systems, inconsistent standards, unstable data 
quality, and strict security and compliance requirements. Missing, duplicated, delayed, incorrect, or 
inconsistent data across systems may directly affect key business activities such as cre dit approval, 
risk warning, fraud detection, and regulatory reporting. 
Financial data governance from a governance framework standpoint includes access to financial 
information, standardization, storage integration, information quality control, security compliance 
and application feedback. It is not meant to be a mere introduction of a certain technical tool, but to 
solve issues like data isolation, inconsistent data definitions, data quality fluctuations, security risks 
etc. via institutional framework, process coordination, responsibility assignment and business 
scenarios. The standardization, reliability and controllability of financial data can only be improved 
when a relatively stable governance mechanism is accomplished for data collection, circulat ion, 
processing and application. 
Data quality evaluation for financial data should be done in a multi -faceted way, comprising the 
following aspects: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, security and 
traceability. Data quality requir ements vary from business to business. The more thorough and 
precise customer information is in a credit business, the better. The identification of risks needs to 
be done in real time with data updates and standardized definitions across systems. Traceabi lity and 
compliance are more important with regulatory reporting. So, data quality evaluation shouldn't just 
be single -indicator checks or the results of scores. It should connect to business scenarios, data 
types, and governance goals and it should lends itself to problem tracing, cause analysis, and 
subsequent improvement. 
Prior studies have focused on the standardization of financial data, financial data quality control, 
security compliance and development of digital finance. But, the relationship betwee n governance 
structures and quality assessment remains to be closer. When evaluating quality in business practice, 
the evaluation should not just result in a score or report. It should be integrated back into certain 
governance activities such as the data sources, field definitions, system interfaces, owning 
departments, and security management. Future financial data governance efforts should focus more 
on process monitoring and business feedback to identify and resolve data issues at the point of data 
collection, processing, usage, and reporting. Financial data governance is the blend of institutional 
structures, tools, and business mandates that can help prevent risks, meet regulatory requirements, 
and drive financial digital transformation.

content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

INTRODUCTION: Patient-reported measures are important tools in assessing cancer care quality, yet they may overlook the interpretive work patients do in making sense of provider and health system actions. Beyond practical aspects, patients read specific actions symbolically, as signals of respect, competence, and concern. This study explored how individuals diagnosed with cancer understand and define high- and low-quality care. METHODS: The authors have conducted semistructured interviews with 58 adults diagnosed with cancer within the previous year across 3 regions of an integrated health system. Interviews were analyzed using thematic coding. RESULTS: Participants consistently framed their experiences through interpretations of specific provider and system actions. Three primary domains emerged: timeliness and responsiveness, proactive coordination and advocacy, and clarity, with kindness identified as a meta theme. Actions including rapid callbacks, proactive scheduling, and clear explanations were understood as both operational efficiencies and evidence that providers were trustworthy and cared about patients. Conversely, delays, poor communication, and lack of coordination were interpreted as indifference or lack of urgency. DISCUSSION: The findings of the authors have underscored that patients interpret care actions through both practical and symbolic lenses. Even when clinical outcomes are favorable, perceived indifference or unclear communication can erode trust and heighten distress. These insights expand quality frameworks by highlighting relational and interpretive dimensions of care. CONCLUSION: Timeliness, coordination, clarity, and kindness are not merely operational goals but signals of empathy and respect that profoundly shape patient experience. Integrating these dimensions into quality improvement efforts can advance cancer care that is clinically effective and responsive to human needs.

解 説 
北海道における小麦の品質特性と用途別品質評価手法 
竹 内 薫 * 
地方独立行政法人 北海道立総合研究機構 
Quality characteristics and processability eval uation methods of Hokkaido wheat 
Kaoru Takeuchi * 
Central Agricultural Experiment Station, HRO, Higashi-6 Kita-1 5, Naganuma, Hokkaido 069-1395 
＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ 
Hokkaido is the leading wheat-producing region in Japa n, and efficient quality evaluation is essential for 
developing high-performance cultivars. This review summarizes wheat production in Hokkaido and recent 
advances in instrumental quality assessment methods for processing suitability as a complement or replacement 
for sensory evaluation, which is labor-intensive and unsuitable for large breeding populations. For Chinese 
noodles, a small-scale method using 50 g of flour enabled reliable texture measurements using breaking force 
and breaking energy, both of which showed strong correl ation with sensory evaluation. Additionally, noodle color 
and discoloration tendencies could be effectively assesse d using spectrophotometry. For sponge cake, key sensory 
attributes related to “melt-in-the-mouth” (crumb hardness, elasticity, and bolus flowability) were translated into 
instrumental parameters using compression tests with a texture analyzer, which aligned well with expert 
evaluations. These methods provide practical tools that en hance the efficiency of wheat breeding and support the 
development of high-quality wheat products in Hokkaido. (Accepted Apr. 23, 2026) 
Keywords : wheat, Chinese noodle, sponge cake, food texture 
キーワード : 小麦, 中華麺 , スポンジケーキ , 食品テクスチャー 
1. は じ め に 
 
北海道は小麦 , そば , 大豆 , 小豆 , いんげんまめ等
の生産量で全国一位 , 米については二位であり , 国内
最大の穀物生産地である 1). 北海道の農業試験場では , 
高品質かつ病害・障害抵抗性に優れた生産性の高い新
品種の普及を目指して品種開発を行っている . その
過程では作物種や用途ごとに様々な品質評価を行っ
ており , 既存の手法で対応できない場合には品質評
価手法自体の開発も行っている . 例として北海道立
総合研究機構中央農業試験場では , 近赤外分光法を
利用した小麦のフォーリングナンバー 2) やテンサイ
のショ糖含量の非破壊評価手法 3), 既存の手法よりも
少量かつ簡易に分析可能なマイクロドウラボによる
小麦粉生地物性評価手法 4), 業務用途に対応するため
の経済性や作業性も考慮した炊飯米評価手法 5) 等の
開発を行ってきた . 
研究小集会では米 , 大豆, 小豆およびいんげんまめ
も含めて品種の品質特性や品質評価について紹介す
ることとしていたが , 本稿では紙幅の都合により穀
類のうち小麦を取り上げる . 北海道における小麦の
生産状況や品種の品質特性を紹介するとともに , 品
種開発等に活用される品質評価手法の開発について
解説する . 
 
2. 北海道における小麦の生産状況および品質特性 
 
北海道は国内最大の小麦産地で , 2023 年の作付面
積は 132 200 ha (全国の小麦作付面積の 57 %) である i). 
品種別に見ると日本麺用の秋まき小麦「きたほなみ」6)
が 68.6 %と最も多く作付けされている ( 表 1).「きた
ほなみ」は子実のアラビノキシラン含有率が低く , 極
めて製粉性に優れ , 小麦粉の灰分が低いことが特徴
である 7). また粉色 , 麺色, 麺の粘弾性も優れ , オース
トラリア産の麺用小麦銘柄「Australian Standard White 」
(通称 ASW) に匹敵する品質である . 次に面積

が大きいのはパン・中華麺用秋まき小麦「ゆめちか 
ら」8) で, 一般的な強力粉よりもグルテンの弾性が強
い“超強力”の特性を持つ . 次いで面積が大きいパン用
の春まき小麦「春よ恋」 9) は製パン性に優れることか
ら実需者からの引き合いが強く , 2024 年産の産地銘
柄別の落札価格は 88 502 円/トンと最高位である ii) . 
最近では北海道で初めての菓子専用品種「北見 95
号」が育成された 10). スポンジケーキ等の洋菓子には
アミロース合成酵素に関わる Wx-A1, Wx-B1 および 
Wx-D1 遺伝子型が全て野生型でアミロース含有率の
高い小麦が適しているとされる 11). 国内で菓子用小麦
粉の原料として最も多く使われている北米産小麦銘
柄「Western White」は Wx 遺伝子型が全て野生型の品
種が配合されており 12), アミロース含有率が高く , ス
ポンジケーキの口どけが良いと評価されている . 北
海道産小麦で菓子用小麦粉を製造する場合には軟質
小麦の中で生産量の多い日本麺用の「きたほなみ」が
原料として使われることが多いが , Wx-B1 遺伝子型が
欠失型でありアミロース含有率がやや低いため , ス
ポンジケーキの口どけが悪いと評価されることがあ
る 13). 新品種「北見 95 号」は「きたほなみ」と比べて
アミロース含有率が高く , かつグルテンの質が弱く
薄力的な特性を示す 10) ことから , 洋菓子用途として
生産・利用が進むことが期待される . 
 
3. 小麦の加工適性評価 
 
小麦の子実は製粉 ( 一次加工 ) により小麦粉となり , 
パン , 麺, 菓子などさまざまな調理加工 ( 二次加工 ) 
に用いられる . これら多様な用途に対応するため , 小
麦品種開発の現場でも子実 , 一次加工 , 二次加工の各
段階で多角的な品質評価が実施されている . 品種開
発のための品質評価の課題点として , 供試できる試
料量に限りがあり , 同時期に多数の試料を分析しな
ければならないことが挙げられる . 品種開発では , 交
配によって得られた膨大な種類の小麦を圃場で栽培
して優れた形質を持つものを選抜するが , 圃場面積
や栽培管理の労力には限りがあるため , 初期～中期
世代は 1 種類あたりの栽培面積を小さくしている . 
この世代では収穫できる子実が少なく , その中から
翌年度に播種する種子も確保する必要があるため , 
製粉できる子実は数十 g から多くても数百 g 程度で
ある. そのため , 客観的で簡便であり , 試料の消費量
が少なくて済み , 可能であれば非破壊的な品質評価
手法の開発が求められている . 
小麦育種の場合 , パン適性については , ブラベンダ
ー試験を含むさまざまな理化学分析手法が開発され
ている 14). また , うどん等の日本麺適性についても , 
食感に関係するアミロース含有率や澱粉の糊化特性 , 
麺の色に直結する小麦粉の測色値が利用されている 15). 
一方で中華麺の製麺適性 16) やスポンジケーキ等の菓
子適性 17) については主に官能評価によって判断され
てきた . 官能評価は人の感覚を使って試料間のわず
かな差異を識別でき , おいしさのような複合的な官
能特性も評価できる点で有用であるが , パネルの募
集, 訓練, 維持にコストを要するとともに , 同時期に
多点数を評価できない等の難点がある . 加工適性に
優れる品種開発には毎年多点数の試料を同条件で分
析する必要があるため , 機器分析によりこれらの課
題を解決する中華麺適性と菓子適性の評価法の開発
に取り組んだ . 
 
4. 機器による中華麺適性の評価法 18) 
 
小麦粉の中華麺適性は色と食感の官能評価により
判断され , 製麺後の変色が少なく , 茹でのびしにくい

さについて , 分光測色計とテクスチャー測定機器を
用いて簡便に評価する手法の開発を行った . 本評価
手法のポイントは , 試料の消費量を削減した点 , 官能
評価の代替として分光測色計とテクスチャーアナラ
イザーを用いた点である . 
小麦の中華麺適性評価法として農林水産省食品総
合研究所の方法 16) があるが , 小麦粉の使用量が 300–
500 g と多く, 前述の理由から製粉量の少ない初～中
期世代の育成系統には適用しにくい . 一方で小麦粉
使用量を 50 g まで減らすと生地量が少なく小型の卓
上ミキサーでも混捏できない . そこで , 次に示す方法
により, 50 g の小麦粉からフードプロセッサーを用い
て生地を調製した . 小麦粉 50 g ( 水分含有率 13.5 % 
換算) に 10 % かんすい・ 10 % 塩化ナトリウム水溶
液 5 mL と純水 11 mL を加えフードプロセッサーで
混合した . そぼろ状の生地をロール間隙 3 mm の製
麺機に通して荒延べ 1 回, 複合 2 回で麺帯を調製
し, チャック付きポリ袋に入れて 25 ℃ で 60 分間
熟成した . 熟成した麺帯は , ロール間隙を狭めながら 
4 回圧延することで最終厚さを 1.4–1.5 mm とした . 
測色には麺帯を直径 2 cm にくり抜いて供試した . テ
クスチャー測定用の麺線は 20 番手 ( 幅 1.5 mm) で
切り出した . 
テクスチャー測定は次に示す方法で行った . 500 mL 
ビーカーに純水 350 mL を入れてマントルヒーター
で沸騰させ , 麺線 10 g を投入して 3 分間加熱した . 
ビーカーをマントルヒーターから外して 1 分間経過
後にゆで麺を取り出し , 20 ℃ の水に 1 分間浸漬して
冷却した . 水から引き上げたゆで麺 5 本をテクスチャ
ーアナライザーの測定台に並べてアクリル製ナイフ 
(底面 60 × 1 mm) で測定速度 0.2 mm/s, 最大歪率 
95% まで圧縮した . この時の最大荷重を破断荷重と
し, 荷重-距離曲線の破断点までの曲線下面積を破断
仕事量とした . 
スケールダウンして調製した中華麺のテクスチャ
ー特性が通常のスケールで調製した中華麺と同様か
検討した . 3 種類の市販中華麺用小麦粉で製麺し , ゆ
で時間を 2–8 分の範囲で変えることにより調製した 
18 種類のゆで麺について破断解析を行った . その結
果, 破断荷重および破断仕事量のどちらとも , 小麦粉
50 g で調製した場合と 300 g で調製した場合とで高
い相関が認められ ( 破断荷重 r = 0.99, 破断仕事量 r 
= 0.97), フードプロセッサーの利用により試料の消費
量を削減することができた . 
中華麺の色やテクスチャーについて , 機器分析に
よる評価が官能評価と一致するか検討した . 北見農
業試験場で栽培された 19 品種・系統について試験製
粉機で歩留 60 % の小麦粉を調製し , 上述の方法で
麺帯色とゆで麺テクスチャーの測定を行うとともに , 
食感と色の官能評価 16) を行った . 評価項目は生麺の
麺帯色の良さ ( 調製直後および調製翌日 ) , ホシの程
度, ゆで麺の食感 ( 調理直後および 7 分後) とし, か
なり不良～普通～かなり良の 7 段階採点法で評価し
た. なお, ホシとは中華麺に現れる黒褐色の斑点のこ
とで, ホシが少ない方が良いとされる . 官能評価によ
る麺帯色の良さの評点と , 分光測色計で測定した麺
帯の L* 値 ( 明度) との間には高い正の相関が , a* 値 
(赤色度) との間には高い負の相関が認められた ( 表 2). 
麺の色が暗く , くすんで「色が悪い」と評価される場
合には L* が低く , a* 値が高いことから , 分光測色
計で麺帯の測色を行うことで麺の色の良さや製麺後
の変色しにくさを評価できる . ただし , ホシの程度は
分光測色計の結果との相関が小さいため評価できな
かった. 
ゆで麺の破断荷重と破断仕事量は , 官能評価によ
る食感の評点と高い相関があった ( 表 2). また, 別の
ゆで麺試料 24 点を用いて官能評価による「ゆでのび」
を評価したところ , 破断荷重と「ゆでのび」の関係が
示された ( 図 1). ロジスティック回帰分析により , パ
ネルの過半数が「ゆでのびしている」と判定する破断
荷重は 2.94 N と推定された . これらのことから , 茹
で時間を一定にした麺線の破断荷重を測定・比較する
ことで , 中華麺の食感 , ゆでのびしにくさを評価でき
る. 
本評価法は中華麺適性の高い小麦育種に活用する
ために開発されたが , パスタのテクスチャー評価に
も応用可能である 20). 本評価法を利用して , 北海道の

5. 菓子用小麦品種開発のためのスポンジケーキのテ
クスチャー評価法 21)–22) 
 
日本では菓子用小麦の二次加工適性としてスポン
ジケーキの膨化程度と「口どけ」の良さが特に重視さ
れている . 膨化程度は菜種置換法やレーザー体積計
で測定した体積および比容積により評価できるが , 
「口どけ」は官能評価が唯一の評価方法である . 複合
的な官能特性である「口どけ」を機器分析により評価
するためには , スポンジケーキにおける「口どけ」と
はどのような特性であるか整理する必要があった . 
そこで , 日本麺用「きたほなみ」 , 菓子用小麦育成系
統「北見 92 号」および米国産銘柄「 Western White 」
の小麦粉について , 製粉業者によるスポンジケーキ
試験を実施した際に , 官能評価の自由記述でどのよ
うな表現が用いられるか分析した ( 表 3). その結果
「口どけ」が良いとされるスポンジケーキはクラム 
(やわらかい内相部 ) の「かたさ」が小さいこと , 「弾
力性」が大きいこと , 食塊の「流動性」(口腔内での食
塊の流れやすさ ) が高いことが分かった . 
そこで , これらの項目について官能評価に対応す
る機器測定法を検討した . 加工適性の異なる 5 種類の
市販小麦粉を供試し , オールインミックス法でスポ
ンジケーキを調製した . すなわち , 小麦粉 100 g, 製菓
用凍結全卵 100 g, グラニュー糖 100 g, 純水 40 g, 
製菓用起泡性油脂 8 g を卓上ミキサー ( ケンミック
スアイコーシェフ PRO, 愛工舎製作所 ) に投入し , 1 
速で 1 分間, 3.5 速で 10 分間ミキシングしてバッタ
ーを調製した . バッター 100 g を 9 × 9 cm の型に入
れ, 180 ℃ のオーブンで 30 分間焼成し , 翌日に官能
評価およびテクスチャー測定を行った . 官能評価は
研究室パネル 6 名が順位法で「かたさ」「弾力性」
「流動性」を評価し , 正規化順位スコアを得た . テク
スチャー測定は , 2 バイトテクスチャー試験 (Texture 
Profile Analysis : TPA) 23)–25) と, 口どけ食感解析を行っ
た. TPA は 35 × 35 × 20 mm に切り出したクラムを試
験片として , 直径 35 mm の円柱プランジャーで最大
歪率 66.7 %, 試験速度 1 mm/s で 2 回圧縮した . 官
能評価の「かたさ」に関係すると考えられる最大応力
のほか, 官能評価の「弾力性」に関係すると考えられ
る特性値を取得した ( 図 3). TPA の弾力性は圧縮 2 
回目の圧縮時間 L2 を圧縮 1 回目の圧縮時間 L1 
で除した値と定義されている 23)24) . 1 回目の圧縮後に
試料高さが復元せず L2 が小さくなると弾力性も小
さくなることから , 弾力性は圧縮後の試料高さの復
元しやすさを示していると考えられる . また, TPA の
凝集性は圧縮 2 回目の曲線化面積 ( 仕事量 ) A2 を
圧縮 1 回目の曲線化面積 A1 で除した値と定義さ
れている 23)–25) . 曲線化面積は圧縮時間 ( 圧縮距離 ) と
応力の積であるため , 試料高さの復元しやすさに加
えて応力の変化も凝集性に反映され , 複合的な「弾力
性」の指標と考えることができる . また, TPA の回復
性は本研究において 1 回の圧縮における圧縮時間 
L1 と除重時間 L1’ の比と定義した . 回復性は弾力
性よりも瞬発的な試料高さの復元しやすさを反映す
る特性値と考えられる . 以下, 官能評価項目としての
「弾力性」は鉤括弧で示し , TPA の特性値は単に

(TPA の) 弾力性と示す . 同様に, 官能評価項目の「か
たさ」「流動性」についても鉤括弧で示す . 
口どけ食感解析は 20 mm 角に切り出したクラム
を試験片とし , 直径 28 mm のガラスシャーレに置き , 
純水 3 mL を滴下してから直径 25 mm の円柱プラ
ンジャーで 5 回圧縮した . 最大歪率は 66.7 %, 試験
速度は 2 mm/s で実施した . 連続で 5 回圧縮した際
の各回の最大応力を比較し , 最も高値を示した圧縮
回を t max として示した . テクスチャー測定はいずれ
も 23 ℃ に設定した実験室で行い , 口どけ食感解析
には 23 ℃ の純水を用いた . 
圧縮試験の最大応力はクラムの「かたさ」との間に
高い相関が認められ ( r = 0.94, 図 4A), TPA の回復性
はクラムの「弾力性」との間に高い相関が認められた 
(r = 0.91, 図 4B). 一方で, 回復性と比べると弾力性と
凝集性は「弾力性」との相関係数が小さかった ( それ
ぞれ r = 0.77, r = 0.27, 図表省略 ). 
官能評価による「弾力性」が高いケーキは圧縮後に
除重すると速やかに復元するが ,「弾力性」が低いケー
キは圧縮により気孔の連続相が挫屈してしまうか , 
あるいは連続相の内面同士が圧着することで復元の
遅延が起こる . そのため , これまで多孔質食品の弾力
性の指標として TPA における 2 回目と 1 回目の
圧縮距離や仕事量の比をとった弾力性や凝集性が使
われることが多かった 26)27) . しかし , 本研究で対象と
したスポンジケーキについては , 1 回目の圧縮後から
2 回目の圧縮が始まるまでの時間に復元速度が遅い
試料が徐々に復元するため , TPA の弾力性や凝集性
では復元が早い試料と遅い試料の差が小さく , 官能
評価で感じられる試料間差を捉えられなかった . 一
方で回復性は , TPA の弾力性や凝集性よりも瞬発的
な復元速度を示しており , 特性の類似した試料間の
微妙な差異を検出するのに適した指標である . 
また, 食塊の「流動性」については , 口どけ食感解
析試験で得られる特性値 (t max) との間に正の相関が
認められた ( r = 0.88, 図 4C). t max が小さい試料は 5 
回の圧縮のうち早期に膨潤・崩壊し , tmax = 5 の試料は 
5 回の圧縮では崩壊しなかったことを示す . 圧縮中
のクラムの様子を観察すると , 官能評価で「流動性」
が低いと評価された試料は吸水性が高く , 膨潤, 崩壊
するのが早かったため , 口腔内で食塊が流れにくか
ったと考えられた . 一方で「流動性」が高いと評価さ
れた試料は吸水性が低く , 加えた水が圧縮の際に染
み出ており , 膨潤・崩壊しにくかった . このため口腔
内でも食塊がさらさらと流れやすかったと考えられ
る. 
また, これらのテクスチャー特性値について , 小麦
育成系統の評価に従事する専門家パネル 7 名が採点
法で評価した「口どけ」評点との関係を調べた . 加工
適性の異なる 6 種類の小麦粉を供試した結果 , TPA 
の最大応力は 「口どけ」との間に負の相関が認められ , 
TPA の回復性と口どけ食感解析の t max はそれぞれ
「口どけ」評点との間に正の相関が認められた ( 図 5). 
開発した手法は , 菓子用小麦育成系統の加工適性
評価に利用されたほか , 薄力粉に他の小麦粉や穀類
粉を配合した場合の食感への影響評価にも利用可能

6. お わ り に 
 
今後も北海道から米 , 小麦, 豆類等の高品質な穀類
を供給し続けるためには , 生産現場における様々な
課題を解決する必要がある . 例えば秋まき小麦につ
いては収量を低下させるコムギ縞萎縮病やコムギ萎
縮病が問題となっており , これらの土壌病害は薬剤
防除が困難なため病害抵抗性品種の作付けが唯一の
対応策である 30) . また, 春まき小麦の基幹品種である
「春よ恋」については穂発芽による品質低下が生じや
すいことや , 圃場で倒伏しやすいといった欠点があ
る. 北海道の穀物生産の課題に対応するためには , 農
業特性を改良しつつ既存品種と同等以上の品質を維
持した新品種の開発が必要である . 食品科学・食品工
学分野の研究は , 品質評価の自動化・簡便化 , 非破壊
評価の導入等の形で新品種開発の効率化に貢献でき
ると考えられる .

拠出 ( 北海道産麦生産流通安定対策事業 ) を財源とす
る受託試験により実施した . 道内の小麦生産者の皆
様およびスポンジケーキの研究についてご指導いた
だいた北海道立総合研究機構の阿部珠代氏 , 小宮山
誠一博士にお礼申し上げる .

title: Research on high-temperature test devices and test methods for blowout preventers using water media
source: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Machine Vision, and Control (AIMVC 2026)
summary: Research on high-temperature test devices and test methods for blowout preventers using water media
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

Reliability verification of blowout preventers (BOPs) in oil and gas drilling and production equipment is difficult under extremely high-temperature and high-pressure conditions, such as deep wells and ultra-deep wells. Traditionally, oil-based media are used for testing. However, because the temperature fluctuation of oil-based fluid is very intense, it will have a significant impact on the test pressure, which not only increases the complexity of operation but also significantly reduces the credibility of the results. Therefore, this paper presents a special physical test device for high-temperature tests of blowout preventers, using water as the working medium. The device supports a maximum simulation temperature of 350 °C, a pressure range of 0–250 MPa, a pressure control unloading system, and an automatic displacement device. Through the combination of experimental measurement and numerical simulation, the variation law of the volume expansion modulus of water within a certain range is systematically revealed. The problem of water phase change at high temperature (310 °C) is also solved. On this basis, the "segmented temperature control-pressure real-time compensation" high temperature and high pressure control strategy is designed, and a complete simulation test scheme is formulated in combination with the actual working conditions. The results show that the phase change caused by the volume expansion of the water medium at high temperature can be effectively controlled by the test device. The test process is stable, the data is accurate, and both the reliability of the test system and the effectiveness of the test method are demonstrated. The reliability of the test system and the effectiveness of the test method. This study opens up a new direction for the high-temperature testing of BOPs and holds significant importance for ensuring the efficient and safe operation of BOPs.

title: Use of complementary and alternative medicine and its association with antiretroviral therapy adherence and quality of life among people living with HIV in urban Indonesia: a cross-sectional study
summary: Use of complementary and alternative medicine and its association with antiretroviral therapy adherence and quality of life among people living with HIV in urban Indonesia: a cross-sectional study
content:
【摘要】本库未获取到该文献全文，以下为出版方/索引库提供的官方摘要：

HIV remains a major global health concern, and complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) is often used alongside antiretroviral therapy (ART). This cross-sectional study assessed CAM use, associated factors, perceptions, and relationships with ART adherence and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) among people living with HIV (PLHIV) in Indonesia. From June to September 2025, 400 PLHIV attending three primary healthcare centers in Makassar completed standardized interviewer-administered questionnaires. Overall, 158 (39.5%) reported current CAM use, predominantly herbal remedies. In exploratory bivariate analyses, CAM use was associated with older age, comorbidity, family support, self-reported mode of HIV acquisition, and hospitalization history (all p < 0.05). CAM users more frequently perceived CAM as safer than conventional treatment (65.2% vs. 40.9%). ART-adherence categories differed between groups (p = 0.006), although high adherence was comparable (87.3% vs. 88.8%). CAM use was associated with a lower EQ-5D-5L utility index in the unadjusted analysis (B = −0.039; 95% CI: −0.065 to −0.013), but not after adjustment (B = −0.020; 95% CI: −0.046 to 0.006). CAM use was not associated with EQ-VAS scores. CAM use was common but was not independently associated with poorer HRQoL. Routine CAM screening and individualized counseling may help identify potential CAM–ART interactions and support safe HIV care.
